News.title: Houthis parade captured US weapons after seizing key global shipping strait with Saudi-backed forces retreating
News.content:
Next

HOUTHI rebels have paraded captured US weapons chanting “death to America” after seizing a key global shipping strait.

The Iran-backed terrorists danced with their stolen weapons by the Red Sea shipping lane as Saudi-backed government fighters were forced to retreat.



The Houthis have made rapid gains against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in recent months, grabbing large areas of Yemen.

And they now control the Bab al Mandab strait, a key stretch of water at the mouth of the Red Sea that leads through to the Suez Canal.



$1 trillion worth of goods pass through the waterway each year.

Yemen’s government pulled back from the vital strait on Sunday, to defend Aden, their interim capital.



The bitter fighting has been ongoing for more than a decade, since the rebels seized capital Sanaa in 2014.

But after years of relative calm, truces were shattered during the US-Israeli war in Iran as the rebels traded blows with the internationally recognised government and even blasting airports in Saudi Arabia.

As the rebel group took the Bab al Mandab strait Saudi Arabia ditched the commander leading its assault in the Houthis.

Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad Al-Salman was moved out to work as an adviser to the defence minister for military affairs.



Chief of the General Staff General Fayyad Al-Ruwaili was put in charge of commanding the joint forces, according to Saudi state media.

Yemeni military sources said the Houthis had advanced to the southern coastal area of Khor Omairh, some 62 miles west of Aden.

The rebels are just 16 miles from government lines at Qawah, another coastal area.



It comes after the Iran-backed militia have seized a cluster of strategic Red Sea islands, working in tandem with Tehran to squeeze off trade routes to the West.

A huge network of submarine fibre-optic cables carrying internet traffic between Europe and Asia also runs through the Red Sea.

Maritime security expert Dr. Ian Ralby warned that the Houthis growing control in the region could pose an existential problem for digital life.

He told The Sun: “You’re looking actually at a third of the world’s internet in that group of cables.”

From multi-trillion pound banking systems to your Friday night Netflix binges, the UK’s online life hangs by a thread in this corridor.



Seventeen submarine cables traverse the Red Sea, handling around 90 per cent of digital traffic between Europe and Asia.

Data centres clustered along the Gulf rely on them, powering cloud infrastructure for multi-national corporations like Apple, Amazon and Google.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But despite how critical they are for everyday life, the cables are surprisingly vulnerable.

Dr. Ralby said: “When it comes to the capability to disrupt, most of us can buy a pair of bolt cutters.”

News.title: Does the PM really think spouting feel-good platitudes & empty promises is a substitute for actually leading country?
News.content:
Next

WELL, Andy Burnham has finally said it: “It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And, to be frank, the Emperor has nothing on.”

Sadly, this was not a stunning moment of self-reflection from a man who seized power for power’s sake and has realised he’s up the creek without a plan.



No, instead, it’s the latest narration of a Commentator in Chief who thinks sharing supposed wise words of his internal monologue is a substitute for leadership.

Last night’s offering was Our Andy’s first speech to the Lord Mayor’s Banquet — an annual affair at the Guildhall in the City of London where Prime Ministers unveil their foreign policy vision.



Burnham’s line that “Britain is back as a positive player on the world stage” would have landed better if he wasn’t talking to a few dozen policy wonks in the City, while over in China the leaders of the world’s superpowers were preparing to meet face to face.

The Prime Minister declared: “I’m talking about a Britain that can believe in itself again, that can hope again, and that can help bring hope back to the world.”



Well, given that his speechwriter was caught on a train at the weekend pumping out this sort of saccharine drivel using AI, I’m not sure what’s worse — if the latest speech was written by robot or human?

Anyway, I’m sure Trump, Putin and Xi will have all this at the top of their agenda when they meet on Thursday.

The meat in Burnham’s speech full of slop was his latest pitch for betraying Brexit and hurling us back into the clutches of EU red tape.

“Because it’s right, and because it is in our interests,” he claimed.



Yet what does that really mean, in practice? Step forward Labour nepobaby Hamish Falconer, our Europe Minister since July.

He has let slip that Brussels is making outrageous demands, far beyond reducing trade barriers in return for EU students flooding into our universities.

Falconer smugly told the BBC it would of course be “reasonable” to agree to Eurocrats punishing Britain with fines if a future Tory or Reform UK government later wished to restore Brexit freedoms by unpicking Burnham’s new sell-out deal.



He simpered: “The EU is worried about that and you can see why.”

There are plenty of words I could use for siding with our negotiating adversaries in the EU, against our own taxpayers, but I’ll stick with treacherous.

The Europeans are running rings around these amateurs but can we really be all that surprised?

What exactly is it that qualified this Red Prince, Falconer, for the important job of negotiating for Britain? Other than being the son of Charlie Falconer — who served as Tony Blair’s constitutional- arsonist Lord Chancellor.

Yes, Daddy tied up our country in the web of equality and human rights laws that now bedevil us, while the boy wonder sells us short abroad.



And what a wonder he is — just take a look at his career in Government so far.

Young Hamish was left red-faced in his previous job as Minister for the Middle East, after declaring that lobbying to free Egyptian activist Alaa Abd El-Fattah from prison there was “at the top of my priority list” — and later that he was “very glad” when his man was let go and arrived safely in Britain.

Unfortunately, Abd El-Fattah was not some cuddly peacenik poet, after all, but quickly exposed as a self-proclaimed racist who called Brits “dogs and monkeys” and demanded “we need to kill more” Israelis and police officers.

Falconer’s track record then barely improved. On social media, he was dubbed Hamas Hamish due to his cosy relationship with the Palestinians.

He has consistently supported the deeply flawed United Nations aid agency UNRWA — which was forced to admit its staff had participated in the murderous October 7 attack on Israel, and generally palled up to Husam Zomlot, Palestinian ambassador to the UK.



You may know Mr Zomlot as the very angry bearded gentleman who regularly popped up at the weekly hate marches that blighted our cities for months — and Falconer even recently hugged the man on camera.

But Zomlot has refused to fully condemn the October 7 attacks, and has played them down.

He even told Sky News in 2023 that the word “terrorist” should not be used to describe Palestinian killers, because they are the real “victims”.

Zomlot also never really properly explained what he meant in 2014 when he hit out at those “fabricating also the story of the Holocaust”, other than to later insist he is not a Holocaust denier.

But Jeremy Corbyn was a guest at his wedding in 2010, naturally.



Obviously, for bungling Burnham, Falconer’s track record qualified him perfectly to lead EU negotiations on behalf of the UK Government.

And you wonder why we are being sold a pup?

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It’s bad enough the PM is relying on being just a commentator, kicking the can down the road at home while playing make-believe abroad.

But if that’s how he’s going to run the show, is it too much to ask that he at least delegate to some competent people?

News.title: Woman, 23, killed after car ‘struck by BMW being chased by cops’ is pictured – as man charged
News.content:
Next

A YOUNG woman who was killed in a horror crash involving a BMW that was being pursued by police has been pictured for the first time.

Jade Langton, aged 23, and Cameron Bell, aged 22, were both tragically killed in the early hours of Sunday morning in Leeds, West Yorkshire.



A blue BMW 123D was pursued after it failed to stop for police at 12.44am on Gelderd Road, cops said.

The BMW then collided with a white Volkswagen Scirocco – which Jade and Cameron were inside – as it was turning into Gelderd Road from Lowfields Road.



West Yorkshire Police said Cameron, 22, the driver of the Volkswagen, was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.

Jade – who was pictured for the first time on Monday – was raced to hospital by paramedics but was tragically pronounced dead a short time later.

On Monday, officers said Leigh Ross, 39, of Harrogate, had been charged with two counts of causing death by dangerous driving.

Ross has also been charged with two counts of causing death by driving while disqualified, two counts of causing death by driving a vehicle while unlicensed or uninsured, failing to stop for police, and aggravated vehicle taking.



The 39-year-old appeared at Leeds Magistrates Court on Monday after he was remanded in custody.

Ross sobbed in the dock as he made his first appearance at court and his voice broke as he was asked to confirm his date of birth and address.

The court heard the offences were so serious they could only be dealt with at a crown court.

Ross was remanded in custody until his next appearance at Leeds Crown Court.

As he was leaving the dock, he looked towards the public gallery and said: “I’m sorry.”



Three other occupants of the BMW – two boys, aged 16 and 17, and a 16-year-old girl – were taken to hospital for treatment for injuries.

They were also arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving before their release on bail pending further enquiries.

Shocking images from the scene show a huge emergency service presence as the road was cordoned off.

A police spokesperson said on Monday: “Officers from West Yorkshire Police Major Collision Enquiry Team are continuing to appeal for any witnesses to any part of the incident.

“Specialist family liaison officers are supporting the families of the two people who died. The families have requested that people respect their privacy at what continues to be a very difficult time for them.”



They added specialist family liaison officers are supporting the families of the two people who died.

“The families have requested that people respect their privacy at what continues to be a very difficult time for them,” the force said.

Any witnesses or those with footage that could help officers in their investigation have been urged to get in touch, quoting reference 13260649342.



The force has also made a referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct which has declared an independent investigation.

It comes after shocking footage emerged of a BMW driving erratically just before a crash.

A dark blue vehicle appears to travel at speed not long before the fatal crash in Leeds.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The motor – believed to be a BMW – was seen careering wildly at a roundabout as other stunned drivers watched on.

However, it is unclear if the clip is related to the horror crash on Gelderd Road just before 1am.

News.title: Labour’s tax raids are killing off jobs for young Brits – and more state spending won’t fix the mess
News.content:
Finish the job







Next

BRITAIN’S youth unemployment problem is a ticking timebomb with almost a million young people neither earning nor learning.

So what should we make of jobs czar Alan Milburn’s much-vaunted 250-page report, which is published today after weeks of briefing?



There are some good ideas — namely the need to reform the hugely complicated welfare system trapping so many young people on benefits.

The proposed doubling in the number of apprenticeships is also welcome.



But there is far too much focus on State intervention and more State spending.

The private sector — which is desperate to help solve the crisis, if only Government would get its boot off the throat of employers — appears an afterthought.

Milburn talks of the need to cut National Insurance payments for bosses who hire under-25s.

But he adds that a cut can only happen “when economic conditions allow”. In Westminster speak, that means never.

Meanwhile, he will pump billions of pounds into a new layer of bureaucracy giving mental health support and personal advisers to prepare teens for work — all while the £353billion welfare bill continues to rise.

A plethora of new rights will be given to young people, while ministers will face a legally-binding “youth test” every time they want to pass a new law.



What young people desperately need are opportunities.

But two-thirds of businesses say they are less likely to hire because of Labour’s Employment Rights Act and soaring business taxes.

Pubs, shops and small firms — places where generations started work in Saturday jobs — have been priced out.

If ministers and Milburn are truly serious about tackling the national Neets scandal, they need to put left-wing dogma aside — and cut taxes and red-tape.

Rwanda EU-turn

LABOUR’S first act after seizing power was to ditch the Rwanda deportation scheme — flushing £700million of taxpayers’ cash down the drain.



Since that vital deterrent was scrapped, nearly 90,000 more illegal migrants have crossed the Channel in small boats to land on our shores.

We now learn that five EU nations are themselves preparing to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, with more than half of all member states eyeing similar deals.

In a humiliating twist, many of them will stay in a camp built for the abandoned UK-funded scheme.

Meanwhile, the bill for hard-working Brits keeps rocketing.

Ministers are shelling out nearly £80,000 a day to ferry migrants around in taxis and buses.



That’s on top of eye-watering costs for accommodation, handouts and legal aid.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

When the Prime Minister cosies up to his EU pals to plot his Brexit betrayal later this week, maybe they will finally talk some sense into him.

If he follows their lead on Rwanda, at least we might get something positive out of Brussels for once.

News.title: Fighter jets scrambled after Russian military planes fly into disputed territory of key American ally
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

PUTIN PRESSURE Fighter jets scrambled after Russian military planes fly into disputed territory of key American ally







Next

FIGHTER jets have been scrambled after Russian military planes flew into a disputed air defence zone of a key US ally.

Several of Vladimir Putin’s military aircraft flew into South Korea’s defence zone over the East Sea in the early hours of Tuesday.



Seoul’s military chiefs had already picked up the approaching Russian planes and deployed fighter jets in response.

The Kremlin’s aircraft entered the zone without giving advance warning, according to Yonhap News Agency.



South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) confirmed the warplanes had since withdrawn without breaching the country’s sovereign airspace.

Military chiefs said: “Our military detected the Russian military aircraft before it entered the KADIZ and deployed Air Force fighter jets to take tactical measures in preparation for contingencies.”

The Korean Air Defence Identification Zone (KADIZ) serves as an early warning system to detect foreign military aircraft closing in on South Korean airspace.

Foreign warplanes are generally expected to give advance notice before flying into the zone, although it is not considered sovereign territory.

But the Kremlin refuses to recognise Seoul’s authority over the area, claiming the zone has no basis in international law.

Putin’s warplanes have repeatedly put South Korea’s armed forces on high alert.



On August 25, Russian military aircraft flew into the same zone near the eastern islands of Dokdo and Ulleungdo, sparking another fighter jet scramble.

Nearly 10 Russian and Chinese military aircraft also entered the zone on June 27 in a joint show of military might.

Bombers and fighter jets flew through the area in succession, prompting Seoul to deploy its own warplanes.

South Korea later lodged an official protest with Moscow and Beijing.

The latest aerial encounter comes just a day after Volodymyr Zelensky warned of the growing military threat posed by Putin’s North Korean ally, Kim Jong-un.



The Ukrainian president said the dictator was feeding Russia’s war machine with dozens of ballistic missiles every month.

He also revealed that intelligence reports suggested the Kremlin was planning to ramp up production of its ballistic and cruise missiles.

Zelensky warned that Kim was using the Ukrainian battlefield as a testing ground to improve his own deadly arsenal.

And the consequences, he warned, could stretch far beyond Ukraine – leaving countries neighbouring North Korea facing a growing military threat.

He urged Britain, Germany, France and Italy to arm Kyiv with more missiles capable of matching Putin’s firepower.



Meanwhile, Nato was forced to scramble fighter jets on its eastern flank last week amid fears of unidentified drones flying towards Latvia and Lithuania from Russia or Belarus.

Residents across parts of the Baltic nations were urged to take cover on Tuesday night as the military alliance activated its air defences.

Among the areas placed on alert was Lithuania’s second-largest city, Kaunas, home to some 300,000 people.

A yellow air raid warning was issued at around 11pm, urging residents in the counties of Vilnius and Utena to head for their nearest shelter.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The alert said: “The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: POSSIBLE AIR RAID ALERT (YELLOW). Find a safe place.



“If you see a suspicious object, keep away, call 112. Wait for the all-clear.”

News.title: United Airlines suffers ‘widespread system outage’ just days after ground stop caused chaos across US
News.content:
Next

UNITED Airlines has suffered a “widespread system outage” just days after the FAA grounded all flights in the US for the second time since 9/11.

Hundreds of flights were delayed as the airline confirmed Monday’s system-wide meltdown after flight chaos rocked the country on Friday.



The airline apologised to customers, causing the problem a “widespread system outage”, saying their “teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible”.

United Airlines has since resolved the tech issue, it said.



It is not clear exactly which systems were impacted by the tech meltdown but some 418 United flights were delayed, according to FlightAware.

A computer issue was stopping airlines from being able to provide final weights for departing flights, according to an internal memo from United’s pilot union seen by Reuters.



It said several applications used by pilots, including crew communications had been taken down by the outage.

The memo said flights already in the air were not affected by the tech meltdown.

It told captains to pay attention to local guidance on whether to take off or stay at the gate.

A United pilot in Houston was seen in a recording posted on the ATC app asking the tower if he could stay at the gate until the system was up and running again.



The airline said there was no indication the system meltdown was a cyber security issue.

A United Airlines spokesperson said: “We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights.

“There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.”

The meltdown comes as thousands were left unable to access their accounts on Monday afternoon as Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank were struck with major tech issues.

And Microsoft experienced widespread issues on Friday, impacting Teams, Outlook and its AI assistant Copilot, leaving thousands of employees unable to complete their work.



On Friday aviation bosses grounded flights across the US because following a shutdown caused by “old copper wires”.

Millions of airline passengers faced cancellations and delays after American airspace was shut down without warning.

The FAA ordered planes nationwide to stay on the tarmac for four hours on Friday “due to extraordinary circumstances” following issues with air traffic control communications.

Chaotic scenes emerged from airports nationwide as travellers were snapped sleeping on floors with baggage piled up in the waiting areas.

In a press conference on Saturday, US transport secretary Sean Duffy repeated that the US government does not think the disruption was caused by a cyber attack.



He told reporters: “We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related.”

Instead, he laid the blame on “an incredibly old telecommunications system”, explaining that work was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre at the time of the grounding.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said the maintenance had been ongoing for years, adding that “it was such an old wire that it was being discontinued”.

Duffy said tech contractor L3Harris was switching out the wires and that the government is trying to find out if the problem was caused by “incompetence” or by a faulty piece of equipment.

News.title: Ed Miliband admits Brits face ‘costs’ in new EU deal as Brexit row erupts ahead of crunch summit
News.content:
Next

ED Miliband has admitted there will be costs to cosying up to the EU ahead of Friday’s crunch summit.

The Foreign Secretary braced Brits for a strings-attached deal that Andy Burnham is preparing to sign with Brussels.



He told Radio Four’s Today programme: “What the Prime Minister will do after this summit is lay out the options and there will be trade-offs. Of course there will be costs and benefits of different options.”

It comes as ministers are expected to sign away hard-won Brexit freedoms and sign Britain up to EU rules on food, carbon trading and youth mobility.



Meanwhile, Mr Miliband was also reminded that Britain’s AI sector is pushing economic growth stats well above those in Europe, which have much tighter regulations.

But the PM’s official spokesman said the main aim of the summit was also to “drive growth”.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch hit back at Mr Burnham for his EU obsession, blasting: “Sort out the economy, fund our defence, cut welfare.

“We don’t need to be in the EU for any of that.”

She also claimed Britain would vote to stay out of Europe instead of rejoining if a referendum was held today.

Reform’s Richard Tice said: “Even Remainiac Ed Miliband admits there are costs to rejoining the EU.



“Freedom of movement with 450million people, sending £750million a week to the EU, and losing our new trade deals to name just a few.

“This entire exercise is Burnham cynically deflecting from glaring mistakes his own government is making.”

Even former PM David Cameron has warned Mr Burnham against rejoining the EU, despite his own role in the Remain campaign in 2016.

News.title: Tremors felt in Australia after huge 6.6 magnitude earthquake rocks Indonesia
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BIG QUAKE Tremors felt in Australia after huge 6.6 magnitude earthquake rocks Indonesia







Next

A HUGE 6.6-magnitude earthquake has rocked Indonesia, sending tremors as far as Australia.

Hundreds of Aussies reported feeling the powerful quake after it struck Indonesia’s Tanimbar Islands at around 6.41am Darwin time.

Geoscience Australia said the earthquake struck 29km beneath the Banda Sea.

More than 380 reports have been lodged by Australians who felt the ground shake.





Initial seismic data put the magnitude at 7.4, locating the quake around 90 miles south-west of Tual, a city in Indonesia’s Maluku Province.

Despite the force of the earthquake, the Bureau of Meteorology confirmed there was no tsunami threat to mainland Australia or its islands.

Indonesia sits along the notorious Pacific Ring of Fire – one of the most seismically and volcanically active regions on Earth.

Shifting tectonic plates beneath the region regularly unleash powerful earthquakes and violent volcanic eruptions.



Indonesia bore the brunt of one of the deadliest natural disasters in modern history in December 2004.

A colossal 9.1-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Aceh province, triggering a catastrophic tsunami.

Devastating waves swept across 17 countries.

In August this year, at least 38 people died after a powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake hit the island.



Astonishing footage showed homes reduced to crumbling shells, with walls and roofs falling into heaps of concrete and twisted wreckage.

The quake’s epicentre was 68km north-west of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province.

Jaw-dropping videos showed terrified locals scrambling to safety as debris came hurtling down.

News.title: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
News.content:
Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn.

Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade.

His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults.

But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state".

Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations.

Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis.

The review says that, in 2024/25, for every Â£1 spent helping young people into work or education, Â£25 was spent on youth benefits.

By 2036, it says the aim should be for that ratio to be Â£2 on benefits for every Â£1 on work support.

News.title: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
News.content:
Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.

Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people.

About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data, external from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.

Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.

He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.

"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.

We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.

News.title: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond
News.content:
Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

News.title: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
News.content:
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.

Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.

She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.

A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".

Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.

This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.

There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.

When the government introduced its draft legislation, external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it, external.

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".

She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.

But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".

Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."

But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.

"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.

"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.

She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.

Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.

When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.

She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."

The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.

"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.

"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."

The committee hearings continue.

News.title: Met Office yellow warning in place as snow could disrupt Tuesday morning travel
News.content:
Parts of northern England and southern Scotland are set to get an early taste of winter as hill snow moves in on Tuesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for snow is valid until midday Tuesday with 5-15cm expected at some locations above 300-400m.

Major routes like the A74(M), A66 and M62 could all have problems with transport disruption.

Some railways are also likely to be affected with longer journey times for train services.

Cold health alerts are also in place, external for northern England issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.

News.title: UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham says ahead of EU summit
News.content:
The prime minister has argued the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit later this week.

Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham compared the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.

He is due to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, after the substance of those deals was set by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door".

In his first major speech on foreign policy, the prime minister said that following the summit he would begin new discussions with the EU about options for "our long-term relationship".

However, he warned it would take time and insisted that "at every stage the British people will be the boss".

Burnham has ruled out major changes before the next general election.

On the UK's current relationship with EU, Burnham said: "It's like the emperor's new clothes â where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.

"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."

Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit, Burnham set out three tests for any agreement.

Firstly, that it must be consistent with Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".

He also said it must improve the original Brexit deal and bring it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

Finally, he said any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to people's everyday lives - a reference to voters in Burnham's Greater Manchester constituency.

He also said the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach".

"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."

Burnham said "Britain was back in the game in a big way" and would be a country that "leads with its values".

News.title: Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
News.content:
A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is "completely unacceptable".

In a post on X, Norris wrote: "Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims.

"This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can be seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".

Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."

"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.

Victims' commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma.

"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."

While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".

She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.

If Brand is found to have broken prison rules, possible punishments enforceable by prison governors can result in restrictions on social visits or loss of privileges such as access to additional time in the gym or loss of TV.

Governors can also impose proportionate restrictions on communications where justified.

This could include blocking specific phone numbers, increased monitoring of calls or restricting contact with individuals where necessary to protect victims or maintain prison security.

News.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
News.content:
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.

This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.

According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.

Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.

"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.

"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.

It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.

GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither has Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from analyst firm Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".

Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.

News.title: Emma Barnett to leave Radio 4's Today for new BBC show
News.content:
Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.

Former Woman's Hour host Barnett has developed a "bold" new show, she says, which will launch in 2027 across BBC Sounds, BBC iPlayer and YouTube.

Her final day presenting Radio 4's flagship morning news and current affairs show will be on Wednesday 18 November.

"For the last nearly six years - it's been incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners," she said in a statement. "Having proudly hosted Woman's Hour and now the Today Programme - I've had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network."

She added: "But it's not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives."

Posting on Instagram, external, she said there would be more information on what her new show would be about soon.

"Watch this space and look ready. I amâ¦ More soon."

Barnett joined Today in May 2024, taking over from Martha Kearney to work alongside co-presenters Nick Robinson, Mishal Husain, Amol Rajan and Justin Webb. Husain and Rajan have since left.

Today programme editor Rebecca Keating said Barnett had brought "enormous energy" to Today, with "a keen focus" on listeners.

She noted how Barnett had a proven "track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate" but how she was "also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench.

"We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture."

In August, Barnett, 41, revealed she had had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis, days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.

She returned to the Today programme explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".

Speaking on her BBC podcast, Ready to Talk with Emma Barnett, last year, she told listeners that finding out she was going through perimenopause at the age of 38 felt like she had been "mugged, robbed".

The broadcaster said it was the "first time in my life I haven't really wanted to be a woman - it's the first time I've thought, I'd really quite like to be a bloke".

Radio 4 controller Mohit Bakaya said he was "delighted she's staying with the BBC" and would "look forward to her new show."

News.title: Barristers must stop using rape myths in trials, justice secretary says
News.content:
Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Winter said to the court "not one of them [Brand's accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave".

Winter also asked the jury if they could be sure that out of the "many, many women" Brand had had sex with over a decade, "he raped just three of them".

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: "[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large."

The charity Rape Crisis says it is "really common for people who experience rape, sexual assault, sexual abuse or other types of sexual violence to find they can't move or speak".

The judge presiding over Brand's case was praised by the Criminal Bar Association and campaign groups for comments he made during his sentencing remarks to dispel rape myths.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

A spokesperson for the BSB said such cases "must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice", adding: "Any other approach may discourage others from coming forward and adversely affect public confidence in the criminal justice system more widely."

Kirsty Brimelow KC, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales which is part of the group examining the need for further training, said it was important for the BSB to remain "independent of the government".

She told BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour that a "regulatory gap" had not been made clear to her and there were already powers to discipline barristers if breaches of the code of conduct happen.

She said training for "vulnerable witnesses" was already undertaken but it could be "problematic" if it was made mandatory.

Brimelow said there were currently a lack of barristers defending cases of rape and sexual assault and the possibility of further compulsory training could see more pushed out.

"What I wouldn't like to see is publicity around one case to take a life of its own rather than looking at what we already do," she told the BBC.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said the justice secretary was "determined to make protections for victims as strong as possible".

"Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts, giving evidence in cases of this nature is a brave act and can be traumatic for victims: they must never feel as though they are the ones on trial," the spokesperson said.

"Independent judges are already able to, and do, give directions to counter rape myths but we always want to keep looking at ways we can improve how the entire justice system treats victims of sexual violence."

News.title: Women's criminal records wiped for abortion offences
News.content:
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.

Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.

Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.

Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".

"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.

"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."

Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."

It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.

"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.

It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.

News.title: UK budget leaves NI underfunded, O'Dowd says
News.content:
Northern Ireland's public funding has worsened relative to the rest of the UK as a result of the Westminster budget, Stormont's finance minister has claimed.

John O'Dowd said the Treasury's figures show that NI will now be funded below its objective "level of need" next year and the year after.

Needs-based funding recognises that it costs more to deliver public services in some parts of the UK compared to others.

The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant has offered Â£1.5bn over the next three years and said if Stormont ministers accept this, that will take funding comfortably above the level of need.

O'Dowd said: "Treasury's own assessment shows that we are underfunded, relative to our current estimate of need, in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

"My officials' analysis also indicates that we are underfunded this year, and therefore in each year of the Spending Review."

It is understood O'Dowd believes that in cash terms this means public services will be underfunded by around Â£450m over the next three years.

It comes as executive ministers held further talks about the budget deadlock on Monday afternoon at Stormont Castle.

News.title: Police officers lied about searches connected to fatal crash, hearing told
News.content:
By the evening of Saturday, 3 March, the families of the three young women "were so worried that they decided to report them missing to Gwent Police", having been unable to contact them for hours and noting their lack of presence on social media

Ross's mother, Claire Ross, and Russon's father, Nathan Russon, went to Newport central police station to report their children missing.

The panel was told logs were created at this time which would help with subsequent enquiries.

During this time, Smith's mother, Emma Borg, had gone to the caravan the young people had travelled to and found her daughter's handbag there but no sign of the group.

Morley told the hearing that the "people in the caravan weren't particularly helpful", making Smith's mother realise that "something was very wrong".

Smith was eventually reported missing by her sister Lauren Doyle a couple of hours later, which included "sensitive information" adding overall to what was described as a "very worrying set of circumstances".

He added that the force also received "some concerning information about the men that was added to the system" which he said he would not read out in public.

The hearing was told that PC Hardwick and PC Livingstone were on a 16:00 to 03:00 shift and were given the "straightforward task of attending two home addresses to take any details from family members and to search".

Morley said this was something that "should always happen" during a missing person's enquiry and was "common sense" - allowing officers to assess whether the missing person might actually be at home, might have left something of importance behind like a note or might have taken something of importance.

The panel heard PC Livingstone had been assigned the search of Smith's house and PC Hardwick that of Russon's, but the two officers went to both addresses together and when they returned filled in the relevant paperwork.

PC Livingstone said she had first spoken to Smith's brother and then her mother.

In relation to the search, the following was written down: "Nothing missing out of the usual.

"Mum and Dad was concerned and Mum believed she went out in the same clothes and has not taken any new clothes with her."

That, the panel were told, was a "dishonest and misleading entry".

News.title: Yellow weather warnings issued for snow as temperatures plummet
News.content:
A spell of cold and wintry weather is set to grip northern areas of the UK early this week, bringing the threat of ice and hill snow.

A yellow weather warning for snow comes into effect in the very early hours of Tuesday following a blast of Arctic air pushing across the UK causing temperatures to plummet.

Cold health alerts for parts of northern England also remain in force from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.

Some snow is forecast over the hills and mountains in the north over the coming days but the wintry chill will be fairly short-lived in the south, where temperatures will rebound to above average by midweek.

News.title: Prince and Princess of Wales arrive in India ahead of meeting with Modi
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived in India for a three-day visit that will include a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The visit is the first time William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together in four years.

Her cancer treatment has limited the amount of international travel she has undertaken but she will be with her husband for several engagements this week.

Most are related to the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, which awards five Â£1m prizes for the best solutions to the biggest climate challenges.

"The princess is enormously proud of what the prince has achieved with Earthshot and is really looking forward to being alongside him for what is one of the most important moments in his year," said a spokesperson for the royals.

"She's seen it develop into something truly remarkable and is excited to experience first-hand just how far it has come."

News.title: Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field
News.content:
Appearing on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Miliband was reminded that in 2023 he said the project would be a "colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism", external.

Asked if it could be assumed he would resign if his successor decided to develop Rosebank, Miliband replied: "No, definitely not because I obey collective responsibility.

"Miatta Fahnbulleh will make the decision on this. As you know, it's what they call a quasi-judicial decision so she looks at all the evidence and then reaches a conclusion."

Miliband said he would not "second guess her decision" on Rosebank.

He added he supported the energy secretary recently giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field after years of uncertainty and a court case.

Pressed further about his previous remarks on Rosebank, Miliband said: "I'm a member of the government and I will abide by collective responsibility on this."

He went on to say there are "direct and very bad impacts at home" for the cost of living linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the Iran conflict.

Miliband added: "What does that teach us? That we can't get economic and energy security from fossil fuels, we've got to keep on with this transition to wind power, solar power, nuclear power; homegrown clean energy we can control."

Catherine Fookes is among a group of Labour MPs, reported to number at least 75, who have signed a letter opposing Rosebank.

The MP for Monmouthshire told Today: "We need to really look at what we're doing and ensure we don't exacerbate our climate challenges and make climate change worse.

"And that's exactly what drilling in the North Sea would do."

Steve Yemm, Labour MP for Mansfield, offered his support to Rosebank and said it would be a "test of whether, as a country, we can support investment and skilled work in the North Sea whilst meeting our climate obligations".

One Labour MP, who is pro Rosebank, said they were increasingly confident the decision would go their way, but added the "gloves will now come off" after Fookes's intervention.

They said people on both sides of the argument had been attempting to avoid so-called "red on red" clashes but predicted Labour MPs would now start to disagree more forcefully in public about the issue.

The same MP accused Miliband of "running two departments" and said the current group of energy ministers were "all his people" and "all coming from the same place".

They said they were becoming increasingly frustrated with Labour MPs who opposed Rosebank and added "Trump is right, we do need to open the North Sea".

Some people in Parliament believe that a decision on the oil field could be made as soon as the end of this month.

News.title: Arkansas city of El Dorado uses travel spotlight to clear its name. Call us 'El Duh Ray Duh'
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When a system failure grounded airplanes nationwide, led to thousands of flight cancellations and disrupted air travel worldwide, a little place called El Dorado suddenly found itself in the spotlight.

The southern Arkansas city of about 18,000 people gained unwanted attention when a radio communications site based there was identified as a possible source of the troubles.

While it may not be the attention they sought, the El Dorado-Union County Chamber of Commerce figured any attention is an opportunity to introduce the world to the town.

“While our community is not to blame for the outage, we want to take this time to point out that, as folks on cable television networks, podcasts, and other outlets talk about El Dorado, we want you to do it the right way,” the chamber of commerce said on Facebook, starting with the name.

The chamber posted a pronunciation guide: “Proper use: El Duh Ray Duh,” although “El Duh Ray Doe” is also acceptable. Calling the city “El Duh Rod Oh” is to be avoided.

“And while we’re at it — tell the masses that our community is growing, we are adding jobs, your children can get their college tuition covered through the El Duh Ray Duh Promise,” the chamber stated.

The chamber also referred readers to the city's website, which promotes the city's tourism and culture.

On Monday, Steven Jones, president of the El Dorado-Union County Chamber of Commerce, said that companies are also eyeing lithium reserves in the city.

Standard Lithium, a Canada-based lithium production company, is developing a project for the mineral's extraction near El Dorado, according to its website.

“We just thought why not capitalize on the marketing and have a little fun,” Jones said Monday.

___
