News.title: Suranne Jones reveals menopause ‘brain fog’ left her unable to remember lines
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Suranne Jones says that menopausal "brain fog" can affect her ability to recall lines on set.

The actor, 48, has returned to the thriller series Doctor Foster for a third and final season, noting that "everyone" on set was aware she was going through menopause.

Speaking to Women’s Health UK, she said: "For my business, the brain fog is awful because you can’t remember your lines.

"You’re just stood there going, ‘I don’t know!’… Everyone (on set) knows about my menopause."

Jones, who played DCI Amy Silva on police drama Vigil—which wrapped up its third series in September—reflected on concluding these major roles.

Speaking about the show’s ending, she said: "I’ve just turned 48 and I wanted to say goodbye to that character in a way.

"All the big things that I’m known for are coming to an end. It feels good to have done Vigil and Doctor Foster will be the last of that.

"It was gorgeous to exec produce on it, to be in the writing room and be more involved because I’ve now got much more experience… But I’m entering my new era of coming."

Jones as Doctor Gemma Foster ( BBC/Drama Republic )

She first gained fame playing Karen McDonald on Coronation Street for nearly 500 episodes between 2000 and 2004. She credits her time on the soap with establishing a strong foundation, saying: "I was introduced to a financial adviser. I bought my own flat. I was introduced to a therapist.

"That became a community – and what a gift for a 20-year-old to have all that advice… By the time I left (four years later), I was a property owner and already working on my mental health."

Jones also described the recovery routine she maintains three times a week while filming.

She said: "The sauna is great for loosening everything and the red light is brilliant for any injuries.

"When I came home (from filming Vigil), I was about to do Doctor Foster, and it had worked so well for Vigil that I was like: ‘This is a lot of money that I’m going to spend on this.’

"But now when I’m filming, I’ll do it three times a week."

The full interview is featured in the latest issue of Women’s Health UK.

News.title: Sadiq Khan secures major funding boost in bid to end rough sleeping in London
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A further £168 million in Government funding has been secured as part of Mayor of London Lord Sadiq Khan's initiative to tackle and ultimately eliminate rough sleeping in the capital.

The three-year financial package will fund shelter and dedicated services to help individuals transition off the streets and into settled housing. A total of £41m is designated for immediate winter measures, forming a key component of Lord Khan’s pledge to eradicate rough sleeping by 2030.

Emphasising the priority of the initiative, Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated: "Ending rough sleeping was my first pledge as Prime Minister because I believe everyone deserves the dignity of a safe place to call home. This has to be a national effort, with everyone playing their part.

"Mayors and local leaders know their communities best, and with the backing of government they can bring together the people and services needed to get people off the streets and help them rebuild their lives.

"The mayor of London has made consistent efforts to reduce rough sleeping across the capital. We want to build on that work, keep up the momentum and make sure nobody is left behind."

Addressing the new support, Lord Khan noted that the funding would "help us break the vicious cycle of street homelessness".

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has pledged to end rough sleeping (Leon Neal/PA) ( PA Wire )

"No one should have to sleep rough. Everyone deserves somewhere safe to stay and the support they need to build a life off the streets," he added.

"It will give boroughs and charities the resources to help people off the streets and into secure homes, with the support they need to stay there.

"The urgency the Prime Minister is bringing to this issue is welcome, and we’ll work closely with the Government, boroughs and charities to help people off the streets this winter and deliver our ambition to end rough sleeping in London by 2030."

The mayor also encouraged members of the public who spot individuals in need of assistance to notify Streetlink.

More than 90 per cent of the overall settlement will be allocated directly to London boroughs, alongside key charities including St Mungo’s, Depaul UK, Housing Justice and Crisis.

Under the provisions, Crisis will receive £300,000 for hotel spaces over Christmas and more than £160,000 for a dedicated hotel for women. Housing Justice is set to receive nearly £1.3m for specialist accommodation designed to assist people moving into permanent housing, while £400,000 is earmarked for a London Youth Hub catering to 18 to 24-year-olds facing street homelessness.

In January, Lord Khan is scheduled to introduce his Homes off the Street scheme, aimed at supplying 500 extra permanent properties for vulnerable individuals requiring intensive support.

Bonnie Williams, chief executive of Housing Justice, praised the announcement: "This is a significant and very welcome investment in ending rough sleeping in London.

open image in gallery St Mungo's CEO Emma Haddad greeting the Queen earlier this year ( Getty )

"It’s encouraging to see the Government and mayor working together with the voluntary sector to turn that ambition into action."

She added: "Getting someone off the streets is the first step, but we need to make sure they have the support to stay off them.

"We know how important relationships, practical support and a sense of belonging are in helping people sustain a home.

"This investment gives us a real opportunity to do more of that work, alongside our members and partners, and help end rough sleeping for good."

Emma Haddad, chief executive of St Mungo’s, also highlighted the importance of the "significant investment in ending rough sleeping in London".

"Every day that goes by without somewhere safe and warm to stay causes people’s physical and mental health to decline rapidly, so any response to homelessness needs the right types of accommodation as well as the right support for people’s individual needs", she said.

"This funding recognises exactly that, as well as the unique circumstances of particular groups of people, with tailored support for women, young people and migrants."

News.title: Tackling London’s illegal sex industry – where women are abused for as little as £7
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Aged just 13, Louisa* was trafficked to the UK. Nearly 30 years later, she is one of many women trapped inside “vicious cycles” of abuse that keep her working on the streets as a means of survival.

Another woman, now in her 70s, has been working the streets for over four decades. And there are others who are hooked on fizzy sweets due to a crack cocaine addition. Isabelle*, who has lost all her teeth, is one of those. She drinks a hot chocolate with 18 sugars when she suffers from withdrawals.

These women work on Langhedge Lane and in surrounding alleys – by day, home to blocks of flats, an industrial estate and a small primary school, but at night associated with London’s illegal sex industry, where men pay women as little as £7 to take part in the “most extreme end of violence against women and girls”.

It is one of the many hotspots in Edmonton and Haringey that is the focus of Operation Amicus, the Met Police’s initiative to target sexual predators and protect vulnerable women involved in street-based sex work.

The three-officer female team that lead the operation are part of a pilot scheme to engage with sex workers and to improve their trust in the police, with the hope it will encourage them to report crimes committed against them. In order to do so, they spend their nights driving around the area in plain clothes and unmarked vehicles – attending hospitals with those who have overdosed, gathering intelligence on men who use their services and supporting women through the justice system.

open image in gallery The female-led team spend their nights driving around Edmonton in unmarked police vehicles and gaining the trust of women on the streets ( The Independent )

While sex work is legal in England and Wales, related activities like soliciting for clients in public places, brothel keeping, pimping and advertising sexual services are all illegal.

However, the police’s handling of such cases has come under scrutiny in recent years, with the Met Police, the British Transport Police and the Crown Prosecution Service all admitting failings in August after serial sex offender Simon Levy was left free to murder two women and rape a third.

The three officers leading Operation Amicus, who The Independent is not naming, said many of these women are afraid to report rape and serious sexual abuse, but that the scheme has shown signs of working.

They are aware of 95 sex workers operating in the area and have regular contact with 40 of those women, which includes arranging emergency accommodation, guiding them towards partnerships for health support and providing them with clothing and mobile phones.

“Being a female on the floor, it’s easier to engage with them,” one officer said. “If you speak to the females and you say you’re police, it doesn’t work. If you stick a uniform in front of them, it doesn’t work. If you give them the same face, not in uniform, and they know that same person is going to attend each time, they will be more open to talking.”

All of the women have heartbreaking stories.

Many are struggling with £200-a-day drug habits, while others are trapped in abusive relationships. The majority are homeless and suffering from previous trauma.

open image in gallery Operation Amicus provides women who attend custody to report sexual offences with clothing and toiletries ( The Independent )

When offered a jumper, one woman said she had returned to the streets after being recently released from prison. She had been offered housing, but this would have involved being placed in the same proximity as her ex-boyfriend – leaving her with no other options but to sleep on the street.

Others have contracted sexual diseases such as syphilis, hepatitis A and HIV through this line of work, but often go without medication as they are not registered to GPs, are constantly on the move and fail to attend medical appointments due to unstable lifestyles.

Operation Amicus has partnered with 11 different organisations spanning policing, healthcare and specialist support services to try and support each woman. Many have resorted to petty theft in order to feed themselves or to avoid street based sex work, with the Met Police working alongside other agencies such as the CPS to recommend rehabilitation programmes rather than criminal penalties.

“Because of the amount of violence the females do receive, they then turn to petty crime as it’s a quick and easy win,” an officer said. “We have to manage that fairly by making sure we can either get them into a partnership to avoid that. They will often steal. One of the females stated to us when we took her to court the other week ‘I’m fed up of being raped now, I’ve turned to theft’. What can you say to that?”

Since being launched in January, the force have started to see positive results. More women are now reporting rapes, while others have shown more interest in engaging with services.

open image in gallery Superintendent Rob Gibbs said the operation is to ‘protect the next generation of girls’ ( The Independent )

One woman, who was struggling with a drug addiction and was unable to live freely in her accommodation as a result of cuckooing – where gangs or individuals take over a vulnerable person's home to conduct illegal activities – has recently agreed to enter a rehabilitation programme.

Superintendent Rob Gibbs, who leads the initiative in Edmonton and Haringey, said: “Women in this area can be seen as the problem and participating in anti-social behaviour, and not seen as victims of violence against women and girls. These are the women and girls at the harshest end of that.

“The level of exploitation is huge here. They are trying to avoid homelessness, they are navigating serious violence and/or rape quite regularly. We need to look at perpetrators and those who are controlling or coercing them.

“There’s a number of issues that might bring someone to this point - domestic violence, sexual violence, human trafficking and it is often linked with drug and alcohol dependency - that is often the lever for people to exploit them.

“What we are looking to do is reduce the harm enough so that we are protecting the next generation of girls.”

*Louisa and Isabelle are not their real names

News.title: Senior Royal Family member ‘asked Heathrow Airport worker to boil an egg in a kettle’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A senior member of the Royal Family once advised a Heathrow Airport employee to boil an egg inside a kettle during a period when catering options were restricted, a new book has claimed.

Heathrow: Gateway to the World commemorates the aviation hub’s 80th anniversary and documents the personnel, passengers and key events shaping its history.

Written by Rosalyn Wikeley, the work includes stories involving high-profile travellers, spanning global leaders, royals and celebrities, who have passed through the west London airport.

In the text, Sonia Dixon, who served as VIP liaison officer at the airport’s exclusive The Windsor suite for over three decades, recalls her interaction with the senior royal during restricted catering conditions.

“Prior to The Windsor suite opening, all VIP suites were airside within terminal buildings, and were only used by diplomats or royals,” Ms Dixon said.

“Only tea, coffee and biscuits were provided.

open image in gallery Queen Elizabeth II pictured arriving at Heathrow Airport after a visit to the United States in 2007 ( PA/Tim Ockenden )

“One senior royal requested a boiled egg.

“I explained that we lacked the facilities to do a boiled egg.

“She said, ‘Pop it in the kettle, my dear, I do’.

“My response was ‘Ma’am, I would, if I had an egg to boil’.”

Heathrow declined to reveal which royal had requested the boiled egg.

The Windsor suite, reserved for the most important of VIPS, comes with a retinue of 96 staff to take care of guests’ every need.

Back in 2021, The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge were said to have used the suite, which cost around £3,300 at the time, ahead of a half-term holiday with their children.

Ms Wikeley also wrote about the late Queen Elizabeth II’s arrival at Heathrow where she took her first steps on British soil as sovereign after the sudden death of her father King George VI in 1952.

Following the news of his death, Elizabeth returned to London from Kenya, where she was undertaking a Commonwealth tour, meaning a mourning dress had to be “smuggled on board for a quick change” before she descended the steps of her aircraft, Ms Wikeley writes.

“Given the unforeseen circumstances, the 25-year-old sovereign returned to a fairly quiet reception, greeted by dignitaries and senior politicians, including then prime minister Sir Winston Churchill, at the foot of the aircraft steps,” the book reads.

open image in gallery King Charles pictured at Heathrow in 2023 ( PA )

“Mere minutes before the now iconic photographs were taken of the Queen descending the aircraft steps, the appropriate mourning dress had to be smuggled on board for a quick change.

“No mourning dress had been packed for the tour.”

The royal family’s relationship with the airport spans decades, with Elizabeth II inaugurating the Europa Building, which later became Terminal 2, in 1955.

She went on to open Terminal 1 in 1969 and then later unveiled the London Underground Piccadilly extension to the airport in 1977.

The King, then the Prince of Wales, and Diana, Princess of Wales, opened Terminal 4 in 1986 and Elizabeth returned in 2008 to officially inaugurate Terminal 5.

During this visit, the late Queen described the new building as “a 21st century gateway to Britain”.

Following an extensive renovation, Terminal 2 was renamed the Queen’s Terminal in 2014.

open image in gallery Diana Princess of Wales leaving Heathrow Airport in 1981 ( PA )

The book also features photographs of famous passengers at the airport musician Sir Mick Jagger, the Spice Girls, Dame Joan Collins and Marilyn Monroe.

According to the airport, passengers have travelled an estimated 40 billion miles through Heathrow since its first flight in 1946.

New images of the Heathrow’s proposed third runway and £33 billion expansion plans are also included as the book nods to the future of the airport.

Heathrow chief executive Thomas Woldbye said: “Heathrow’s 80th year has been about more than celebrating eight decades of travel.

“It’s been an opportunity to recognise the extraordinary role Heathrow has played in shaping British culture and aviation history.

“But while we’re immensely proud of our past, our ambitions are firmly focused on the future.

“As we mark this milestone, we’re looking ahead to the next chapter of Heathrow’s story, and the role we’ll continue to play in connecting people and places for generations to come.”

Heathrow: Gateway to the World, will be available to purchase online through Assouline from November 19 before being sold at Harrods stores across all Heathrow terminals and in Assouline boutiques from November 20.

News.title: Air conditioning units and wine fridges among wealth status symbols – report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

More than a third (35%) of people perceive owning an air conditioning unit as a marker of wealth, in signs that the summer heatwaves could be influencing what is seen as covetable, according to research.

Among people earning £100,000 or more, nearly a fifth (18%) said they have one in their home, rising to 31% in London and to 51% amongst affluent people aged under 35, HSBC UK said.

The research also found that 23% of people with incomes of £100,000 or more own a wine fridge.

Meanwhile, 8% own an overseas holiday home, 7% own collectable cars and 6% belong to a private members’ club.

Kitchen islands were also owned by 31% of affluent people surveyed.

Xian Chan, head of wealth at HSBC UK, said: “The findings of our report highlight the evolving nature of what people feel constitutes wealth and symbolises affluence.

“Last year’s kitchen island has made room for new aspirational markers, namely the wine fridge and home air conditioning.

“The consistent trend we are seeing is that popular markers are more synonymous with home comforts and small daily indulgences than traditional material status symbols.”

Among the general population surveyed, people typically think someone needs an annual income of at least £347,000 to be considered wealthy, HSBC UK said.

YouGov surveyed 2,000 people across the UK, including 1,000 UK adults representing the general population and 1,000 people with a gross personal income of £100,000 or more.

News.title: Still Game reunion confirmed as hit comedy set to return to stage
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Still Game will return to the stage in 2028, the creators behind the hit sitcom have announced.

The play, Still Game Live: Heaven Sent, will go on a 10-show run at the Ovo Hydro in Glasgow from February 2028 – nine years after the show came to an end.

In a statement revealing the news, star creators Ford Kiernan and Greg Hemphill said: “We had FOMO (Fear of moving on) Haud oan! Whit’s been happenin? It’s been far too lang… Craiglang.”

The ninth and final series of the BBC comedy aired in 2019 before the cast said an apparent goodbye in the live show Still Game: The Final Farewell.

On Monday though, the Hydro teased a comeback on social media in a video showing the empty arena before a camera pans to the two identical hats worn by Jack and Victor.

And on Tuesday, it was confirmed that fans will be able to make last orders at The Clansman with tickets going on sale from 10am on Friday.

The cast previously set a string of box-office records with their hugely popular live shows in 2014, 2017 and 2019.

The show will run for 10 shows between Friday February 18 and Sunday March 5 2028.

News.title: Retirees warned that pension ‘loyalty penalty’ could cost thousands of pounds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Pension savers could risk paying a “loyalty penalty” by allowing their retirement pots to be eroded through fees costing thousands of pounds more than they may need to pay, Which? is warning.

The consumer group looked at pension drawdown – a way of taking money from a pension pot while keeping the rest invested so the pension pot can potentially continue to grow.

This option allows savers who have reached the stage when they are taking an income from their pension to choose how much and how often they want to withdraw, while the rest of the money remains invested.

Which? analysed the annual fees payable with 18 drawdown providers, using different pension pot sizes.

The biggest pot size Which? analysed was £750,000. The consumer group calculated that, taking into account the most competitive fees and the most expensive, over 10 years, accounting for annual investment growth of 5%, a drawdown customer could potentially pay more than £60,000 more in fees with the most expensive option versus the cheapest.

Which? also said a survey of more than 1,700 drawdown customers aged 55 and over in September found that when setting up their pension drawdown plan, half (50%) had remained with their existing pension provider, rather than shopping around.

Paul Davies, a pensions expert at Which? said: “Retirees today are under immense pressure to make every pound in their pension count, but blind brand loyalty could quietly cost them tens of thousands of pounds over their retirement.

“Platform fees and hidden charges compound over time, quietly chipping away at your future spending power.

“It pays to shop around and be deliberate about what you actually need from a platform.

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

“Just a few hours spent comparing providers today could preserve a substantial chunk of your nest egg for the years ahead.”

Becky O’Connor, head of pensions at PensionBee, said: “Retirees need to make the most of the savings they have built up through working life.

“Paying attention to the value for money offered by their drawdown plan, including investment performance, management of volatility, technology supporting flexibility and ease of drawdown, fees and customer service, is important.

“But not all drawdown arrangements are the same and it can be very difficult to compare plans from different providers due to different charging structures and services.

“Asking questions of your provider, doing your own research, seeking guidance from Pension Wise, and speaking to an independent financial adviser are the key ways to help people make good decisions on where to keep retirement savings.”

Marc Stewart, head of financial advice distribution at Skipton Building Society, said: “A pension may need to support you for decades, so it’s important to shop around and consider whether your pension still offers good value and suits your needs in retirement.

“But fees shouldn’t be looked at in isolation.

“Investment performance, withdrawal levels and changing income needs can all play a part in how long a pot lasts.

“Savers should be looking at the whole picture, rather than focusing on one number alone.

“Reviewing your pension regularly and understanding both what you’re paying and what you’re getting in return can help you make more informed decisions about your retirement.”

James Wilson, long-term savings policy adviser at the Association of British Insurers (ABI), said: “It’s important that savers understand any charges when accessing their pension, but comparing on cost alone only gives half the picture.

“Each provider will have an individual investment approach and offer different drawdown options to their customers, which will come with different fees, risks and potential returns.

“Retirement is a huge life stage, and what is right for one saver may not be right for another.

“Anyone considering drawdown should always shop around to find the product that best suits their needs.”

A spokesperson for M&G said: “Not all pensions are the same, and cost alone doesn’t tell you whether a pension is delivering value.

“Charges matter, but so do investment performance, the range of assets customers can access and the features they receive for their money.”

The spokesperson added: “Any meaningful assessment of pension value needs to look at that whole picture, not charges in isolation.”

News.title: Wall Street slides as Nvidia casts shadow over tech stocks
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Asian stocks fell sharply at the start of a huge week for AI following the shock exit of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang over a string of extramarital affairs.

South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi fell 3.6pc and Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.4pc after another night of drama for the $4tn (£3tn) chip giant.

Just hours after Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, called for a “dramatic shake-up” at Nvidia , it emerged Mr Huang was considering a possible comeback.

Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the boss of Epic Games, were among prominent figures to sign a public letter demanding that Nvidia “bring Jensen back”.

Meanwhile, several unnamed tech executives set up a “war room” to coordinate a “Stand With Jensen” campaign, according to The Financial Times.

The Wall Street Journal also reported overnight that Nvidia could be looking to scale back some of the aggressive financing it has deployed to prop up other AI companies.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies said: “These concerns are more real and are likely to have an impact on a number of companies in the supply chain.”

Taiwan’s Taiex, a beneficiary of the global AI frenzy, sank 6pc, with shares of its leading chipmaker TSMC down 5.7pc.

Allies in Silicon Valley, including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the boss of Epic Games, have pushed for Mr Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia despite an ongoing investigation into his conduct by the company’s board.

The chip giant will unveil its latest quarterly results on Tuesday after triggering a wave of turmoil for the tech sector.

AI giant Anthropic is expected to list in New York this week with a valuation of $1.4tn, doing so at a time when valuations are coming under pressure.

By Monday morning, several major AI supplies had suffered a drop in their share price, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung down 4.3pc and 4.5pc, respectively.

OpenAI investor SoftBank Group also slipped 3.7pc, while memory maker Kioxia dropped 7.7pc. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron was also down 7.1pc.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “Nvidia’s results tomorrow may outweigh everything and will largely put a bow on a bumper earnings season in what has been a bumpy period for markets.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Asian stocks mostly fell Monday as the tech sector struggled to recover from the crisis at Nvidia after boss Jensen Huang stepped down.

Mr Huang, a pivotal figure in the artificial intelligence boom, resigned Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The 63-year-old’s departure raised concerns about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a build-out that has helped propel global markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the world.

Reports that Mr Huang was in talks for a spectacular return to the hotseat, did not appear to be having much of an impact in Asia, with Taiwan’s Taiex index plunging 6pc as chip giants TSMC and MediaTek were hammered.

South Korea’s Kospi sank more than 3pc owing to steep losses in SK hynix and Samsung, while Japan’s Nikkei lost more than 2pc with Advantest plunging 11.1pc and Kioxia 7.7pc.

There were also losses in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Bangkok, Manila and Jakarta, though Hong Kong, Mumbai and Wellington rose.

News.title: How an NHS midwife overhauled maternity care in the world’s most dangerous place to give birth
News.content:
In her nearly 20-year career as an NHS midwife, Isata Dumbuya saw only one woman die. But in her first week working in a government maternity hospital in rural Sierra Leone, she witnessed the deaths of four mothers.

Her Sierra Leonean colleagues seemed resigned to such tragedies. Yet for her, these avoidable deaths were a huge shock: they brought home the enormity of her career change, and the challenges she now faced.

She had returned to Sierra Leone to pass on her NHS experience and training, but she had never seen anything like this.

“I did not know what to do – in all my experience,” she recalls. “There were [medical] conditions that I was seeing there that I had never seen in my life because they would not be allowed to happen in the UK.”

After a long and successful career in the UK, the mother-of-five had been inspired to return to her birthplace after seeing reports of the appallingly high mortality rates faced by mothers.

At the time women in Sierra Leone had a one-in-17 lifetime chance of dying during pregnancy, delivery or its aftermath. Today the lifetime risk is one in 52.

She found the government hospital in Kono overwhelmed, short-staffed and poorly organised.

Her new colleagues were exhausted and fatalistic from the relentless deaths.

“In this time, the only thing I was useful for was crying.

“I [had a lot of doubt] because I’m like ‘I can’t do this’. I really don’t know how.

“And also, when you are looking at the people around, they are so fine with it, because they had to do some serious level of emotional shutdown to cope with all this.”

News.title: England stun world champions Spain in one of their greatest victories
News.content:
There was so much to admire. England began the night testing Spain’s first-phase passing to breaking point. They began the second half counter-attacking Spain for two goals from Ezri Konsa and White. Then after Elliot Anderson’s red card, this was a different England. With Trafford in inspired form, they held off the relentless Spain for long enough.

Harry Kane scored his 93rd England goal from the spot and was replaced before the end so that Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy could give the midfield one more lease of life. By the end, the excitement meant that Kane was unable to take his seat on the bench, and he stood alongside Tuchel in the technical area, cajoling and advising.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. Tuchel’s pool of talent is deeper than it was for his predecessor but there is also a greater maturity to the way they play. The England manager called it the greatest performance of almost two years in charge “given the circumstances… who we play, where we play” and as ever for England just slightly too late.

The defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England showed on this night. They were under the hammer after Anderson threw an arm over the shoulder of Lamine Yamal and was dismissed before Mikel Oyarzabal converted the penalty that followed. “Thirty minutes against Spain in Spain feels like three hours,” Tuchel said, although Spain had a long way back after the blitzing they took at times in the first hour.

News.title: Scotland’s ugly win seals weekend of domination for northern hemisphere
News.content:
This was far from pretty. In fact it was downright ugly. If Wales’s historic win over New Zealand on Saturday will be spoken of for generations, this turgid 15-12 victory for Scotland over Australia had probably been forgotten, even by the 65,095 who witnessed it, by the time they caught the tram home. But it capped a spectacular weekend for northern hemisphere rugby.

One should never read too much into results one year out from a World Cup; different conditions, home advantage, different stages in teams’ development cycles, and so on. But it was difficult not to feel at least some encouragement from a weekend in which France ended a five-match losing streak against world champions South Africa in one of the most thrilling Test matches of recent times, Wales ended their All Blacks hoodoo with an epic display of defensive resolve, and Scotland won a grim arm-wrestle against Australia. With England and Ireland thrashing Japan and Fiji respectively, only Italy’s loss in a tight one against Argentina prevented a clean sweep.

It will be interesting to see how the southern hemisphere responds over the next couple of weekends, but you have to say, this new Nations Championship format has breathed a bit of life into the global game. Even if it was in very short supply at Murrayfield on Sunday.

After the barnstorming games in Paris and Cardiff, expectations were high heading into the match, but it proved to be a messy, attritional affair, not helped by a greasy pitch and two teams absolutely desperate for a win. First-half tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey put Scotland 12-5 up at half-time, with Harry Potter having replied for the visitors.

News.title: Record-breaking England hammer Australia to force series decider
News.content:
Good morning from Adelaide Oval. For England fans waking up back home, things are a going a little better now than they were in Perth 48 hours ago.

Having been asked to bat first again, they are 102 for one after 18 overs, and going nicely. Tom Banton has made a fine fifty, while Joe Root is doing what he does. You know the drill: look up and he’s on 30, and so on.

The man to go was Ben Duckett, whose tough times in Australia continued, when he picked out a fielder in the offside ring for nine. The ball was short and wide, and the stroke pretty ugly. Anyway, without him, England have managed to build a bit of a platform. The pitch is classic Adelaide, lacking the pace and bounce of Friday in Perth, and it helps that Australia have left out their new find, Mahli Beardman, who is being “managed”.

Naturally, there is also still a lot of chat about sandpaper. David Warner was supposed to be here for Fox but is not, having attended to a family commitment in Sydney last night, according to the station.

More significant, though, was the intervention of Chadd Sayers, a one-cap seamer who was on the sandpaper tour. He is commentating for SEN and has backed Khawaja up strongly. He believes all players knew that sandpaper was being used in two Tests and says there was a 60-90 minute meeting involving all players about taking collective responsibility. Cummins said the opposite.

News.title: Ireland stay in hunt for final place despite complacent display
News.content:
Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Nations Championship fifth-round Test between Ireland and Fiji at Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

Ireland are third in the Northern Hemisphere standings, having played a game less than England and France above them, but a point bonus victory this evening would put Andy Farrell’s side level with Steve Borthwick’s men and keep them in the mix for top spot. Meanwhile, Fiji are rock bottom of the South Hemisphere table, with a miserable points difference of -133, and lost 54-17 to France last time out.

Tadhg Beirne, who is poised to captain his country for the first time on home soil this evening, said Ireland are aiming to carry on the positive momentum following their 42-12 win over Argentina eight days ago, but feels his side can still improve. “The big focus for us is to continue building on our performance, particularly from last week,” he remarked.

“We laid down a foundation of how we want to play, but we’re certainly not satisfied with that. I think there were patches of us playing really well there, but there were also patches where we weren’t to the standard that we’re going to hold ourselves to.”

News.title: Botham’s grandson inspires Wales to historic win over All Blacks
News.content:
The second half of Wales’ Nations Championship started with a hard-fought 28-21 bonus point victory over Japan last Saturday. Steve Tandy’s side sit fifth in the Northern Hemisphere table, but just five points separate them from second-place England, and they still have a tonne of pride to play for as they aim to finish as high as possible in the group.

Speaking ahead of the encounter, Tandy said: “We’re excited for the opportunity we have against New Zealand. It was good to get the win last Saturday, but some elements of our execution weren’t where we wanted.

“We have to go up another level this weekend and be more ruthless. We have one of the best teams in the world coming. We want to be better and put in an 80-minute performance.”

Meanwhile, New Zealand arrive in the Welsh capital in imperious form, having won their opening four Nations Championship matches and boasting a +73 points difference. South Africa’s defeat has opened the door for the resurgent All Blacks to pounce, and they’ll be brimming with confidence following their eye-catching 43-21 triumph against Scotland at Murrayfield a week ago.

As for the team news, Tandy has made four alterations to the starting XV that overcame Japan. Taine Basham is poised for his first international appearance since the 2024 Six Nations, while James Botham, Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Adam Beard also begin the contest. The influential Aaron Wainwright is out with a minor calf problem.

All Blacks Head Coach has ordered 10 changes to the 23-man squad that brushed Scotland aside. Forwards including George Bower, Asafo Aumua, Josh Lord, Anton Segner and backs such as Richie Mo’unga, Anton Lienert-Brown and Fehi Fineanganofo all start for the heavily rotated visitors. Full-back Beauden Barrett will captain New Zealand for the first time, in his 149th Test, while Will Jordan is unavailable because of a hamstring issue.

Kick-off is at 14:10, with team news following now.

News.title: Joseph a star in the making as England revel in role of bullies
News.content:
England have made wholesale changes, with only five members from the starting XV against Australia remaining. Henry Pollock starts at eight, Will Joseph earns just his second cap on the wing and Archie McParland is set for his international debut off the bench.

“Japan are a very well-coached side who will challenge us in different ways, and we know we will need to bring intensity throughout the game,” said Borthwick. “The atmosphere at Allianz Stadium last week was incredible. The players really fed off the energy in the stadium, and we are really looking forward to being back on Saturday [today].”

Japan’s first game of this month’s fixtures ended in defeat as they lost 28-21 against Wales in Cardiff last weekend. That defeat means they have just one win from their first four games of the Nations Championship, which came against Italy in the opening game, and they sit second bottom in the southern hemisphere standings.

“We have had really good training to prepare us for the game we are expecting against England,” Jones said. “We had two days of very settled and pretty training but Wednesday was quite dirty. We had to adapt to certain situations and in the end we did it really well. I was really pleased with the players, really pleased with their effort, really pleased with the way they adapted to the situations. I am looking forward to going to Twickenham with this young Japanese team that is going to play the house down.”

Kick-off from Allianz Stadium is at 4.40pm.

Sports.title: England U21 3 France U21 2: Max Dowman nets last gasp winner for Young Lions in clash with £600MILLION of talent
Sports.content:
Next

MAX DOWMAN was the Young Lions’ late hero as Lee Carsley’s side proved their worth in a HALF-A-BILLION-POUND bout in the South West.

There was nearly £600MILLION worth of talent in both the England and France Under-21 squads on Monday night at Aston Gate, more than THREE times the estimated value of usual occupants Bristol City.



And Arsenal talent Dowman, 16, the man with the biggest reputation, proved England have the best bang for the buck as he won the game on his first ever start for the U21s.

Dowman’s 89th-minute winner added to first-half goals from Mikey Moore and Divin Mubama to outweigh a second-half double from France substitute Giovani Vesini.



France didn’t lose a single match during their Euros qualification process, averaging over three goals per game as they cruised to qualification.

Carsley’s outfit proved too strong in the opening 45 minutes and it took Moore, 19, who was making his first ever start for the U21s, just six minutes to put England ahead.

The Tottenham ace, currently on loan at Koln, was played in by Ethan Nwaneri before he tucked a curling effort into the bottom corner.

Arsenal loanee Nwaneri – currently at Borussia Dortmund – was involved again for the second, delivering a pin-point floated cross to the back post to find Mubama, 22, on the half-hour mark.

Manchester City loanee Mubama – currently at Southampton – judged the flight of the ball perfectly, nodding it back across goal and into the opposite corner to double England’s lead.

But France hit back with 10 minutes to play when Versini’s shot slipped through Tommy Setford’s gloves and into the back of the net as the rain hammered down.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Versini added a second just five minutes later when he curled in a stunning effort from 25 yards out.

But just when it looked like England’s night had been spoiled, up stepped superstar Dowman to save the Young Lions.

The playmaker, who became England U21’s youngest-ever player when he made his debut last week, tapped home a pass from Harrison Armstrong with just over a minute left to play.



Carsley knew that his side had not been tested during their qualification campaign for the Euros, beating the likes of Kazakhstan and Andorra on their way.

But this performance against comparable opposition showed that England might just have the quality to pull off a historic three-peat in the summer when they bid to win their third European Championship in a row, having lifted the title under Carsley in both 2023 and 2025.

On getting the better of France, Carsley said: “What I would say about this squad is, I have got a lot of expectation for them. I think they can really achieve something special.

“France are one of the best teams I have seen so far. I have watched a lot of Germany, Spain and France ahead of the next six months. France are definitely up there with the best teams that I have seen.”

Speaking about Dowman, Moore said: “He is a top kid. You forget how old he is. I was saying on the bench that my little brother is 17, and he feels older to me than my little brother.



“It is weird seeing how well he is doing at such a young age. I think he has been top and everywhere he goes he is taking the next step and he just needs to keep going and keep pushing.”

Sports.title: Man Utd star suffers knee injury days before Mauricio Pochettino set to take charge as manager
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED keeper Karl Darlow has suffered an injury setback ahead of Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival at Old Trafford.

The Wales stopper, 36, skipped training on international duty and is set to miss the Nations League match with Portugal in Cardiff on Tuesday.



Darlow, a summer signing from Leeds on a free transfer, has been back-up to United No1 Senne Lammens this season and made his debut in the Carabao Cup 3-2 loss to Brighton.

Wales boss Craig Bellamy, who started Darlow in a 3-1 defeat to Norway on Saturday, said: “We’ll check on Karl.



“His knee just flared up a little bit.

“He has not been playing on a regular basis so we were aware of that before it.



“We’ve given him as much time to recover.”

Darlow missed the majority of pre-season as well as the last international break which spanned four matches due to the same knee problem.

New United boss Pochettino, who replaces the sacked Michael Carrick, arrives in the UK later this week after USA‘s clash with Haiti in the early hours of Wednesday.

He has already sent some off his staff ahead to get cracking.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Long-time assistants, Jesus Perez and Toni Jimenez, as well as his son, Sebastiano, jetted into Manchester on Sunday.

Assistant coach Miguel D’Agostino and physical trainer Silvia Tuya have remained with the US and will head across the Pond after the game with Haiti.

Pochettino hinted that some of his USA players may wind up joining him at Old Trafford.

He said: “I know that you asked the players before. All good players always have dreams.

“To reach the last level – and I see United is one of the teams that is in the last level – it’s a dream for many of the players.



“But now I see they need to be focusing in today, in tomorrow’s game, in their day clubs.

“I know really well for more than two years every single player and I see they are all players with an unbelievable talent.

“And of course, in the future when that happens, we are going to pay attention.”

Sports.title: Meet forgotten ex-Chelsea star, 51, central to England’s decision to axe Jordan Pickford for James Trafford
Sports.content:
Next

ENGLAND boss Thomas Tuchel has hinted he is planning to change his No1 with James Trafford making a strong case for Jordan Pickford’s place.

But Tuchel, 53, can’t be the only one credited with that decision as he holds the Three Lions’s goalkeeping coach Henrique Hilario‘s opinion in very high regard after their many years working together.



Hilario, 51, spent two years as part of the German tactician’s coaching staff at Chelsea.

And the Portuguese coach followed the ex-Bayern Munich boss at Wembley last year when the latter replaced Gareth Southgate at the helm.



Following the former Paris Saint-Germain boss’ arrival, Pickford, 32, remained England’s undisputed starting goalkeeper all the way until last summer’s World Cup.

But it seems like Hilario has seen something special in Trafford, 24.

The former Borussia Dortmund boss and his goalie coach were impressed with the Leeds star’s shot-stopping abilities but also agreed he is better with the ball at his feet than his Everton counterpart.

That led to the England boss splitting game time with each keeper making three starts in the last six Nations League matches.

However, Trafford appeared to have made a stronger case for the position after a stunning display on Sunday’s historic 3-2 victory against world champions Spain in Madrid.

The ex-Manchester City ace sealed the Furia Roja’s first defeat in two years after a heroic last-gasp double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Aymeric Laporte.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

It seems like Hilario’s instinct has paid off and showed why Tuchel extended their cooperation after a successful stint at Chelsea that saw them winning the Champions League in 2021.

The former goalie signed for the Blues in 2006 from Nacional as third-choice behind Petr Cech and Carlo Cudicini.

And the ex-Portugal international spent almost a decade providing back-up before retiring in 2014 after being part of two FA Cup victories and another two League Cup trophy wins.



Two years after hanging up his gloves, the Porto academy graduate returned to Stamford Bridge under then manager Antonio Conte as assistant goalkeeping coach.

Hilario was then promoted two years later by Maurizio Sarri and remained in that role under Tuchel too.

Sports.title: Man Utd must go all out for stunning £130m Cole Palmer transfer – and axe £300k-a-week Bruno Fernandes to pay for it
Sports.content:
Next

THE new Generalissimo is heading for Old Trafford.

However, no army chief can be assured of success unless his troops truly believe in themselves — and the battle plan.



And in London, the Manchester-born player who has worn two shades of blue is exactly what Mauricio Pochettino needs in his red battalion.

For Pochettino, the key to getting it right will be ridding his dressing room of symbols of the old guard and replacing them with acolytes ready to follow his orders.



That means Ineos, Omar Berrada, Jason Wilcox and the United board giving Poch the tools to do the job, whatever the impact on the “bottom line”.

On making big calls that the merchandising arm of the club might not like…



While getting him out of Chelsea will surely take a British-record fee in excess of £130million, Cole Palmer fits both the Poch playbook and the United DNA.

Apart from anything, he’s a Wythenshawe lad who grew up supporting the Red Devils and idolising Wayne Rooney.

That means a sacrifice — cutting through the noise and the game of contract bluff and telling Bruno Fernandes it is better for all sides for the Portuguese to move on.

Before that, though, new manager Poch and the Old Trafford hierarchy must make it clear to Chelsea’s top brass that they are willing to pay whatever it takes to bring Palmer, 24, back to his home city.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

More of the same will not do for United. It’s what got them in this huge mess in the first place.

When he walks into Carrington on Thursday, Pochettino will inherit a dressing room compiled under SIX different managers.

Luke Shaw, Poch’s one-time teenage “son” at Southampton, was signed by Louis van Gaal, who also gave Marcus Rashford his debut.

Jose Mourinho added Diogo Dalot, while successor Ole Gunnar Solskjaer brought in Harry Maguire and Amad Diallo, as well as Fernandes.

And then it was Erik ten Hag, who landed Mason Mount — Poch let him go as Chelsea chief — Leny Yoro, Matthijs de Ligt, Joshua Zirkzee and Noussair Mazraoui.



That came before a summer splurge in 2025 under Ruben Amorim that saw Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Benjamin Sesko move in.

This summer, with Carrick at the wheel, no left-backs or strikers joined — but Youri Tielemans, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos arrived in midfield.

All adding up to a side that will travel to Anfield on Sunday in the relegation zone… and potentially rock bottom of the pile.

Radical change, both in personnel and mindset, is required. Tough choices. Big calls.



Fernandes, 32, has been an outstanding player for United since his arrival in 2020 from Sporting.

In addition to 341 appearances and 113 goals, he was part of the sides that won the FA Cup and Carabao Cup.

Fernandes ended last term as Football Writers’ Association Footballer of the Year and winner of the PFA award, too.

Yet the public row with Carrick and last week’s floating of the contract issues were a signal that a parting of the ways would be mutually beneficial.

Especially if United can line up Palmer, who knows exactly what Pochettino demands.



It was the Argentine who gave Palmer his big break, bringing him from an irregular role at Manchester City to a starting one at Stamford Bridge.

In his three-and-a-bit seasons in Pep Guardiola’s squad — learning from a master — Palmer made 37 appearances, just 13 of them starts.

But the attacker signed off with City’s goal in the 2023 Uefa Super Cup shootout win over Sevilla.



His first Chelsea term — working with Poch — brought 40 starts, five games off the bench, 25 club goals and an England debut. The season ended with his strike against Spain in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin.

Pochettino took a gem and honed it, giving Palmer the responsibility and freedom he craved, those hours of running on the training ground at Cobham rewarded.

Those hints and suggestions that Palmer has a hankering for home will not go away.

He can’t go back to City but if United can prise him out of SW6, it would supercharge the atmosphere in and around the club.

Poch would add a world-class talent with a willingness to put in the hard yards.



And he could be a dressing-room disciple — able to articulate the manager’s message, pass it on and explain why it works for everyone.

Chelsea, of course, will not want to lose him.

But they didn’t want to lose Enzo Fernandez, either. And a huge offer on the table might soften that resolve. Money talks.

IF YOU had been asked to name England’s first-choice back five in the summer, it probably wouldn’t have been: James Trafford, Ben White, Ezri Konsa, Marc Guehi and Lewis Hall.



Things move quickly in football.

Thomas Tuchel’s September promises over what he wants his side to be have been made good.

Watching England hustle, harry and monster Spain for more than an hour on Sunday night was what feel-good football is supposed to be.



Tuchel will never completely shift the shadow of Argentina in Atlanta until he proves he can handle the pressure-cooker situations at Euro 2028.

But something significant is being built. Something substantial. The FA’s faith in Tuchel looks more than justifiable.

AT WEMBLEY on Thursday, Harry Kane was rightly feted for his feats for his country.



But just 24 hours earlier, a few miles away, one of the players who emerged alongside the England captain was ploughing a lonely furrow on a field in Chiswick.

Working with a personal coach, Dele Alli found himself surrounded by school matches, rather than the international stage he once strutted.

The hope, a devout one, is that there could yet be a way back for Dele, even if, at 30, it may not be at the very highest level.

He is certainly giving himself the chance.

SO, IN THE END, Arsene Wenger decided he did not want to be football’s standard bearer against Gianni Infantino.



The ex-Arsenal boss considered the idea of running for the Fifa presidency for more than a week before passing on the option, with French FA head Philippe Diallo instead nominated by Uefa ahead of Wednesday’s deadline.

Yet if anyone is going to bring Infantino down, you suspect it will be a US politician, rather than any of football’s movers and shakers.

Democrat Congressman Jamie Raskin has Infantino — and, of course, Donald Trump — in his sights at his expected role as the new head of the House Judicial Committee, with the power to subpoena witnesses to give evidence under oath.



It was the FBI-led raid on Zurich that eventually ended Sepp Blatter’s Fifa reign.

And Raskin could be the weapon Uefa lacks the wherewithal to wield.

IT DIDN’T work for Thomas Frank at Tottenham.

A marriage of inconvenience, leading to one of the biggest Danish tragedies since Hamlet.

Spurs fans will be preparing the fusillade they are sure to aim at Frank when they visit Crystal Palace at the end of January.



New Selhurst boss Frank, though, remains a thoroughly decent man and a good manager.

He will show that — and get the Eagles flying again.

THE MORE that Cricket Australia attempts to close the Sandpaper-gate scandal down, the worse the cover-up looks.



Pat Cummins denied he had knowledge of the ball-tampering plan after admissions by Usman Khawaja and David Warner.

But those denials were then blown apart by Cape Town 12th man Chadd Sayers.

It could be a summer of hell for the Baggy Greens.

Sports.title: ‘It’s a lonely place’ – How working as a FARMER helped turn James Trafford into England goalkeeping superstar
Sports.content:
Next

JAMES TRAFFORD has always had safe hands.

The Leeds United shotstopper, 24, produced a heroic display for England in their 3-2 Nations League win over Spain.



But before he established himself as one of the top goalkeepers in the country, he helped his dad, David on their family farm in North Cumbria in the Lake District.

Trafford would care for the lambs, help them give birth and mix manure with lime when he was a young boy.



Last year, the 6ft6in goalie told SunSport: “The first time I did lambing was aged 11. I had to put my hand up them and pull.

“That was far too disgusting and, although it was cool to have experienced that, it wasn’t the best thing.



“I also had to muck out. We mixed manure with lime to get the right soil pH acidity. And being in the slurry pit was horrible — the stench.”

Early years

Trafford was brought up in Cockermouth, where England cricket hero Ben Stokes was raised.

He briefly attended Cockermouth School, just like Stokes, however he left in year 7 to chase his football dreams at Manchester City’s youth academy aged 12.

The £40million star has never forgotten his roots and the strong work ethic he developed from his years on the farm put him in good stead for a career in football.



Loan spells at Accrington Stanley and Bolton, where he won the EFL Trophy in 2023, prompted Burnley to pay Manchester City £19million for his services.

He achieved promotion with the Clarets in 2024, conceding just 16 goals in 45 games in the Championship – a Football League record.



The following season Burnley were relegated from the Premier League back to the Championship, but Trafford’s performances stood out and encouraged Manchester City to re-sign him for £31million, a transfer record fee for a British keeper, in 2025.

Frustratingly for Trafford, after starting the season as first choice, City manager Pep Guardiola bought Gianluigi Donnarumma and he was frozen out of the side.

Mental health

Speaking on Football Daily’s The Football Interview in November, Trafford revealed how his time at City affected his mental health and why he had to move to Leeds United in the summer.

He said: “What a horrendous, horrendous feeling. Not playing.

“You are ringing a lot of people and just venting. Like most people, you have a [bad] day at work and you ring someone up.



“I ring my dad, I ring my mum, I ring my missus, I ring my mates. I like ringing my mates and we can just have a good talk about it all. It’s quite funny.

“I had to play regularly this season for my own mental wellbeing. You just lose yourself not playing.

“Maybe I’m different, I don’t know, but the feeling of not playing every week, it felt horrendous.



“I just had to play every week this season for that mental feel-good and to keep progressing with my career and edging me closer to achieving the dreams I want to achieve.”

Keeping grounded

Away from football, Trafford is a down-to-earth and humble personality.

When his busy schedule permits, he returns to Cumbria to see his family, enjoy his mum’s roast dinners, and catch up with best friend, Spencer Fulton, an aspiring rugby league player.

Testament to his level-headed approach to life, just two weeks after he played for the Three Lions at Wembley in September, he enjoyed some downtime with mates playing darts in the Black Bull on Cockermouth’s Main Street.

He has admitted in the past if he wasn’t a footballer, he likely would have become a farmer, and isn’t above returning during his summer’s off to wrap fleeces and clip sheep.



In 2024, Trafford appeared in Farmers Weekly, alongside his dad David, a weekly reader of the magazine, on a tractor.

He spoke about how his farming background prepared him to become a professional footballer.

Trafford told Farmers Weekly: “You draw on it the most in the tough times. You know, when it’s nailing down outside and you really can’t be bothered.

“Every farmer knows that regardless of the weather, you still have to go out. You still have to work all day. You just have to do your job and do it as best as you can.



“That sort of upbringing, seeing my mum and dad graft as hard as they can, has always stuck with me.”

Trafford even sees comparisons between football and farming.

He said: “Being a goalkeeper is tough. You’re the only one who wears a different coloured kit. Even that on its own, you stand out.



“Like farming, goalkeeping can be a really lonely place. But it’s also a really good position on the pitch because you have that sense of importance and you try and keep everything together.”

Career choices

But, a career in football was not what his granddad, Bill, had in mind for Trafford

He wanted his grandson to continue the farming family legacy, or become a jockey.

Trafford told SunSport: “Grandpa Bill, god bless his soul. I have two cousins then my sister and I.

“Grandpa always said, ‘he has to be a farmer’ but he really wanted one of us to be a jockey — but we were all too tall!”



Horse racing’s loss is football’s gain, as Trafford wrestles Jordan Pickford to be England’s first pick between the sticks.

The pair share a great bond off the pitch, although Trafford has outlined his determination to be England’s permanent No1.

Sunday night’s outstanding performance in Madrid has gone a long way in convincing England boss Thomas Tuchel that it’s time for a changing of the guard in the nets.

Sports.title: Why Mauricio Pochettino appointment could spell the end for Jason Wilcox at Man Utd
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED have turned to Mauricio Pochettino to rescue their disastrous season following the sacking of Michael Carrick.

The Red Devils sit 18th in the Premier League table after a dismal start to the campaign that saw standards slip at Old Trafford.



And SunSport’s Manchester United correspondent Samuel Luckhurst believes the Argentine will immediately lay down the law to an under-performing squad — though a power struggle with the hierarchy could be brewing.

Speaking on SunSport’s The Luckhurst View, he said: “He is someone who is going to demand a hell of a work ethic from the players.



“They’ve not worked hard enough this season. And that wasn’t entirely down to them.

“I know that a fellow journalist said recently that, ‘sacking Michael Carrick, it’d be tantamount to shooting Bambi.’



“Well, it wasn’t. It wasn’t like that whatsoever. He should have been put out of his misery a few weeks beforehand. And also he was responsible for this very lax culture that he’d allowed to creep in.

“And it’s bizarre that someone who was so successful at the club as a player allowed that to happen. And you look at the running stats, you look how low down you are. I think they rank 20th out of 20 for the athleticism of squads in the Premier League.”

Our United man thinks Carrick ultimately paid the price for his own attitude as a player.

He added: “We’ve seen it from the very start of the post-Ferguson era when David Moyes came in and said, ‘I’m going to make you run more.’ And United players, among them Michael Carrick, bristling at that constructive criticism.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“It seems like every manager since then has had an issue with them not being fit enough or not running enough.

“So for that alone, a lot of United supporters will want to get on board with Pochettino cracking the whip with them.”

While Pochettino is expected to whip the dressing room into shape, his arrival raises major questions about how he will coexist with technical director Jason Wilcox.

United have handed the former Tottenham boss the title of head coach rather than manager — a structure that has previously caused friction.

Luckhurst added: “Given his background at Tottenham, he has to be the main man. He has to be the boss.



“That’s why he only lasted a year at Chelsea with their complicated structure.

“Whereas at Tottenham, I think the sporting director or the technical director was gone a year after Pochettino left. And then they didn’t really bring anyone else in while he was there.

“So that’s going to be a fascinating dynamic to see how that plays out with Jason Wilcox, who of course is the director of football.

“I think from United fans’ perspective, it’s a polarising appointment because he has been in gradual decline since he didn’t get the job in 2018.

“And he didn’t really leave his imprint on PSG where he was only there for 18 months.



“The fact that he was in club football exile with the United States felt peculiar given his age going into that job at that time, even though it had the lure of taking charge of the States in a home World Cup and then of course extending his contract as well.

“So there are a lot of misgivings about him, but also clearly given the work that he has done and some of the non-negotiable aspects that he’ll impose on this team, there are elements about his coaching style that United do need, not that that’s particularly difficult given where they are in the table.”

Luckhurst thinks Pochettino and Wilcox may end up in a power struggle that only one man emerges from.

He explained: “I don’t think Pochettino is going to back down over that.



“That’s one reason why he lasted only a season at Chelsea. There were too many issues with the hierarchy. And I think they had two sporting directors at the time.

“And that’s just not what he was used to from his time at Tottenham. And he did have relative success at Tottenham. It will be a fascinating dynamic.

“And he’s there on a two-and-a-half-year contract. I would be amazed if in two and a half years time, Pochettino and Jason Wilcox are still at United.

“It already feels like something would have to give there. And most United supporters would not be sorry to see the back of Jason Wilcox, clearly.”

Despite sitting in the relegation zone ahead of a daunting trip to Liverpool, Samuel insists Pochettino must aim far higher than mere survival.



With 28 games remaining and the gap to the Champions League places standing at just 10 points, United still have time to salvage their campaign.

Our man said: “I don’t think it’s difficult for Pochettino to just get them out of the relegation zone, but they’ve still got to be looking at trying to finish in the top four.

“They’ve got what, 28 games left. They’re ten points off the top four.

“Given how other teams are so inconsistent, erratic. Liverpool are quite streaky, Chelsea are erratic.

“City, I think we’re all expecting them to be deducted points at some point. Well, it’s got to happen sooner rather than later, given the integrity of the league is at stake there.



“Brighton have been brilliant, but you still wonder whether they’re going to be able to keep it up for the next six months.

“So, and also I look at that United squad and as dismal as the defence is in, Carrick did not help things by playing square pegs and round holes.

“It’s not going to be difficult, I think, for Pochettino to merely get them out of the relegation zone.

“But the fact that we’re even talking about, you know, will Manchester United finish in the top ten or where should they be aiming for is a problem in itself.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But I maintain that in terms of the firepower on that squad and what they’ve got up top, they should still be looking to at least challenge for Champions League qualification.”

Sports.title: Who does Robert Pattinson support? New James Bond’s football team revealed
Sports.content:
Next

ROBERT PATTINSON is officially the new James Bond.

The British actor has replaced Daniel Craig and his debut appearance as 007 is expected to come in 2028.



Away from his roles as in The Twilight Saga and Batman, Pattinson is reportedly a huge football fan.

And he revealed that missing matches was one of the worst things about being a Hollywood star.



Who does Robert Pattinson support?

Pattinson was born in south-west London in Barnes.

As a youngster he was a keen footballer – despite admitting he wasn’t very good – with his talents in playing the piano and guitar.

But despite living south of the river, his footie alliances were in the north of the capital.

Pattinson is a massive Arsenal supporter.

Following his announcement as the new James Bond, throwback photos emerged of Pattinson with Theo Walcott at the Emirates.

The actor revealed in an interview with The Metro: “I miss reading the sport section [of English newspapers]. I miss the football… Arsenal.”



And asked on the red carpet who his favourite player was, Pattinson replied: “Emmanuel Petit.”

The French midfielder played for the Gunners from 1997 to 2000, winning the Premier League and FA Cup under Arsene Wenger in his first season at the club.

That summer he went on to win the 1998 World Cup with France.

Petit also played for Monaco, Barcelona and Chelsea.



In 2022, Pattinson joked that he had restarted football training to be able to play with his daughter.

He told GQ: “I just have this terror of passing it back, and I go straight back to being a 10-year-old, and kicking it in the wrong direction. People being like: ‘Wow! What an idiot!’

“Eventually, I’m probably gonna have a child. So I’ve started training myself so that I can be somewhat… so that I can play soccer with a three-year-old.”

Sports.title: Michael Carrick seen for first time since Man Utd sacking as fans say ‘looks five years younger already’
Sports.content:
Next

MICHAEL CARRICK looked refreshed and replenished after being publicly spotted for the first time since his dismissal as Manchester United manager.

Carrick, 45, was sacked in controversial fashion on Thursday following United’s worst start to a season in 40 years that’s left them in 18th place in the league.



The club legend revived his former team last season after replacing Ruben Amorim and leading them to third place. But he only managed one win in all of his ten Prem games this season, losing four of them.

The Red Devils moved quickly and replaced the former midfielder with Mauricio Pochettino, who will take charge of his first game on Sunday against rivals Liverpool at Anfield.



But Carrick has also moved on – it seems – as he was seen attending a gig by The Courteeners at Alexandra Palace in London over the weekend.

The ex-England international posed for a photo during the event in which he looked relaxed as he smiled for the camera.

And fans quickly noticed that the years appear to have fallen off Carrick since getting away from the chaos at Old Trafford.

A supporter tweeted: “He already looks 5 years younger.”

Another agreed: “He does indeed!”

A third added: “Carrick looks 20 years young already.”

This fan wrote: “Carrick enjoying life I see.”

Another posted: “The wrinkles went away.”

And a comment echoed: “Man de-aged like 10 years WTF.”

"I'm confident Thomas' extensive experience in the Premier League will help us achieve our goals for the rest of the season."

Is Thomas Frank the right man for Crystal Palace? Have your say in the comments section.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Domestic football isn't the only thing on Frank's agenda. Palace are embarking on their first campaign in the Europa League, having won the Conference League under former manager Oliver Glasner last season.

‌



The Eagles are 20th in the 36-team table after four games. They host Spanish side Real Sociedad next Thursday, a fixture sandwiched by two vital Premier League games against Coventry and Hull, who are two and four points above Palace respectively.

Palace are also still in the Carabao Cup. Frank's side will host Sunderland in a quarter-final clash on Wednesday, December 16.

Sports.title: Inside England’s World Cup recovery including squad overhaul and Thomas Tuchel change
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel says England’s glorious night in Madrid shows they have finally moved on from the World Cup.

England enjoyed one of their greatest victories on foreign soil as they beat world champions Spain and ended their 43 game unbeaten run.

It has put Tuchel back on course to achieve the dream of ending England’s wait for silverware after the heartbreak of losing to Argentina in the summer.

Just 123 days on from that painful night in Atlanta, England showed they have learned their lesson with a “statement win” against Spain.

‌



But it took a player summit, rebuilding belief and confidence together with fresh ideas and Tuchel used a now tried and trusted football line by insisting they had to go through a “process” to get there.

Thomas Tuchel questions Elliot Anderson red card after 10-man England hold off Spain READ MORE :

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Harry Kane took centre stage at a players’ meeting at the start of the first England camp back in September as the squad had their say over what went wrong at the World Cup.

England famously surrendered their 1-0 lead against Argentina, they sat deeper and Tuchel made a string of defensive substitutions - and ultimately paid a heavy price.

‌



Tuchel took on board the players’ views while also ushering in a raft of new players and, by the time the England boss named his squad for this camp, only half of the 22 outfield players in the United States survived the cull.

It has been branded Tuchel 2.0 and the former Chelsea and Paris Saint Germain boss said it was needed “to improve, you need to bring in new players for competition, young players, new energy, fresh energy.”

View 4 Images England have bounced back from their World Cup heartbreak in Atlanta

You could see from the way England approached and started the win against Spain - as they were fast out of the blocks, pressed high and attacked - that this was a strong mindset and back to what Tuchel does best.

‌



If England lost their nerve in the summer then they were back to throwing caution to the wind and proving they belong among the world elite.

Tuchel said: “We took the next steps after the World Cup, and I'm very proud of the performance. It's a real statement victory. The way we won is not only just winning, but the way we won and the way we played the third phase is very impressive.

“Full credit to the players. You could see the steps that we take between every single match, and that's why I'm very, very happy. It's a full package. It's a full package of belief, of courage, of commitment, of togetherness, of relying on each other and stepping up on in this moment.

“And then you need also quality, and we showed the quality today in all aspects of the game, big in defending, or in the high press, or in the low block, in the build-up game or in the set pieces, or in the goal, in the duels.

‌



“It was a complete performance that makes me very proud, and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry.”

View 4 Images Thomas Tuchel wants his England side to keep pushing forward

The Football Association always have a review after each tournament and it is done in a very corporate way as it featured a former civil servant and a former British Army officer.

If that was a box-ticking exercise, then it was the players who really put their views across to allow England to move on from the hangover in the summer to a much better positive place.

‌



The foundations for the Spain win were built in Croatia last month when the handbrake was released with a 7-0 win and then you had the pace, energy and high press from the off in Madrid. Spain could not live with England.

If England sank deep against Spain then it was more about the brave defending from the Mexico win when they had been reduced to ten men rather than Argentina when they just retreated. Tuchel accepts the players had real input and ideas in their meetings.

Tuchel added: “It took me a while to digest and see the way forward, how we can help and adjust and improve, and how we can do this together. Clarity came then in the first camp.

View 4 Images England defended for their lives to get over the line (Image: Thomas COEX / AFP via Getty Images)

‌



“We had of course reviews and so on, but clarity came then together with the players. And straight away we had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went.

“So once camp started, the ideas became more clear for me. Even if it was not so easy the first week, like to overcome and arrive with different emotions. Some were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team.

“Some had digested it, some had not digested it. But it was important to have this kind of process together to again overcome and everyone committed that we want to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“Full credit then to the players how they buy into it like from meetings and training and you straight away see it's amazing that it came together like this now.”

‌
