Sports.title: James Trafford now in pole position to oust Jordan Pickford and become England No.1
Sports.content:
James Trafford now in pole position to oust Jordan Pickford and become England No.1

James Trafford starred for England as the Three Lions beat world champions Spain in Madrid, with the Leeds keeper now vying to become the long-term number one

View 2 Images James Trafford was superb as England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid

James Trafford has put himself in pole position to be England’s long-term No1.

‌



‌



Leeds keeper Trafford’s heroics in Spain have only reinforced Thomas Tuchel’s belief that he has the potential to succeed Jordan Pickford. Tuchel has identified Trafford’s ability to play out from the back plus also his reflexes, shot stopping and calm mentality as his major qualities.

‌



Trafford made three sensational late saves against Spain to further state his case but it is clear that Tuchel is ready to move on from Pickford. Everton keeper Pickford has been No1 for the best part of his decade but there were question marks over some of his performances at the World Cup.

‌



Tuchel used the Nations League to share the games between the pair but it was noticeable that Trafford got the two Spain games who were the best opponents and they also wanted to use his ability to play out from the back.

England boss Tuchel pointed to Trafford’s match-winning saves as being as important as a Harry Kane goal and said the competition is exactly what he wants.

Tuchel said: “That is very important. You need this bit of luck combined with quality. He is a good shot stopper and he has the reflexes. And he proved it on that stage, so this gives him a lot of belief.

‌



“You always have to deserve your place. You will never get a gift and just get a game. So he deserved to play.

“But we also expected this kind of performance. Was not only the last save, but also the build-up play and not lose the focus. And now it's on him to keep going for it.

‌



View 2 Images Trafford was named player of the match after his stunning late saves

“It’s no headache at all. I'm so far away from a headache that I cannot imagine. So it's what we wanted, and this is the best thing that can happen to all of us, also to Pickers.

Sports.title: Ezri Konsa aims dig at defeated Spain as he lays out England's targets under Thomas Tuchel
Sports.content:
Ezri Konsa aims dig at defeated Spain as he lays out England's targets under Thomas Tuchel

England produced an impressive backs-to-the-wall performance in Madrid to beat Spain and are now ready to push for silverware in the Nations League and Euros

View 2 Images Ezri Konsa is confident England can win trophies (Image: Diego Souto/Getty Images)

Ezri Konsa says England would have thrashed world champions Spain 5-0 if they were not reduced to 10 men.

‌



‌



England produced one of their all-time great performances in Madrid to end Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run and were 3-0 up and in cruise control when they had Elliot Anderson sent off. Arsenal centre half Konsa then had to help 10-man England man the barricades and hold on for dear life as Spain roared back to make it 3-2.

‌



But Konsa insists that if England had kept 11 men on the pitch then the end result would have been very different because they completely outclassed the No1 team in world football.

‌



Konsa said: “It was a special night, a game we wanted to win, a game we knew we could win. We stuck to our game plan. You guys saw the game at Wembley and I thought we did really well. A few individual errors cost us and they almost did again but we stuck together, 10 men, and dug deep. If we had 11 men on the pitch we would have scored two more.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



“We went 1-0 up and Harry, our captain, told us to keep going and to keep our food on the pedal. This is their first loss in 44 games so it speaks for itself. Coming here and getting the win was special and massive.”

Spain have dominated the international stage since winning the Nations League and they went on to win the Euros in 2024 and the World Cup last summer. They beat England at Wembley in September but it was a hard luck story for Thomas Tuchel’s men because Kane missed a penalty to give his side a 3-1 lead. And instead Spain came back to win 3-2.

‌



It looked like a familiar story might be unfolding even after Kane, Konsa and Ben White scored in the Metropolitano Stadium and then England were put on the back foot by Spain’s comeback. But Konsa says getting the job done shows how England have matured, they have moved on from the World Cup defeat to Argentina and now they have the belief they can beat the best.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



View 2 Images Ezri Konsa scored England's second goal vs Spain (Image: Michael Regan/The FA via Getty Images)

Konsa also says that winning the Nations League will be key to strengthening belief they can then win more trophies in the future and give them confidence ahead of the Euros in 2028. He said: “Yes, 100 per cent. The Nations League is a trophy at the end of the day. Silverware going into the Euros would be massive for us. We want to win the Euros and we know it is on home soil. That will give us a massive boost.

‌



“It is very important. You end it with huge confidence going into next year’s set of games. We are taking it camp-by-camp. We are not taking it too far forward. But going into March we will have a lot of confidence.

“There’s a top mentality, we have world class players. Everyone knows what we can do once it clicks. You saw the first half and until the red card how much quality we have. We dominated the game and for us we believe in ourselves and the manager. We just want to go out and show everyone what we can.

Article continues below

“The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our food on the pedal. That is what we did. Argentina was different, different circumstances. Playing with 10 men against the world champions would always be difficult. The amount of balls coming into the box we dealt with really well.

“The World Cup has gone now. We have passed that. We are focused on winning each game and we know we have the Euros coming up.”

Sports.title: 'Two Man Utd stars let me down on my worst day ever - it was an embarrassment'
Sports.content:
'Two Man Utd stars let me down on my worst day ever - it was an embarrassment'

A Manchester United legend has explained that two of his most trusted stars once let him down on a particularly dark day in the Red Devils' rich history

View 2 Images Sir Alex Ferguson called out Rio Ferdinand and Patrice Evra

Sir Alex Ferguson once noted that Rio Ferdinand and Patrice Evra contributed significantly to his "worst ever day" as Manchester United manager. The legendary Scot enjoyed a remarkable career at Old Trafford between 1986 and 2013, with plenty of highs to reflect upon in his retirement.

‌



‌



One of the world's most dominant teams during that period, Ferguson guided the Red Devils to a staggering haul of 13 Premier League titles, 19 domestic cups and a pair of Champions Leagues. However, the sensational highs during Fergie's reign were not without their crushing lows.

‌



The worst of which, in the 84-year-old's opinion, came in the form of a 6-1 battering on home soil to fierce rivals Manchester City in October 2011, which turned the Theatre of Dreams into a cathedral of nightmares. City had lived in United's shadow for most of their time in the Premier League until 2008, when they were bought out by the Abu Dhabi United Group.

‌



Man Utd turned me down after two interviews but I still want to work in England READ MORE :

Their spending started immediately, as they looked to breathe a new lease of life into the Cityzens, while Ferguson playfully laughed off the club as United's "noisy neighbours," given his hold on Greater Manchester. City proved that moniker null and void when they ran out 6-1 winners in enemy territory on October 23, 2011, however.

Already a goal down thanks to Mario Balotelli's first-half opener, Jonny Evans handed City a numerical advantage just two minutes after the break. The Northern Irishman brought down Balotelli on the edge of his own area as the last man, with Mark Clattenburg reaching into his top pocket and brandishing a red card in his direction for denying a goalscoring opportunity.

Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



The proverbial floodgates then opened. Balotelli bagged his brace with 30 minutes remaining, with Sergio Aguero finding the back of the net just nine minutes later.

If the game wasn't already out of reach by the time Darren Fletcher pulled one back to make it 3-1 with less than two minutes left to play, Edin Dzeko found two of his own either side of stoppage time, with David Silva also making the scoresheet at the death.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Reflecting on the disturbing showing at full-time, Ferguson admitted that it was his worst day at the office, while also digging out Ferdinand and Evra for their part in a shambolic defence. He said: "It was a bad day, there is no doubt about that; it was my worst ever day.

‌



"Jonny Evans's sending off was a killer for us. With 10 men, we kept attacking - it was crazy football and ended up being an embarrassment.

"We should have just said, 'We've had our day.' I believe you shouldn't bring down a man on the edge of the box.

‌



View 2 Images Sir Alex Ferguson was unhappy with Rio Ferdinand and Patrice Evra (Image: Getty Images)

"Evans is young, but he should let Balotelli go through and see what he can do. I thought with the experience we've got - Rio Ferdinand, Patrice Evra - they would have defended more, but we just kept attacking.

Article continues below

"Sometimes there has to be common sense about it. It was a bad day. I can't believe the scoreline. Even as a player, I don't think I ever lost 6-1. That's a challenge for me too."

City went on to win the Premier League title that season on goal difference, thanks to Aguero's iconic strike to secure a 3-2 win over QPR in their last match of 2011/12 - sparking a new era of dominance in Greater Manchester, albeit at the Etihad Stadium.

Sports.title: How Arsenal star Ben White went from reviled England exile to match-winner under Thomas Tuchel
Sports.content:
How Arsenal star Ben White went from reviled England exile to match-winner under Thomas Tuchel

Ben White was one of England's heroes in their 3-2 win over world champions Spain, having revived his international career under Thomas Tuchel following a mysterious issue under Gareth Southgate

View 4 Images Ben White has completely turned around his fortunes with England (Image: Chris Brunskill/Getty Images)

There were many individual winners on Sunday night in Madrid - James Trafford and Lewis Hall chief among them - but Ben White's unique story makes his performance in England's remarkable victory stand out above the rest.

‌



‌



Picked to start at right-back by Thomas Tuchel, White was outstanding, providing two telling moments in the second half. First in the 57th minute, he gathered Jude Bellingham's pass and slotted underneath Unai Simon to make it 3-0. Then, with the game on the line in the 84th minute, he made a fantastic recovery tackle to deny Nico Williams a sight of goal.

‌



Both moments were crucial, with his goal turning out to be the difference between the two sides as England celebrated one of their best performances of the Tuchel era.

‌



Right-back has traditionally been viewed as a position of strength for England, who can call upon the likes of Reece James and Trent Alexander-Arnold. Yet after missing the World Cup through injury, White has re-emerged onto the international scene with a point to prove.

In the cauldron of the Metropolitano Stadium, he proved it. The Arsenal defender's words post-match hinted at something deeper than happiness at a job well done. "Just proud to be a part of it," he told ITV. "Glad to be here, for sure."

Black Friday special! Click here to sign up to Mirror+ for just £1 a month!

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

'No reason to doubt his commitment'

White's match-winning performance in Madrid came just days after he was booed onto the pitch at Wembley while replacing Alexander-Arnold in the win over Croatia. It seems that the 29-year-old's commitment to the national team is still not clear in the minds of many match-going fans after he quit the squad during the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

‌



"I hope it doesn’t happen again. He’s a player of us. Since I’m in charge, he’s desperate to come and to be with the group,” Tuchel said when asked about the boos after the Croatia game.

“Since I’m in charge, I can only judge him on what I see and what I experience, and he’s on the highest level. He can really help us to win football matches, and like I said, he’s part of our group, and we protect our group, and I’m protective of our group, he deserves to be with us.”

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

View 4 Images Ben White scored his second goal in eight caps for England (Image: Sebastian Frej/Getty Images)

‌



Tuchel then added: “He’s a high-quality player, and I honestly don’t even know what happened (when he left the 2022 World Cup squad) and what were the deep reasons and the situation that he left camp. So, like I said, until I’m in charge, there is no reason to doubt his commitment or his passion."

That was the message from Declan Rice when he spoke before the Spain match. “Ben has moved on from what's happened in the past, he's totally focused on playing for England. When he's been fit and available he's constantly put himself forward to play for England," White's Arsenal teammate said.

‌



“He loves being here, it's not like he doesn't like being here, he loves playing for England, loves being around the lads."

Shadow of Qatar

There is no question over whether White is good enough to merit a place in England's squad. The question - for some at least - is whether somebody who ruled himself out of contention in the past is worthy of reconciliation now.

‌



The issue is the mysterious nature of his withdrawal back in 2022. England said it was for personal reasons, but reports later emerged of a falling out between the Arsenal defender and Gareth Southgate's assistant manager - and Michael Carrick's recent assistant at Manchester United - Steve Holland on the training pitch in Qatar.

White refused to be considered for selection while Southgate was still in charge and has only been welcomed back into the fold since Tuchel took over. The real reason behind his international exile isn't about to be made public.

‌



View 4 Images Ben White withdrew from England contention in 2022

"Obviously people don't know the full story, because I [have] never said anything and I won't put anyone under the bus or share any of that," White told BBC Radio 5 Live last week. "I think that is probably the best way."

‌



Rice appears to be frustrated by the perception surrounding his team-mate. "It's so long ago now, it's nearly five years and it doesn't need to keep getting brought up," he said. "We need to look forward to the future and what Ben White is going to do in an England shirt, that's the most important thing.

“It's a pointless conversation, Ben has moved on, no-one talks about it around the dinner table, no-one speaks about it in the pool, we just play football and do what we need to do.”

‌



Letting football do the talking

View 4 Images Thomas Tuchel has brought Ben White back into the England fold (Image: Jacques Feeney/Offside via Getty Images)

It was a knee injury which prevented White from going to the World Cup in the summer. He's come back firing this season for Arsenal, providing three assists in seven Premier League appearances, and has a great chance of becoming Tuchel's first-choice right-back.

‌



With Chelsea's James struggling with injuries and Alexander-Arnold not getting regular game time under Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, Tuchel will value White's performances for title-chasing Arsenal.

White's athletic ability makes him a threat on the overlap - as he showed in scoring on Sunday - but it also makes him a perfect match for England's man-to-man press, while his aggressiveness is also a valuable characteristic.

Article continues below

The former Brighton and Leeds famously said he doesn't watch much football in his own time. He is clearly not fond of speaking to the media. But if he lets his football do the talking, then his international career will have plenty more years left to run.

Sports.title: 'I didn't know' - Price's controversial 145 checkout at Grand Slam explained
Sports.content:
Gerwyn Price produced a controversial 145 checkout en route to a routine Grand Slam of Darts victory over Sebastian Bialecki on Monday night in Wolverhampton.

Price, the three-time champion in Wolverhampton, came through 5-2 against Poland's Bialecki to book his place in the knockout stage.

However, there was controversy during the final Group E match as Price hit a 145 finish when he had 135 remaining in the fourth leg of the match.

What happened?

Image: Price defeated Bialecki to reach the last 16 in Wolverhampton

'The Iceman' needed 135 to hold his throw, and he thought he had taken it out.

After hitting T19 he asked referee Charlie Corstophine what he had left and was told 88.

However, he actually needed 78.

With 88 in mind, Price incorrectly hit T16 and D20 to finish off the leg and was given the hold.

Of course, Price believed he had gone the correct route for what he needed and went on to set up a last 16 date with Ryan Searle.

What did Price say?

"I didn't know until I just walked in [to the press conference]," said Price. "I hit the first treble and I asked what I'd got left and he said 88.

"So I went treble 16 double top and he said game shot."

The Welshman admitted he was glad he didn't know or it would've weighed on his mind.

He added: "I know. I swear to God, I didn't even know until I came back here. I'm glad I didn't know because it probably would have played on my mind."

What does the PDC rulebook say?

6.4.6 Errors in arithmetic shall stand as detailed on the scoreboard unless corrected prior to the next throw of the player whose score is in error. Any error in the score can be corrected by the Referee at any time until Game Shot is called in

that leg.

6.4.7 If the incorrect score resulted in a leg win the result will stand unless corrected prior to the start of the next leg.

Price on new format

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Price thrashed Peter Wright 16-8 to triumph at the Grand Slam of Darts in 2021

Both players went into the contest with one win each after beating Joe Hunt, which made it a straight shoot-out with only the group winners reaching the knockout stage this year.

Price had opened his week with a 5-3 win over Hunt on Saturday, racing into a 4-0 lead before Hunt won three legs in a row. Bialecki needed a deciding leg to beat Hunt 5-4 on Sunday.

The new format has already seen Ross Smith, Jonny Clayton and Luke Woodhouse suffer shock exits and Price said: "I prefer the old one [format], obviously. I've had some good memories here. You can slip up once, but in this one you can't.

"As you can see, a couple of good boys have gone, and they probably thought they'd have a second chance. But once you lose a game, that's it; you're gone."

Sports.title: British doubles No 1 criticises ATP bosses at trophy presentation absence
Sports.content:
British doubles No 1 Henry Patten has taken a swipe at ATP bosses for their absence from a trophy presentation in Turin on Monday.

Upon receiving the year-end doubles No 1 trophy from chief tour officer Andre Silva, alongside his Finnish partner Harri Heliovaara, Patten called out the ATP chairman Andrea Gaudenzi and CEO Eno Polo.

"For us, it's a really big deal. It's a real shame that the ATP chairman and CEO don't think the same." Patten said.

"It would have been nice to have them on court with us today, but here we are by ourselves."

Sky Sports News has contacted the ATP Tour for comment.

Patten and Heliovaara enjoyed a sensational season, winning Wimbledon for the second time in their careers and lifting trophies in Adelaide, Doha, Dubai, and Madrid.

The duo have repeatedly criticised the ATP's approach to doubles, including their proposals that would include smaller draws and reduce prize money for the 2028 season.

Patten and Dutch player Sem Verbeek spearheaded an open letter, signed by over a hundred other players - including former champions Bob and Mike Bryan - calling for the reform project to be scrapped.

Speaking to Sky Sports Tennis, Tim Henman said: "He [Patten] made his thoughts pretty clear about the lack of representation from the chair and the CEO on the tour.

"There is the conversation around massive reform in the doubles world, potentially cutting the doubles draw in half and that would save prize money that could go into the singles, so those doubles players are feeling like their jobs are in jeopardy.

"This is a great platform as the doubles is getting incredible support."

What the open letter opposes

Halving draw sizes. ATP Masters 1000 doubles draws would be cut in half to 16 teams, while smaller ATP 500 and 250 tournaments would drop to just eight teams



Cutting prize money. The share of tournament prize money allocated to doubles would drop from 20% to 10%, shifting roughly $20 million (£15 million) away from doubles specialists to fund early-round singles payouts



Heliovaara also addressed the crowd, thanking Patten and their team, saying: "I'm going to say that Henry is the best partner in the world for doubles. I've been lucky enough to play with him for two and a half years.

"We shared a lot of wins, a lot of losses, but most of all, a lot of time everywhere in the world, really. On the court, off court, it's been a very nice, amazing trip together. But it's not just the two of us, I think it's also our team there in the box, in the spotlight today.

"I would like that we also give a big hand to every one of them. It's a lot of sacrifices from us, from the team, and obviously our families at home. Everybody who has helped us to achieve something like this. And to have a trophy like that at home, we will be very proud for a very long time."

Patten and Heliovaara will now turn their attention to the task at hand in Turin, where they are 1-0 in round-robin play. They defeated Orlando Luz and Rafael Matos in a match tie-break on Sunday.

Sports.title: Record-breaker Robertson speaks out after Scotland's bad loss to Switzerland
Sports.content:
Andy Robertson created Scotland history then delievered a scathing assessment of their Nations League collapse against Switzerland.

On the night he became the men's record appearance holder with 103 caps, Sebastien Pocognoli came under pressure with a bruising 4-0 defeat in St Gallen.

"That cannot happen in international football," he told BBC Scotland after the match.

Image: stats

"I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it. These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden, who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."

The Scots were comfortable against the much-changed Group B1 winners until the 22nd minute when midfielder Lewis Ferguson put through his own goal.

Image: Lewis Ferguson conceded an own goal after a positive Scotland start

The unforced error deflated the visitors, who lost wing-back Aaron Hickey to injury before the break, and there was more damage in the 47th minute when Samuel Ballet's drive was touched in by Winsley Boteli before Alvyn Sanches hammered in a third just four minutes later, with substitute Zeki Amdouni adding a late fourth.

The Scots finished third in the group behind Switzerland and Slovenia, with seven points from 18, missing out on a promotion play-off spot next year and a more favourable seeding for the European Championship qualifying draw next month.

The Belgian boss' first campaign as Steve Clarke's successor has been underwhelming to say the least with just two wins - both against bottom side North Macedonia - from six fixtures and Pocognoli now finds himself under the spotlight just months into his tenure.

The key moments from Berit Sitterstadion

2: SAVE! A comfortable save for Angus Gunn but Isaac Schmidt is given too much time to get a shot away. An early warning.

17: CHANCE! John McGinn hooks the ball over the bar as Scotland continue to pile on the pressure.

22: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Disaster for Scotland as Lewis Ferguson sticks out his leg and sends the ball into his own net.

24: CLOSE! Almost an equaliser from Aaron Hickey. He gets his head to Andy Robertson's cross, but it's just past the post.

36: INJURY! Hickey pulls up holding his hamstring and his night is over.

42: CHANCE! Nathan Patterson sends the ball in to McGinn but he heads straight at the goalkeeper. An opportunity missed.

44: CHANCE! That should be a second for Switzerland! Adrian Bajrami gets on the end of the cross but somehow heads the ball well off target.

47: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Samuel Ballet plays a one-two with Remo Freuler, and Winsley Boteli gets the last touch to put the Swiss two up.

51: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Alvyn Sanches gets on the end of a ball from Boteli and fires across Gunn and into the net.

66: SAVE! Gunn pulls off a save to deny Ballet a fourth for the hosts and Luke Graham is there to block Zeki Amdouni's follow-up effort.

72: OVER! Scott McTominay gets on the end of Kieran Tierney's cross and somehow blasts it over the bar.

85: SUB! Kristi Montgomery replaces Ferguson as he makes his Scotland debut.

89: GOAL SWITZERLAND! Amdouni's shot from the edge of the box takes a deflection off Graham as it goes past Gunn.

What now for Pocognoli?

Image: It has been a tough start for Sebastien Pocognoli

Almost a year on from the elation of Scotland beating Denmark to reach the World Cup, it now looks like a struggle to reach Euro 2028.

Scotland will be in Pot 3 when the draw is made next month, and there is a lot of improvement needed before the qualifying campaign then kicks off in March.

In his first six games as Steve Clarke's successor, Sebastien Pocognoli has won just two. Both against North Macedonia.

They had a decent first 20 minutes in St Gallen, but this was not Switzerland's best team.

Murat Yakin was without Granit Xhaka, Dan Ndoye, Manuel Akanji and Johan Manzambi and they still made it look easy against the Scots who managed just one shot on target. A tame one.

How much time should the new Scotland head coach bet given? Following the man who led the nation to three major tournaments was always going to be a hard act to follow, but the team appears to have regressed.

Pocognoli positive about Scotland's future

Image: Sebastien Pocognoli has two wins from his first six matches as Scotland boss

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli speaking to BBC Scotland:

"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game, if I'm really honest and objective.

"I think we had some very good moments in the game, we started the game like we wanted, aggressive away from home.

"I think if we were in confidence, we would not produce the moments we produce in the game.

"I think we create good moments on the ball, on pure bravery decisions to play forward through the lines or the pressure.

"We create chances also for pressing, sometimes we should have to manage better the transition from pressing, but it is all the things we want to see.

"So the next step is to have the quality to just finish this action, and the more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things.

"We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."

Robertson: 'That can't happen, we've got to step up'

Image: Andy Robertson is demanding a reaction from Scotland

Scotland captain Andy Robertson speaking to BBC Scotland:

"First half we were in the game but lost a stupid goal. But I thought we had chances and should have made it one each at half-time.

"We talked about it at half-time, we told ourselves to keep going and the time you get to 50 minutes, you're 3-0 down? That cannot happen in international football.

"That's what happened tonight. We were playing against a good team. But while we were in the game in the first half, you have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down, it's a tough place to come and that. A really tough night for us."

Sports.title: Rice: More to come from Arsenal's £105m 'bargain'
Sports.content:
Arsenal's Kroenke family owners tend not to get involved in transfer dealings but when it came to Declan Rice, and the prospect of spending £100m on a player for the first time, they needed to be sure that it was a sensible investment.

So, in the conference room at Arsenal's training ground, co-chair Josh Kroenke asked to be walked through the deal by Mikel Arteta, former sporting director Edu, then executive vice-chair Tim Lewis and now chief executive officer Richard Garlick.

"My eyebrows raised because I didn't know if we were in that phase just yet to go after a player like that," Kroenke recalled. He wanted to know what he would bring and how Arteta would use him. He wanted reassurance that he could hit the ground running.

Kroenke left the meeting in no doubt about the deal, either financially or in footballing terms. A club-record approach to West Ham was greenlit and Rice has of course gone on to prove an inspired addition, his new deal reflecting his importance.

"Declan Rice, we got him half price," is the refrain among Arsenal supporters. A player instrumental in their Premier League title success, who insisted "it's not done" then did more than anyone to drive them over the line, is now tied down for his peak years.

He has brought Arsenal even more than the club anticipated, arriving as a No 6 before being unshackled as a rampaging No 8, then reverting to a deeper role this season.

Image: Declan Rice is playing deeper and on the right side of a midfield pivot this season having played as a left-sided No 8 two seasons ago

He scores, creates and dominates physically. His deadly set-piece delivery is another string to his bow.

"He is becoming a total player," said Arteta, who has even called on him at right-back. Of course, Rice filled in admirably in that role. "A total player has to be able to do as many things as possible and he has the capacity to do that," added Arteta.

Image: Declan Rice has played in different positions for Arsenal

Rice's adaptability and willingness to evolve his game have been themes of his time at Arsenal and the same traits were apparent to those who worked with him at West Ham, where he made an instant impression on his former team-mate Jack Wilshere.

"I love Declan, first of all a person," Wilshere tells Sky Sports. "I could see that straight away when I went in. He was very humble, his eyes were open, he wanted to learn, he would ask the right questions, and he just went from strength to strength.

He is definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world

"His footballing ability speaks for itself, but I wouldn't say he's someone who it came naturally to. He had to work on his right foot, on his left foot. But physically, he was always a beast and that would help him get out of certain situations."

Wilshere also noted the leadership qualities that have come to the fore at Arsenal. "Even when I went there and he was 19 or 20 and finding his way in the team, he had natural leadership and a natural aura about him that you could see," he says.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Declan Rice laugh at Chelsea fans after setting up a goal for Arsenal

"He has a good understanding as well. When you look at players making big moves now, for me, one of the most important things around it is timing. I think Dec got his timing right.

"He spent a good few years at West Ham becoming a hero, becoming an important member of that team, trying to get that team up the table to finish high as possible. He won a trophy with them, and then he decided to go and compete for bigger things."

Wilshere and Rice crossed paths again following his move to Arsenal, where Wilshere, now head coach of Luton Town, was working as an academy coach and shadowing his old team-mate Arteta.

"I know how important he was to Mikel at that time when Mikel brought him in, and how he was going to be that shining light of the team who would always be present," he says.

"That's another thing that's really impressive about him: his robustness. He plays every single game. He dominates every single game physically."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Declan Rice sing Ice Ice Baby at Arsenal's trophy parade

Rice's record bears it out. Last season was his most demanding yet as he made 55 appearances in all competitions for Arsenal, many of them while managing hamstring nerve pain, before making a further eight for England at the World Cup during the summer.

He is an incredible athlete who continues to show remarkable resistance to injury. He has only missed five out of 119 Premier League games since his arrival at Arsenal. Only four outfield players have played more minutes in the competition in that timeframe.

His reliability is invaluable to Arteta and Rice continues to find ways to improve. Having moved back to the base of midfield this term, switching to the right side of the pivot to accommodate Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes, he has become notably more incisive with his passes.

According to Opta, Rice ranks second among Premier League players - and top among midfielders - for line-breaking passes this season, behind only Jan Paul van Hecke. He also ranks second only to Martin Odegaard for line-breaking passes in the final third.

Image: Declan Rice is second in the line-breaking passes category

He is sometimes criticised for sideways passing but he is averaging nearly twice as many line-breaking passes than last season, showing clear development in yet another area of his game.

The hope for Arsenal is that Rice will continue to unlock more levels after committing his future to the club. And certainly, that is the expectation from those who know him.

"I actually think there's more to come from Dec," adds Wilshere. "I've said it for a few years now. To be fair, he has started to add goals, but I still think he can add more with his physical ability, with his ability to strike the ball off his left foot, right foot.

"But he's already a top player and definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world."

A sensible investment indeed.

Sports.title: Rice verbally agrees new Arsenal contract
Sports.content:
Declan Rice has verbally agreed terms on a new long-term contract at Arsenal, Sky Sports News can reveal.

Sky Sports News has been told his new deal will bring him in line with Bukayo Saka, who is the highest-paid player at the Emirates.

Rice and his representatives have been in negotiations for several months, with the club keen to tie down one of their most important players, even though he still has 18 months left on his existing contract, with a further year's option in the club's favour.

Rice was named Arsenal's Player of the Year last season when they won the Premier League title and this new deal will take him into his early 30s.

The 27-year-old joined Arsenal from West Ham for a club record £105m in 2023. He's gone on to be a key member of Mikel Arteta's leadership group, and someone who the Spanish coach has built his team around.

Image: Declan Rice has verbally agreed a new Arsenal contract

Speaking on Saturday ahead of England's final Nations League group game in Spain, Rice confirmed that he was close to an agreement.

"I'm a player that always sets myself targets, always pushes for more. I've always been stable in the clubs I'm at. The new contract is hopefully on the horizon soon.

"I'm extremely lucky I'm at a club like Arsenal where the manager shows me so much trust. I've so many team-mates who put so much energy and effort into me. I'm extremely lucky that I don't have to worry about that stuff. It makes playing football a lot easier."

Analysis: Best in the league? Rice is the complete midfielder

Sky Sports' Sam Blitz:

Arsenal are not just tying down Declan Rice - one of their most important players - to a bumper new deal, they are tying down arguably the Premier League's best player into his remaining peak years.

And this season is the best version we've ever seen from Rice.

The England midfielder has started the campaign on fire and tops the Premier League assist charts at the moment with five - all of them from open play.

But this creative spark from Rice has come despite the Arsenal man playing a deeper role in Mikel Arteta's set-up. A sitting midfielder, yes - but still as attacking as ever.

No midfielder in the Premier League has made more final third passes or passes through the lines than Rice this season.

His number of final third entries has nearly doubled compared to two seasons ago. And his recent goal for Arsenal against Bayern Munich in the Champions League summed up how he is influencing the top end of the pitch a lot more.

That goal cancelled out Harry Kane's strike for Bayern. Rice is Arsenal's superstar equivalent.

Rice can do everything in midfield for Arsenal. He can hurt teams by running through them, or passing through the lines. He can score, as well as create. He can damage from open play, or from his deadly delivery from corners and free-kicks. He is the complete midfielder.

Odegaard yet to begin new Arsenal contract talks

Image: Martin Odegaard is yet to agree a new contract

Meanwhile, another huge figure in the Arsenal starting XI - captain Martin Odegaard - has said he has not yet begun negotiations over a new contract, even though his current deal expires at the same time as Rice's.

Speaking while on international duty with Norway, the Arsenal captain said: "I'm happy and hope I can be there for a long time to come, but so far we haven't started on that.

"There is no stress about it. I am where I am, and I am super happy with it. Things are going well, and it is not something I am stressed about. As I said, I want to be there for a long time to come. I am enjoying myself a lot."

Sports.title: WTA chair on Pegula-Andreeva hot mic incident: It's not bad for viewership
Sports.content:
WTA chief Valerie Camillo says private comments made by Jessica Pegula about Mirra Andreeva being overheard on a YouTube livestream is "not bad for viewership".

Camillo personally apologised to Pegula, describing the broadcast of on-court conversations during a practice session at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells as "regrettable and unacceptable".

The Tour, who operated the livestream, had intended for the microphones to capture ambient sounds from the court but failed to inform participants.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tim Henman and Jamie Murray discuss who they think is the best female tennis player this year

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player 'This spirit, this fighting mindset' - Andreeva told Sky Sports she was determined to win WTA Finals

A broadcast showed the American in conversation with her coach Mark Knowles, calling the 19-year-old a "diva" and saying she has lost respect for Andreeva's coach Conchita Martinez for not calling out her behaviour.

"Someone actually asked me if we planned it or did it on purpose to draw attention to the event," Camillo told Sky Sports' lead tennis commentator, Jonathan Overend.

"I wish that we were so crafty and strategic but we can't put ourselves in any situation where we put our athletes at risk. Our number one objective as a member services organisation for our players is to protect our players.

"What Jess said is competitive banter. I don't think there was anything particularly salacious in it. But having mics lying around that aren't being properly managed is not how the WTA expects to execute and operate.

"It created a viral moment. It created a lot of dialogue. But that's not intentional and not something you should expect to see us doing in the future.

"I've had this conversation here that I come from a variety of different sports. Before joining the WTA, I exclusively worked in male sports. I worked at the NBA and majorly baseball and it's quite common for there to be competitive banter that is brought into the forefront.

"It's up to the athletes for what they feel comfortable with and what they don't. But a little drama isn't bad for ticket sales.

"It's not bad for viewership. It's not bad for commentary. That's just a reality."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the semi-final match between Andreeva and Pegula at the WTA Finals

Andreeva laughed off the hot mic moment and went on to defeat Pegula 6-3 6-4 on Saturday, in a match that gained an extra layer of intrigue to reach the WTA Finals title match.

She concluded a stunning week with a second victory over Elina Svitolina to win the season-ending tournament.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the WTA Finals title match between Andreeva and Elina Svitolina.

WTA finances and maximising financial opportunity

Image: Valerie Camillo aims to find extra revenue streams for the WTA

The WTA was forced to replace the venue for the season-ending event from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in July, which represented a major financial setback for the governing body.

The deal with the Saudi Tennis Federation (STF) included record prize money over a three-year period, but the ongoing tension between Iran and the United States made planning for the Finals more challenging, eventually forcing the tournament to move to Indian Wells in California.

The body is projecting operating losses of £17.3m ($23m) for 2026 and expects to hold roughly £11.3m ($15m) in cash by the end of the year, according to The Telegraph. Camillo remains confident of finding extra revenue streams through in-house media rights and sponsorship growth to create financial stability.

"Our ambition for the WTA Finals is equal prize money [with the men's tour]. That's our ambition, just as we expected of the Grand Slams. All of our combined 1000 events will have equal prize money in 2027," she said.

"We've been building fandom. We've been operating globally. We've been creating superstar athletes through our platform for many, many decades, and so the athletes have the opportunity not to just earn on the court, but also to control their own brands and monetise that off the court.

"WTA intends to remain in its position as number one in the hearts and minds of fans, in the mindset and investment of our sponsors, and we want to be building an even greater platform on which our great athletes can compete, not only one that they can enjoy from the ferocity of the crowd, but also one that enables them to maximise their financial opportunity to the best of our ability."

WTA intends to have 'better controls' of revenue streams

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player British tennis player Jodie Burrage called on the WTA to take further action after she was subject to death threats and social media abuse following her defeat in the Chennai Open

One of the WTA revenue streams comes from selling data, match data, court feeds to data companies with the betting industry a large part of that.

British tennis star Jodie Burrage called on social media platforms to hold people accountable for sending death threats and abuse.

Burrage, who was playing her first WTA Tour match since Wimbledon last summer, received death threats and online abuse following a first-round defeat at a tournament in India.

The 27-year-old shared a raft of abusive messages sent to her Instagram account. Alongside the video, Burrage wrote: "Nice welcome back to the tour. I remember why I left."

Camillo said: "The complexity of official data to these partners is sort of an industry inside thing. But the reality is that through having official partnerships, you actually can have more integrity and controls.

"If you don't have relationships with these variety of platforms, you can turn into a little bit of the wild, wild west. It's not to say that there isn't a financial element to these relationships. That would be disingenuous. Of course there is. But it does also enable us to have a partnership that leads to better controls."

Sports.title: Old foes Taylor and Van Barneveld to reunite for Ally Pally charity pro-celeb
Sports.content:
Phil Taylor and Raymond van Barneveld will renew their iconic rivalry as non-playing captains at a special pro-celeb event at Alexandra Palace next month.

Two of darts' greatest names will lead teams featuring world champions and celebrity guests on Thursday December 10, with £5 from every ticket sold donated to Prostate Cancer UK.

Taylor and Van Barneveld famously contested the 2007 final at the Circus Tavern in Purfleet, one of the sport's most memorable matches.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at some of the best checkouts from World Championship Finals from 1995 to 2007

Almost 20 years on, they will bring that competitive spirit to the captaincy as their teams battle for the Rivals Reunited trophy.

The evening will serve as a test event ahead of the World's move into Alexandra Palace's larger Great Hall, giving fans an early opportunity to experience the new setting before the venue hosts the tournament for the 20th time.

Phil Taylor said: "Raymond and I have had some great battles over the years, and the competitive instinct never goes away. It should be a good laugh, but I'll still be making sure my team know we're there to win!"

Raymond van Barneveld added: "Phil says it's a bit of fun, but I know what he's like - he'll want to win just as much as I do! It will be great to be back at Ally Pally together, and hopefully my team can give the fans plenty to cheer about."

The action gets under way at 7pm.

Two-time world champion Adrian Lewis, radio presenter Jordan North and social media personality Woody, will feature for Team Taylor.

Team Barney will include three-time world champion John Part, radio presenter Chris Stark and comedian Lloyd Griffith.

Sky Sports remains the home of darts with the Grand Slam of Darts (November 14-22) and World Darts Championship (December 11-January 3) all live. Stream darts and more through NOW with no contract.

Sports.title: Tuchel and England must learn lessons of history, Seville and Southgateism | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
I may have the body of a weak and feeble German, but I have the heart and stomach of a manager of England. And I think it foul scorn that Spain should dare to invade the borders of my realm. Or, for that matter, any one of 24 qualified teams for Euro 2028, because at the end of the day there are no easy games at this level, I’ve always said that.

The words, there, of Thomas Tuchel, England’s Faerie King, speaking to TalkSport shortly after the glorious 3-2 defeat of the Spanish possession armada at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

OK, Tuchel didn’t technically say any of this. He was instead wry and spiky. He made a joke about people moaning about his team on the radio, which just goes to show he’s a good lad and one of us (disclaimer: when he wins). But this is England. And beating Spain can do some strange things to you.

Not just because Spain are the defining team of the past 20 years, six-time international trophy winners and current world and European champions. But because Spanish football culture is the global template for tone, texture and tactics, the ultimate source of the Football Association’s slightly dog‑eared footballing blueprint.

Beating Spain is like beating your super-smart but slightly controlling younger brother. It’s getting one over on that other way of playing, punitive high technique, death by possession, patience over urgency. Even better, Tuchel’s team did so in Madrid with a performance based around the hard‑running physicality that English football sees as part of its deep sporting soul.

As such it will be tempting to see this Nations League victory as a springboard, a Rubicon crossed, a shattering of the Iberian ceiling. With some justification; England have the talent to win a home European Championship two years from now. But it feels just a little bit easier to visualise now.

There was something new in seeing Spain not just outmuscled but outplayed in the first half, reduced to whinging about fouls, unable to take the ball away. Not only because England’s pressing was smart and relentless but because of the players’ ability to keep possession in tight spaces.

It is also true that a quick glance back at recent history tells us exactly how much of a golden dawn a win such as this can be. Which is: zero, zilch, nothing. No golden dawn at all.

In reality there are no Rubicon moments, no decisive levellings-up, only staging posts and warning signs, even in victory. This is the most important point about a night such as this. It won’t tell you where you’ll end up. But it may tell you how to keep heading the right way, if you’re ready to learn from recent history.

As it happens, recent history is in the room with us right now, clearing its throat, rattling its chains, trying to shift the Ouija-board dial. Here is an interesting fact. Spain have only twice conceded three goals at home in a competitive men’s international. The second time was on Sunday night, when England won 3-2 in Madrid after going 3-0 up. And the first time was 15 October 2018 when England beat Spain 3-2 in Seville after going 3-0 up.

View image in fullscreen Gareth Southgate embraces Marcus Rashford after the win against Spain in 2018. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/The FA/Shutterstock

The parallels between those games are numerically improbable. At the time of win No 1 Gareth Southgate had been in permanent charge for 684 days and one narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was his 29th game. At the time of win No 2 Tuchel had been in charge for 683 days and another narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was Tuchel’s 28th game.

That Southgate moment was greeted with understandable optimism. You know the kind of language used because it’s out here now, too. New dawns. Statement victories. Rise of a Golden Generation. Not just a benchmark but a springboard as well, an astonishing feat of carpentry if true.

So was it that? Answer: no. In fact Seville 2018 was arguably the moment Southgate-ism reached a stylistic ceiling. England played a fast-paced game of counterattack that night. The team was an attacking mix, a midfield of Winks‑Barkley‑Dier, with Sterling‑Kane‑Rashford in front. England scored 27 goals in six games the following autumn, starting most with a back four and a double pivot, ending 2019 with a 6-0, a 7-0 and a 4-0. This felt like something new.

The Covid break pretty much killed that mini-era. Or rather, it was allowed to kill it, because coaches have choices too. England went 42 weeks without a game. By November 2020 they were losing 2-0 in Belgium with a back five and a deep defensive midfield.

The Euros had already been postponed for a year. In the summer of 2021 England started the final against Italy with another back five plus Declan Rice and Kalvin Phillips, and congealed into a kind of footballing rice pudding as the game reached its crisis point.

Here is an unprovable counterfactual. If football had rolled on, if England had not had an empty year to look down and get scared, they might have retained enough momentum to go harder against Italy in that final and win it.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But then, the Southgate era was gruelling for many of those players. There is a separate study to be made of the way so many key early Garethistas disappeared or entered a slow decline. That October 2018 team turned out to be a pop‑up thing of shifting parts, evidence of the complex, zigzagging nature of team building.

The would-be golden generation included Ben Chilwell, Eric Dier, Joe Gomez, Ross Barkley, Harry Winks and Marcus Rashford. Nathaniel Chalobah made his only appearance as a sub in added time, and still has the second-shortest England career, after Martin Kelly.

Rather than a golden dawn of ultimate glory, England entered a more talent-appropriate era of losing late-stage games against good opponents. If anything the Spain victory added to the ambient pressure around those tournaments, helping to create the sense it is now unthinkable for England to lose, because we have an image of them as winners, and English winning is the best winning, the only real winning.

The lesson remains the same now, the need to avoid both portents of doom and the lure of a golden new hyper-future. In this sense Tuchel is encouragingly restless both in defeat and victory. Even his new-season touchline look – tailored, sombre, all black – has an agreeably priestly, hair‑shirt energy; less Elizabeth I, author of the introductory quote above, more Martin Luther on his way to a business meeting in an out‑of‑town spa hotel.

View image in fullscreen England’s team of today contains talent from Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich. Photograph: Manuel Queimadelos/Quality Sport Images/Getty Images

Tuchel’s best quality is his obsession with analysis and objectivity. On Sunday night he was already talking about the need to improve. This can be an obstacle at times (see: process-based Argentina substitutes). But it is also a rejection of complacency, ornament, frippery. This England are better than their 2018 equivalent. That team had seven players from Leicester and Arsenal. This one has key parts from Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich, including the current Ballon d’Or winner and a £300m midfield tripod.

The balance of the attack in Madrid was good, not just the most seductively talented players but the best parts for the plan. Anthony Gordon is an interesting figure in this respect, an intelligent, culturally adaptable, tactically aware footballer, whose game is nonetheless basically running up and down. Elite teams seem to have a place for this role now. Flank-scurry energy node. Right-sided gallop unit. Lewis Hall was also very good again. Any team looks better with a genuine left‑footed full-back, like hanging a picture straight on the wall.

Mainly what Tuchel did in Spain was to select a team with no indulgences, full commitment to a tailored gameplan, no celebrity passengers. And that style is not fixed. See also: Trent Alexander-Arnold against Croatia, and some excellent passes against a deep block even on a middling night. Stick that behind your ear as well, Thomas.

Teams are hugely complex things. Tuchel had to get to know his players. The idea you can simply bolt on an elite manager and expect instant progress was always a bit silly. No dips or lulls, no adaptation. This might work if you come from the same cultural system. But plonking on a brain from someone else’s body is still a way of looking for shortcuts, the managerial equivalent of sticking it in the mixer and hoping for the best. There you go. Give us a final fix on 75 years of inherited domestic culture.

Tuchel is now a little further along with all this. He even did the backs-to-the-wall thing better, waiting to the last moment to press the defensive emergency button, the sight of Dan Burn rumbling out a signal to both teams that this really is the end of the night, like turning on all the lights and getting the DJ to play Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Quick Guide Dowman becomes England U21s' youngest scorer Show Max Dowman (pictured) became England Under-21s’ youngest-ever goalscorer by grabbing the late winner in a 3-2 friendly victory over France at Ashton Gate. Lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals. The Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance. Carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association Photograph: Michael Steele/The FA Collection Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Sunday night was a wonderful game. It was England’s most complete performance under Tuchel. But the lesson hasn’t changed. Trust the process, not the results. Keep doing the ruthless, adaptive things that got you there. England will at some point have to beat the best. And the Nations League is a very useful tool. Win it next summer and taking that final step starts to look a whole lot less of an Arthurian fever dream.

Sports.title: Nations League: Wirtz doubles up as Germany rout Netherlands to top group
Sports.content:
Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany delivered a 5-0 rout of the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday, reaching the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners.

Brajan Gruda contributed a goal and two assists, with Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck also on the scoresheet as the hosts delivered their most impressive display so far under Jürgen Klopp’s leadership.

It was Germany’s biggest win over their neighbours since a 7-0 victory in 1959, and the Netherlands’ first defeat since Xavi Hernández took over as coach in August. The Dutch have still advanced to the last eight by finishing second, with Germany’s fifth goal taking Klopp’s side into top spot.

The visitors had the first good chance when Jurriën Timber found Crysencio Summerville unmarked on the penalty spot, but the winger lost his footing before getting a shot away. Germany then went close as the Berlin native Scherhant hit a post after connecting with a cross from his Freiburg teammate Philipp Treu.

Nine minutes later, Scherhant had another chance from the same spot and this time curled a lovely effort across the face of goal and inside the far post. Germany pushed for more goals after the break, and Wirtz delivered with a superb solo effort on the hour, lifting a shot in off the left post from the edge of the penalty area.

Schlotterbeck headed in from Gruda’s free-kick with 65 minutes gone, and the RB Leipzig winger laid on another goal six minutes later when he tore down the right and found Wirtz, who hammered home from close range. Gruda then added one of his own, tapping in a Scherhant shot which rebounded off a post.

Wirtz said: “We don’t mind who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly … We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we’ve taken some great steps in our development as a team.”

View image in fullscreen The Netherlands keeper Bart Verbruggen cannot keep out Brajan Gruda’s effort as Germany score their fifth goal. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

“Everyone will go home with a smile on their face – and for at least the next three or four months, no-one will be questioning the German national team,” Klopp said afterwards. “Instead, they’ll be thinking: ‘This could really turn into something.’ We have wonderful footballers, great characters … the lads are even surprising themselves.”

Greece had to settle for third place in Group A2 despite a 1-0 home win over Serbia. Giorgos Masouras scored the second-half winner in Volos, but the hosts missed out on a quarter-final place on head-to-head goal difference, their 7-0 defeat by the Netherlands on Friday proving costly. As group winners, Germany will be seeded in Friday’s draw and will avoid England, France and the winners of Group A4 – probably Portugal – in the last eight.

Switzerland completed a dominant campaign in Group B1 by thrashing Scotland 4-0 in St Gallen. Slovenia finished second in the group, claiming a promotion/relegation playoff place, as Danijel Sturm’s double helped them secure a 3-0 win over North Macedonia.

Lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals. The Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance. Carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association Photograph: Michael Steele/The FA Collection Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

In League C, the Faroe Islands beat Moldova 1-0 to complete an unbeaten campaign and earn a playoff place. Slovakia, already guaranteed Group C3 top spot, earned a 2-2 draw with Kazakhstan thanks to Adrian Kapralik’s last-gasp leveller.

Iceland finished Group C4 unbeaten with a 3-0 home victory against Luxembourg securing first place. Second-placed Estonia beat Bulgaria 2-1 to book a playoff spot.

In League D, Gibraltar earned a 1-1 home draw with Malta thanks to Carlos Richards’s late equaliser, while Lithuania defeated Liechtenstein 2-1 in Kaunas.

Sports.title: Switzerland roll over sorry Scotland to increase the pressure on Pocognoli
Sports.content:
A match that should have been about 103 was instead about four. Andy Robertson is due acclaim for becoming the most capped player in Scotland’s history but how the full-back will wish the moment had arrived in different circumstances.

A second-string Switzerland team pulled Scotland apart, raising further and significant questions about the suitability of Sébastien Pocognoli to carry out the job his paymasters boldly entrusted him with. Scottish FA giddiness about Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke, a hugely successful leader of the national team, is looking increasingly ridiculous. “I don’t think you’ve got time in international football,” said Robertson as dust settled here. Ouch.

This was a horrible night for Pocognoli, who is under serious pressure just three months into his tenure. Scotland’s players looked a disillusioned and disorganised lot. Pocognoli has never previously managed in international football, which renders it reasonable to ask his qualifications to improve this grim scenario. Scotland have finished a distant third in a favourable Nations League section. Ramifications exist for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in December. Pocognoli is taking a pounding in the court of public opinion.

“The score is painful,” said Pocognoli. “I see a lot of good things in the way that we try to play. The result is heavy but the players gave everything. They enjoy playing like this.” An eye test suggests otherwise. Scotland are overly generous in defence, lame in midfield and powder-puff in attack. It is quite the mix.

Pocognoli’s demeanour during pre-match media duties suggested he was irritated by the early questioning of his approach. The Belgian is unwilling to deviate from the deployment of three centre-backs whether Scotland are at home to North Macedonia or away to Switzerland. While the prospect of facing a highly impressive Swiss team would ordinarily make Scots gulp, there was cause for hope in St Gallen. Not only had Switzerland already won Group B1 but they were in makeshift form.

Switzerland’s lack of cohesion was apparent during an opening spell where the visitors looked decent. A flurry of set pieces and a John McGinn half volley that dipped over Yvon Mvogo’s crossbar emphasised Scottish attacking intent. On a difficult pitch, Switzerland’s first 20 minutes lacked purpose. As good as things were to get for Scotland, alas.

View image in fullscreen Andy Robertson’s record-breaking match was a game to forget for Scotland. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

There appeared no real danger as Zachary Athekame fired in a hopeful cross from the Swiss right. Scotland had an abundance of cover inside their own penalty area. The problem was that one of those charged with clearing lines, Lewis Ferguson, instead poked the ball past Angus Gunn. No own goals are pretty; this one was especially ugly. Ferguson had needlessly panicked.

Scotland attempted an immediate response as Aaron Hickey headed wide. The Brentford man had to be withdrawn before the interval, apparently damaging his left hamstring when making a defensive intervention.

Hickey, whose career has been seriously disrupted by injury, was understandably distraught. Although Switzerland were by now in control, McGinn spurned a glorious opportunity five minutes before the interval when heading straight at Mvogo. Adrian Bajrami spared McGinn’s blushes with an even worse miss at the opposite end before the teams headed for their orange wedges. The half had been humdrum in nature.

Ferguson shanking the ball out for a Switzerland corner set the tone for a spell where the game was put firmly out of Scotland’s reach. Samuel Ballet burst forward from midfield before playing a one-two with Remo Freuler and slamming towards the Scotland net. The ball was heading in before Winsley Boteli made certain, with the video assistant referee dismissing Scotland’s appeals for offside. The ease with which Ballet evaded those in navy blue was as striking as the space Freuler found himself in. Scotland’s structure, once a staple, was nonexistent. Five defenders and two deep lying midfielders were being gleefully ignored by the rampaging Swiss.
