Sports.title: Haas sticks with Camara for Las Vegas GP, Hirakawa in for FP1
Sports.content:
Rafael Camara will race again for Haas at Formula 1's upcoming Las Vegas Grand Prix, as Ryo Hirakawa takes Ollie Bearman's seat for the opening practice session.

Both Hirakawa and Camara have now raced for the team following the dismissal of Esteban Ocon, who was stood down during the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Hirakawa, contesting the World Endurance Championship finale in Monza - later winning his third WEC title - was unavailable for the previous F1 round in Brazil and this presented Haas an opportunity to bring Camara in for an early debut.

Camara will stay in the car for Las Vegas, as he gathers valuable experience for his full F1 debut next season with the team. Bearman meanwhile has only given up his seat for one FP1 session so far this year, so will do so for the final time to present Hirakawa with more track time in the VF-26.

Hirakawa scored a point in his Mexico City F1 debut, albeit after Oscar Piastri and the two Alpine drivers were handed post-race penalties, and impressed team principal Ayao Komatsu with "very good mental conviction - [he was] so clean. He delivered what we expected."

Ryo Hirakawa, Haas F1 Team Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

Camara endured a tougher debut run, as conditions at Interlagos were incredibly variable. The Brazilian built up through the weekend and showed good pace by the end of FP3, but the rain arrived ahead of qualifying and made his life more difficult.

After rescuing his car from a spin in Q1, Camara got as far as Q2 - but put his car into the wall at Turn 12 having been unable to get the correct rear-axle braking in low-grip conditions.

He thus qualified 13th and started 11th with other drivers taking grid penalties, but a tough stint on the intermediates put Camara towards the back of the field.

Read Also: Formula 1 Why Camara should take heart from a tough F1 debut in Brazil

It is uncertain whether Camara will stay in the car for the rest of the season, given his position at the top of the F2 drivers' standings; he may wish to complete the season, but this will largely be at the behest of Haas and Ferrari.

Hirakawa could feasibly return to the car in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, should Camara return to F2 for those rounds.

Sports.title: What is left to fight for in F1 2026?
Sports.content:
A five-way battle for P2 in the drivers’ championship

Kimi Antonelli romped to his maiden world title to become Formula 1’s youngest world champion, but behind him it’s all to play for – and closer than ever.

As the highest-scoring driver across the latest eight rounds, Max Verstappen has climbed to second in the championship, but that doesn’t mean he’ll comfortably be this year’s runner-up. George Russell, Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris lie within 33 points of the Red Bull driver, with a maximum of 75 points still available.

Whoever takes second and third will then get the privilege to attend the FIA’s end-of-season gala as podium finishers – a prospect which typically is enjoyable to some drivers and daunting for others.

Team boss Toto Wolff said Mercedes’ priority may now be securing a 1-2 in the drivers’ championship, perhaps softening the blow of a disheartening campaign for Russell, but not everyone cares as much.

“I'm not going to say it doesn't mean anything, but it's not something I focus on,” Hamilton said of the prospect of finishing second. “I think winning the championship is the only thing any of us really care about. I mean, maybe some people do care about the other positions, but for me, my sole focus is on making sure that we secure second in the constructors' championship.”

It certainly doesn’t matter to Verstappen. “For me personally, I don't care if I'm second, third or fourth,” the Dutchman said of his championship chances back in Singapore. “It doesn't do anything. But I just want to have fun till the end, you know, try to go for a day’s success.” Eight consecutive podiums, including three wins from the last five rounds, seem to prove his point.

Another three chances for Oscar Piastri and Isack Hadjar to win

Oscar Piastri, McLaren, Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Oscar Piastri and Isack Hadjar have two things in common: they are the only top-team drivers who have been comprehensively outperformed by their team-mates and the only ones who have, so far, failed to win a grand prix in 2026.

Both of them have taken a couple of podium finishes each without ever having a real chance of victory. The fact that they never qualified on the front row doesn’t help.

That is not too surprising from sophomore Hadjar, who is paired with the formidable Verstappen, but for Piastri, it is a little more puzzling; the 2025 title contender has struggled to adapt his driving style to F1’s new machinery, especially when it comes to finding the limit.

“It's definitely something I've been working on a lot. There's been signs of progress with that, but it's just taking longer than I'd hoped,” he admitted back in Mexico.

Hadjar is in a very different situation. “This year, for some reason, I feel like I haven't driven much,” he said in Brazil, having missed three races after injuring his wrist in August. “You know, Saudi, Bahrain cancelled, and then I had a two-month break during the summer break, and now I feel like I have a lot left in the tank. I'm a bit sad that we're already on the end, because I feel like I can still go a long way this year.”

To be fair, Hadjar had his share of misfortune in the previous rounds. “That's what makes it more frustrating for me right now,” he added. “The last couple of races, I couldn't even be in the top five, except for Malaysia – there's always been something happening on Sunday.

“But it's going to click. It's just a matter of time, and on my side, I think pace has been decent, so I just want to keep pushing, and anything can happen with the conditions. So, just stay very, very sharp.” He was rewarded with a podium finish in Brazil; will he do even better next?

Red Bull vs McLaren for P3 in the constructors’ championship

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

The main battle in the constructors’ championship will be Red Bull against McLaren for third position. Second-placed Ferrari admittedly isn’t mathematically out of reach, but it enjoys a 95-point advantage over Red Bull, with 129 available to score. Such a plot twist would require three debacles from the Scuderia and consistent podium finishes from Hadjar.

With Red Bull on 415 points and McLaren on 398, however, it’s all to play for. Red Bull surged to the front of the pack in the last couple of months – it collected 152 points from Azerbaijan to Mexico, with McLaren down on 59 – but the MCL40’s latest upgrade helped Norris to victory in the Brazilian GP.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies described McLaren as “a bit faster” in the Interlagos race, though the wet conditions weren’t quite representative of what they will likely be in Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi – but further updates are expected in Nevada.

“It's thanks to these [latest] upgrades that we are now in condition to fight for the victory, combined with the conditions surely,” McLaren team boss Andrea Stella said. “And these upgrades, first of all, they will be complemented by some more parts that come in Vegas. And they form the foundation for what will be next year's car.

“So, it's encouraging for the trajectory of McLaren that we seem to be able to transform our development into performance on track.”

Read Also: Formula 1 McLaren to upgrade MCL40 F1 car at its bogey track Las Vegas

Haas vs Audi for seventh position

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team, Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

With Racing Bulls and Alpine solidly fifth and sixth in the standings, our attention now turns to Haas and Audi – a tale of two seasons.

F1’s new era began in impressive fashion for the American team, with Oliver Bearman finishing seventh in Australia and fifth in China. The 17 points collected across these two weekends represent more than half of Haas’ current tally of 31, as the team lost ground throughout the campaign amid consistency issues with the VF-26.

This is intriguingly reminiscent of the team’s first season, exactly 10 years ago, with Romain Grosjean then scoring 18 points in the first two events before the team’s eventual tally plateaued at 29.

Meanwhile, Audi’s maiden F1 campaign after fully taking over the Sauber squad started with low-key form, with its first power-unit somewhat struggling relative to most rival engines. But the R26 has become a consistent points scorer at the hands of Gabriel Bortoleto and Nico Hulkenberg – hence how it has made up a 19-point deficit to Haas, now lying just three points adrift.

So the momentum firmly is with Audi, which has actually outqualified Haas in 18 out of 20 grands prix so far – especially as the second Haas car is now driven by Rafael Camara, who made his debut last time out in Brazil. Despite the rookie’s raw pace, his lack of experience might prove costly in such a tight fight.

“I really want to manage expectations here,” Haas team boss Ayao Komatsu said in Brazil. “And then that means I'm not putting any pressure on Rafa, right?

“Of course, as Haas F1 Team, we are in a tight championship battle with Audi. But, again, that's not his problem, if you like – that's on us. Our job is to really just create an environment that doesn't have any of those extra pressures.”

Read Also: Formula 1 Why Camara should take heart from a tough F1 debut in Brazil

Aston Martin to spring a surprise?

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Aston Martin’s 2026 has been nothing short of a disaster, particularly amid the Honda power unit’s lack of power, reliability and driveability – which has been painfully obvious on many occasions.

‘Painfully obvious’ might also accurately describe a dejected Lance Stroll’s lack of enjoyment, as he retires from most races and his answers to the media – which never were that loquacious in the first place – have become near-monosyllabic.

Fernando Alonso hasn’t been much happier, but to his credit, he has made an impact whenever it was remotely possible. Aston now has seven points to its name, courtesy of the two-time champion’s starring drive to eighth in Malaysia.

It’s unlikely Alonso can shine in Las Vegas – the Honda powertrain’s deficiency may be too stark with that near-2km full-throttle portion along the Strip – but a winding track like Lusail might be a decent opportunity to clinch a result for Aston.

As it happens, the team is just five points behind ninth-placed Williams – which has scored just one in the latest 14 grands prix – in the constructors’ championship. All Aston needs would be for Alonso to take one seventh-place finish, assuming its rival doesn’t score more than one point by the end of the season.

“We turn up at every event with the motivation, drive, and passion that we had earlier in the season to score every point possible,” Williams team principal James Vowles told Sky Sports F1 in Brazil. “What I'm more indicating is it's just a much harder task now, but it doesn't mean that the team isn’t motivated.

“Actually, I'd be surprised if you didn't look around and find people actually surprisingly in a good spirit. They can see what's coming in the future, but our goal still to the end of the season is to make sure that our last point scored wasn't a few races ago.” It will be a tall order.

Sports.title: Retaining Lawson isn't enough – Red Bull must stop treating him like a failure
Sports.content:
Liam Lawson never failed at Red Bull Racing in 2025. It was Red Bull that failed Liam Lawson.

Retaining his services for another year isn't just a logical decision, but perhaps the first sign that the organisation is changing the habits it developed under Helmut Marko. Yet there may be one more step it needs to take to avoid failing Lawson again.

It needs to stop treating its young drivers – Lawson included – like goods with an expiry date.

There's hardly anyone who would disagree that the New Zealander not only deserved to stay in F1 after his performances this year, but also earned that right under the pressure of having no clarity over his future for so long. Many would probably have cracked or become frustrated, but Red Bull trained him well in how to shield himself from that pressure and not let it affect his performance.

His strongest spell of the year coincided with a period when the paddock was increasingly asking the same question, and doing so more and more loudly: what else does this guy have to do to secure his future?

The final confirmation came after a run of five races in the points, four of which he finished seventh, putting him in a class of his own in the midfield. That run also included some stunning qualifying performances and bold moves on track. He's ninth in the standings, with more than double the points of Pierre Gasly, who occupies the next position in the championship table. And it's largely thanks to Lawson's contribution that Racing Bulls now looks set to secure its best result in the team's history.

Lawson's 2026 is surely his strongest season to date, at least in F1. But it's also the first in which he's actually been able to prove what he's capable of without being called up as a stand-in or rushed into an impossible task, as happened in early 2025.

Liam Lawson, Red Bull Racing Photo by: James Sutton / Motorsport Images

Lawson's dreadful couple of races for Red Bull didn't really come as a surprise to anyone – apart, seemingly, from the organisation itself. Yet expecting him to deliver something substantially better in the circumstances of his promotion – being placed in the same garage as Max Verstappen after just 11 F1 starts – was like expecting a newly graduated medical student to perform open-heart surgery on his second day in the job. Or a firefighter being sent into a burning skyscraper on his first call, without even having rescued a cat from a tree.

Yet those two races remain a somewhat defining part of how Lawson is perceived today – and perhaps one of the reasons why it took so long to confirm his future. The idea that he's someone who had his chance and failed still seems to dominate some people's assessment of Lawson, both outside and within Red Bull.

But if you simply forget those couple of months – which the New Zealander himself seemed to suggest he had done, whether consciously or as a form of self-protection – the picture looks completely different. He did well when standing in for Daniel Ricciardo in 2023, and then had a strong end to the season when he finally replaced the Australian a year later.

But Lawson's F1 career to date, despite him never changing employers, has been incredibly fragmented. There were those two short spells with the Faenza team, then the mad rush into Red Bull, followed by his demotion. Funnily enough, even this year – the first in which he's about to finish the season with the same team he started pre-season testing with – he was still called up for three races to stand in for Isack Hadjar.

Still, there's one important thing to remember about Lawson's 2026. It's not just his best year. It may be his best precisely because he's finally been able to show what he's capable of when he's not being used as an emergency solution to fill a suddenly vacant cockpit. This year's VCARB 03 is the first car he can truly call his own in Formula 1, having worked on its development last year and tested it properly ahead of the championship.

Lawson's also more experienced, yes. But he's still just 24, which is somewhat difficult to comprehend given how much he's already been through in F1. And if it weren't for the failure of March 2025, he'd now be seen as banging on Red Bull's door rather than fighting for the right to stay with Racing Bulls.

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

The subsequent decision to deny Nikola Tsolov a place in order to retain Lawson isn't just an indication of how highly Red Bull rates the New Zealander's season. It's also perhaps a clear sign that the organisation is beginning to move away from Marko's uncompromising approach and his tendency towards sudden, dramatic decisions.

There's no denying that the Austrian built something incredibly successful with his junior programme, and the results of his work speak louder than any criticism. Even on the current grid, there are plenty of former Red Bull juniors who were brought into F1 by Marko. But it's also true that some drivers never reached their full potential under that system.

The best of the best, including the two four-time world champions produced by Marko's approach, are the ultimate proof of his judgement. Yet there are also drivers like Jean-Eric Vergne, Sebastien Buemi and even Daniil Kvyat, who potentially had more to offer had they not been overlooked, shown the door or promoted too early.

There are more names to go through – and, after all, most of them also owe their careers and their successes in other championships or teams to Red Bull and Marko himself. But there's an undeniable feeling that some of them could have delivered more for the organisation that picked them up at a young age.

Lawson's F1 career could now have ended just as Vergne's did at the end of 2014, when the Frenchman wasn't retained by Toro Rosso after three seasons but didn't get his promotion to Red Bull when Sebastian Vettel decided to leave for Ferrari.

Jean-Eric Vergne was a match for Daniel Ricciardo at Toro Rosso, but their F1 careers took very different paths Photo by: Sutton Images

Marko rushed Kvyat into the senior team instead, despite Vergne comfortably outscoring the Russian in their single season together. JEV never found another seat in F1, despite having previously been almost a match for Daniel Ricciardo. Kvyat was in the same position as the inexperienced firefighter Lawson would find himself in a decade later – and lost his Red Bull drive just over a year after being promoted.

But if Red Bull really is changing its approach, it also needs to stop treating Lawson as a failure. Because it wasn't him who failed a year and a half ago, but a system in which everyone was judged by the same yardstick: if you're as good as Verstappen, you'll survive. But not everyone is – not only in terms of absolute talent, but also in the way they develop. After all, generational talents are generational talents precisely because they're rare.

There's some talk now about Lawson having world championship potential – which is typical F1. When someone impresses, there's always going to be talk about it. It's a nice phrase to attach to a talented driver, but it's about as meaningful as writing someone off completely after two races.

Lawson's 2027 will probably begin against a backdrop of speculation that it could be his final year in F1. Because over the years under Marko, Red Bull has conditioned us to believe that its young drivers have an expiry date, and that if they haven't somehow made it into the senior team before that date arrives, they must make way for the next generation.

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Manuel Eletto / Getty Images

But is that really the right approach?

That may be a question Red Bull needs to answer for itself. And if retaining Lawson really does signal a change, maybe the organisation should make it clearer that things will be different from now on – that a driver who is performing shouldn't have to fear being shown the door simply because he's become too experienced.

World championship potential or not, Lawson has proved he's good enough to race in F1 – and to do a great job for the team he's racing for.

And continuing to treat him like a failure isn't going to help that team get the best out of him, either.

Sports.title: Inside Turkey’s revamp for the return of a modern F1 classic
Sports.content:
Finding the right balance is often a challenge in modern Formula 1. That applies to the technical regulations: striking a balance between satisfying drivers and purists on the one hand, and delivering the spectacle F1 wants to offer younger fans on the other, with a constant stream of overtaking moves for, let’s say, the TikTok generation.

But that balancing act also applies to the calendar and the venues F1 visits. Many of the recently added destinations are temporary circuits in glamorous locations such as Miami, Las Vegas and Madrid, but these are not necessarily the tracks that get diehard fans excited.

Next year, however, a race will return to the calendar that has the potential to combine the best of both worlds. Istanbul is a global city – the bridge between Europe and Asia – and therefore the kind of destination F1 likes to have on its calendar. But the circuit, located on the Asian side of the Bosphorus, is also one that appeals to drivers and fans, particularly because of its famous Turn 8.

Ahead of the Turkish Grand Prix's return, Motorsport.com sat down with Eren Uclertopragi, president of the Turkish Automobile Federation (TOSFED). He shares the ambition of bringing both aspects together: an event that meets the standards of modern F1, while retaining a circuit that diehard fans enjoy.

“Yes, I think the same,” Uclertopragi said. “From a fans’ perspective, we are always more eager to watch the races in old-school tracks, so it's good that F1 accepted our proposal and that, also with the great help of FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem, we are back on track. We all miss the old races, but at the end of the day, from the commercial side, we also need the races like Madrid. We need both, the modern street tracks and tracks like Istanbul, Monza and Silverstone.”

Start of the 2005 Turkish GP Photo by: Lars Baron / Getty Images

That said, all permanent circuits have to adapt to meet the standards of modern F1, both in terms of facilities and the overall presentation of the event. The layout in Istanbul will remain intact, but a great deal will change around it.

“There will be major upgrades to the circuit,” Uclertopragi explained. “We will modernize our circuit to the level F1 reaches right now. We are, of course, working on the infrastructural side. We will try to cover most of the grandstands and we will try to make fan zones to do whatever is necessary to give the best experience to the fans.”

That last point is a crucial pillar of the plans. Istanbul Park has been a drivers’ favourite in the past, but according to Uclertopragi, the biggest challenge for the next five years – the duration of the new contract – is to make it a fan favourite as well; there is a lot of work to be done in that respect.

“It was always a drivers’ circuit, but now we’re trying to make it a fan circuit as well,” he said. “That starts with the traffic control and crowd management. The surrounding roads have already been constructed in a new way, so that there are now incoming roads and outgoing roads. The traffic flow will be improved to make the experience of getting into the circuit and getting out of the circuit better.”

Fans watch the 2005 Turkish GP Photo by: Bryn Lennon - Getty Images

The latter is particularly important, as traffic during previous editions of the Turkish Grand Prix was rather chaotic. It is an issue Uclertopragi is well aware of.

“We know what we have to do. We have started already planning the infrastructure and we are expanding the paddock as well. The capacity will be doubled and the infrastructure will be done from scratch. Apart from that, we will improve our hospitality units, including using our famous Turn 8.”

One aspect is particularly noteworthy in this overhaul of the event: the Turkish GP will be organised very differently in the coming years compared to previous editions. TOSFED is not only the Turkish motorsport federation, but now also the promoter – something that should mean more direct lines of communication and greater ability to actually turn ambitions into actions this time.

“The management of the circuit has been handed out to TOSFED, so that is creating a new flow with regards to getting things done as a promoter. Everything will be in my hands and with the support of the state, so we will try to do whatever is necessary,” Uclertopragi said.

“The worst part is that prior to our management, the circuit was managed by a private company and their prioritization was not the sport, not the fans, not Formula 1. So unfortunately we had problems with the fan experience and that is why we are prioritizing that fan experience right now.”

How Istanbul Park plans to avoid further asphalt issues

Aerial view of Istanbul Park in 2026 Photo by: Miragest

Aside from that, Uclertopragi knows that the fundamentals still need to be right. The layout will not change, and the asphalt needs to be in better condition. The surface proved problematic during F1's most recent visits, prompting several drivers to describe it as “driving on ice” – especially when it rained in 2020, the weekend when Lewis Hamilton secured his seventh world championship.

“Yeah, there was a problem with the asphalt back then, I totally support you on that,” Uclertopragi admitted.

“We were not a big fan of resurfacing the top layer with only a short period of time to go before the race. Part of the problem was that there were no races held at the circuit, so there was no race prior to F1 and that meant we had the surface problem.”

Unsurprisingly, the organisers in Istanbul are keen to avoid a repeat of those problems in 2027.

“Currently, we are in close cooperation with the FIA and experts from the circuit,” he continued. “Of course, we will need to change the kerbstones and so on, but the layout will be the same. And I guess we will not be changing the tarmac this time.

“It will remain the same and currently we are hosting ‘experience events’ at Istanbul Park for at least 30 weeks a year. After the renovation and upgrades we will start holding national and international races again, prior to Formula 1.”

This should prevent F1 drivers from once again being confronted with an unpleasant surprise when it comes to grip levels.

Can the Turkish GP stay on the calendar beyond 2031?

Fans at the most recent Turkish GP, in 2021 Photo by: Ozan Kose / AFP via Getty Images

All of this is initially being done with the five-year contract in mind, but Uclertopragi wants Istanbul to remain on the calendar beyond the initial deal, meaning the investments are aimed at the longer term.

“We are looking into a longer period. That's why the projects that we are having right now about the circuit will be going beyond five years. We are discussing internally and with the state how we can expand this project without leaving the calendar again,” he said.

Uclertopragi knows all too well what is needed to achieve that: delivering on the aforementioned promises. If that happens, he believes the rest will follow naturally.

“For sure, our commitment is for five years first of all, but if we deliver the standards that Formula 1 is looking for, then it will be beneficial for both parties. As long as we deliver the commitments we had and if we will have happy fans in the next five years, then I think it will be beneficial for both parties to keep Istanbul on the calendar,” he concluded.

Sports.title: McLaren to upgrade MCL40 F1 car at its bogey track Las Vegas
Sports.content:
McLaren will introduce upgrades to its MCL40 at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, with the new parts labelled as “the foundation for next year’s car”.

The team launched its 2027 front wing concept in Brazil, with team principal Andrea Stella describing it as an improvement for driveability and predictability; McLaren returned to form at Interlagos, with Lando Norris clinching pole position and victory in wet conditions. This ended a five-round podium-less streak, the squad’s worst since the first half of the 2023 campaign.

“After the upgrades in Hungary, it was encouraging that we were in a position to win – we should have won Madrid, really,” Stella said, referring to the unfortunate timing of the Virtual Safety Car in Spain, which likely cost Norris the victory at Madring.

“But after that, other people took upgrades and we lost this position. I think we also paid the price of not having had great qualifying sessions. It would have been interesting to see Lando starting from the front in races like Austin or Mexico; it would have been definitely a fight for podium.

“But it's thanks to these upgrades that we are now in condition to fight for the victory, combined with the conditions surely. And these upgrades, first of all, they will be complemented by some more parts that come in Vegas. And they form the foundation for what will be next year's car. So, it's encouraging for the trajectory of McLaren that we seem to be able to transform our development into performance on track.”

Las Vegas has not been a happy hunting ground for the papaya team. Back in 2023, McLaren had become a consistent podium contender, but both cars were out in Q1; Oscar Piastri scored a solitary point, while Lando Norris bottomed out and heavily crashed on lap three.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

The following year, the eventual constructors’ champion qualified just sixth and eighth, uneventfully driving to sixth and seventh in the race, 27 seconds adrift of the top five.

Last season, Norris did take pole; he and Piastri held on to second and fourth in the race as title rival Max Verstappen prevailed, but both cars were disqualified due to the MCL39s’ rearmost skid blocks being too worn.

Based on the MCL40’s specificities, Stella doesn’t necessarily expect the Nevadan track to favour McLaren this year, with full throttle down the near-2km Strip portion.

“It's a very different circuit layout, Vegas; long straights,” the Italian commented. “We know – we have seen this in Monza, we have seen this in Baku – that when the requirement is to develop top speed, not necessarily McLaren is the best car. We know that this also somehow relates to our [shorter] gear ratios that are not ideal when you need to go above a certain level of top speed.

“But having said that, we approach Vegas with some optimism because the car is faster now. This race will give us – and not [just] us but everyone, I think – a bit of understanding of how to use the tyres and where the car is good, where their car or our car is less good. So there's information to be capitalised for Vegas as well.

“So we look with some optimism. Also, Vegas, we want to go there and have a good result, because it's been probably, of all the races in the calendar, the one that we've been struggling the most. And even last year that we had a good race, we made our life bad with the problem that we had with the skid. We look forward to Vegas, have a good result there and finally be in peace with this venue.”

Sports.title: The surprising convergence behind F1's increasingly competitive 2026 season
Sports.content:
As George Russell took pole for F1 2026's curtain raiser in Australia by a whopping eight tenths over Mercedes's nearest rivals, you could see the collective heads drop in the paddock.

With this season the first year of all-new regulations, both on the chassis and power unit side, there were genuine fears of a 2014 repeat, with Mercedes out in front and the competition fighting over scraps.

Mercedes certainly did try to make the most of its early advantage, despite its power unit's reliability woes, as it has now sealed both the drivers' and constructors' title with three rounds to spare.

But the second half of the season after the summer break paints a different competitive picture. A picture in which all four top teams have had their chance to shine, owing to the ebb and flow of powerful upgrades being fast-tracked as part of a frantic in-season development race.

Lando Norris dominated either side of the summer break with wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, and what should have been a third win in Madrid. That followed a strong spell for Ferrari with one win apiece for Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc.

Later on, Red Bull made perhaps the most impressive comeback of all by clawing back one second, enabling Max Verstappen to take three wins over the past five races.

The end result is that Mercedes outscored Red Bull by just a single point since the summer break, while Ferrari could have been closer with better race weekend execution. McLaren has firmly been the fourth-fastest team only for Norris to excel in the wet in Sao Paulo last week.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Anadolu via Getty Images

Constructors' standings since the summer break

Position Team Points 1 Mercedes 227 2 Red Bull 226 3 Ferrari 172 4 McLaren 133

That convergence is best observed in qualifying, with the top four teams covered by three tenths in Singapore and Mexico. Austin was a difficult race for McLaren, but Kimi Antonelli, Verstappen and Leclerc all qualified within 0.230s at COTA. The absolute highlight was a thrilling qualifying session at the inaugural edition of Madring's Spanish Grand Prix, where the top five qualified within 0.195s across four different teams.

The new regulations have caused the top teams to enjoy a bigger advantage over the midfield than last year, which some feel is down to the cost cap restricting smaller teams from catching up. However, the fight at the front is demonstrably closer than what most observers expected during the first year of a new regulations cycle, especially given the added variable of power units being a bigger differentiator.

Why is that the case? When Autosport asked McLaren chief Andrea Stella that question, the Italian believes that under the budget cap, F1's four top teams have all converged in terms of the quality and quantity of their personnel, and with it the quality of ideas and methodologies at the front end of the field.

"In my view, teams have never operated at these standards," Stella said in Austin. "Four teams, and even the other teams, keep developing at this rate within a cost cap and somehow everyone has found a way to deliver lots of upgrades.

"The second consideration is that car performance is an expression of the expertise and know-how that you can realise from an engineering point of view. When you have a group of people that have established methodologies, knowledge, a certain way of working together, then they deploy this expertise and know-how to attack a certain group of regulations, and they achieve a certain level.

"Ultimately, it's the same people that attack a new regime of regulations, so I'm not surprised that, because it was close in the past, it's close in the present. In the second half of the season things are converging, but this is because it's just the quality of the team that gets reflected into the technical product."

Andrea Stella, McLaren Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur noted the rate of aerodynamic development is much steeper than in previous years, which explains why car performance can fluctuate so much weekend to weekend. "The first six races of the season were a bit difficult compared to Mercedes, they were perhaps six, seven tenths faster than us, and we came back all over the season. Now we score more points than everybody after Madrid," he said in Sao Paulo.

"We won races in June, McLaren in July, Red Bull in August or September, and we came back. What is true is that the first year of new regulations, the gradient of upgrades is much higher. Each time we are bringing something, we are doing a step. Look at McLaren this weekend [in Brazil], where McLaren deployed a new front wing to good effect].

"It's the story of the season. We had this kind of rotation, but I think this convergence of performance is good for the championship and good for the show."

Red Bull chief Laurent Mekies also pointed out the new regulations appear more restrictive at first, though the number of innovations this year - such as the Ferrari pioneered rotating rear wing - suggest there's still plenty of scope to exploit the fine print.

"The convergence is probably happening earlier than what we all thought," the Frenchman said when quizzed by Autosport about the subject in Brazil. "I'm guessing somehow, it's perhaps an indication of fairly restrictive regulations. That being said, you see cars with visibly different concepts, and you see four top teams fighting.

"What is fair to say is that to be already in the second part of 2026 we're in a situation where you turn up at a race weekend and you don't know which one of the four top teams is going to win the race, I think it's great for the sport. Now we have a top five in qualifying separated by two tenths. It's a strong combination of the development race and absolute perfect execution if you want to win on Sunday."

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

That means 2026's world champion Mercedes will have its work cut out next year to defend both of its titles. Team boss Toto Wolff was under no illusion that this regulations cycle would be a repeat of the 2014 era.

"The competition has been getting tougher between Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull and ourselves," Wolff acknowledged. "It's four teams that can win races and will be challenging for a world championship. And I have no doubt that it's going to be very difficult for us next year. So for me, the 2027 season has started now. It is about learning in the three last races."

Echoing Stella's thoughts about the four big teams operating at a similar standard right now, Wolff added: "It looks like maybe the most competitive era that is about to start, because the teams have become so professional in capability, in resource, that these kind of runaway seasons, I don't see them anymore, whether it's four in a row or eight in a row.

"You can see how quickly it goes from being dominant, and within a few races you realise that your upgrade doesn't work, and you fall back and you're just third on the road.

"I wish it was the era of Mercedes running away with another few championships, but I don't think it's the reality. It's a completely new challenge."

Sports.title: The Antonelli you don't know: Inside the Mercedes garage with F1's new world champion
Sports.content:
Mercedes mechanics have learned to watch their backs. Not because of the dangers of a pitstop, but because of Kimi Antonelli. Formula 1's newly crowned world champion has a rather unusual habit. He approaches members of his crew, greets them and, when they least expect it, gives their nipples a pinch - so nobody appears to be safe!

It is just one of the many practical jokes through which the 20-year-old Italian has developed a special relationship with the people who work on his W17. But behind the mischief, seemingly so far removed from the image of a world champion, lies something much more significant.

Success has roots that are not always visible. To understand them, you sometimes have to look beyond what happens on the track. In Antonelli's case, that means listening to the people who share the work, pressure and emotions of a grand prix weekend with him.

Their accounts paint a picture of a young man who has earned something that even a world championship cannot guarantee: the trust and respect of those around him. It is a relationship that developed naturally, rooted in an attitude Antonelli learned long before reaching F1, when he accompanied his father Marco to races with his own team. Growing up around workshops and racing circuits taught him a valuable lesson: before becoming a racing driver, you have to learn how to be part of a team.

"When he comes into the garage, it's quite a show," said Nathan Tupper, who works on the power unit of Antonelli's car. "He grabs everyone, pinches people's nipples, slaps them all over and generally causes chaos. At the end of the day, he's 20 years old. That's just Kimi."

Ash Jones, the second senior mechanic on Antonelli's car, agrees: "There are so many practical jokes that it would be difficult to list them all. He comes over, says hello and then gives you a pinch. That's how he jokes around with us. He likes having a good relationship with everyone, laughing and having fun together."

The jokes do not even stop when the circumstances would seem to demand maximum concentration. Tom Mason, Antonelli's number one mechanic, has seen it countless times: "It always makes me laugh watching him getting ready to get into the car before qualifying. He's still joking around, grabbing the guys, tickling them. Even when the pressure is enormous, he's there having fun. He's incredibly relaxed."

The driver who has displayed such remarkable maturity on the track is the same young man who, the moment he walks into the garage, becomes a 20-year-old eager to have some fun. Birthdays are another occasion for the Mercedes mechanics to be on their guard, as Antonelli has introduced a tradition of celebrating his colleagues by covering their faces in whipped cream.

George Russell, Mercedes, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Hector Vivas / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Callum Wooldridge, who works on the front end of Antonelli's car, explained why the ritual has become so popular within the team. "When you work in Formula 1, you spend so much time away from home that sometimes you end up celebrating your birthday during a grand prix weekend,” he said.

"It's not always easy. Sometimes you really miss being at home. Kimi started this thing with whipped cream in people's faces, and I don't think there are many other garages in the paddock where something like that happens. It's funny. It happened to me on my birthday in September last year."

The practical jokes have helped create an environment in which the relationship between the driver and his crew has become unusually close. "It's one of the best atmospheres I've ever experienced working with a driver," said Jones. “With Kimi, you feel completely comfortable. It's like talking to one of the guys you work with every day. There's no awkwardness, no tension when you speak to him."

Antonelli's race engineer Peter Bonnington actively encourages that sense of familiarity. "Bono encourages us to interact with him, to have a laugh," Mason explained. "Kimi is very approachable and loves joking around with the guys. It's a really good environment to work in."

The early tests, the crashes and the kid in the blue cap

To discover another side of Antonelli, one must go back to 2024, when Mercedes began the testing programme designed to prepare him for his F1 debut. Franck Bougeard was one of the mechanics involved in those sessions and his first encounter with Antonelli came in the spring, during a test in Austria. Kimi was just 17, wearing a blue cap with a rather unruly head of hair sticking out from underneath.

"I remember all that hair coming out of his cap, looking a bit messy," said Bougeard with a smile. "He really looked like a little kid. And there he was, about to drive a Formula 1 car." Bougeard's memories also include Antonelli's early crashes, as the young Italian began exploring the limits of an F1 machine.

"At Abu Dhabi, he crashed and damaged the chassis. Luckily, we'd brought a spare one, which is something we hardly ever do at those tests,” he said. "I don't even know why we'd brought it, but thank goodness we had, because we needed it."

Antonelli crashed on his F1 session debut in Monza, 2024 Photo by: Zak Mauger / Motorsport Images

Then came Monza, and another accident: "At that point I was starting to think, ‘brilliant, every time this kid leaves the garage, we're going to end up changing a chassis!’ He was very quick, but sometimes he pushed too hard. He needed to learn where the limit of the car was, and a few crashes were part of that process. That's exactly why we were there, to give him the opportunity to learn."

After his accident at Monza, Antonelli returned to the garage visibly upset about the extra work he had caused. "He kept apologising," Bougeard recalled. "He was saying how sorry he was for having destroyed the car again. I told him it wasn't a problem and that the important thing was that he was OK. Then I asked him: 'What did your dad say?'"

Kimi's answer has stayed with the mechanic ever since.

"He gave me a telling-off for half an hour,” he said. Bougeard also wanted to know how Antonelli's mother had reacted. Kimi explained that she had been terribly frightened, to the point of tears. So here was a teenager already capable of driving an F1 car, yet still dealing with the sort of family situations familiar to countless young people.

His father telling him off, his mother worrying about him, and Kimi returning to the mechanics to apologise. But Marco Antonelli also features in another memorable episode, as during a test in Abu Dhabi, after learning that his son had crashed into the barriers, he rushed towards the scene of the accident, even crossing the circuit to reach him.

"Marco was on the other side of the track. When Kimi crashed, he immediately set off to get to him,” said Bougeard. "I had to speak to him afterwards. I said: 'Marco, there are professionals here, there are ambulances. The last thing I want is for you to get run over by an ambulance while you're crossing the circuit!'"

Marco admitted he had been wrong. But those early accidents are more than just amusing memories. Tom Mason recalled that when Antonelli joined the Mercedes race team at the beginning of 2025, one of the young driver's biggest concerns was creating too much work for his mechanics.

Antonelli endured many a tough lesson before becoming world champion Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"Whenever he made a mistake, he felt incredibly bad about it,” said Mason. “He kept apologising for the damage to the car and for all the work he'd caused us. Eventually, I told him he needed to stop worrying about that."

Mason remembered exactly what he wanted the young driver to understand. "I told him: 'You don't need to apologise to us. If something goes wrong, you don't have to worry about the car or the work we have to do. We're happy to do our jobs. As long as you give everything you've got, we'll do exactly the same for you.'"

There had inevitably been some uncertainty before Antonelli arrived, as Mercedes was saying goodbye to Lewis Hamilton after a hugely successful partnership and handing his car to an 18-year-old rookie.

"We didn't really know what to expect," Mason admitted. "We'd worked with Lewis for so many years and knew his habits inside out. With Kimi, everything was going to be new. I wondered how many accidents he might have, how long it would take him to adapt and how much extra work he might create for us."

There were difficult moments, particularly during the 2025 season. But Mason stressed that even at his lowest points, Antonelli never brought tension into the garage. "Spa was particularly difficult for him,” he added. “But we weren't angry. If anything, we felt sorry for him because we could see how much he was suffering. He was so young and had an enormous amount of pressure on his shoulders."

But one quality has particularly impressed Antonelli's number one mechanic: his ability to move on quickly from disappointment. "He can have a terrible weekend, or a practice session where everything goes wrong,” he said. "When he gets out of the car, he's angry. You can clearly see it. But the next time you meet him, he's already completely different. He comes back into the garage full of enthusiasm, ready to start again. He doesn't carry that negativity around with him. It's almost as if he starts again from zero every time."

For Mason, that attitude makes a considerable difference to the way the team operates. "If a driver is constantly in a bad mood, the people working with him eventually end up feeling the same way,” he claimed. "With Kimi, it's the opposite. He's so positive that his enthusiasm rubs off on everyone. For me, having to coordinate the work of the guys, that's an ideal situation."

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Two days to learn everyone's name

There is another detail on which all five mechanics agree: Antonelli knows the people who work on his car personally, and he learned their names remarkably quickly. "That's one of the things that impressed me most," said Ash Jones. "He knows everyone in the garage. Not just their names, but details about their personal lives too. If you tell him something about yourself, he remembers it."

Tom Mason remembered an episode from the days before Antonelli officially joined the race team. "When we found out Kimi was coming, I spoke to Rosa, his press officer,” he said. “I suggested organising something so that we could all get to know him. Rosa told me Kimi was really enthusiastic about the idea, but first he wanted to do something with the guys who'd worked with him during testing."

Antonelli had no intention of forgetting the people who had accompanied him through the previous months. "He was very conscious of that," said Mason. "He wanted to make sure he met up with the people from the testing programme first, the guys who had been with him up to that point. Then he would get to know everyone else."

And when he finally arrived in the race team's garage, the introductions were remarkably quick. "After a couple of days, he already knew everyone's name,” added Mason. "And that's incredible when you think about how much he had to learn at the same time: a new car, how the team operated, all the procedures, working with the engineers. Yet he still found the time to get to know every single person."

It is an attitude that seems to run through the Antonelli family. Nathan Tupper explained that Marco had also developed a spontaneous, affectionate relationship with the mechanics. "You can be working away and suddenly someone comes up and gives you a hug from behind. You turn around and discover it's Marco,” he said. "That's just how he is. They're a very open, affectionate family. They make you feel part of their world."

Callum Wooldridge remembered the young driver he first met at the beginning of 2025: “He was still a little shy and needed time to settle in. As the months went by, he opened up more and more. Today he's not shy at all. He jokes with everyone.

"But really, he's still the same person. He's just learned to feel at home. He's part of the family now. He behaves exactly like the rest of us. And the nice thing is that his attitude doesn't change depending on the results. Whether he's had a good day or a bad one, he's always the same kid."

Antonelli's crash during FP3 in Melbourne Photo by: Mark Thompson / Getty Images

Melbourne: When the mechanics worked a miracle

Yet life in the Mercedes garage is not all jokes and laughter, as Jones recalled what happened in Melbourne at the start of the 2026 season. Antonelli had badly damaged his car during FP3, leaving the mechanics facing a race against time to get it ready for qualifying.

"After qualifying, I went to speak to him," Jones said. "He told me: 'I've no idea how you managed to get my car back on track.' He genuinely couldn't believe it!" So Antonelli's second place on the grid made the day even more special.

"He was incredibly grateful for what we'd done. He just kept thanking us,” he said. "That's something that has really stayed with me." It is an episode that helps explain just how personally the Mercedes mechanics have experienced Antonelli's journey to the world championship.

"When Kimi has a bad day, we feel bad too," said Wooldridge. "Whether the problem is down to him or the car doesn't really matter. We're so close that we all go through the same emotions together. It's like being on a rollercoaster."

For Jones, the turning point in believing Antonelli could genuinely win the world championship came at Monza, where the Italian sensationally fought his way to victory from 19th on the grid. Wooldridge, meanwhile, chose Austin, where Antonelli converted an unexpected pole position into a victory delivered with remarkable maturity.

Nathan Tupper's most vivid memory is the emotion of Antonelli's maiden grand prix win in China - the race after Australia - whereas Bougeard, who first met Antonelli when he was still a teenager taking his first steps in an F1 car, prefers to look at the entire journey.

"It's incredible to think how much he's grown in such a short space of time,” he said. "We knew he had talent, but I never imagined he'd come this far, this quickly."

Marco Antonelli talks with Simone Resta, Deputy Technical Director of Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

A world champion who is still a kid at heart

There is one remark from Bougeard that perhaps sums up Antonelli better than any other. "It's difficult not to like him,” he claimed. "Even if you woke up one morning thinking you really didn't want to put up with Kimi that day, the moment you see him, you change your mind. He's got a great sense of humour and loves teasing people. He gives you the feeling that he's genuinely enjoying what he does."

Antonelli's story is full of contrasts. The kid with the messy hair who turned up for his first F1 tests. The young driver that apologised profusely after destroying a chassis, while his father told him off and his mother worried about him. And the 20-year-old who is now the youngest world champion, but still wanders around the garage playing practical jokes on his mechanics.

Antonelli has grown up. He has learned to handle pressure and earned authority within the team, without losing the spontaneity that characterised him when he first joined the Mercedes programme. His mechanics have watched an extraordinary talent develop. They have rebuilt his cars after accidents, shared his disappointments, celebrated his first victories and experienced the tension of a championship battle that would have seemed impossible only a few months earlier.

Then, on Sunday evening in Mexico City, came the hugs and the tears. It was not simply the joy of a team celebrating a world championship. It was the emotion of people who had watched a young man grow up, got to know him and, somewhere along the way, become genuinely fond of him.

The world title is just the next step on that journey.

Sports.title: Hamilton tells F1 to spend £50 million in promoting under-represented talent | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has called on Formula 1 to publish data revealing how far the championship is representative of people from different backgrounds.

The seven-times world champion founded Mission 44, an organisation to promote black and other under-represented groups, in 2021.

Hamilton said polling conducted by the organisation shows support among fans for broadening representation. Almost two-thirds of 3,000 people polled across the UK, US and Brazil said F1’s leadership should do more to widen participation, while 55% agreed the series “talks about inclusion more than it delivers”.

In order to promote new talent in the championship, Hamilton’s review made three recommendations. These include a commitment to invest £50 million over five years promoting new talent.

The organisation’s review, called Igniting Inclusion, also recommends the series, the FIA and all 11 teams report data on representation to an independent organisation for tracking. The data would include “who joins, who is promoted and who leaves, by gender, ethnicity and socio-economic background.” This partner would “publish one, sport-wide picture each year” and give annual awards recognising progress made by teams.

Igniting Inclusion also urges teams to create a published number of early-career places each year which would “build thousands of paid routes into motorsport by 2030.”

“Formula 1 is inspiring millions of young people around the world,” said Hamilton. “But inspiration means nothing without opportunity. We can’t tell young people to dream big and then not open the doors when they try to make those dreams a reality.

“F1, the FIA and every team must push harder and move faster. We need real investment, more opportunities and greater accountability. We’ve shown that change is possible. Now we need to go further. The talent is out there, and the future of our sport depends on unlocking it.”

Sports.title: Racing Bulls boss Permane “should talk up” need for cost cap changes – Vowles | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Williams team principal James Vowles says the leading midfield team of 2026 should want to see changes to Formula 1’s cost cap.

Vowles claims the cap, introduced in 2021, has had the unintended effect of making it harder for midfield teams to catch up to the top four front-runners – Red Bull, Mercedes, Ferrari and McLaren. He argues the spending limit is taken up by salary and car development costs, leaving too little for teams to invest in their facilities.

“Before the cost cap came in, there were more points scored by the teams that weren’t the top four teams,” he told The Fast and the Curious. “Quite a bit more points, actually.”

“So back then about 10% of the podiums were [scored by] the teams that were in P5 to P10 [in the championship]. Now it’s 5%.

“There’s been one winner in 130 grands prix that wasn’t a top four team, one winner.” This was when Pierre Gasly won the 2020 Italian Grand Prix for AlphaTauri, the team now known as Racing Bulls. Vowles said that was a result of “my mistake” when he was a strategist at Mercedes.

“So what I’m really bringing to everyone’s attention is the following. What we’ve done with the cost cap is we’ve made it better for the top four teams.

“The gap between all of us is bigger than it’s ever been before. The amount of points that we are scoring is less than ever before.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Vowles said other teams which are trying to catch up to the front-runners face the same problem.

“We are investing and – here’s the kicker to it, so is Aston Martin – we’re investing huge amounts more than we did before the cost cap. That was the difference.

“Williams wasn’t putting the money in, they didn’t have the money. Force India [Aston Martin’s former identity] weren’t putting the money, they didn’t have the money. So the world today is actually a completely different financial element.

“But I’m being hurt by trying to catch up to others, which is holding me back. And by the way, not just me. It’s holding back other teams as well at the same time.”

Vowles feels other midfield teams which are limited by the cost cap should be pushing for changes too. “I think Alan Permane should talk up about this as well, by the way,” he said.

Permane’s Racing Bulls team is on course to finish fifth in the championship this year behind the top four teams. However Racing Bulls shares an owner with Red Bull and largely exists to prepare new drivers for the chance to join the bigger team.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Last month Permane said he isn’t interested in significant changes to the cost cap, arguing that major investments can be spread over multiple seasons.

“I don’t think we would support a wholesale change to the cost cap rules to start being able to spend huge amounts more money because I think it’s served us very well for the six years we’re into it now. I think it’s served Formula 1 very, very well.

“I think maybe there are tweaks to do, for sure. If you want to spend a whole lot of money on [capital expenditure], you can. The mechanism’s in there.

“So if James wants to go and spend $100 million on something, he can do that. You just pay it off over the X number of years. So, the mechanism is already there.”

However Vowles insisted it is not possible to make investment on the scale teams need under the cost cap without significant compromising their competitiveness.

“We have 30 years of under-investment in Williams,” he said. “And at the moment, the way we are competing up and down the grid is whatever money you spent six years ago has defined the tools you have around you. Simple as that.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Vowles said a midfield team which wants to “fight for world championships and fight for wins” needs to be able to be able to spend more than they can at the moment without compromising their car development.

“I can do all the expenditure I want, but we wouldn’t get a car out the door if I built the facilities for a period of time because I’m having to pay this wooden amount of money that goes into a black hole as a result of it,” he said. “That’s not sporting equity at all.

“Sporting equity would be we all play with the same tools, the same characteristics. It’s unfortunate, it’s not their fault, we didn’t have investment for 30 years.

“But also, we shouldn’t define a sport by what we spent in our chequebook six years ago before the cost cap came in, which is fundamentally what we’re talking about now. So it’s not quite true to say that. You can’t spend the money without it having a large performance hit, which others won’t have to go through.”

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said Camara “made his debut under extremely challenging conditions and showed us and the world why we signed him for 2027” in Brazil.

Hirakawa was unavailable to participate in Brazil as he was racing in the World Endurance Championship at Monza. The Toyota driver clinched the title, for the third time in his career, alongside team mates Brendon Hartley and Sebastien Buemi.

Sports.title: Poll: How many F1 drivers could have won the championship in Antonelli’s car? | Debates and Polls
Sports.content:
In the last two seasons, drivers from at least two different teams could have won the world championship.

But in 2026 it seems no one was going to beat one of the Mercedes drivers to the world championship. Andrea Kimi Antonelli won the title with a 119-point lead over Verstappen, with 100 points still available. Even if he scores nothing between now and the end of the season, he is assured of the title by at least 36 points.

It’s always been an unavoidable fact of Formula 1 that every driver gets a different chance to win the world championship: often within the same team. George Russell has had more technical problems than his team mate.

But would Russell have beaten Antonelli to the title if they each had the other’s car? And which of the other 20 drivers are quick enough to have won the title in Antonelli’s car?

When the 2026 season began the grid featured 12 grand prix winners, four of which were world champions.

Which of them – plus their rivals – could have won the world championship in Antonelli’s car?

Does Fernando Alonso have a third world title in him? Was it just unreliability which cost Russell the crown? Could another driver who had never won a race before 2026 have claimed the title like Antonelli did?

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

I say

Although Russell has had the worse luck of the two Mercedes drivers this year, it doesn’t explain the 130-point gap between them at the time Antonelli clinched the title. Therefore I don’t think it’s realistic to say Russell would have beaten Antonelli had they spent the year in each other’s cars. So which of the other 20 drivers could have beaten Russell in Antonelli’s car, taking it as read that they would have enjoyed a slight reliability advantage? I’d confidently back the four existing world champions. Charles Leclerc certainly looks like a potential champion based on his form compared to Lewis Hamilton and past Ferrari team mate Sebastian Vettel. Carlos Sainz Jnr is another multiple race-winner who measured up well against Leclerc so he gets the nod too. I’d put Oscar Piastri on the list for the same reason, notwithstanding his tough campaign this year. Both Cadillac drivers are experienced and successful enough to be considered championship contenders. Ordinarily I wouldn’t pick either as being quicker than Russell, but he’s had such a difficult year I’m adding them to my list. Isack Hadjar has been extremely impressive in his second year in F1, and if Antonelli can win the title in his second season I see no reason to rule him out. Although Liam Lawson has been strong in the midfield, his brief stint at Red Bull did not persuade me he’s a champion in the making in quite the same way. Pierre Gasly got his chance at a Red Bull cockpit too soon and is now showing the kind of consistent speed that championship campaigns are made of. He makes the cut too. It’s tempting to add more names to the list, particularly the likes of Gabriel Bortoleto and Oliver Bearman, but at the moment I don’t feel confident to call either potential future world champions. How many drivers could have won the title in Antonelli’s car? I reckon half the grid. Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Sports.title: Ignore social media echo chamber and trust F1 over Middle East races – Wolff | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff says Formula 1 is right to go ahead with its plans to race in the Middle East.

Many sports including other motor racing series cancelled events in the region due to the US-Iran war. However F1 commercial rights holder Liberty Media held its Moto GP event in Qatar last weekend, despite one manufacturer staying away due to concerns over the safety of travelling to the region.

F1 confirmed this week it has abandoned its back-up plan to relocate the final round of 2026 to Imola in Italy if its planned events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi cannot go ahead.

Wolff said those questioning the wisdom of racing in the Middle East should pay less attention to media coverage and listen to those in charge of the series.

“For me, with our social media feed, we are always at risk of seeing what we want to see,” he told the BBC. “I believe you need to trust what the authorities say. You need to rely on the commercial rights holder, that’s F1, and the FIA as our governing body.”

However Wolff said no staff will be forced to attend the final two rounds and anyone choosing not to could hand an opportunity to a replacement.

“I strongly support that if someone doesn’t want to go to Qatar or Abu Dhabi, personally doesn’t want to, then I’m very fine with that,” he said. “We don’t want to oblige anyone. There’s not going to be any sanctions, or so on, on teams.

“If you don’t feel right about going there, then I have respect for that, and don’t go. It gives an opportunity maybe to someone else to be tested and to see how another person would perform in the future. That’s how I would approach it.”
