World.title: HOW to skip ‘Hell Affairs’ when applying for your Smart ID Card
World.content:
Minister of Home Affairs Dr. Leon Schreiber coined the phrase, "From Hell Affairs to Hope Affairs," referring to his digital bank branch rollout. Image: File

14-million new Smart ID Card applications … that’s what the Department of Home Affairs still has to process, according to its latest data. However, anyone trying to phone ‘Hell Affairs’, as it’s unaffectionately known, already knows the drill. The line rings for one minute before being automatically cut off. Emails go unanswered, too.

We’re messaged repeatedly at The South African by readers who contact the department and simply get no answer. One such reader, Terence Barthus, finally went in person to apply for an unabridged birth certificate. On his first try, the queue moved so slowly he left at midday. Day two came, he arrived earlier, but it hardly moved for five hours. By the third day, when he was finally assisted, he was told the certificate would take about six months, not the three as promised.

SMART ID CARD OVERHAUL

The old green ID book is touted as the most forged document in Africa. Surely, its time for an upgrade … Image: File

It was Home Affairs Minister Dr. Leon Schreiber who coined the phrase, “from Hell Affairs to Hope Affairs.” When he took office in 2024 he described the department as, “synonymous with corruption and poor service delivery.” Now we have the Home Affairs@home partnership, launched in March 2026. By November 2026, Schreiber announced that 753 bank branches were now offering Smart ID Card replacement services. Together with traditional Home Affairs offices, that means 967 locations.



The walk-in service at applicable banks takes as little as five minutes, with no prior booking or paperwork required. At last count, South Africa still has 14-million green barcoded ID books in circulation, held by citizens and permanent residents. Since the Smart ID Card began circulating in 2013, approximately 34.7 million have been issued. That comprises 25-million reissues and 9.7-million first timers.

DEADLINE FAST APPROACHING

Nevertheless, the old green ID book loses its legal recognition on 31 March 2028. That’s just 501-days away, as of publishing on Monday 16 November 2026. To process the outstanding replacements. ‘Hell Affairs’ must average approximately:

893 000 cards per month.

cards per month. 206 000 per week.

per week. 29 300 every day.

That’s an annualised processing rate of more than 10-million cards – about 2.7 times the record 4 million issued during 2025. The scale of the challenge is considerable if the department is to meet its own deadline.

NOT EVERY SMART ID CARD APPLICANT CAN SKIP THE QUEUE

Not all the participating bank branches are operational as yet, with Nedbank the next to go online. But they should be by 2027. Image: File

Moreover, bank branches only handle Smart ID Card replacements and green ID book upgrades. They do not handle:

First-time applicants. That includes 16-year olds with no form of ID.

Children’s documents, such as birth certificates, which are the starting point for any Smart ID Card.

Naturalised citizens and permanent residents, who aren’t yet covered, though ‘Hell Affairs’ says it plans to extend services to them by March 2027.

So, if you’re in one of these above groups, sorry, but you have to plan for the full ‘Hell Affairs’ experience. Go early, take a chair, a book, a flask of coffee, you name it …

SMART ID CARD ONLINE APPLICATION EXPLAINED

Nevertheless, for those who can get a Smart ID Card without visiting Home Affairs, you’d be silly not to take advantage:



Walk into a participating Absa, Capitec, FNB or Standard Bank branch with no booking, if you are eligible.

Apply online. Home Affairs runs the online service across two separate websites: eHomeAffairs is where you apply and pay, register a profile, complete the online form, upload your documents and settle the fee.

While the second is My Home Affairs Online, which is where you book your in-person biometric appointment.

You need both, in that order: Apply and pay on the first, then book an in-person visit on the second.

WHO CAN USE ONLINE ROUTE ONLY?

The next step from the department is bypass the card and go straight to a digital ID. But there are no timelines for that as yet. Image: File

The online system is built for South African citizens aged 16 and over who are or have access to:

Applying for a first Smart ID Card.

Replacing a lost, stolen or damaged card.

Upgrading from the old green ID book.

Have or know your valid 13-digit ID number.

ID number. A South African cellphone number, for the OTP.

An active email address.

A photo/digital copy of your current ID (JPEG or PDF, under 2MB).

STEP BY STEP TO NEW SMART ID CARD

One you are registered on eHomeAffairs with your ID number and personal details, do the following:

Log in and select ‘Apply for Smart ID Card.’

Download the BI-9 form online and complete it, indicating first-time application, replacement or upgrade.

online and complete it, indicating first-time application, replacement or upgrade. Lost or stolen cards need a SAPS case number to be processed.

Pick a participating branch for your biometrics.

Pay the fee and keep your proof of payment.

Attend your appointment with your ID, proof of payment and booking confirmation.

Wait a maximum of three weeks for the SMS saying your card is ready.

WHAT IT COSTS

First-time application (16 and older): Free

Citizens aged 60 and older: Free

Replacement, re-issue or upgrade: R140

Temporary Identity Certificate while you wait: R70

But what do you think? Have you tried the bank branch route for a Smart ID Card? Or have you recently endured a ‘Hell Affairs’ queue? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: Tech shares slide ahead of Nvidia results, Anthropic IPO
World.content:
LONDON - Technology stocks struggled to recover on Monday from the crisis engulfing Nvidia after its chief Jensen Huang quit, with the latest earnings from the AI chip giant as well as Anthropic's huge market debut dominating the agenda.

Investors will also be keeping close tabs on the first trilateral summit between Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, taking place on the sidelines of the APEC gathering this week featuring nations from around the Pacific Rim region.

European stocks began the week little changed, after tech shares mostly led declines across Asian indices.

"Key European equity indices held firm in the face of a mountain of questions about whether the AI boom is slowing down," said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

Nvidia reports its quarterly earnings Tuesday after the Wall Street close, offering a fresh chance to assess the outlook for a bellwether AI company whose value has plunged since Huang's shock resignation last week.

He quit following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and another with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

His exit raised concerns about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a buildout that has helped propel global markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the world.

"Nvidia's financial results will certainly be a litmus test for the market," Mould said.

"The results themselves may show a business at the top of its game, but the prime focus will be on what Jensen Huang's departure means for strategy," he added.

Nvidia expects third-quarter revenue to surge to around $108 billion.

Another key moment for the AI trade comes Thursday, when shares in Claude-maker Anthropic are expected to start trading.

Analysts expect it to raise around $65 billion in the IPO, which could value the five-year-old start-up at $1.3 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable companies.

In Asia, tech-heavy indices struggled at the start of the week.

Taipei plunged six percent, Seoul sank more than three percent and Tokyo lost more than two percent at the close.

There were also losses in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Bangkok, Manila and Jakarta, though Hong Kong, Mumbai and Wellington rose.

Also in view this week are US retail sales data and the minutes of the Federal Reserve's October meeting, which could provide signals on the outlook for US interest rates.

In company news, New World Development plunged almost 50 percent in Hong Kong after the heavily indebted property firm unveiled plans for a $3.2 billion rights issue that reignited concerns about its financial health.

World.title: Tuchel learns lessons as England reign in Spain
World.content:
MADRID - Thomas Tuchel took most of the flak when England blew their chance to reach the World Cup final, but he showed he had learned his lessons on a glorious night in Spain.

The German described Sunday's dramatic 3-2 win over the world champions in Madrid as the best performance of his reign as the Three Lions topped their Nations League group.

The visitors were exceptional for an hour inside the Metropolitano, roaring into a 3-0 lead with a penalty from Harry Kane before goals from Ezri Konsa and Ben White early in the second half.

England threatened to completely overrun Luis de la Fuente's men but Elliot Anderson's sending-off in the 63rd minute changed the game.

Mikel Oyarzabal punished England by scoring the resulting penalty and Nico Williams added another as Spain came forward in waves. But the visitors held firm, helped by some brilliant late saves from goalkeeper James Trafford.

The impressive result means England progress to the Nations League quarter-finals as Group A3 winners while Spain are licking their wounds after a first competitive defeat since March 2023.

The match carried echoes of England's rearguard action to beat Mexico by the same scoreline in the World Cup last 16 after they were reduced to 10 men.

But that performance was overshadowed by a heartbreaking 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina in Atlanta, where Tuchel packed his defence in the second half, ceding ground to the South Americans.

- Tuchel stays positive -

This time it was different.

Tuchel's first change, in the 78th minute, was to shore up his midfield, bringing on Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly for Kane.

Later he introduced Leeds forward Dominic Calvert-Lewin to ensure his side still had an attacking outlet, also introducing defenders Djed Spence and Dan Burn.

Tuchel hailed a "statement victory".

World.title: UN climate chief warns of AI 'double-edged sword' at COP31
World.content:
ANKARA - The UN's climate chief highlighted the "great potential and great peril" of artificial intelligence in the battle against global warming on Monday as COP31 host Turkey launched an initiative aimed at tackling the issue.

Named after the Turkish Mediterranean city hosting the UN talks, the voluntary "Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge" seeks to tap the technology's potential in finding climate solutions and assess its growing environmental risks.

The pledge has received 80 endorsements so far, including countries and companies, but only a small number of nations are among them for now.

"We have arrived at a technological moment of both great potential and great peril. AI and other frontier technologies are a double-edged sword," UN climate chief Simon Stiell said at the launch of the pledge.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow. AI benefits must outweigh its growing costs," Stiell said.

AI is being deployed in a broad range of applications, from improving weather forecasts to monitoring industrial emissions and optimising renewable energy.

But the data centres that power the technology consume huge amounts of energy and water, fuelling anger in communities whose utility bills have soared and raising concerns about their growing carbon footprint.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged AI companies in June to disclose their environmental impact and commit to powering every data centre with renewable energy by 2030.

A UN study has found that the facilities consumed more electricity than all but 10 countries in 2025 and could be ahead of all but five by 2030.

Their water consumption could meet the annual basic water needs of the entire population of sub-Saharan Africa by 2030, according to the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health.

About 30 percent of the electricity consumed by data centres comes from coal, followed by renewables at 27 percent, natural gas at 26 percent and nuclear at 15 percent, according to the International Energy Agency.

- 'Creating momentum' -

Only 10 countries have signed up to the COP31 pledge so far, with the United States, China and European Union missing from the list.

Major AI players such as chip designer Nvidia, ChatGPT developer OpenAI and Claude's Anthropic are also missing, but the pledge was signed by the World Business Council for Sustainable Development, a group whose members include Amazon, Google and Meta.

"CEOs and boards need to step up and align business and investment plans with the world's agreed climate goals," Stiell said.

Tomas Lamanauskas, deputy secretary-general of the UN's International Communication Union (ITU), which worked with Turkey on the pledge, stressed that Monday marked the launch of the initiative, with the hope of gaining more endorsements.

"Eighty is not a limit," Lamanauskas told AFP. "I think it's about creating momentum. ... We'll be working with others to come on board as well."

Turkey's Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir told the panel that the backing so far "demonstrates growing support for our shared ambition".

"We must both reduce AI's environmental footprint and harness its potential to modernise industry, improve energy efficiency, strengthen climate resilience, and accelerate green development," Karcir said.

But Jill McArdle, corporate campaigner at nonprofit group Beyond Fossil Fuels, called the AI pledge a "distraction" whose "promises are vague".

"The AI pledge risks giving Big Tech a green stamp without requiring it to address the real climate impacts of its infrastructure," McArdle said.

World.title: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott receive honorary Oscars in career firsts
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - Hollywood royalty Glenn Close and Ridley Scott both received an honorary Oscar on Sunday, the first golden statues of their decades-long careers, at a lavish gala bringing together industry elites.

Screen legend Close has been tipped for Academy Awards eight times during her five-decade career, including for her roles in "Fatal Attraction" and "Dangerous Liaisons."

British director Ridley Scott, known for box-office hits including "Alien", Blade Runner" and "Gladiator", is a nine-time nominee but had also never won the award.

The honorary Oscars, awarded annually by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, celebrate cinema legends for their careers and contributions to the film industry.

US actor John Malkovich, who is tipped for Oscars glory for his role in dark comedy "Wild Horse Nine," introduced Close as "a friend and a treasured colleague."

"She is a true master," said Malkovich, who starred alongside Close as the arch seducer in "Dangerous Liaisons."

"Glenn is unafraid to go there, and I love that about her."

- 'Happy ending' -

Close, who dedicated the award to her daughter, earned a standing ovation.

"As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not, though some years I thought I might have a chance," said the actress, who earned her first nomination for 1983 hit "The World According to Garp."

"I have always felt that the great honour is to be in the room," she added.

Three-time Best Director nominee Scott received his gong from Matt Damon, who paid tribute to the master of the modern screen epic.

"It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand," said Damon, who worked with Scott on 2015 box office smash "The Martian."

The director did not attend the event at the Ray Dolby Ballroom in the heart of Hollywood, but expressed his gratitude in a pre-recorded video.

Director Christopher Nolan and actors including Tom Holland, Charlize Theron, Olivia Wilde and Penelope Cruz were among dozens of star attendees.

The 17th edition of the awards, which precedes the Golden Globes in January and the Oscars in March, also paid tribute to legendary animator Floyd Norman.

Norman, who began his career in 1956 at Walt Disney Animation Studio, becoming the studio's first Black animator, contributed to dozens of films including "Mary Poppins" and "The Jungle Book."

"On occasion, even movies have a happy ending," the 91-year-old said.

"This special evening, here's my happy ending."

World.title: Number Of The Day | 17% | 16 November 2026
World.content:
When telecoms companies merge, will customers share the gains?

Telkom's share price rose by as much as 17% amid renewed talks about a possible acquisition by MTN. For investors, the prospect of a buyer for the entire company creates an immediate question about value. For mobile customers, however, a different question matters: would a bigger operator deliver better service, or leave people with fewer meaningful alternatives?

That distinction is the heart of the debate about consolidation in telecommunications. A transaction can make commercial sense for the companies involved and still require a much harder public-interest examination. South Africa's mobile market

already includes powerful operators, and removing an independent competitor would change the choices available to consumers.

The promise of scale

Telecommunications businesses depend on expensive networks. Coverage, capacity and reliability require continuing investment, while infrastructure can take years to build and maintain. Combining operations might reduce duplication and help an enlarged business direct resources towards improving its network. Telkom also brings more than a mobile subscriber base: its history as a fixed-line operator gives its infrastructure an additional strategic dimension.

But efficiencies are not the same as consumer benefits. A merger might lower costs for the combined company without producing cheaper data, better coverage or more responsive service. Those outcomes depend on what management does with the savings and, crucially, on whether customers can take their business elsewhere when promises are not met.

Why the smaller rival matters

Competition is not simply a contest between the two biggest networks. The presence of another credible operator can influence pricing, packages and the urgency with which market leaders respond to customers. Even when a rival is smaller, the ability to win dissatisfied subscribers gives the larger companies a reason to keep improving.

That pressure can weaken if customers have fewer credible choices. On the other hand, an operator that cannot invest adequately may struggle to provide meaningful competition, regardless of how many brands remain in the market. The relevant test is therefore not a simplistic preference for more companies or fewer companies. It is whether the structure left behind would support sustained competition and investment.

A decision beyond shareholders

A proposed MTN–Telkom deal would face scrutiny from competition authorities and communications regulator ICASA. Telkom's ownership structure introduces another layer: government remains a substantial shareholder, alongside a stake held by the Government Employees Pension Fund. Any proposed transaction must navigate commercial interests as well as the implications of changing control over an important communications business.

Those hurdles are not administrative footnotes. They are the mechanism through which questions about market power, infrastructure and the public interest receive attention beyond the boardroom. Nor should a dramatic share-price increase be mistaken for evidence that a takeover is certain to happen.

The strongest argument for consolidation would be one that survives a consumer test. If a larger network can invest more and compete more effectively, the benefits should become visible in the prices people pay, the reliability they experience and the alternatives still available to them. Until those outcomes are clear, a 17% market reaction says far more about investor expectations than it does about the future of South African mobile services.

References

eNCA, Number of the Day, 16 November 2026 (Gareth Edwards and Francis Herd).

World.title: Five things to know about Bond, James Bond
World.content:
LONDON - British box office magnet Robert Pattinson was named on Monday as the new James Bond, thrusting the "Twilight" and "The Odyssey" heartthrob into one of the world's most famous film franchises.

Here are five things to know about the man with a licence to kill.

Born on paper

James Bond started life on the page, his name taken from the cover of a Jamaican bird-watching book because his creator, British author Ian Fleming, wanted something as mundane as possible.

Fleming was able to draw from some rich real-life experiences, having served in naval intelligence during World War II.

One of Commander Fleming's key missions was Operation Goldeneye, aimed at sabotaging ties between Spain and Germany -- which later gave him the name for his Jamaican home, and inspired the 1995 movie.

His first novel, "Casino Royale", was released in 1953 and was a huge hit, chronicling the escapades of a larger-than-life secret agent and giving the British public a brief escape from the grim reality of post-war rations and hardship.

He went on to write 13 more Bond novels and penned the children's story "Chitty Chitty Bang Bang" for his son, which also came to the screen as a hit musical.

Fleming died in 1964 at the age of 56, just two years after the first Bond film appeared.

Big money

The figures vary, but Bond is one of the most successful film franchises of all time, having spawned 25 official films.

Industry data site The Numbers places Bond in third place for worldwide box office takings, behind only the Marvel Cinematic Universe and Star Wars.

While franchises such as King Kong and Godzilla have been around longer, Bond is more regular, rarely going more than two or three years between instalments.

The longest gap was between Timothy Dalton's last outing, 1989's "Licence to Kill", and Pierce Brosnan's "GoldenEye" in 1995.

Underlining the immense value of the franchise, Amazon bought the Bond rights from MGM for a cool $8.45 billion in 2021.

International agent

The various Bonds of the past 60 years have included Englishman Daniel Craig and Roger Moore, Scotsman Sean Connery, George Lazenby from Australia, Timothy Dalton from Wales and Irishman Pierce Brosnan.

In the novels, Bond is the son of a Scottish father and Swiss mother -- both of whom die in a climbing accident when he is a boy.

Codenames

The codename "007" has a specific meaning.

The "00" designation signifies the agent's licence to kill, while the "7" is his identification within the elite unit of MI6, Britain's external intelligence service.

The M designating Bond's boss comes from the "Missions Department".

Q, who furnishes Bond with all his nifty gadgets, gets his moniker from "quartermaster" -- a military term referring to the person in charge of supplies.

The bad guys have their own codenames.

"SPECTRE", the organisation that causes Bond so much trouble, is short for "Special Executive for Counter-intelligence, Terrorism, Revenge and Extortion".

A famous fan

One big name who gave Bond an early boost was President John F. Kennedy, who cited "From Russia With Love" in his top 10 books.

Reportedly, it was also the last film he ever watched before leaving for Dallas in November 1963.

World.title: 'Not competitive' Brazil can improve, insists Ancelotti
World.content:
SINGAPORE - Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti on Monday promised an improved performance in the year-ending clash against Singapore, admitting that his squad was "currently not competitive."

The Selecao lost 3-2 against Japan in a friendly in Singapore on Saturday, where Ancelotti and skipper Raphinha were red-carded after Japan scored the dramatic clincher in stoppage time.

"Given that the team is currently not competitive, I want to do more," Ancelotti told reporters in Singapore, where Brazil play on Tuesday.

The Italian, Brazil's first-ever permanent foreign coach, said: "I want to do more because I enjoy being here, so that the team can become more competitive on the global stage.

"The priority is to play well first (tomorrow) and to do well."

Ancelotti, 67, is coming under increasing pressure, following a string of underwhelming performances including two defeats, two wins and a draw in Brazil's last five international outings.

Japan avenged a 2-1 defeat by Brazil in their previous meeting at this year's World Cup, when the South Americans beat them in a round-of-32 clash.

After Saturday's loss, Ancelotti faced a barrage of criticism, including from former Brazilian national team star Romario.

Ancelotti brushed off Romario's remarks, saying "like anyone he has the right to express an opinion."

But the former Real Madrid coach, who reacted with fury after Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to Japan's winning goal on Saturday -- which was upheld by VAR -- said that his team "didn't deserve to lose" against Japan.

Japan face Paraguay on Tuesday in the second match of the double-header at Singapore's National Stadium.
