World.title: TSC picks Cheptumo Ayabei as new Chief Executive Officer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Teachers Service Commission headquarters in Nairobi. [File, Standard]

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has picked Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer, making him the first person with a disability to head the commission.

Ayabei emerged top in interviews conducted on Monday, beating four other candidates, including the commission’s acting chief executive, Dr Evaleen Jesang Mitei, to become the country’s top teachers’ employer.

His selection ends a prolonged search for a substantive head of the commission, which has operated under acting leadership since the departure of former CEO Nancy Macharia in June 2025.

Ayabei, who hails from Baringo County, is currently TSC’s Director of Finance, having served at the commission for more than two decades. He joined the institution in 1999 as a Finance Officer before rising through the ranks to become Director of Finance in 2009.

His elevation marks a significant milestone for the representation of persons with disabilities in the country’s public institutions.

Ayabei was the first candidate to face the selection panel at 9am at the commission’s headquarters in Upper Hill, Nairobi. He was followed by Mitei at 10am, Robert Odette at 11am, Lawrence Ngai Kaburu at noon and Farah Abdi Saman at 1pm.

The five candidates were shortlisted from 124 applicants who responded to a fresh  issued on September 29. Applications closed on October 30.

Ayabei holds a Bachelor of Education degree in Mathematics and Economics from Kenyatta University and a Master’s degree in Finance and Banking from the University of Stirling in the United Kingdom. He is also a Certified Public Accountant.

Before joining TSC, he worked at the Ministry of Education between 1990 and 1999.

He takes over at a critical time for the commission, which oversees the employment, deployment, promotion and discipline of teachers across the country. He will inherit mounting pressure over teacher shortages, recruitment, promotions, transfers and the management of the teaching workforce.

The recruitment process had faced legal challenges, with a petition filed at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Kisii seeking to halt the exercise.

The case, filed by Evans Morara Nyangongo under Cause E038 of 2026, challenged the fresh recruitment and raised questions about Mitei’s participation in the process while serving as acting CEO and seeking the substantive position.

Nyangongo sought to stop the commission from proceeding with the appointment until the issues raised in the petition were determined.

However, the court dismissed both the application and the suit, with no orders as to costs, clearing the way for the interviews.

In its defence, TSC maintained that the decision to advertise the position had been made collectively by the commission’s board and not by the acting CEO.

In a replying affidavit, TSC chairman Jamleck Muturi John maintained that Mitei had neither participated in the board’s deliberations on the recruitment nor influenced the process.

The fresh recruitment followed an earlier court decision that nullified the previous exercise over procedural irregularities, forcing the commission to restart the search for a substantive chief executive.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: TV host Amr Adib comments on Egyptian state selling lands to pay off debt
World.content:
Egyptian media host Amr Adib on Sunday commented on the Egyptian government’s reliance on selling land to generate liquidity and address financial crises over the past few years – citing the Ras el-Hekma deal as an example.

He questioned whether the government could replicate this approach with new tracts of land in the Red Sea Governorate, given what he viewed as a lack of liquidity among investors and the mounting burden of external debt.

During his show “al-Hekaya” (The Story) broadcast on MBC Masr, Adib said that selling land has become a frequent solution the state has turned to in recent years in order to deal with a variety of issues.

“Over the last few years, every single crisis you faced was resolved only by selling land—just like what happened with Ras el-Hekma deal. In fact, two days before the Ras el-Hekma agreement was signed, the US dollar exchange rate was approaching LE 70”, he explained.

Help from the UAE

Revisiting the details of the Ras el-Hekma deal, Adib noted that the agreement provided the state with liquidity that helped it overcome financial pressures over the past two years.

He highlighted the role played by the UAE in making these funds available.

He remarked: “The Emirati leadership, with great generosity and solidarity, provided Egypt with a substantial cash sum—this was far beyond a typical corporate transaction. It is precisely what allowed the country to catch its breath over the last two years; otherwise, things might have spiraled downward.”

While acknowledging that the deal spurred economic activity, attracted investments, and generated tax revenue for the state, Adib emphasized that he still does not support relying on the sale of land as a recurring solution to crises.

“I am not in favor of selling land, even though some see no harm in it, even if the sale of Ras el-Hekma did indeed trigger economic activity, job creation, investment, and tax revenue for the state.”

Are there any investors?

Discussing the allocation of new land in the Red Sea Governorate, Adib recounted a conversation he had with a prominent businessman, who expressed concern about the difficulty of finding investors capable of purchasing the land, given the current liquidity crunch.

Adib quoted the businessman as saying: “Go ahead and invite someone to take this new land—nobody has any money, and those who do are holding onto every penny.”

The TV host linked these concerns to what he described as a global shortage of capital, saying: “The real issue is that there is simply no money—not in Egypt, not in the region, not in Europe, and not in America. So, if you’re looking for capital, it’s just not there; no one has the money to give you.”

US$165 Billion in External Debt

Moving beyond land sales, Adib addressed the broader question of how to repay the country’s external debt—which he stated amounts to $165 billion.

He called for a conference or the formation of a committee of experts and specialists to develop practical strategies for managing this debt.

Urging experts to provide clear solutions, he remarked, “I have yet to see a seminar or conference focused on how we might actually repay these debts; the discussion always centers on how the debt was incurred in the first place. Organize a conference or a committee to put forward proposals or concepts. No one in Egypt is answering the question: what are we going to do to pay off this debt?”

Adib continued, “I appeal to the experts: tell us, what do you see as the way forward? How could the debt be restructured or rescheduled? What are Egypt’s potential sources of revenue? We have nothing to hide.”

World.title: Teacher at Kafr Mansour Primary School suspended for alleged assault on pupil
World.content:
The Undersecretary of the Ministry of Education in Qalyubia, Yasser Mahmoud on Sunday ordered the suspension of a teacher at the Kafr Mansour Primary School in Kafr Shukr, pending investigations into reports that the teacher had allegedly assaulted a third-grade student and caused bleeding.

Mahmoud has referred the entire matter to the Administrative Prosecution for investigation.

He also requested a detailed medical report from the Health Insurance Hospital regarding the child’s condition, in order to determine whether the bleeding was a result of the teacher’s assault or another cause.

The Undersecretary explained that he visited the school where the incident took place, accompanied by a legal committee.

He also spoke with the student’s classmates, who confirmed the incident occurred as reported.

The father of the injured student was summoned to check on his son’s well-being and to hear his complaint.

Upon his arrival, the Undersecretary—in the presence of the legal committee—asked him when he first learned of his son’s injury.

The father replied that his son had returned home from school on Monday complaining of abdominal pain.

He added that his son was assaulted after asking for permission to use the restroom. He noted that, upon the child’s return from school, he discovered the boy was passing blood in his urine; he subsequently took him to the hospital for medical examinations and necessary treatment.

The father added that, upon learning the teacher had beaten his son inside the classroom, he went to the educational administration office in Kafr Shukr on Wednesday to file a formal complaint against the teacher.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Two new trains enter service on Egyptian Metro Line 1
World.content:
Egyptian Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir on Sunday oversaw the entry into service of the first two new air-conditioned trains on Metro Line 1.

These are part of a deal to supply 55 new trains – comprising 495 air-conditioned coaches – for Metro Line 1 (Helwan–New El-Marg), contracted with the French company Alstom.

Accompanied by French Ambassador to Cairo Éric Chevallier, the Chairman of the National Authority for Tunnels Tarek Gewaily, several ministry and authority officials, and representatives from Alstom, Wazir took a ride on one of the new trains from Saray al-Qubba Station to Sadat Station.

He then inspected the train’s modern technical and technological features, emphasizing the importance of continuing to develop existing lines and providing safe, modern, and high-quality transport services to citizens.

The minister emphasized that the new train deal is a cornerstone of the plan to modernize the fleet for the first line.

It includes the supply of 55 air-conditioned trains, as well as the provision of modern equipment for the Tora workshop, compatible with the technology of the new trains.

The agreement also covers maintenance services for a period of eight years, along with comprehensive overhauls for each train, including all necessary spare parts.

State of the art trains

He further explained that the new trains feature advanced technical and technological specifications designed to ensure the highest levels of comfort and safety for passengers.

These include modern air-conditioning systems, secure passageways between carriages that allow for easy movement within the train, and surveillance cameras, installed both in the driver’s cab and throughout the carriages.

This will enable the monitoring of the driver’s actions and the real-time transmission of this data to the control center.

The minister noted that this system is incorporated into all modern public transport modes, including the metro, the Light Rail Transit (LRT), and the high-speed electric train network.

A comprehensive control center will be established for all electric-powered rail transit systems, Wazir explained, alongside a unified control center for the entire railway network, which spans a total length of approximately 10,000 kilometers, to ensure rigorous oversight and continuous monitoring of operations.

The minister noted that the new trains feature LCD screens inside the carriages to display information and instructions, as well as screens above the side doors to indicate the final destination.

They also include designated spaces for wheelchairs, equipped with securing mechanisms for people with disabilities, and illuminated electronic maps showing the route and stations, all of which help make the metro easier to use, particularly for those with hearing impairments.

The minister emphasized that the state’s objective goes beyond just adding new trains to the first line; rather, it is implementing a comprehensive development process for every component of the system.

This initiative aims to achieve a qualitative leap in service quality, operational efficiency, and safety and security standards.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Showdown looms between Trump and Democrats over air traffic control meltdown
World.content:
The shutdown that snarled American aviation last week showed that fixing the country’s antiquated air traffic control system could hardly be more urgent. But the political conditions needed to drag it into the 21st century look increasingly elusive.

After thousands of delays and cancellations that disrupted the plans of more than a million people journeying to weddings, family events, funerals, work commitments and sports events, travel was nearing normality early Monday.

But recriminations over the nationwide ground stop are escalating, with the Trump administration shifting blame and demanding tens of billions more in funding while newly empowered congressional Democrats warn there will be no blank check.

Key questions include what caused the shutdown and whether it could happen again, especially with the traditional mass exodus at Thanksgiving looming; whether the White House has a plan and the capacity to fix the issue; how much will it cost to address; and how long it will take before a new system comes up to speed.

Any successful modernization effort would require a unified national effort, bipartisan purpose, a president with political capital to catalyze action, and a government trusted to undertake big infrastructure projects. All this raises the question of whether the administrative machinery that won World War II and the Cold War is still capable of nimbly doing big things swiftly and on budget.

The fallout from Friday’s ground stop suggests that few of those conditions exist, and the sudden exigency of upgrading the air traffic system will only heighten pressure on a lame-duck Congress that may struggle to keep the government open next month.

Air traffic control funding and reform are also likely to become an early test of the hazardous political era that will dawn when Democrats run Congress next year opposite a GOP president.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy looks on as technicians fix a sound issue during a press briefing at the Department of Transportation headquarters building in Washington, DC, on November 14. Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images

Trump finally weighs in

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy toured Sunday talk shows demanding action from Congress while assuring Americans they were safe in the air. “There hasn’t been investment in this network for decades … it’s the worst-kept secret in Washington. And the question becomes, well, when do we make the investments?” Duffy said on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

A complicating factor is that the latest incident appears to have been caused by the act of modernizing the system itself. This only underscores the complexity of overhauling hardware that is already over-stressed by air traffic volumes it was not designed to accommodate while it remains in operation.

Duffy told CNN the meltdown was triggered by an operation to change obsolete copper wire that apparently resulted in floods of data overwhelming the wider network. His explanation at least was an improvement on his imprecise White House news conference with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday, which produced few answers at a time when airports were mobbed by grounded travelers and then turned into a Trump-boosting session. “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin said, unironically, as chaos deepened and the commander in chief was most notable for his rare silence.

Trump finally weighed in Sunday on Truth Social, blaming failures on the Biden administration and demanding Congress fund modernization with a huge package rather than in “drips and drabs.” But he seemed just as concerned with other priorities, including a judge’s order temporarily halting his plan to replace a beloved public golf links and park in Washington with a championship course.

Friday’s graphic illustration of the air traffic control quandary might be the spur needed to prod Congress to act.

But the president’s approach and record mean a new funding request will be contentious, especially when Democrats take over. The administration’s knee-jerk style of governing was on display Friday, when Duffy upped his request for funding from $30 billion to $50 billion without providing any details on why or how funds would be spent.

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer for the party’s leadership in the chamber, said it was “rich” for Duffy to complain since Congress had already given the administration what it wanted with $12 billion in Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill,” of which only a third had been spent.

“I will support whatever level of money is necessary to fix this problem. We should fix this problem on a bipartisan basis,” Van Hollen said on “State of the Union.” But he warned, “If they need more, they should come up and justify it.”

Democratic Rep. Jim Himes claimed the administration had helped cause the debacle, blaming Elon Musk for forcing 1,300 Federal Aviation Administration employees to retire or resign and firing 400 probationary employees as part of Department of Government Efficiency purges last year. “What you’re seeing is the wages of what Elon Musk did, where he just gutted an entity that affected millions of Americans last Friday,” Himes said on CBS’ “Face the Nation.”

President Donald Trump departs Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, on November 15. Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images

Does Trump have the bandwidth to fix the problem?

The Trump administration’s recent struggles and controversies hardly enhance confidence in its capacity to govern effectively and to fix air traffic control.

The far easier task of restoring the Reflecting Pool on Washington’s National Mall — a Trump pet project — turned into a farce. The White House is currently gripped by a scandal over Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief instrumental to shaping Trump’s AI policy who resigned over extramarital affairs, including with a woman described by a US official as a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

Meanwhile, Trump still hasn’t ended a war with Iran he promised would take mere weeks. It flared up again this weekend and will shortly head into its 10th month. And on Friday, the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles.

The loss of public trust in Trump was underscored by the GOP’s disastrous losses in the midterm elections.

The administration’s failure in some cases to spend money appropriated by Congress on its intended purpose will bolster demands from lawmakers for strict conditions attached to any new funding.

Duffy is quite correct to say that underfunding and delays in upgrading air traffic control have been a common thread across multiple administrations. But there is growing concern over the current White House’s management of the situation.

A report by the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan federal agency, warned in September that while the FAA had made progress in modernizing outdated air traffic control systems, “it could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions.” The report warned that the FAA lacked a lifecycle cost estimate or master schedule for related projects — a failing it said could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems.

No one could argue that Friday’s emergency came as a surprise. Lawmakers and administrations have been warning for decades that the system is old and overburdened, and its problems speak to a wider failure to overhaul critical infrastructure.

Trump has often compared US airports unfavorably with modern travel facilities in China and in the developing world. But modernization efforts in the US are often hampered by infighting in Congress and a dysfunctional budget process as the government careens between shutdown crises and fiscal cliffs.

A traveler looks for his luggage at Los Angeles International Airport on Friday, November 13. William Liang/AP

While Trump put the blame on Biden, Republican majorities have regularly clipped funding requests for aviation industry modernization from Democratic presidents. In 2011, Van Hollen, then a member of the House, warned that “our nation’s aviation infrastructure critically needs rehabilitation” and accused GOP leaders of paring back funding to 2008 levels. In 2015, President Barack Obama’s Budget Director Shaun Donovan warned Republicans that their $255 million cut to a $2.6 billion FAA request would slow modernization that “would lead to worsening air traffic delays and higher replacement costs in the future.”

In 2025, Democrats raised concerns about Trump’s $12.5 billion FAA request, warning that even Capitol Hill Republicans and those in the White House were divided on priorities. “Before we pour billions into the nation’s air traffic control system, we should ensure we have the policies, implementation plan, timing, and funding level right so we are not throwing hard-earned taxpayer money at projects and programs that will not actually fix the problem,” Democratic committee members wrote in a letter to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation panel’s chairman Ted Cruz.

Last week’s debacle at America’s airports will heighten such questions and may degenerate into a confrontation between a Democratic Congress and a Republican president next year.

Illinois Democratic Sen. Tammy Duckworth accused Republicans of finding money for Trump’s vanity projects during two years in control of Congress. “But none to fix our air traffic control system? Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch,” she wrote on X.

But Duffy is pleading for help

“I have systems that are from the ’90s. I have radar that are from the ‘60s and ‘70s,” he told CNN. “We can fight about all kinds of things in America, but let’s not fight about this.”

In theory, an air traffic control emergency that could compromise the safety of every American flyer is crying out for bipartisan compromise.

The question now therefore is whether the nation’s deep and enduring polarization will again thwart efforts to solve one of its most pressing crises.

World.title: Army soldier files whistleblower complaint against the Pentagon over Iranian strike that killed 6 US service members
World.content:
One of the US Army soldiers that survived an Iranian strike that hit a makeshift operations center in Kuwait and killed six has submitted a whistleblower complaint alleging that the Pentagon did not listen to concerns about the lack of proper protection for troops, according to a copy of the disclosure obtained by CNN.

The complaint, submitted last week to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS, comes as Democrats are poised to launch wide-ranging investigations into the Trump administration and its handling of the Iran war when they take control of Congress in January.

CNN has reached out to the congressional committees and the Pentagon for comment.

Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom outlined why he submitted the report in an exclusive interview with CBS’ Norah O’Donnell on “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday, describing the March 1 attack as a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.”

“We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn,” he said. He added that some people described the operations center as a “trailer park.”

The six US Army Reserve soldiers killed in the strike at Kuwait’s Shuaiba port were the first US service members killed in the US’ war with Iran. Dozens, including Ramsbottom, were wounded.

While senior Pentagon officials said at the time that the building was fortified, a source familiar with the site previously told CNN it was only surrounded by concrete barriers that would provide protection from car bombs but had nothing to shield it from drones or missiles. CNN also previously reported that the attack came quickly and with no warning or sirens to alert troops to evacuate or get into a bunker, according to a source familiar with the situation.

Ramsbottom said he brought up the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors in various meetings and was told: “We don’t have to worry about protection.” Military leaders later said that they were going to try to get a counter-drone system sent to the site, but “it never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested,” he said.

The installation did not have a physician or a fixed aid station when the drone strike happened, according to the whistleblower report. There was only one ambulance at the site.

Ramsbottom has made similar claims in interviews with multiple outlets since the attack. In an interview with CNN affiliate KOAA news in April, he recalled that while the facility had protections for “legacy threats” like mortar fire or car bombs, it wasn’t prepared for modern drone warfare.

“It was well-fortified for that type of thinking from pre-Russian invasion of Ukraine. It was a pretty well fortified base. But it wasn’t well prepared for the type of fight that we’re getting into,” he told the news station.

At a press conference after the attack in March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the US has “incredible air defenders,” but acknowledged that “one” projectile had made it through in the attack.

“Every once in a while you might have one — unfortunately, we call it a squirter — that makes its way through. And in that particular case, it happened to hit a tactical operation center that was, that was fortified, but it — these are powerful weapons,” he said.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who sits on the House Armed Services Committee and is the top Democrat on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has asked Hegseth to appear in a classified briefing to answer questions and provide “all force protection assessments” about the facility at the Shuaiba port.

World.title: Estonia to shut its border with Russia, blaming Moscow for foiled arson plot
World.content:
Estonia is to close its border with Russia after blaming Moscow for a suspected attack on a defense technology company, Estonia’s prime minister said Sunday.

Eight people have been detained after allegedly attempting an arson attack on the company overnight on Saturday, authorities say. No one was injured.

Estonian security services say the attempted attack was carried out on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU.

“If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face,” Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement Sunday.

“Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable,” he added.

Border crossings will be closed from December 1, and Michal did not say when they would reopen.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Russian state news agency TASS that the move is part of a wider pattern of “Russophobia.”

“We’ll check all this for veracity,” Zakharova said. “But if these are their real plans, then they’re part of another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia.”

Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the “attempted sabotage” this weekend was “yet another reminder that Russia’s hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine” and that “hostile actions must have consequences.” He said he expected further sanctions to be adopted targeting Russian individuals and entities at a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Brussels, Belgium on Monday.

Ukraine has commended Estonia for its move to close the border, hailing it as an example of effective action against Russian hostility and encouraging Europe to take note.

“Estonia has shown that Russian sabotage can and should have consequences beyond diplomatic condemnation,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X. “This approach deserves wider support across Europe.”

Russia has long been accused of carrying out sabotage and other hybrid attacks against Europe but has repeatedly denied the claims.

Back in September, European officials pointed the finger at the Kremlin following a series of incidents that appeared to target NATO members.

A railway line on which several former Western diplomats were traveling was struck by a Russian drone near Ukraine’s border with Poland, while another drone – likely of Russian origin – was shot down in Lithuania. A third drone also washed ashore in Poland.

Elsewhere, a Danish helicopter was narrowly missed by a Russian flare, and Dutch rail traffic was significantly disrupted after metal pipes that had been fitted across the tracks triggered short circuits, turned traffic signals to red and forced trains to an inconvenient stop.

Despite denying involvement, Moscow has remained the alleged culprit. European NATO-member allies have deemed the actions an escalation of conflict against the bloc – characterizing the attacks as measures designed to antagonize without triggering all-out war.

World.title: Turns out the AI king wasn’t untouchable
World.content:
Big Tech CEOs have an aura of invincibility.

A small handful of men have amassed extraordinary power and run a collection of the world’s most valuable tech companies that make cutting-edge products fueling global markets and the economy. They’ve seldom been tested and never brought down. OpenAI tried and failed to fire its CEO Sam Altman. Elon Musk hung on to power after badly damaging Tesla’s reputation during his stint in politics.

That invincibility myth was shattered Thursday when Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO for 33 years, ally of the President of the United States and cofounder of the world’s most valuable AI company, resigned.

Many business leaders have been taken down by scandals like Huang’s – the downfall of former CEOs of American Apparel, Boeing, Intel, McDonald’s and Hewlett-Packard all played out in somewhat similar fashion.

But none come close to the magnitude and significance of Huang’s ouster.

“This is one of a kind,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. “In the corporate world, this is by far the biggest fall.”

It sends a clear message: If Huang can be forced out, any leader can.

It took a public scandal

Huang appeared untouchable.

He very well may have been – up until this week, before his infidelity spilled out into public view and could no longer be ignored by the board.

Nvidia and Huang had been synonymous for decades. He maintained an extraordinarily flat organization, with 60 direct reports and no clear succession plan. He boasted that the company was structured such that he was uniquely qualified to run it.

Huang’s genius was the stuff of legend. He correctly predicted in 2013 – a decade before ChatGPT – that the company’s graphics processors would serve as the foundation for AI. He was right, and his company became the first ever to be worth $5 trillion on the stock market.

The Nvidia Groq 3 LPU chip. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images

So the board failed to challenge Huang, despite numerous missteps and bad bets along the way. It was apparently unfazed by reports dating back more than a year about Nvidia’s odd relationship with Megaspeed – the major Nvidia customer run by Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Jensen Huang had a relationship. The board failed to investigate Huang when the New York Times reported last month that US intelligence feared Alice Huang may be a spy, or when photos of its CEO and Alice Huang were plastered all over the internet.

It took the scandal becoming an unavoidable topic of public conversation this week for the board to hire an outside counsel to investigate. It took another revelation – by The New York Times that Huang had an alleged affair with an executive who reports to him – to ultimately force him to resign.

That made the board negligent in its duties, said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors.

“The single biggest failure of corporate boards is succession planning, and there’s no evidence that was done here,” said Minow. “We love to think about superstar CEOs and founders, but they’re never as special as they think they are.”

Huang’s aura of invincibility stems from one of his favorite boasts: Nvidia’s humble 1993 founding during a meeting held at a Denny’s – and how its shaky beginnings forced him to repeatedly save the company from near extinction. He made the company’s motto: “Our company is 30 days from going out of business.”

Jensen Huang holds up a wafer lined with chips at the company headquarters on January 17, 2002. Julie Jacobson/AP

But the board misjudged that past success as evidence of Huang’s unique talents, Minow said.

The biggest risk for the life of a company, she argued, is not failure – because when a company is on the verge of destruction, everyone is working together and problem solving. Instead, the biggest risk is when the company is doing spectacularly well: No one can sustain that hockey stick-like growth, and the board starts attributing success to intangible things like its uniquely talented leaders.

“That puts a lot of pressure on the snowflake genius from Denny’s,” Minow said. “It’s like a baseball team with a winning streak no one can explain. The whole team starts wearing lucky socks. Nvidia’s board thought it had its lucky CEO.”

The myth of the invincible tech CEO

Huang may have wielded incredible power at Nvidia, but more recent tech founders have worked to place a buffer around themselves even more durable than Huang’s.

Huang is an outlier among his tech CEO peers: He controls just 3.6 percent of his company’s shares. Many founders, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and soon-to-be public Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei all have dual class stock arrangements that give them significantly more voting power over common shareholders – and effectively unilateral power over their corporations’ governance.

Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta, walk to a press briefing with President Donald Trump on September 29, 2026. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Even those stronger insulators are permeable. Shareholders aren’t powerless against dual class stock structures or seemingly untouchable CEOs: They can bombard companies with lawsuits – which have already started against Nvidia.

And it’s not clear that even a CEO as wealthy and powerful as Musk could survive a scandal like Huang’s. Musk’s friendly, hand-picked Tesla board began a CEO replacement search and successfully pressured him to return his focus to the company after spending much of 2024 and 2025 engaged almost exclusively in the political spotlight, damaging Tesla’s global brand in the process.

“There’s a lot of myth-making in tech that there’s one person who is uniquely qualified to run the company,” said Sonnenfeld. “That’s not true: They have human frailties, they’re imperfect, and they’re replaceable.”

Nvidia board’s decision here was cut and dry: Anyone else at Nvidia would have been let go if they had engaged in Huang’s alleged conduct. Huang may have put his company’s trade secrets at risk of theft by a foreign competitor. He lost trust with Nvidia’s customers and demonstrated a lack of candor with his board. Huang lost the legitimacy to lead.

So that means the CEO – even the visionary leader of the chipmaking bedrock of AI – can be held responsible, just like any other employee who may have violated the company’s code of conduct.

And, on Thursday, he was kicked out of the company he built.

World.title: Beyond the GERD: Ethiopia’s shifting regional balance
World.content:
The dispute between Egypt and Ethiopia is no longer a mere quarrel over a completed dam, deadlocked negotiations, or traded diplomatic barbs.

Crucially, Addis Ababa now views the Nile’s waters as a cornerstone of a grander ambition to reshape its regional standing—an agenda that links hydropolitics with demands for Red Sea access to tilt the balance of power across the Horn of Africa.

The recent launch of the “Nile and Red Sea Strategic Forum” in Addis Ababa underscores this shift.

While legally registered as a civil society organization rather than a state body or formal negotiating party, its mandate extends well beyond traditional civic work.

The forum is designed to mobilize scholars, policy experts, and legal specialists to shape public discourse, draft policy, and bolster Ethiopian diplomacy on both the Nile dispute and maritime access—all while forging external partnerships to advance state strategy.

What matters here is not the forum’s immediate size or clout, but the trajectory it signals.

Moving past reactive rhetoric during moments of crisis, Ethiopia is building a permanent apparatus—spanning research, law, and media—to continuously manufacture arguments and lend intellectual and legal legitimacy to its positions both at home and abroad.

Even more telling is the deliberate fusion of the Nile and Red Sea dossiers. Through this framing, water is elevated beyond merely just technical management, and maritime access is elevated beyond a commercial bid to lower shipping costs.

Both are cast as existential matters of national security and inherent historical and geopolitical “rights” designed to rally both the Ethiopian public and international institutions.

Egypt must read this message clearly: Addis Ababa is actively widening the arena of contention. It aims to pivot the debate away from the technical operating rules of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) toward a wholesale renegotiation of the regional order.

The core questions are now far broader: Who holds the authority to manage shared resources? Who dictates the rules of engagement? And what place does Ethiopia claim in the strategic equation of the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?

Remarks made two days ago by Ethiopian Minister of Water and Energy Habtamu Itefa reinforce this reality.

Declaring that the GERD’s completion proved his country’s resilience against external pressure, he noted that the expertise gained will streamline future water projects.

Though he named no specific initiatives, his message is unmistakable: Addis Ababa views the GERD as an opening chapter, not a final destination.

Even without hard evidence of signed contracts or secured financing for new dams, waiting until excavators break ground before responding would be a grave strategic miscalculation.

As Ethiopia builds the institutional machinery to craft and export its narrative, Egypt can no longer afford a reactive posture, perpetually responding to facts on the ground set by others.

Egypt must urgently evolve its own strategic toolkit—the pressing question now is how.

World.title: LNTA, Nightlife Liberia Launch Festive Season Calendar Featuring Over 70 Events
World.content:
Monrovia – The Liberia National Tourism Authority (LNTA), in collaboration with Nightlife Liberia, has launched the “Never Done Jamming” festive season campaign, unveiling a calendar of more than 70 entertainment events scheduled across Liberia from November 2026 through January 2027.

The initiative, anchored by the Liberia Nightlife Essentials Calendar, brings together concerts, music festivals, beach parties, cultural celebrations and other entertainment activities under a coordinated platform aimed at promoting Liberia as a festive season destination.

The campaign seeks to strengthen domestic tourism, attract international visitors and encourage members of the Liberian diaspora to spend the festive season in the country.



As part of the initiative, LNTA’s Unforgettable Liberia digital platform will provide access to the event calendar, updates on upcoming activities and timely notifications, enabling residents and visitors to discover and participate in entertainment and cultural events across the country.

The platform is also expected to increase visibility for local entertainers, event organizers, hospitality establishments and other businesses operating within Liberia’s tourism and entertainment sectors.

The partnership reflects LNTA’s efforts to promote tourism through public-private collaboration, digital innovation and entertainment-driven initiatives.

By bringing together Liberia’s nightlife, cultural attractions and hospitality experiences, the “Never Done Jamming” campaign seeks to showcase the country’s entertainment offerings while creating opportunities for tourism-related businesses during the festive season.

The campaign is expected to run through January 2027.
