World.title: Liberia’s Waste Economy: Can the Country Turn Plastic Pollution into Opportunity?
World.content:
A solar-powered backpack made from discarded advertising banners by Liberia’s Ignite EcoGear, turning waste materials into useful products. Photo: Liberia’s Ignite EcoGear

By Aria Deemie

Liberia’s waste-recycling initiatives are growing, but limited funding, machinery and infrastructure are preventing them from operating at scale.

The country’s waste policy provides a framework for recycling and private-sector investment, but weak data and implementation gaps remain.

At COP31, waste pickers and climate leaders are calling for greater investment, recognition of waste workers and a shift toward preventing waste rather than simply managing it.

Discarded advertising banners are being turned into solar-powered backpacks in Liberia. At Ignite EcoGear , the materials are repurposed into bags fitted with solar panels, rechargeable batteries and LED lights, giving discarded materials a new use.

Archie Forpoh, who runs the initiative, sees waste as an opportunity to create products and businesses. “Waste is not the end of a product’s journey; it can be the beginning of another opportunity,” he said.



While Forpoh sees waste as an opportunity to create products and businesses, waste pickers say their contribution to recycling must also be recognized.

“We make a living from waste, we work with waste, but we do not want to become waste,” said María Soledad Mella Vidal, a Brazilian waste picker and representative of the International Alliance of Waste Pickers.

Her words speak to a wider challenge facing countries such as Liberia, where waste collection and recycling initiatives are growing but investment, infrastructure and recognition remain limited. At the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, waste has been elevated as a priority in the COP Presidency’s Action Agenda for the first time, drawing attention to waste reduction, recycling and the people whose livelihoods depend on recovering discarded materials.

The COP31 Zero Waste Action Agenda aims to halve the projected increase in global annual waste generation by 2035. For Liberia, the question is whether existing initiatives can grow into a functioning waste economy.

Lucia N. Yeenee, founder and executive director of Zero Plastic Liberia , said the organization was established in 2024 in response to plastic pollution and weak waste management systems.Its activities include community clean-ups, environmental education, youth mentorship and campaigns. Yeenee said the organization has expanded across eight counties, engaging more than 15,000 students and community members in 2025. It has also mobilized 80 community members in Grand Bassa County, whom it calls eco-warriors, to help organize clean-ups and educate residents about environmental protection. The organization has partnered with more than 11 institutions.

Zero Plastic Liberia volunteers take part in a community cleanup as the organization works to reduce plastic pollution and promote better waste management in Liberia. Photo: Zero Plastic Liberia

Despite collecting more than 150 tonnes of waste, Zero Plastic Liberia still sorts and stores much of its recovered plastic because it lacks the facility and machinery to process it at scale.

“Liberia must move from seeing plastic as waste to recognizing it as a resource and an opportunity,” Yeenee said.

“The challenge is not that Liberia lacks people willing to act. The challenge is that we have not invested enough in the systems that can turn their commitment into sustainable results,” she added.

Liberia has a policy framework intended to address some of these gaps. The Environmental Protection Agency published the National Solid Waste Management Policy in October 2024. It outlines measures to improve waste collection, separation, recycling and recovery, while encouraging private investment and public-private partnerships.

The policy also calls for extended producer responsibility, incentives for recycling markets and health protections for waste workers. But these commitments depend on implementation, financing and enforcement.

Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency Executive Director Emmanuel Yarkpawolo said the government was considering legislative measures to strengthen plastic waste management. A proposal submitted by Senator Augustine Chea of Sinoe County is under consideration, while the EPA is preparing its own draft. Public consultations are expected after COP31.

Liberia also lacks reliable national data on the amount and types of waste generated, collected and processed, Yarkpawolo said.

“That data is not clear right now,” he said.The challenges are evident around W(h)ein Town, Monrovia’s largest landfill and the country’s only engineered landfill. In a September 2024 investigation , this reporter documented residents’ concerns about unsafe water, damaged reservoirs and waste spilling into homes. In 2026, residents again called for the landfill’s closure , citing health and environmental risks.

Waste piles up at the W(h)ein Town landfill near Monrovia, where residents have raised concerns about water contamination and health risks. Photo credit: Sammy Russ Vaye

Speaking at the Zero Waste Museum in Antalya during the launch of the Fair Ton initiative, Carlos Silva Filho, senior adviser to the COP31 Climate High-Level Champion and adviser to the Zero Waste Foundation, said reliable data is essential to attracting investment.

Carlos Silva Filho, senior adviser to the COP31 Climate High-Level Champion, speaks during the launch of the Fair Ton initiative at the Zero Waste Museum in Antalya, Türkiye. Photo: Aria Deemie

“When we look in terms of funding, the first thing we need is reliable data. If we do have reliable data, I’m sure that funds will come. Because we really need to understand what is there, what is needed, and plan and implement this alternative infrastructure and system,” he said.

He also stressed the need to recognize the people who collect and recover waste.

“We really need to understand and value the people that are working on a daily basis to ensure that we have a livable, clean, and healthy environment,” he said.

Silva Filho said waste recovery is also an economic development opportunity, reducing dependence on the extraction of finite natural resources.

“And third, because we really need to understand that it is also an economic development matter. Because we cannot continue extracting raw materials and natural resources from the planet, because they are finite. They will run out. We are really going at the speed of light, so we need to recover those resources that we already have,” he said.

For Desmond Alugnoa, Africa program manager for the Zero Waste and Climate Program at the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives , building a successful waste system starts with organizing communities and including informal waste workers.

Alugnoa said waste pickers should be part of a wider movement because their daily work gives them practical knowledge of how different materials can be recovered and reused.

“Waste is generated by every individual and every household. Now, to collect all of it, you require a big movement. You require a strong movement,” he said.

He identified source separation, or sorting waste where it is generated, as another essential step. It does not require expensive bins, he said.

“The most basic infrastructure you need is not fancy waste bins. It’s just any container that you can put waste in. That is good enough,” Alugnoa said.

Organic waste can be separated for uses such as composting and biogas production, while plastics can be sorted and prepared for recycling. But processing waste at a commercial scale requires land, storage space and suitable machinery.

“If you are going to recycle it yourself, you need some basic machinery that is efficient,” he said.

Asked about a youth-led effort in Liberia reportedly using plastic in charcoal production, Alugnoa warned against burning plastics because of the pollutants released in the process.

“When you burn plastics, it emits a lot of pollution. And those pollutions that are emitted are very toxic to human health,” he said, cautioning that such projects risk becoming false solutions.

He pointed to Ghana’s efforts to organize waste pickers as one lesson Liberia could consider. The Green Africa Youth Organization ,with support from the Ministry of Local Government and development partners, launched the Federation of Informal Sector Waste Workers Associations of Ghana on July 31, 2026. The federation brings together waste worker leaders from all 16 regions and gives them a platform to engage government, municipalities and businesses. Ghana’s Minister for Labor, Jobs and Employment, Abdul-Rashid Pelpuo, confirmed the union’s formation as lawful under the country’s Labor Act.

Ghana also has entrepreneurs developing products from construction waste, electronic waste and plastics, including school desks made from recovered plastic.

For Liberia’s waste businesses, however, access to start-up funding remains a major obstacle. Alugnoa said grants and philanthropic funding are often better suited to covering the initial costs of land, storage and machinery than loans.

“There should be more philanthropy-based funding for the CAPEX, the capital cost, which is the cost that you incur setting up the business,” he said.

He also urged young entrepreneurs not to expect quick returns.

“Do not see it as quick money,” Alugnoa said, advising businesses to start with public education and source separation to obtain cleaner materials that are easier to process.

Some private recycling activity is already taking place in Liberia. Yarkpawolo said a facility on Bushrod Island collects plastic sachets and bottles and turns them into products such as washing buckets, plates and plumbing pipes. He said some materials are also exported to Sierra Leone. The scale of the operation and its contribution to the country’s overall waste recovery remain unclear.

But recycling is not only about the materials recovered or the products made from them. It also depends on recognizing the people who collect and sort waste and the environmental services they provide.

Brazilian waste picker Severino Lima Jr., president of the International Alliance of Waste Pickers, said their work should be treated with dignity, not charity.

“I am not a poor, pitiful thing. I don’t live in the landfill just to survive,” Lima said. “It is a dignified form of work that needs to be improved and humanized.”

The alliance is developing the Fair Ton platform with Fundación Avina , Red LACRE (the Latin American Network of Recyclers), and Global Methane Hub . The methodology combines scientific research and local knowledge to measure the materials recovered by waste pickers and the greenhouse gas emissions avoided through their work. It aims to generate evidence that can help secure recognition and financing for waste picker organizations.

Silva Filho said the COP31 Solutions Platform is intended to connect projects and help turn climate commitments into local action.

“This is where ambition becomes implementation,” he said. The platform aims “to connect the different initiatives, to accelerate results, to maximize climate action, and to deliver solutions on the ground at the local level for the people.”

For Yeenee, Liberia’s opportunity lies not simply in collecting more waste but in changing how the country produces, uses and disposes of materials. That will require stronger systems to support communities, create opportunities for young people and prevent plastic from becoming pollution.

“We must stop asking how to manage the waste we produce and start asking how to prevent waste from being produced in the first place,” she said.

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership , a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

World.title: Raise Your Hand Foundation Backs Faith University, Says It Has Sponsored Over 600 Liberian Students
World.content:
BOYS TOWN, Margibi County – The United States-based Raise Your Hand Foundation says it has sponsored more than 600 Liberian students since 2008, providing financial assistance to university students struggling to complete their education due to economic hardship.

By Edwin Genoway, Jr.

The foundation’s Country Representative, Leviticus Whamah, disclosed this during an engagement with journalists following his presentation to the graduating class of Faith University in Boyce Town, Margibi County.



Whamah said the organization, headquartered in Roseville, California, has worked with several universities and colleges across Liberia to provide scholarships to students who face difficulties paying their tuition and other academic expenses.

He explained that the foundation’s intervention is primarily intended to prevent students from abandoning their education because of financial constraints.

“Since 2008, we have sponsored over 600 students in Liberia,” Whamah said, naming institutions such as Nimba University, Grand Bassa University, Stella Maris Polytechnic, Bomi Community College, the University of Liberia and AMU among its partner institutions.

According to him, the foundation provides full tuition scholarships, graduation-fee assistance and, in some cases, transportation and accommodation support for students experiencing severe financial difficulties.

“Our major work here has been providing scholarships. We make sure we provide scholarships to those who find it very difficult to continue their university education,” he stated.

Whamah explained that students seeking assistance must already be enrolled at a university that works with the foundation. They must also be recommended by their institution’s admissions office, which is expected to identify students genuinely experiencing financial difficulties.

He emphasized that the foundation does not directly provide admission funding to high school graduates who have not yet enrolled in a university.

“The first thing is that you must be in school, but you are having challenges going to school. Maybe you are dropping every semester because you cannot get your tuition on time. We work with these kinds of people to sponsor them,” he explained.

Whamah further disclosed that the foundation’s scholarship program places particular emphasis on science-related disciplines rather than covering every academic program.

He said the organization had previously engaged Margibi Haven College over a proposed partnership to support female students pursuing science-related courses. However, the initiative did not progress following the departure of the institution’s president and the lack of subsequent institutional support.

Faith University Credits Foundation for Institutional Support

Meanwhile, Faith University President Rev. Dr. Tailey W. Garley has credited the foundation for its contributions to the institution’s academic programs, infrastructure and human capacity development.

Garley described the foundation as an important partner that has supported the university since its early days, including sponsorship for nearly all of its programs and contributions to infrastructure development.

He said one of the foundation’s most significant contributions has been its investment in human capacity, noting that several teachers at the institution, from early childhood development through higher academic levels, have benefited from its sponsorship.

The university president also disclosed that the foundation was fully sponsoring a current workshop organized for the institution.

According to Garley, the sponsorship covers participants’ transportation reimbursements, learning materials, meals and souvenirs.

He said the support demonstrates the foundation’s commitment not only to students but also to strengthening the institution and improving the capacity of its workforce.

University Defends Academic Standards

Addressing questions about Faith University’s academic performance compared to other higher institutions, Garley acknowledged that the university lacked the empirical data needed to make evidence-based comparisons.

However, he described Faith University as an institution where academic competition is strong and students earn their honors based on merit.

He also rejected allegations of academic misconduct, insisting that the university does not tolerate bribery and that instructors do not sell pamphlets to students.

To support his argument about the quality of the institution’s academic preparation, Garley recounted an experience involving the chief executive of an information technology firm.

He said the executive contacted him after the university’s information technology students demonstrated strong performance, expressing surprise at their level of competence.

According to Garley, the executive told him he was “very shocked” by the students’ performance, which the university president cited as evidence of the institution’s learning environment and academic preparation.

Third Commencement Set for November 28

Garley also announced that Faith University will hold its third commencement convocation on November 28.

He explained that students undergo career-development seminars and are required to take an exit examination as part of the university’s graduation process.

The university president said these activities are intended to prepare graduating students for life beyond the classroom and assess their readiness to enter the professional world.

The collaboration between Faith University and Raise Your Hand Foundation highlights the role of institutional partnerships in supporting higher education, particularly in a country where financial challenges continue to prevent some students from completing their studies.

With the foundation reporting more than 600 scholarship beneficiaries since 2008, its leadership says it remains committed to supporting Liberian students, while Faith University’s president maintains that the partnership has also contributed to the institution’s broader development.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-Minister Jailed, Ex-VP Behind Bars, Economist Grounded. Opposition Sees a Pattern Leading to Weah
World.content:
Monrovia – The rice arrived in April 2023: 29,412 white sacks stacked in a warehouse, a gift from Saudi Arabia for Liberians made homeless by floods and fires. Officials in suits and Saudi aid workers in green vests posed in front of the pile for the cameras.

By Rodney D Sieh

Three and a half years later, the man at the centre of that photograph, former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, faces 10 years in prison. On Friday, inside the Temple of Justice in Monrovia, Judge Ousman Feika refused his request for a new trial and sentenced him and several co-defendants over the diversion of more than 25,000 bags of that rice. Prosecutors said the rice ended up on market stalls instead of with disaster victims. Within hours, Kemayah’s lawyers said they would appeal to the Supreme Court.



By the weekend, Weah’s Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) had issued a statement that went well beyond the case. It warned that its patience “must not be mistaken for weakness.” It accused President Joseph Boakai’s government of using courts and prisons as “instruments of political intimidation.” And it raised, without quite stating it, a question now common in Monrovia: after Kemayah, will they come for Weah?

‘Reckless, Provocative’

George Weah is the only African to have been named world footballer of the year. He grew up in a Monrovia slum, governed Liberia from 2018 to 2024, and handed over power peacefully after losing the 2023 election to Boakai, then 78, a veteran politician. Weah, now 60, has made no secret that he wants his old job back.

The CDC’s statement opens by condemning a publication it attributes to Philibert Browne. The party says the publication invokes Weah’s name in a way that is “reckless, provocative, and potentially harmful” to his reputation and his personal safety. It did not say what the publication alleged. It asked the government to guarantee the former president’s “security, dignity, and fundamental rights,” and criticised official “silence.”

There is no public sign that Weah is under investigation. But his party is clearly preparing supporters for that possibility, and setting up any future case against him as political before it begins.

A List of Grievances

To make its case, the CDC lists people. Each name carries a story.

Kemayah. He was Weah’s chief diplomat and now leads his own small party, the Movement for Economic Empowerment. The CDC says Weah chose him to deliver his message at the party’s Martyrs’ Day rally in Kinjor, Grand Cape Mount County, on November 7, six days before he was sentenced. His family has suffered too. His mother, known as Ma-Watta, died in March, and the family links her decline to the stress of his arrest.

Jewel Howard-Taylor. Weah’s vice president, 63 years old and the ex-wife of the jailed former warlord-president Charles Taylor. She has been in Monrovia Central Prison since August on drug-trafficking and money-laundering charges. Her lawyers asked that she be allowed to await trial outside jail because she suffers from asthma. The court refused.

Samuel Tweah. Weah’s finance minister and the most senior official of his government to be prosecuted, accused over the handling of more than US$6.2 million. A jury acquitted him in May, and the CDC celebrated. Then Judge Feika, the same judge who sentenced Kemayah on Friday, ruled that the integrity of the proceedings had been compromised. He set aside the not-guilty verdict, declared a mistrial, and sent all 15 jurors to prison for contempt. Tweah has since written to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, calling his prosecution part of a campaign to weaken the CDC before the 2029 vote.

Samuel Jackson. A well-known economist and television commentator. In October, he was seen at the Temple of Justice being helped along by two men because he was struggling to walk. Since then, he has posted a photograph of himself lying in bed and pleaded for permission to travel abroad for medical treatment. He wrote that he wants fair treatment, not sympathy.

County superintendents. The officials who run Grand Gedeh and Grand Cape Mount counties, both of which recently hosted large CDC rallies, lost their jobs. The party says that is no coincidence.

Holes in the Narrative

Look closely and the list is uneven.

The CDC includes Thelma Duncan-Sawyer, Weah’s former deputy foreign minister, among those suffering “accelerated judicial action.” But the jury in the rice case appears to have acquitted her. It cleared three defendants in all. A court determined to punish the opposition does not usually set its targets free.

Jackson’s case is a personal tragedy, not an obvious political prosecution. He is charged with manslaughter and related offences over the March death of his wife, Toni Khumalo Jackson, a South African lawyer. Police say forensic evidence points to negligence. Jackson says she was injured in a fall, and he denies the charges. His health deserves humane treatment from the court. That does not make his prosecution a political act.

The superintendent claim is murky as well. Grand Gedeh received a new acting superintendent in September, months after the CDC’s June rally there. And Boakai has dismissed officials across his own government without explanation this year, including his own justice minister.

The Government’s Own Goals

Still, the government has handed its critics plenty of material.

The Tweah case is the clearest example. Overturning a jury’s acquittal and jailing the jurors who delivered it may have been legally justified. If the proceedings really were compromised, the court had a duty to act. But to a political audience it looks like a system that will not accept a not-guilty verdict for a CDC minister. Every jury that has sat in Criminal Court ‘C’ since then has known what happened to the last one.

Kemayah was convicted on a split verdict. The jury did not find him guilty of theft, and a prosecution witness testified that he halted the rice distribution once reports emerged that sacks were being sold. Liberia’s police chief publicly linked Howard-Taylor to the country’s record cocaine seizure, even as other officials insisted the two cases were separate. And when a president fires people without saying why, others will supply the reasons.

The biggest problem is a simple one. Every high-profile defendant so far served under Weah. Until the anti-corruption drive reaches someone close to Boakai, the charge of “selective justice” will keep landing.

Taking It Abroad

The CDC says it will “document abuses” and take its complaints to “domestic, regional, and international institutions.” In practice, that means West Africa’s regional bloc ECOWAS, foreign embassies and human rights monitors, following the path Tweah has already taken to the United Nations.

The statement closes on a line meant to rally supporters and to be read by diplomats: “Political opposition is not a crime. Loyalty to a former President is not a crime.”

Who Answers the Question?

Liberia is a small country of about five million people. It spent 14 years at war and two decades rebuilding fragile institutions. Its courts are now carrying a heavy load. The government says they are finally delivering accountability. The opposition says they are being used against it. Most Liberians are left somewhere in between: they want officials punished for stealing from flood victims, and they also want to be sure the judges are fair.

Kemayah’s appeal, Tweah’s retrial, Howard-Taylor’s trial and the government’s willingness to prosecute its own people will decide which account wins. For now, the CDC has asked the question. The government has not yet answered it.

World.title: Editorial: Tread Carefully, Mr. President, Washington Is More Than One Address
World.content:
THE BOAKAI ADMINISTRATION has spent much of the past two years enjoying something rare for a small West African state: an easy relationship with the most transactional White House in recent memory. Monrovia has said yes when Washington asked. It offered to take Kilmar Abrego Garcia when U.S. courts blocked his return to El Salvador. It agreed to accept up to 1,200 deportees who are not Liberian. It has been quick with warm words. In return, it has received goodwill, access, and millions of dollars in “migration management” support.

A Liberian government is right to want that kind of goodwill. Building a foreign policy on it alone is a mistake, and the events of the past few weeks show why.

FIRST CAME THE MIRROR. The U.S. State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statement on Liberia is among the bluntest assessments Washington has published about this country in years. It calls corruption the primary brake on Liberia’s democratic consolidation and economic growth. It reports that multinational firms are routinely charged fees that appear nowhere in their contracts, that accounts of extortion at several levels of government are common, and that political cronyism shapes decisions that should be made on merit. The report gives the government some credit for asset declarations, contract probes and the push for a specialized corruption court. But the overall verdict is clear. The same Washington that applauds Monrovia’s cooperation on deportations does not trust Monrovia with its investors’ money.



THEN CAME THE MICROSCOPE. On September 23, Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia filed Senate Resolution 886. It would require the Secretary of State to report to Congress within 30 days on Liberia’s human rights record, including how deportees sent here are treated. It also asks for every agreement, every financial transaction, and every assurance exchanged between the two governments on removals, and a summary of meetings between Liberian officials and their U.S. counterparts. If the report is not delivered on time, U.S. security assistance to Liberia is frozen by law.

Resolutions like this have so far died on party-line votes in a Republican-led Senate. That was the arithmetic of the old Congress.

NOW COMES THE BALLOT BOX. The November 3 U.S. midterm elections have reshaped Capitol Hill, and Democrats made major gains in both chambers. A new Congress is sworn in in January. The senators who have spent two years asking unanswered questions about third-country deportation deals, about secret payments, and about governments that take Washington’s money without telling their own people will return with a far stronger hand.

It would be dangerous for anyone at the Executive Mansion to assume that a good relationship with one American president means a good relationship with the United States. Congress controls the budget. Congress confirms ambassadors, writes conditions into foreign aid, holds hearings and issues subpoenas. A relationship built on personal rapport with one administration can unravel fast once the questions start arriving from the other end of Pennsylvania Avenue.

LIBERIA HAS BEEN HERE BEFORE. Governments in this country have often mistaken the favour of whoever sits in the White House for the friendship of the American people. The relationship that survived wars, coups and Ebola did so because it rested on wider foundations: Congress, the diaspora, American churches, universities and civil society. Members of both parties have for decades kept Liberia on Washington’s agenda, from aid packages after the war to pressure for a war crimes court. Neglecting those foundations to please one administration would be a costly mistake.

WE THEREFORE URGE the Boakai administration to act before the new Congress is seated, not after:

• Bring the deportation agreement before the Legislature. Article 34(f) of the Constitution requires it. A deal Liberians’ own representatives have never seen will look worse when U.S. senators read it out in a hearing.

• Publish the numbers. How many people have arrived, from where, where they are held, what Liberia has received, and on what terms. The government says it took no compensation, yet U.S. records show millions in support. Explain the difference now, in Monrovia.

• Treat the Investment Climate Statement as an agenda for reform. Every unofficial fee and every captured state enterprise named in that report gives a sceptical Congress grounds to put conditions on aid.

• Engage both parties. Liberia’s ambassador and its lobbying in Washington should spend as much time in Democratic offices on Capitol Hill as they do at the White House.

No one is asking President Boakai to pick a fight with the Trump administration. Liberia cannot afford one and does not need one. But careful diplomacy means planning for the Washington that comes next, not just the one in power today. Some of the senators who will have more power from January are already asking hard questions about Liberia, and Monrovia should prepare its answers before the hearings begin.

World.title: U.S. Senate Scrutiny: Liberia’s Deportation Deal
World.content:
U.S. Senator Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, filed Senate Resolution 886. It asks the U.S. Secretary of State to give Congress, within 30 days of the resolution’s adoption, a formal statement on Liberia’s human rights practices.

Monrovia – When Liberia agreed in August to take in up to 1,200 people deported from the United States, people who are not Liberian and, in most cases, have never set foot in Africa, the government in Monrovia described the arrangement as an act of hospitality. Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah said the arrivals would be received as “guests.”

By Rodney D. Sieh

In Washington, at least one senator wants to know what kind of welcome they are actually getting.



On September 23, U.S. Senator Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, filed Senate Resolution 886. It asks the U.S. Secretary of State to give Congress, within 30 days of the resolution’s adoption, a formal statement on Liberia’s human rights practices. The measure was referred to the Foreign Relations Committee, and Liberia is now among a growing list of countries whose role in President Donald Trump’s “third-country” deportation programme has drawn this kind of congressional scrutiny.

What the resolution demands

The two-page resolution has no preamble and no accusations. It is a list of questions, and the questions reveal what U.S. lawmakers suspect.

It asks the State Department for all credible information on alleged abuses by the Government of Liberia: arbitrary arrest and detention, torture, denial of due process, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and human trafficking or forced labour. It asks specifically about how non-citizens removed to Liberia by the U.S. are treated.

It goes further. Washington would have to disclose:

• whether U.S. security assistance could end up supporting abusive practices;

• conditions in the places where deportees are held;

• every agreement and financial transaction between the two governments relating to removals;

• information on everyone sent to Liberia in 2025 and 2026;

• what assurances on their treatment the U.S. sought or received;

• a summary of meetings between Liberian officials and Washington-based U.S. officials over the same two years.

The legal tool is Section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, a Cold War-era law. It lets Congress, through a simple resolution, demand a human rights report on any country. The penalty is what gives it force: if the State Department misses the 30-day deadline, U.S. security assistance to that country is frozen until the report is delivered. The resolution is also privileged, which means its sponsor can force a floor vote even if Senate leaders would prefer to avoid one.

One of the largest deals of its kind

The Liberia arrangement stands out even within an aggressive global programme. Rights monitors count at least 35 countries that have signed third-country deportation agreements with the Trump administration. By their count, about 22,000 people had been sent to 26 countries other than their own by early August, and Liberia’s deal is the largest by number.

The two governments reached a six-page agreement in September 2025. It became public in March 2026 and does not say how many people Liberia would take or from which countries. The figure of 1,200 surfaced only in August, when Monrovia announced it days before the first flight landed.

The arrival on August 20 at Roberts International Airport did not go smoothly. Several of the 20 deportees, mostly Latin Americans including Cubans and Venezuelans, refused to leave the plane. U.S. agents restrained some of them. Six were later flown on to Equatorial Guinea, a fourth country none of them came from. It was the first reported case of deportees refusing to disembark in a third country and being moved on to another.

Money and the ‘no compensation’ claim

Section 1(b)(3) of the resolution seeks disclosure of every financial transaction linked to removals, and this is where Monrovia is most exposed.

The Liberian government has said repeatedly that it neither demanded nor received any compensation for accepting deportees. Yet the U.S. awarded Liberia US$5 million this year for “migration management,” and The New York Times, citing federal data, reported that US$7.5 million was wired to the country. Liberian officials have said accommodation, food and onward travel would be paid for by Washington and an international partner organisation.

The arrival on August 20 at Roberts International Airport did not go smoothly. Several of the 20 deportees, mostly Latin Americans including Cubans and Venezuelans, refused to leave the plane.

Monrovia may well argue that support for running the programme is not the same as payment for agreeing to it. But a State Department report delivered under oath-like statutory obligations would put the exact figures on the public record, in Washington, for the first time.

The constitutional question at home

The Senate resolution also lands on a dispute inside Liberia that has not been settled. Article 34(f) of Liberia’s Constitution gives the Legislature the power to approve treaties and “other international agreements.” Critics, among them Nimba County Senator Samuel Kogar and the Liberian scholar Robtel Neajai Pailey, argue that the deportation deal never came before either House and is therefore unconstitutional. Kogar asked publicly whether the arrangement had been brought before both Houses of the Legislature.

If the State Department is compelled to produce a full list of agreements with Monrovia, Liberian lawmakers would be handed, from a foreign capital, documents their own executive has not formally submitted to them.

Why Liberia, and why it matters

For a global readership, the context matters. Liberia was founded in the 19th century by freed Black Americans and has been one of Washington’s closest partners in Africa. In court filings during the 2025 attempt to deport Salvadoran Kilmar Abrego Garcia to Liberia, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security described Liberia as “a thriving democracy” and said its constitution provides strong human rights protections. Abrego Garcia’s mistaken deportation had made him a symbol of the immigration crackdown.

Resolution 886 would test that description against the State Department’s own evidence. That is awkward for both governments. Washington’s annual human rights reports on Liberia have in past years documented harsh prison conditions, lengthy pre-trial detention and weak courts, the same conditions deportees could face if they are held or charged.

Will it pass?

Probably not, at least not soon. Kaine filed Resolution 886 alongside 14 other new 502B resolutions covering countries from Belize to El Salvador, following earlier ones on Ghana, Eswatini, Rwanda, South Sudan and others. Previous attempts to force them through have failed on largely party-line votes. In May 2025, the Senate rejected a motion to discharge his El Salvador resolution 45–50, and in June 2026, a similar motion on Honduras failed. Republicans have dismissed the efforts as political theatre.

Even so, the resolutions keep the deals in the news, set out on the record what Congress wants to know, and could matter if the balance of power in Washington changes. Kaine’s office says the administration has pledged at least US$410 million to build its network of deportation partners.

The bottom line

Resolution 886 is unlikely to stop a single deportation flight to Liberia. It does make the arrangement harder for either government to keep quiet. The questions it asks (who was sent, what was paid, what was promised, and where the deportees are now) are the questions Liberians have been asking since August. The Boakai administration can answer them now, in Monrovia, or wait for the answers to come out in Washington.

World.title: Liberia’s Long Wait for a Second U.S. Grant
World.content:
Monrovia – Liberian diplomats in Washington had good news to share last week. On November 10, the U.S. Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) hosted a reception for a Liberian technical team in town to help lay the analytical groundwork for a second MCC compact. A compact is a five-year grant that is not a loan and does not have to be repaid. Liberia’s ambassador to the United States, Dr. Al-Hassan Conteh, told guests that cheap and reliable electricity remains the country’s biggest obstacle to growth. He also listed roads, governance, private-sector jobs, skills and environmental safeguards as priorities.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The Embassy’s account of the evening was upbeat. Behind it is a harder story. Liberia has been trying to win a second compact for nearly a decade, and the U.S. agency it is courting is smaller, more political, and less certain about its future than at any point since it was founded in 2004.



What the MCC is, and why it matters

The MCC is different from conventional U.S. aid. Countries do not apply; they have to qualify. Each year the agency grades poor countries on 22 independent indicators covering governance, economic freedom, and investment in people. To qualify, a country must pass at least half of them and clear two compulsory “hard hurdles”: personal freedom and either control of corruption or government accountability. Countries that qualify can then spend years designing projects with MCC staff before any money arrives.

The first compact showed what a successful partnership can achieve. It was worth about US$257 million, signed in Washington in November 2015 and carried out between 2016 and 2021. Most of the money went to rebuilding the Mount Coffee Hydropower Plant, which was wrecked in the civil war and is now Liberia’s largest source of electricity. The compact also funded road maintenance and reform of the power sector. MCC officials still describe it as a success.

Ten years of trying

What followed was a long wait. After the first compact closed in 2021, governance problems and weak scores on key indicators kept Liberia from moving to a second one.

The breakthrough came in December 2024, when the MCC board picked Liberia as the only new country eligible to develop a compact that year. Weeks later, the Trump administration began its review of foreign aid. The MCC came close to being shut down, and many of its programmes, including several in Africa, were cancelled. Liberia’s compact survived, but in August 2025 the board put off a decision on its continued eligibility. In December 2025 the board reaffirmed it. Finance Minister Augustine Ngafuan called it “a truly good Christmas” for Liberians.

The process has moved slowly since then. MCC teams have visited Monrovia and met the electricity regulator. Liberia formed a Compact Development Team, now led by National Coordinator Alieu Fuad Nyei, whose members were in Washington this month. Its first big task is a “constraints analysis,” a study of what is holding back growth. Electricity and roads have again come out on top. At the start of the year, local reports said work on the compact documents could run until the end of 2027.

The Embassy’s release names no dollar figure and no signing date. Ngafuan has said publicly that the compact could be worth around US$500 million, more or less, but nothing has been agreed.

A new item: mining

One detail in the release stands out. An Assistant Minister of Mines and Energy is in the delegation to give “technical support on the mining project.” Mining had no part in Liberia’s first compact.

The addition fits the times. In 2025, the MCC added two new tests, “America First” and “American Returns,” to how it picks countries and programmes. Neither is in the law that created the agency. Minerals are a priority in Washington, and Liberia is building a framework for a state-owned National Minerals Company. Monrovia appears to be pitching the compact in terms the current administration wants to hear. Whether that helps or complicates a programme meant to reduce poverty is a question the delegation should be ready to answer.

The scorecard: passing, with weak spots

The MCC released its FY2027 scorecards this month. Liberia again cleared both hard hurdles and the half-scorecard rule, which keeps it in contention. But it failed indicators on child health, girls’ primary education completion, women in the economy and employment opportunity, and it slipped on measures it had passed a year earlier. Critics in Monrovia point to an awkward contrast: Liberia passed “control of corruption” on the MCC scorecard, while the State Department’s own Investment Climate Statement calls corruption the main brake on the economy.

The Liberian delegation is headed by Mr. Alieu Fuad Nyei, National Coordinator of Liberia’s Compact Development Team (CDT), and comprises a multidisciplinary group of economists, financial and investment specialists, energy professionals, environmental and social development experts, and senior technical officials from relevant government institutions.

An agency in trouble

The larger risk is in Washington, not Monrovia. The Congressional Research Service, which advises U.S. lawmakers, describes an agency under heavy strain:

• Funding. The administration asked for only US$224 million for the MCC in FY2026. Congress approved more but also rescinded hundreds of millions, and further cuts have been proposed for FY2027.

• Africa sidelined. All of the MCC’s new selections in 2025 were outside Africa, from Fiji to Ecuador.

• The board. The MCC board has only one private member, which is just enough for a quorum. That member is due to leave in December 2026 unless Congress acts, and no replacements have been named. Without a quorum, the board cannot make decisions, including on Liberia.

• Time. On average it now takes about five years from selection to the start of a compact.

The November 3 U.S. midterms add another variable. Democrats made strong gains, and Democratic senators have been among the MCC’s loudest defenders against the cuts. A new Congress could restore funding and protect the agency. The same lawmakers have also been the sharpest critics of Liberia’s deportation deal with Washington and the most likely to examine governance claims closely.

The bottom line

Liberia is in a better position than at any time in the past decade: eligible, still passing the scorecard and backed by an MCC team that wants the partnership to work. But eligibility is not money, a fact the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia stressed when Liberia was first picked. The deciding factors over the next year are only partly in Monrovia’s hands. Liberia has to keep passing the scorecard and turn analysis into projects that can be financed. Washington has to keep its MCC board working and its budget intact.

The board’s next meeting is scheduled for December. For the delegation now in Washington, the reception was a pleasant evening. What matters more is whether the MCC is still able to act on its plans for Liberia a year from now.

World.title: Liberian Prosecutor Accuses Police of Singling Out Tricycle Riders in Traffic Crackdown
World.content:
MONROVIA, – A government prosecutor has publicly challenged the Liberia National Police (LNP) over what he calls “selective justice” in its traffic enforcement. He says commercial tricycle riders are being fined while taxis and illegal private transport operators are left alone.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Wonlue Garpue is a City Solicitor and Prosecutor with the Ministry of Justice, assigned to the West Point Magisterial Court.



In a weekend statement, he said he backed the police’s road safety drive but urged the force to “apply the law equally to all.”

Tricycles, known locally as “kehkeh,” are three-wheeled motorised taxis and one of the cheapest ways to get around Monrovia. Garpue said riders are fined US$50 for carrying two passengers in the front seat. That is a heavy penalty in a country where many people live on a few dollars a day.

“If carrying two passengers in the front seat of a kehkeh is a danger and carries a US$50 fine, then taxi drivers must also be stopped,” he wrote. He said taxis in Monrovia and elsewhere regularly carry four passengers in the back and two in the front, which he called “even more dangerous. But no policeman stops them.”

He also pointed to private cars running unofficial taxi services on routes such as Red Light to Broad Street and Duala to Paynesville. Those cars, he said, have no commercial plates, are not painted the yellow required for commercial vehicles, and carry no passenger insurance. “But they are never ticketed.”

“Why only kehkeh riders?” Garpue asked. “Kehkeh riders are also Liberians. They are young men trying to feed their families. We should not use them as easy targets for $50 fines while taxis and private cars go free.”

He said he was not defending riders who break the law. He called on the police to set up checkpoints that stop tricycles, taxis and private transport cars alike. “That is true road safety and true justice,” he said. “We stand with the Police for safety. We stand with the riders for fairness.”

It is unusual for a sitting Justice Ministry prosecutor to criticise the police so publicly. Both institutions are part of the same justice system.

A costly trade

For riders, a US$50 fine eats into already thin margins. Kollie Z. Koiyan, president of the Liberia Tricycle and Motorcycle Association, has said a brand new tricycle is purchased at US$3,500 and members pay US$150 to the Ministry of Transport to register their vehicles and obtain a license plate. He added that tricycle owners also pay US$130 for insurance while the drivers pay US$35 for a license.

Drivers have complained before. In May 2025, commercial drivers staged a go-slow protest. Their union spokesperson accused the Liberia National Police Traffic Division of issuing multiple, high-cost tickets for minor offenses–even when drivers have valid licenses, registrations, and insurance. The Ministry of Transport later said the dispute had been settled after talks between police and union leaders.

The police have a safety case to make. Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman has said motorcyclists and kehkeh riders have the highest accident rates. According to the Liberia National Police, 478 traffic accidents were recorded in the first three months of 2026, leaving 71 people dead and 309 injured.

Officials and exemptions

Garpue’s complaint lands in a long-running debate over whether the powerful in Liberia follow the same road rules as everyone else.

In April 2025, the House of Representatives summoned the Inspector General of the Liberia National Police (LNP) over a traffic citation issued to one of its members, Rep. Anthony F. Williams of Electoral District #2, Maryland County. At a meeting attended by more than 15 lawmakers, the legislators argued that elected officials should be granted exemptions from such regulations due to security concerns. Reports said the House majority ordered the Liberia National Police (LNP) to revoke a traffic ticket issued to one of its members.

The tension came back in February 2026. The Justice Ministry issued a circular cracking down on siren misuse, stating that “siren privileges are not attached to public office, rank, status, or position.” Within days, senior Justice and police officials appeared before lawmakers. Deputy Justice Minister Cora N. Konuwa told them “There is no intention to stop lawmakers from using sirens and or the third lane.”

The dispute goes back to the 2018 Amended Vehicle and Traffic Law. That law exempted from traffic stops the convoys and vehicles of officials including the President, Vice President, Cabinet ministers, the Speaker, the Chief Justice, Associate Justices, members of the Legislature, and the Liberia National Police. Critics contend that the law permits exemptions from traffic stops and shields certain officials from enforcement measures that would otherwise apply to ordinary motorists, raising concerns about equality before the law and road safety. Senator Abraham Darius Dillon called it bad; it is against the public good and against public safety.” Supporters say the exemptions ensure officials can move quickly during emergencies and security operations.

Some officials have been cited. In 2025 a traffic court fined former Solicitor General Cllr. Syrenius Cephus US$50 for operating a vehicle with expired registration and without a visible rear license plate. Cephus accused the Liberia National Police of singling him out for political reasons.

A force under strain

The police also face real limits on what they can do. In late 2025, Coleman urged lawmakers to supplement the Liberia National Police’s draft 2026 budget with an additional US$12 million, warning that the force is facing critical manpower shortages. The LNP is estimated to have approximately 5,000 officers, well short of the required authorized strength of 12,000.

The shortages are worst outside the capital. In Sinoe County, police said they were grappling with severe operational difficulties due to the lack of functional patrol vehicles, motorbikes, and other essential logistics. In Grand Kru, a deputy commander said logistics alone cannot address the county’s broader security needs without sufficient manpower on the ground.

Public trust is another problem. Assessments and surveys have identified persistent challenges affecting the Liberian National Police, particularly with respect to public confidence and perceived corruption. Coleman launched a new recruitment drive in 2026 and warned that “No applicant should pay money to secure a place in the Liberia National Police,”

For riders like those Garpue speaks for, the question is not whether traffic laws should be enforced. It is whether everyone on the road has to obey them.

World.title: Lusaka Man Wins K6,000,000 playing JetX on betPawa
World.content:
Lusaka Man Wins K6,000,000 playing JetX on betPawa, Zambia’s Largest Recorded JetX Win

Four bets in one JetX flight each paid the K1,500,000 maximum, for a total of K6,000,000.

Davis, a construction worker from Lusaka, has won K6,000,000 on JetX at betPawa. Four bets he placed in the same flight each paid K1,500,000, the maximum win per bet on JetX at betPawa.

SmartSoft Gaming, the developer of JetX, has confirmed it as the largest JetX win recorded in Zambia.

How Four Bets Paid K6,000,000

Davis staked K72 in total: one bet of K12 and three of K20, all on the same flight. The new version of JetX on betPawa now lets players place up to four bets per round, and he likes to use all four.

In JetX, the multiplier climbs as the jet flies, and each bet pays its stake multiplied by the point at which it cashes out. His K12 bet reached 125,000x, and each K20 bet reached 75,000x.

Stake Multiplier Win K12 125,000x K1,500,000 K20 75,000x K1,500,000 K20 75,000x K1,500,000 K20 75,000x K1,500,000 K72 K6,000,000

Each operator sets its own maximum win on JetX. At betPawa, it is K1,500,000 per bet, so all four of Davis’s bets paid the maximum. With four bets, K6,000,000 is the most a player can win in a single JetX round at betPawa. Read how JetX works.

What Davis Said

Davis placed his four bets and stepped away from his phone.

“I just left the phone whilst I was in the kitchen. I found it running, and I decided to just leave it be until it went all the way to the very end,” he said.

The result took time to sink in.

“I was in disbelief. I couldn’t even read out the amount, and I could not sleep,” he said.

The first person he told was his mother. When he asked what she would like, her answer was a borehole at her farm.

“As we speak, they are doing the work right now,” Davis said.

He is using the rest of the win for other needs.

His advice to other players is simple.

“These games have no master; it’s all about luck,” he said.

The full interview with Davis is on the betPawa winner page.

pawaTech owns and operates the betPawa brand and licenses it to local operators in each market, who manage the brand and customer service locally. In Zambia, betPawa is licensed by the Betting Control and Licensing Board (BCLB) with licence number #CL-001083/2-2026.

World.title: PSMD PS urges retirees to embrace entrepreneurship
World.content:
Public Service Management Division (PSMD) Permanent Secretary Lois Mulube has urged public officers approaching retirement to embrace entrepreneurship and use their experience, skills and retirement benefits to contribute to national development.

The remarks were made during the official opening of a two-day Pre-Retirement Training Module Validation Workshop held at Chikwa Lodge in Lusaka today from November 16 to 17, 2026.

Ms Mulube said retirement should be viewed as an opportunity for continued productivity rather than the end of one’s economic life.

She explained that pre-retirement training is important in equipping retiring public officers with the right mindset, financial literacy and entrepreneurial skills to manage their retirement benefits and establish sustainable businesses.

“It equips retiring public officers and citizens with the transformational mindset, financial literacy, and entrepreneurial tools required to successfully manage their hard-earned retirement benefits,” Ms Mulube said.

Ms Mulube further noted that the training will help prevent retirees from falling into economic vulnerability after leaving public service, adding that this will encourage them to become resilient business owners, investors and job creators in support of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Meanwhile, Director of Future Search Margaret Chanda said the two-day workshop is aimed at subjecting the draft pre-retirement training module to rigorous validation to ensure that it responds to the needs of retiring public officers.

Ms Chanda said the module is designed to transform the mindsets of retiring public officers and citizens so that they can meaningfully contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

“This module has been designed as a transformative tool. It aims to re-orient the mindsets of our retiring public officers and citizens so that they can meaningfully contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda,” she said.

She noted that the validation process is important in ensuring that the module is relevant and practical for officers from different professional backgrounds and geographical locations.

Ms Chanda also acknowledged the collaboration between Future Search, the National Institute of Public Administration (NIPA) and Chalim­bana Local Government Training Institute in developing the training module.

World.title: Security guard jailed four months in Chisamba
World.content:
A 20-year-old security guard of Chikonkomene area in Chisamba district has been sentenced to four months imprisonment with hard labour for stealing a bag of maize from his employer.

Webster Mulala, a security guard at Bush Cut Farm, was convicted and sentenced by Chisamba Subordinate Court Resident Magistrate, Susan Magalashi, after he pleaded guilty to theft by servant, contrary to the laws of Zambia.

Particulars of the offence were that on November 3, 2026, Mulala, being a servant as a security guard at Bush Cut Farm, stole one bag of maize weighing 50 kilogrammes valued at K340, the property of his employer.

Magistrate Magalashi convicted Mulala after he admitted the facts as true and correct.

In mitigation, Mulala pleaded for leniency, saying he was still in Grade Nine pupil and is taking care of his grandmother, adding that he committed the offence because of hunger.

In passing the sentence, Magistrate Magalashi said hunger should not be a reason to steal, especially for an employee.

She said the accused should have asked for a salary advance instead of stealing from his employer.

“You are a security personnel charged to protect the property of the owner. However, I have heard your mitigation and I have taken into consideration that you are a first offender,” Magistrate Magalashi said.

She said she was imposing a custodial sentence to send a message to the community, especially to those employed in a similar position.

She then sentenced him to four months’ imprisonment with hard labour, with effect from November 13, 2026.

Earlier, Public Prosecutor Lydia Nyoka told the court that Mulala ran away around 22:00 hours on the material day after his two fellow security guards found him in the maize field.

“On 3 November, 2026, at around 22:00 hours, Austin Choombe, a security guard at Bush Cut Farm, heard footsteps from behind and realised that it was Osten Mutinta, a fellow security guard, who asked to accompany him to the maize field,” the facts read in part.

The court heard that Mulala was later apprehended and taken to Chisamba Police Station where he admitted to the charge under a warn and caution statement administered to him in Tonga.

The court further heard that Mulala led police to the recovery of the stolen maize

World.title: Nkandu urges Topstar to guarantee quality
World.content:
Minister of Information and Media, Elvis Nkandu, has urged TopStar Communications Limited to focus on quality, affordability, and customer care as it serves the Zambian people.

Mr Nkandu said this when TopStar Communications Limited Management paid a courtesy call on him at his office today following his appointment as Minister of Information and Media.

He said TopStar remains a key partner to the government and to the people of Zambia in the broadcasting sector.

The minister has since commended TopStar for the progress made in expanding coverage, especially in rural and peri-urban areas, but said a lot more needs to be done.

“Government’s goal is to leave no one behind, and no Zambian should be left in the dark because of where they live or what they earn,” Mr Nkandu said.

Mr Nkandu has meanwhile assured TopStar that the government will continue to provide a stable and predictable policy environment for it to invest and grow.

He added that in return, the government expects TopStar to continue to be a responsible, patriotic and people-centered corporate citizen.

He has since commended TopStar for the progress made in expanding coverage, especially in rural and peri-urban areas, but said a lot more needs to be done.

Meanwhile, TopStar Chief Executive Officer, Jimmy Luo, said the company has started the process of expanding its business by creating more channels for local content.

Mr Luo said the firm has also advanced its plans of installing solar power systems to cater for viewers who are in areas which are not connected to the national grid.

World.title: Serenje business community elects interim Chamber of Commerce executive
World.content:
The business community in Serenje district has elected, Maxwell Kabanda, to lead the interim executive of the reconstituted Serenje District Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCI).

Mr Kabanda was elected during a meeting facilitated by the Serenje district administration.

During the meeting, businessmen and women in the district voted for Mr Kabanda to head the interim executive as the Chamber seeks to strengthen business representation and promote economic development.

Speaking after his election, Mr Kabanda said the SCCI would support the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda by ensuring that Serenje is well positioned to benefit from economic opportunities.

“We do not take this election for granted. We are going to buy into the Grow Zambia Agenda to ensure that Serenje finds its rightful position in terms of economic growth,” he said.

Meanwhile, Serenje District Commissioner Ellen Mibenge has urged the newly elected interim executive members to begin their work immediately.

Ms Mibenge congratulated the officials for winning the confidence and trust of their fellow business leaders, but reminded them that their positions came with responsibilities.

“However, this is not a ceremonial title but a call to duty. Serenje has waited for a long time for a functional Chamber of Commerce,” she said.

Other officials elected include Francis Sichone as Vice President for Commerce, Trade and Industry, while Kennedy Mulenga was elected Vice President for Administration and Operations.

The rest are Juliet Musonda, Felix Mukabe, Andrew Mwana, Justin Chiyesu, Bennis Ngandwe, Ida Mutaware and Christopher Musonda as members of the executive committee.

World.title: Mufulira entrepreneurs urged to leverage on the district’s location
World.content:
Mufulira District Commissioner, Evaristo Chilumba, has urged local entrepreneurs to leverage the strategic positioning of the district near the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to engage in trade and establish successful enterprises.

Mr Chilumba states that the proximity of Mufulira to the neighboring country offers vast opportunities for cross border commerce, which can only be harnessed if traders are empowered with the necessary knowledge and entrepreneurial skills.

He emphasized that cross border trade goes beyond simply buying goods on one side of the border and selling them, noting that it requires a strong business mindset and a clear understanding of market dynamics, costing and pricing, customs procedures, regulatory requirements, financial management, and business risk management.

He was speaking during the official opening of a capacity building workshop for women and youths in entrepreneurship, under the Enhancing Capacities of Women and Youth Enterprises for Regional Trade (ECoWYERT) project, in Mufulira.

“Mokambo Border should not only be known as a place where people cross to buy and sell goods. It should be seen as an economic gateway through which local businesses can access wider markets, develop supply relationships, and create employment,” he said.

Mr Chilumba challenged youths and women to look beyond the immediate opportunities of informal trade and focus on building sustainable, growing enterprises across key sectors such as agro processing, general merchandise, transport, logistics, packaging, and other trade support services.

He noted that the workshop is critical because it equips small scale entrepreneurs with practical skills to identify viable business opportunities, calculate trade costs, determine appropriate selling prices, and understand basic cross border compliance requirements.

Speaking at the same event, UNDP ECoWYERT Country Project Coordinator Wilfred Mufwambi, explained that the presence of the programme in Mufulira is deliberate due to its proximity to Mokambo Border.

“Our overarching goal is to strengthen the capacities of youth owned micro, small and medium enterprises, particularly those led by young women from rural and peri urban areas, to take advantage of opportunities under the African Continental Free Trade Area,” he said.

Mr Mufwambi echoed the call for local enterprises to participate across entire value chains, including agricultural production, agro processing, packaging, transportation, and logistics, rather than limiting themselves to trading existing products.

“Mokambo should therefore be viewed not merely as a border crossing point, but as an economic gateway through which local enterprises can connect to wider regional markets,” he added.

Mr Mufwambi also underscored the commitment of the project to inclusivity, noting that it deliberately prioritizes underserved groups by setting targets to ensure that persons with disabilities account for at least two percent of overall beneficiaries, while displaced populations account for at least one percent.

He explained that the training forms part of the ECoWYERT project, an initiative implemented by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in collaboration with partners such as the International Trade Centre, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, Federation of Women in Business, the Trade Development Fund, and the Borderless Trade Capacity Building Alliance.

Mr Mufwambi stated that in Zambia, the programme targets 7,000 women and youth beneficiaries and is expected to create approximately 30,000 jobs in the country, as part of a broader regional initiative spanning six countries, namely Botswana, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Malawi, South Africa, Zambia, and Zimbabwe.

He challenged the participants to translate the practical skills gained during the training into tangible business decisions so that young people and women in Mufulira become active participants and beneficiaries of regional trade rather than mere observers.

World.title: Mumbwa district to contribute over 1,000 megawatts solar power
World.content:
Mumbwa District Commissioner, Namukulo Hayumbu, says the district is positioning itself to contribute over 1,000 megawatts of solar power by 2031 towards the 10, 000 megawatts national target outlined in the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Ms Hayumbu says Sunshare Energy Company alone is expected to generate 1,000 megawatts in phases while Kitumba Mine is set to contribute over 100 megawatts of solar energy to the national electricity grid.

She was speaking when members of the Central Province Planning Authority (CPPA) paid a courtesy call on her in Mumbwa.

“I am happy to announce that Sunshare under phase one has just completed a 100 megawatts Nambala Solar Power Project that will have a generation capacity of 500 megawatts at the maturity of the project. The site for an additional 500 megawatts of solar power is at an identification stage. We have Kitumba Mine which has already contributed 50 megawatts of solar power to the national electricity grid,” she said.

She said Mumbwa will also play an active role in the actualisation of the 10 million metric tonnes of maize by 2031 and the 5,000 tourist arrivals target.

Ms Hayumbu explained that Mumbwa has fertile soils that can support a variety of crops, particularly maize and soya beans that are critical to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

She also disclosed that the Mumbwa District Administration is doing everything possible to publicise the blue lagoon and the Kafue National Park in order to increase tourist arrivals as a way of contributing to the 5, 000 target.

Meanwhile, CPPA Vice Chairperson, Samuel Ng’ambi, who was impressed with the solar power project, advised investors to work closely with the Mumbwa Town Council and other stakeholders to ensure developmental projects are well-coordinated.

Mr Ng’ambi said capital projects should be undertaken in accordance with the laid down environmental management regulations to safeguard human life and the environment.

He said the CPPA is concerned about the continued failure by some investors to undertake developmental projects without involving the councils in their planning.

Mr Ng’ambi said investors have an obligation to adhere to the provisions of the Urban and Regional Planning Act and Zambia Environmental Management Authority (ZEMA) Act when undertaking development projects.

Sunshare Assistant Manager, William Mutawa, said the company remains committed to upholding the provisions of the Urban and Regional Planning Act as well as the Zambia Environmental Management Authority Act in its operations.

Mr Mutawa also disclosed that the 100 megawatts Nambala Solar Project has been completed and that it is now awaiting commissioni

World.title: Parents urged to obtain children’s birth certificates
World.content:
An Early Childhood Education (ECE) teacher at Ntulo Primary School in Kawambwa District has urged parents and guardians to ensure that their children obtain birth certificates.

Benken Sebente says birth certificates are critical to establishing the birth identity of children and enable them secure access to essential services.

Mr Sebente added that birth registration is important because it provides children with legal proof of identity and helps them access services such as education, healthcare and other social services.

” Birth certificates are also important in the education sector, as they are among the documents required during the enrolment of children in school,” he said.

Mr Sebente noted that early birth registration helps prevent difficulties that children may face later in life when they need official documents to access various services.

Mr Sebente has therefore encouraged parents and guardians to make birth registration a priority by ensuring that their children are registered immediately after birth.

He added that creating awareness on the importance of birth registration was necessary in ensuring that every child has a recognised identity.
