World.title: Africa: The End of a Cancer Is in Sight for the First Time in Public Health History
World.content:
guest column

To mark Tuesday’s World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day, global health leaders highlight the progress achieved and prospects of consigning cervical cancer to the annals of history.

For the first time in public health history, the end of a cancer is in sight. We already have the tools to make this possible. With HPV (human papilloma virus) vaccination, screening and timely treatment, cervical cancer could become the first cancer ever eliminated.

Each year more than 600,000 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer and about 280,000 lose their lives. Behind every number is a woman whose life, family and future matters. When a mother dies, her children will be left to grow up without her love, protection and support. These maternal orphans are among the often-invisible victims of cervical cancer, their loss echoing across families, communities and generations.

Women in the world’s poorest places are the most affected.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The disease burden is profoundly unequal. Cervical cancer disproportionately affects women and families in the world's poorest communities, and 19 of the 20 countries with the highest burden are in the World Health Organization (WHO) African Region. Beyond the physical suffering caused by advanced disease, too many women face stigma, silence and formidable barriers to lifesaving care.

That’s why WHO made a forceful call to action in 2018. Countries have been rising to the challenge. In 2020, even in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO Member States adopted a ‘Global Strategy to Accelerate the Elimination of Cervical Cancer’. The strategy set ambitious but achievable targets: 90% HPV vaccination coverage for girls, 70% screening coverage for women, and 90% access to treatment for those with precancerous lesions or cancer.

Science, solidarity and commitment are delivering results.

At a time when the world often seems overwhelmed by intractable problems, cervical cancer elimination offers a different story: one of science, solidarity and sustained commitment delivering results.

Progress is accelerating. Australia and Sweden are approaching the historic milestone of eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem, while Rwanda is demonstrating that similar progress is possible in Africa, with several districts already meeting key WHO elimination targets.

Six years after the strategy's launch, the landscape has changed dramatically. Vaccine supply constraints that once threatened progress have largely been overcome, and there are now more HPV vaccines on the market. Today, 166 countries have introduced HPV vaccination into their national immunization programmes, including Burundi, Papua New Guinea and Ukraine in the past year alone. India recently rolled out one of the world's largest HPV vaccination campaigns, reaching more than 11 million girls.

Meanwhile, scientific advances have enabled a simplified single-dose schedule for most girls, making vaccination easier and more affordable to deliver at scale. Ninety-six countries already report implementing a one-dose schedule. Global HPV vaccination coverage has now reached 33%.

Screening and treatment are advancing alongside prevention provided by vaccination.

Screening and treatment have advanced too. More countries are adopting HPV testing, which is more effective at identifying women who need preventive treatment than the traditional Pap test or visual inspection performed with vinegar in low-resource settings. Today’s HPV tests even allow a woman to collect her own sample, offering more options for privacy and convenience, while portable thermal ablation devices are enabling nurses to treat precancerous lesions in minutes, even in remote communities. Science is opening new frontiers too: artificial intelligence-assisted screening could soon improve early detection and further accelerate progress toward elimination.

Behind these advances stands something just as powerful: a growing global movement.

The heroes of this global movement are survivors, advocates, health workers and community leaders who are turning the promise of elimination into a reality.

In Kenya, nurse Martha Wanjiru travels in a mobile clinic across the highlands of Kiambu County, bringing screening services directly to women in urban settlements and rural communities while educating them about their health. Kenya is now advancing a national elimination action plan, transitioning to single-dose vaccination and expanding integrated screening services.

In Sierra Leone, healthcare worker Sallay Carew takes her bullhorn into Freetown’s crowded marketplaces, loudly breaking down stigma as she encourages women to be screened. Today, screening services are available across all 16 districts. Through a training partnership with Zambian colleagues, Sierra Leone’s gynecologists are now performing life-saving cervical cancer surgery, with treatment provided free of charge. Women who once had to travel abroad for care can now receive it in their own country.

Bravest of all are the survivors driving change. In Zambia, Karen Nakawala used her radio show to broadcast her battle with cervical cancer to the whole country. Organizing HPV vaccination drives and screening campaigns to push toward the WHO targets, Karen’s “Teal Sisters” network is now over 100,000 strong. The sisters even accompany one another through treatment and survivorship. In Malaysia, Selina Yeop is building a grassroots network of survivors. With teal-colored fashion shows, peer support groups, and heads held high, they are changing how their country talks about cervical cancer. Across borders and continents, survivors are connecting, organizing and leading.

Their efforts are being matched by political commitment. Last year, governments meeting at the World Health Assembly reaffirmed their determination to eliminate cervical cancer and established 17 November as World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day.

These achievements deserve applause. But progress is not permission to slow down. Too many women are still being left behind.

Governments must sustain investment in vaccination, screening and treatment, until every woman and girl can access the services she needs, regardless of where she lives. Women living with HIV deserve particular attention. They face a six-fold higher risk of developing cervical cancer. While the HIV/AIDS movement delivered extraordinary results in the last four decades, on this count, we are falling short. A complete package of care must include the services that women need too: that means cervical cancer screening and treatment. As countries adapt to a changing global health financing landscape, it is more sustainable to invest in cervical cancer prevention than to face the consequences of the disease.

Industry also has a critical role. Vaccines, tests and treatment technologies must be available at prices that enable all countries, especially low- and middle-income countries, to continue scaling up access. Elimination will only be possible if innovation is matched by affordability.

Close 

Be part of making history on this World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day

Our message is simple: history is waiting to be made, so choose to be part of it.

The tools exists. The strategy is clear. The momentum is real.

Now we need every government, every health worker, every community leader, every parent and every advocate to help carry this movement forward. Vaccinate your children. Get screened. Support someone you love to access care. Advocate for services in your community. Put on a teal ribbon and start a conversation: tell others that you, too, are standing up for women’s health, for the end of cancer, and for the unifying power of public health.

If we sustain the commitment that countries and communities have already shown, cervical cancer can become the first cancer humanity eliminates as a public health problem. Millions of women and girls will live longer and healthier lives. And future generations will know that when the world had the chance to end this suffering, we chose to finish the job.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is WHO Director-Genera. Dr Princess Nono Simelela is Advisor to the Minister of Healt of South Africa. Prof Groesbeck Parham is Consultant Gynecologic Oncologis at the University of Zambia. Richard Freeman is Executive Officer of WHO. Dr Prebo Barango is WHO Cross-Cutting Specialist for NCDs and Special Initiatives. Claire Kimilu is Consultant, WHO Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative.

World.title: Sudan: Sudan's State Collapse - Canary in the Coal Mine for International Peace and Security
World.content:
Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) are community-led volunteer networks made up of Sudanese citizens, many of them young people, that serve as the primary humanitarian lifeline for millions of civilians amid Sudan the ongoing and devastating civil war.

guest column

Sudan's harrowing state implosion since war resumed in 2023 presents a warning for other states in Africa and elsewhere currently heading in that direction as well as stark dilemmas for U.S. foreign policy.

Just as Somalia's state collapse provided an instructive example in the 1990s, Sudan is experiencing a much more consequential slide into a country where multiple international security and peace threats emerge, from chemical weapons to interconnected conflicts throughout a broad regional swathe to the world's most devastating humanitarian crisis. Sudan's state collapse is a canary in the coal mine for similar countries at risk from Libya to Lebanon to Haiti to multiple neighbors, first and foremost South Sudan.

Sudan's collapse is a canary in the coal mine for countries at risk from Libya to Lebanon to Haiti to multiple neighbors.

At a moment when there are more simultaneous conflicts globally since WWII, Sudan's war stands out in its size and scope. The numbers are staggering. It is the world's largest displacement crisis, with 14 million people rendered homeless by the violence. It is the world's largest hunger crisis, with 40% of the country's population facing acute food insecurity. And it is arguably the world's largest sexual violence crisis. The UN's Tom Fletcher concluded, "Sudan is an atrocities laboratory: sieges, denial of food, weaponized sexual violence…"

As the fighting rages on, the crisis only will metastasize, as fertilizer and fuel shortages due to the Iran conflict increase the cost of food, thus driving millions more into extreme hunger.

The funding gaps are gaping, with UNICEF, the World Food Program, and the UN High Commission for Refugees all facing shortfalls between 70 and 85 percent of assessed needs. That directly translates into more starving kids, more virulent epidemics, etc.

The roots of Sudan's collapse share commonalities with other states in extreme distress.

Sudan's case is extreme but not isolated. The roots of its collapse share commonalities with several other states in extreme distress.

First, state capture. For decades, Sudan's rulers and their external collaborators have hijacked state institutions for private gain, creating a classic violent kleptocracy. A coalition of thieves of state ruled the country, and then fell out over its spoils, as thieves do, tearing the country apart in the process. The worst abuser of human rights, the genocidal militia known as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), was originally a collection of racist militias known as the Janjaweed, subsequently organized by Sudan's long-time dictator Omer al-Bashir to fight an incipient rebellion in Darfur. Unsurprisingly, as those militias grew in power and acquired greater wealth, they turned on their former government benefactors and made a play for raw power, leading to massive civil war, total state collapse, and the possible further partitioning of the country.

Second, resource extraction. Sudan's rich resources, particularly oil and gold, have been pillaged by successive governments, allied militias, rebel groups, and unscrupulous external actors. Parasitic multinational networks have created an assembly line of violently extracted and smuggled raw materials in Sudan and many other failing states, enriching a handful of insiders and outsiders while the communities and countries are ravaged economically and environmentally. The result is war as an economic system fueled by resource extraction, smuggling, checkpoint taxation, and the fleecing of humanitarian aid efforts. In Sudan and other African states such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, and the Central African Republic, the global acceleration in the price of gold has led to ever more violent contestations over control of the mining and trafficking of conflict gold, particularly to the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE imports well over $1 billion worth of illicit gold from Sudan per year.

Third, environmental poisoning. As part of the gold rush in Sudan and many other countries, increased artisanal mining is contributing to public health emergencies resulting from chemicals poisoning the groundwater, soil, and communities surrounding the mines. Agricultural communities near the mines in River Nile state now say that crop production has decreased by up to 80% to 90% due to toxic chemicals used in gold mining.

Fourth, external intervention. The Cold War construct of the United States versus the Soviet Union has been replaced in Sudan by a raging rivalry between the UAE backing the RSF and Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, Iran, and Russia backing the rival Sudan Armed Forces. At a recent international donors' conference in Berlin on the Sudan crisis, the UAE and Saudi Arabia tanked the joint communique because the Emirates couldn't even agree to the Saudi insistence on preserving "state institutions." The rise of the so-called Middle Powers has created a more complex chessboard in war-torn states from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Yemen where external actors pour in arms and/or trade in conflict resources such as gold with no consequences, as they pursue conflicting agendas related to influence and resources that make mediation efforts much more challenging.

Fifth, weapons systems. Provided by Iran, Egypt, Türkiye, and especially the UAE to the belligerents, attack drones have become the weapon of choice in Sudan, representative of a trend also seen in conflicts as far afield as Iran, Ukraine, and Mali. The use of these drones has completely changed the nature of warfare. The usual ebb and flow of conflict related to seasonal rains has been rendered moot; attacks on civilian targets can be mounted from further away with deadly accuracy. The cost of a quick and dirty "offensive" can be minimal for the attacker, but devastating for the target, usually civilian. Recently, there has been a surge of drone attacks on food distribution efforts, which ties drone strikes directly to increased starvation. Even more alarmingly for international security, the Sudan Armed Forces were recently found to be using chemical weapons—chlorine gas bombs—in violation of international arms treaties.

UNICEF/Mohammed Jamal A woman searches through the burnt remains of her shelter at a displacement camp in Darfur, Sudan.

Sixth, failed crisis response. In Sudan, international efforts at brokering a semblance of peace, creating accountability for massive war crimes, providing consistent humanitarian assistance, and countering abject state collapse have all failed spectacularly. More broadly, in response to wars around the world, the UN system and various regional entities have proven unable to develop crisis response mechanisms relevant to evolving conflict dynamics.

Seventh, eroding U.S. relevance. The United States still has the most leverage over the external patrons in Sudan, and using that in coordination with a more sophisticated mediation effort would hold the biggest potential for peace in Sudan. But the U.S. has been unwilling to use that leverage in any meaningful way, particularly regarding US allies UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt, who are all pouring gasoline on Sudan's inferno by supporting the armed factions. The US says it is focused on getting both sides to accept a humanitarian truce and to commit to an inclusive political dialogue to lead to a civilian government, but the cold reality is that kind of soft diplomacy can never succeed without changing the conflict's lucrative financial incentives, which in turn requires impacting the calculations of the external backers to the conflict. Sudan and other crisis-torn countries perceived to be less strategically important have been downgraded on the Washington mattering map, leaving in tatters peace processes and the failed elite bargains on which they were built.

Eighth, regional security risks. Sudan's war now risks spreading into a regional war, as several of its neighbors have supported one faction or another. The recent resumption of war in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, is a case in point, as Ethiopia has been supporting the RSF (a claim they reject), and now the Sudan Armed Forces may be supporting the Tigrayan rebels against the Ethiopian government (a claim the SAF deny). Sudan's state collapse and Ethiopia's renewed conflict are now risking a wider regional war, which could engulf other countries including Eritrea, Chad, and others, while also having connections to Yemen. This is already creating significant concerns for U.S. foreign policy in the region, which could escalate.

The playing field in Sudan and other collapsing or failed states has become wildly skewed in favor of elite networks that have captured state institutions for their own gain; in Sudan's case, the contest over these hijacked institutions has led to their utter destruction. At the same time, an assault has unfolded on pro-democracy and anti-corruption human rights advocates, the free press, independent legislatures and judiciaries, women's organizations, and any other independent voice.

A different crisis response paradigm is needed - kleptocratic war machines, including their multinational facilitators, need to be dismantled.

In response to this new, more dangerous era, a different crisis response paradigm is needed. To level the playing field and give peace and democracy a chance, the kleptocratic war machines, including their multinational facilitators, need to be dismantled, or at least more substantially weakened, and the incentives that sustain these war economies need to be disrupted.

This can be achieved if the US, UK, European Union, and other states with influence deployed much more robust sanctions against networks of corrupt officials, weapons suppliers, conflict gold traffickers, and companies they control, as well as anti-money laundering measures. Whole-of-government pressure of this nature is usually reserved for high-level national security issues. It's time to enhance the tools used for Sudan and other developing cases of state collapse.

Additionally, non-governmental organizations can create impact through campaigns aimed at undermining the reputation laundering strategies of some of the key arms-providing countries, like Emirati and Saudi sportswashing efforts using commercial branding deals with leagues, teams and tournaments from multiple sports around the world. More systematic and focused countering of the networks and actors benefiting from chaos and predation is critically needed.

Simultaneously, the constituencies for peace and reform in Africa need far greater support. Without more tangible assistance to the local groups pressing for system change, it's hard to imagine progress.

In Sudan, that means supporting the Emergency Response Rooms, women and youth organizations, unions, local peace committees, and other local institutions that can provide the backbone of social reconstruction, and not trotting out the same tired, failed diplomatic models of power sharing involving only the most heavily armed factions. Sudan is Exhibit A for how that mediation strategy has spectacularly failed.

This is a moment to rethink how the U.S. and the world respond to national implosions and to cobble together … a more effective way forward.

Sudan's complete state collapse and ensuing rising threats to international peace and security - along with a massive border-crossing humanitarian crisis - are a harbinger of things to come for other countries on similar trajectories that begin with predatory state capture.

This is a moment to rethink how the United State and the world respond to such national implosions, and to cobble together the coalition of civil society organizations, multilateral institutions, and concerned governments that can begin to envision a more effective way forward.

Sasha Lezhnev is a Senior Policy Adviser at The Sentry, which John Prendergast co-founded.

World.title: Africa: Facebook Exposure Is Behavioral Intelligence - Not Vanity Metrics
World.content:
guest column

In March 2026, as Nigeria implemented its measles-rubella vaccination campaign, the World Health Organization (WHO) Africa Infodemic Response Alliance was listening to what happened online. It revealed how people were receiving, questioning and interpreting the intervention in real-time.

This demonstrates why public health must take social media seriously as a source of behavioral intelligence to inform interventions. Today, people socialize, trade, network, find love and seek information on social media. Public health must meet people where they already are. As of April 2026, there were an estimated 5.79 billion social media user identities worldwide, equivalent to about 70% of the global population.

To be sure, social media metrics cannot prove behavior change, but that does not make them "vanity metrics." When interpreted carefully, they can provide valuable behavioral intelligence about how people encounter and respond to an intervention.

Facebook is a useful case study of using social media to promote health

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

With over 3 billion users globally, Facebook offers a useful case study. Its metrics broadly capture exposure and engagement. Impressions and reach tell us how often content was displayed and how many people saw it, while likes, shares and comments show how people engaged with it.

Impressions: How often did people encounter the message?

Imagine a public health program places banners promoting vaccination against HPV (human papillomavirus - the leading cause of cervical cancer worldwide) at strategic locations across Abuja, Nigeria, such as at major intersections, markets, schools, bus stops, pharmacies and health facilities. A mother might pass one while taking her daughter to school, encounter another on her way to the market and see the campaign again at a health facility.

Each encounter creates another opportunity for the message to register. But we cannot assume she read every banner, understood the message or subsequently vaccinated her daughter.

Facebook impressions work similarly. An impression is counted each time content is displayed on a screen, including repeat displays to the same person.

Reach: How many different people saw the message?

Using the same banner example, imagine one mother passes the same banner 20 times while another encounters the campaign only once. Impressions capture those repeated opportunities for exposure. Reach asks how many different people had an opportunity to encounter the campaign?

Facebook reach estimates the number of unique users to whom content was displayed. If an HPV vaccination post reaches 500,000 people, it does not mean they all paid attention, agreed with the message or vaccinated their daughters. But it tells implementers something important about the breadth of the campaign.

Likes: What resonates?

A 'like' is often the easiest metric to dismiss. Someone can like a post about cervical cancer screening without ever getting screened. Someone can 'like' one of my Keep Walking With Dr. Bill videos while remaining sedentary.

But a 'like' is nevertheless a small behavioral signal. Someone encountered something and decided it was interesting, agreeable, useful or emotionally resonant enough to respond.

When certain messages consistently generate stronger reactions, program teams should investigate why. Maybe personal stories resonate more than statistics; messages about protecting one's family perform better than messages emphasizing individual risk; or hopeful messages generate stronger reactions than fear-based ones.

A 'like' does not prove behavior change. But patterns of likes can generate hypotheses that programs can test and use to improve content.

Shares: What are people willing to pass along?

Now imagine a mother who sees one of the HPV vaccination banners around Abuja, takes a photo of it and shares it with her networks on WhatsApp. Her decision to share the message tells us she considered the information relevant or important enough to pass along to others.

A Facebook share is similar. Someone deliberately passes a post within their own networks, becoming an informal messenger for the intervention.

Again, sharing does not prove behavior change. But if certain HPV vaccination messages are shared far more frequently than others, implementers should ask why. Was it the language, messenger, image, practical information or way the content addressed a common concern?

Conversely, people may also spread misinformation and disinformation.

Comments: What are people telling us?

Comments may provide the richest behavioral intelligence of all. They allow people to ask questions, express fears, share experiences, challenge claims and sometimes spread misinformation.

Comments can transform social media communication into conversation.

As Project Director of VITAL, an HPV vaccination initiative in Nigeria, I saw this firsthand. Under one Facebook post, a caregiver asked, "What is the full meaning of HPV?" Another asked, "What is HPV vaccine and can someone about 20 take it?"

These were important questions. The first revealed a basic knowledge gap that could easily be overlooked by implementers accustomed to talking about "HPV." The second showed interest but also uncertainty about eligibility, a potential barrier to taking the next step.

Neither told us whether the individuals ultimately sought vaccination. But both told us what our audience needed from us. We answered their questions immediately and used those questions to improve content.

Close 

Measuring behavior change from social media interventions

To confirm if behavior changed as a result of VITAL, we conducted an end-of-project evaluation comparing caregivers exposed to the social media campaign with a control group.

Girls in areas exposed to the campaign had 48% higher odds of being vaccinated, while exposure was associated with an 8.9 percentage-point increase in the probability of vaccination compared with the control group.

The evaluation also helped us understand how the intervention may have worked. Exposed caregivers reported greater motivation to vaccinate, better knowledge of where to obtain the vaccine and greater perceived ease of getting their daughters vaccinated. Interestingly, the campaign did not significantly improve factual knowledge about HPV vaccination. It appeared to work more through behavioral drivers such as motivation and ability to act than simply by increasing knowledge.

As WHO's listening analysis shows, when public health listens carefully to what people are telling us on social media, reactions stop being vanity metrics and become intelligence for better action.

Dr. Ifeanyi Nsofor is a public health physician, behavioral science researcher, and global health equity advocate. His work focuses on applying behavioral science and digital approaches to improve health outcomes globally. He is Co-Founder of the Africa Behavioral Science Network.

World.title: Mozambique: Regulating Smarter - How Mozambique's Tobacco Control Bill Can Protect Public Health, Farmers and the Economy
World.content:
Mozambique is right to modernize its tobacco control framework. The 2007 law was written before products that do not burn tobacco existed. The Tobacco Control Bill is a chance to align the law with today's science and with international practice. But regulation based on evidence has to do more than lower smoking rates. It also has to weigh what each measure means for the farmers, retailers and workers who depend on the sector, and for the public revenues it generates.

Starting from the science

The evidence points to one distinction in particular. Most of the harm from smoking comes from combustion, so non-combusted products are better for adult smokers who would otherwise keep smoking. The Bill would reflect this if it recognized two categories within the definition of tobacco products: combusted tobacco products and smokeless alternatives.

A clear definition does more than tidy up the legal text. It gives the whole value chain, from growers to retailers, a predictable basis for planning. It also lets adult smokers see which products carry lower risk, which supports a gradual shift away from smoking. That shift will be easier to manage for the people whose incomes depend on tobacco if it happens in an orderly way and not through sudden disruption.



Science-based regulation also needs standards. Testing methods developed for cigarettes do not necessarily suit smokeless alternatives. Japan, the Philippines, New Zealand, Switzerland, Nigeria, South Africa and more than 20 other countries have already set dedicated technical standards for these products. If Mozambique requires product standards and pre-market notification, it protects consumers, makes it easier to tell legitimate products from illicit ones, and gives compliant businesses a level playing field. Legitimate operators then do not have to compete with unregulated products that avoid scrutiny and pay no tax.

Health warnings follow the same logic. Identical warnings on combusted and smokeless products suggest that the two carry the same risk, which discourages smokers from switching. Most countries already differentiate between them. Doing so in Mozambique would improve the accuracy of the information consumers receive, and it would do so without giving up the warnings themselves.

Protecting minors and adult smokers together

None of this weakens protection for young people. The Bill should require minimum age laws for all products, combusted and smokeless. It should also use standards on packaging, flavours and nicotine limits so that products do not appeal to minors, and set advertising and sales rules that keep marketing aimed at adult smokers. A regulation that restricts access for minors and gives adult smokers accurate information about lower-risk options serves public health better than one that treats all products as the same.

Where good intentions can cost livelihoods

Some provisions in the current draft would do less for public health than for the economy they affect. As drafted, the Bill would effectively prohibit the sale of tobacco in convenience stores and at duty-free outlets, even though these are legitimate products sold in these channels worldwide. Bans on sale and display are very hard to enforce and tend to push demand toward the illicit market. There the State loses revenue and no one controls the product. Most countries regulate the sale and display of tobacco and do not ban it.

Mozambique can do the same, using the regulatory tools already in the Bill, without cutting the number of retailers so far that it deprives them of income and makes it harder for adult users to reach smoke-free products. Duty-free sales deserve the same protection. These channels are transparent and work closely with customs against illicit trade, and they sustain airport revenues and retail jobs in travel hubs.

Farmers and sustainable development

The impact on farmers is not as visible as the effect on retailers, but it matters just as much. Tobacco supports 120 000 farming households (900 000 people) in 5 provinces and contributes 5% to Mozambique's export earnings. As worded, some provisions would prohibit activities that were never meant to promote tobacco or nicotine products, including agronomy programmes and charitable contributions. Agronomy programmes give growers technical support, improve yields and help them adopt more sustainable practices.

Banning them under the label of advertising could reduce farmers' productivity and incomes, and weaken the investment in sustainability initiatives, such as sustainable farming practices, reforestation or energy efficiency, that makes the sector more sustainable over time. The same broad wording could stop normal commercial transactions and conflict with constitutional principles on access to information. Narrowing it would keep restrictions on genuine promotion while protecting farmer support.

Close 

Retailers and consumers also need information. Smokeless alternatives are newer and less well understood than cigarettes. Allowing commercial communication and online information about them, with safeguards so that it reaches only adult smokers, helps make the transition credible. Advertising of all tobacco and nicotine products should still be tightly restricted, and the rules need to be workable for businesses and enforceable by the authorities.

A balanced path forward

The recommended amendments make tobacco control more precise and more enforceable, and they do not make it weaker. They keep protection for minors in place, give adult smokers accurate information and a path to lower-risk products, and avoid measures that cost farmers and retailers their incomes while giving the State little back. A Bill built on evidence, and open about what it means for the economy and rural livelihoods, is more likely to be respected, enforced and sustained.

World.title: Ghana: Bishops Denounce Galamsey, Drug Trafficking and Social Tensions
World.content:
Accra — Environmental damage caused by illegal mining, rising drug trafficking, growing indiscipline among students, and ongoing intercommunal conflicts and tensions are among the main concerns raised by the Bishops of Ghana in a statement issued at the end of their annual Plenary Assembly.

The meeting was held at the Divine Providence Pastoral Centre in Jamasi, in the Diocese of Konongo-Mampong, Ashanti Region, from November 3 to 14, 2026. Its theme was: "Communion, Participation and Mission: Preparing the Catholic Church in Ghana for Its 150th Anniversary in 2030".

The Bishops reiterated their concern over "the damage caused by illegal and irresponsible mining (galamsey), particularly the pollution of waterways, the destruction of forest reserves, the degradation of agricultural land and threats to public health".



The Bishops call for a state of emergency to be declared in the areas most severely affected by illegal mining, in order to promote responsible and environmentally sustainable mining practices.

"Regulatory bodies, security agencies, traditional authorities, religious leaders and all citizens must pool their efforts and resources to defeat this common enemy. The fight against galamsey must address networks of complicity, provide sustainable alternative livelihoods and promote community participation in environmental protection," they stated.

The recent seizure in France of three tonnes of cocaine from a Ghanaian port (see Fides, 23/9/2026) has once again drawn attention to the worrying scale of drug trafficking involving Ghana. The Bishops denounce "alarming levels of drug trafficking and substance abuse", which pose a threat to public health, family stability, the development of young people and national security.

"We urge the relevant authorities to step up intelligence-led law enforcement, including the application of appropriate sanctions and stronger border controls, while also strengthening public education and rehabilitation services. Families, schools and religious institutions must likewise reinforce preventive education and support for those affected by substance dependence," the Bishops said.

"Of particular concern is the growing indiscipline in some educational institutions, including even some of our own faith-based schools," the statement continued. The Bishops listed several incidents, including "violence, disrespect for authority, examination malpractice and acts of vandalism".

They also described as deeply distressing reports of sexual abuse involving minors in schools, allegedly perpetrated by adults entrusted with their care. Such behaviour, they stressed, undermines the educational mission of schools and the moral foundations of society. The members of the Episcopal Conference therefore called on the authorities to conduct thorough investigations into these cases.

Close 

"We are deeply troubled by the continuing conflicts and tensions between communities in various parts of the country, particularly in Bawku and Kalba-Gbinyiri," the statement continued. These long-standing conflicts (see Fides, 4/8/2025) have claimed lives and undermined social cohesion.

"While acknowledging the recent reduction in violence in these areas, we urge all parties to exercise restraint, renounce violence and embrace dialogue, reconciliation and peaceful coexistence," the statement said.

At the ecclesial level, the Episcopal Conference has also outlined a programme of preparation for the celebrations marking 150 years of evangelization in Ghana. Entitled "A Journey of Faith, Mission and Hope", the program will dedicate each of the next three years to one Person of the Most Holy Trinity, in preparation for the 2030 anniversary:

2027: Year of Jesus Christ, the Son of God;

2028: Year of the Holy Spirit;

2029: Year of God the Father.

The year 2030 will mark the culmination of the celebrations. The date for the official launch of the initiatives will be announced at a later stage.

World.title: Mozambique: Lam Warns of Possible Flight Disruptions Due to Jet Fuel Supply Constraints
World.content:
Maputo — The publicly-owned company Air Mozambique (formerly known as Mozambique Airlines, LAM) has warned of possible flight schedule changes as a result of temporary constraints in the supply of aviation fuel (Jet A-1).

The constraint may also contribute to reduction in the number of flights and potential cancellations in the coming days.

In a statement addressed to passengers, partners and the general public, the company said it had been notified by fuel suppliers of limitations in Jet A-1 availability, a situation that could affect the normal operation of its flights.

"The supply constraints could directly affect the company's regular flight schedule, forcing the airline to adjust departure times, reduce its transport capacity and, in some cases, cancel certain flights in the coming days", reads the document.



However, the company said it is working with fuel suppliers and aviation authorities to minimise the impact of the situation, because " operational safety and passenger assistance remain its main priorities."

The Company also advised passengers to check the status of their flights before travelling to the airport and to ensure that their contact details associated with bookings are up to date so they can receive timely notifications of any changes.

The airline also said affected passengers would be entitled to free ticket rescheduling or refunds, in accordance with its current passenger assistance policy.

Air Mozambique apologised for the "inconvenience the situation may cause and thanked passengers for their understanding and cooperation."

The warning comes amid recurring fuel supply difficulties, against a backdrop of disruptions in international markets, particularly those associated with the conflict in the Middle East.

In recent months, energy sector operators and business associations have expressed concern over logistical delays, rising transportation costs and increasing pressure on petroleum product supply chains.

World.title: Africa: Can the AU's Reparations Agenda Speak for All Afro-Descendants?
World.content:
analysis

African Union leadership on reparations should build a common platform for solidarity while supporting decentralised avenues of justice.

The African Union (AU) designated 2025 as the Year of Justice for Africans and People of African Descent Through Reparations, extending it into a 2026-2035 Decade of Justice. The agenda seeks to address historical injustices, including slavery, colonialism, apartheid and genocide, and encompasses Africans and people of African descent worldwide.

However, some Afro-descendant groups question whether the AU has sufficient diaspora consent and legitimacy to negotiate reparations claims on behalf of African Americans, Afro-Latin Americans, Afro-Europeans and others. Despite shared ancestry, these communities experienced different injustices and may have distinct priorities for reparations.



Since 2022, individuals and organisations in the United States (US) and Europe have questioned whether the process affords Afro-descendant communities meaningful influence or relegates them to secondary roles within a state-centred initiative.

In April 2026, the American Descendants of Slavery Advocacy Foundation New York chapter objected to foreign representation and efforts to subsume its reparations claims under a Pan-African agenda. It emphasised the injustices of slavery in the US and generations of dispossession. African American claims often focus on unpaid labour, Jim Crow, racial violence and exclusion from wealth building. Broader concerns include colonial dispossession, genocide, cultural destruction and wealth extraction.

The debate also includes African complicity in the slave trade implemented by the West. While leaders in Benin and Uganda and traditional leaders in Ghana and Cameroon have acknowledged and apologised for Africa's role, the AU has issued no apology.

The AU and Caribbean Community (CARICOM) have developed the proposed Global Reparations Fund, which Africa would manage. The fund raises questions about how to allocate resources equitably across distinct historical harms while avoiding bureaucratic obstacles and competing agendas.

This does not mean the AU's agenda lacks support from people of African descent. African cooperation with Afro-descendants on reparatory justice dates back to the 1993 Abuja Pan-African conference, and the 2001 United Nations (UN) Durban Declaration and Programme of Action against racism.

Institutional partnership grew in 2021 following the first joint summit with CARICOM. The AU drew on CARICOM's 10-point reparatory justice plan of 2014 and the March 2026 AU-backed UN resolution describing transatlantic slavery as the 'gravest crime against humanity.'

Although the US voted against the resolution, the Congressional Black Caucus endorsed it, praising the AU's leadership and suggesting that African American advocates and lawmakers would back a common global agenda.

Cooperation and support have progressed to direct participation. Ghana, whose President John Mahama is the AU's reparations champion, facilitated the appointment of Ron Daniels, National African American Reparations Commission convener, to Ghana's Global Advisory Council on Reparatory Justice in September 2026. Several US civil society organisations have called for closer alignment with the AU and CARICOM.

But the reparations agenda's credibility depends on building lasting solidarity between the AU and people of African descent. To achieve this, the AU should recognise all historical wrongs, affected communities, responsible actors and remedies, including those associated with African participation in the transatlantic slave trade. It requires respecting affected communities' authority to define and pursue their distinct claims.

There are signs that these concerns are being incorporated into the AU process. The AU's Economic, Social and Cultural Council 2026 forum called for the process to reflect affected communities' priorities. But it did not explicitly grant them a share in decision making.

A credible AU agenda should accommodate scrutiny rather than equating diverse claims with disunity. A coordinated and decentralised approach can draw on the contributions of the AU and people of African descent, strengthening the reparations process.

Jamaica illustrates how national initiatives can reinforce a common agenda. In September 2026, it petitioned King Charles III to refer questions concerning the legality of enslavement and Britain's reparatory obligations to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The petition, backed by CARICOM, could complement the AU proposal to seek an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice.

The contribution of people of African descent and diaspora organisations could strengthen reparations advocacy in Africa through research, public education, litigation, political mobilisation and transnational campaigning. They can engage Western governments, legislatures, universities, businesses and other institutions implicated in historical injustices.

This could raise public awareness, mobilise political support, press responsible institutions to acknowledge their roles and sustain demands for reparatory justice even when commitment within the AU or CARICOM weakens.

In turn, the AU can strengthen localised reparations efforts through diplomatic advocacy, shared principles, research support and coordination among states and affected communities. It can facilitate international legal initiatives and promote common standards for acknowledgement, compensation, restitution, rehabilitation and guarantees of non-recurrence.

Argentina shows how a common platform could amplify community claims. Afro-Argentine communities have long challenged the invisibility of their history. In 2023, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination welcomed Argentina's recognition measures but raised concerns about the lack of information on reparations for historical injustices.

Argentina's vote against the 2026 UN resolution, alongside the US and Israel, complicates the challenge. The AU's agenda and diaspora networks could enhance Afro-Argentine, community-led claims internationally, connect local advocates with wider movements and bring these demands into the public debate.

Close 

For African Americans, whose initiatives have largely been pursued at local and state levels, a stronger international movement could help elevate their claims to the federal agenda and encourage bipartisan engagement.

Questions about agency and representation do not stem solely from people of African descent - they also arise within Africa. In Namibia, Herero and Nama descendants, victims of the 1904-1908 genocide under German colonial rule, challenged the 2021 joint declaration under which Germany offered Namibia €1.1 billion in development aid over 30 years. They objected to their exclusion from negotiations and the lack of direct benefits to affected communities.

To make its reparations agenda a common platform, the AU needs a strategy to strengthen minority voices. The agenda will be judged by its ability to unite distinct struggles for justice while respecting affected communities' rights, priorities and agency.

World.title: Mozambique: Supreme Court Limits Number of Media Outlets That Will Cover Mondlane's Trial
World.content:
Maputo — Mozambique's Supreme Court has chosen specific media outlets to cover the trial of Venâncio Mondlane, former presidential candidate and leader of the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola).

Mondlane is accused of five criminal charges related to post-election mass demonstrations. The mass demonstration he called to protest against the alleged fraudulent results of the general elections held in October 2024 started peacefully but then degenerated into rioting.

He is accused of having committed the following crimes: public apology for a crime, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to crime, instigation and incitement to terrorism. Recently, the Council of State, the advising body to the Mozambican President, decided to lift Mondlane's immunity in order to allow him to stand trial.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to Pedro Nhatitima, Supreme Court spokesperson, the trial, which was scheduled to start on November 17, has only 45 seats for media companies, namely: the publicly-owned Televisão de Moçambique (TVM) and Rádio Moçambique (RM) and the daily newspapers "Jornal Notícias and "Diário de Moçambique." It includes the private TV channels STV, TV Sucesso, TV Miramar, as well as the Portuguese News Agency (LUSA), and the Portuguese Radio and Television (RTP).

"Other national media outlets will have to compete for four rotating spots by registering via an electronic platform. For correspondents from foreign media outlets, only one spot has been made available, which is also subject to registration", the spokesperson said. He did not reveal the criteria for the appointment of companies in question.

He explained that the general public will have access to 10 spots, while other institutions and civil society organizations will also benefit from reserved places, including the country's Bar Association, the Support and Monitoring Group for the Implementation of the Phases (GAMIF), the Centre for Public Integrity (CIP), and the Centre for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD).

The limited spots for journalistic coverage of the trial are deemed as a measure to restrict press freedom in Mozambique.

According to Borges Nhuamirre, a senior journalist and member of the Mozambican chapter of the regional press freedom body MISA (Media Institute of Southern Africa), for the first time, the Mozambican justice system is set to try a high-ranking politician, while journalists face limitations in their coverage of the proceedings.

"This can only be described as a regression for press freedom and, by extension, freedom of expression. Excluding the press from covering an event of significant public interest, on the grounds of a lack of space, can only be defined as a restriction on freedom of the press and, consequently, on the freedom of expression of the Mozambican people, who constitute the audience for the media outlets that have been excluded", Nhamirre wrote in his Facebook account.

Close 

The Supreme Court spokesperson also revealed that the trial will be presided over by five judges and will involve two deputy attorneys general, a legal assistant, two defense attorneys, and a total of 29 witnesses.

World.title: Ecuador's president denies US operates military base despite reports of troop buildup
World.content:

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation signaled an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil.

"Sometimes there's a specific mission. Sometimes there's a specific operation," Noboa told the news outlet Altavoz, describing U.S. personnel at Taura Air Base as carrying out "temporary activities" under a bilateral security agreement, including intelligence-gathering drone flights.

"We work together. It's not an American base. It's an Ecuadoran base," he commented.

THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

Noboa's remarks came about a month after AFP had documented an unusual deployment of U.S. military aircraft, dozens of tents and construction of new infrastructure at the air base.

The investigation identified approximately 20 U.S. military flights arriving at Taura between June and mid-October, along with internal documents confirming the presence of American troops.

Several flights originated from U.S. military installations, including Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama.

The buildup also raised legal concerns among senior Ecuadorian military officials.

AFP cited a September letter in which then-Air Force commander Gen. Mauricio Salazar asked military leaders to clarify the legality of the deployment. Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to a less senior role, the report said.

The increased U.S. military presence comes after Ecuadorian voters rejected a Noboa-backed referendum in November 2025 that would have amended the country's constitution to lift its ban on foreign military bases.

US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS

Despite the referendum's defeat, Quito and Washington have deepened security cooperation to combat drug trafficking and transnational organized crime.

Human Rights Watch has described the United States as Ecuador's primary security partner in its crackdown on organized crime, providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.

The watchdog characterized the partnership as "perilous," warning that "both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war."

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, President Donald Trump has designated several Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and authorized military strikes against vessels in international waters suspected of drug trafficking.

WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES

Ecuador has also emerged as a key ally in Trump's crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working together to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country's foreign minister told Fox News Digital in September.

Roberto Kury said closer cooperation with Washington had delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, citing drug shipments intercepted through U.S. intelligence and joint operations.

"There is an intelligence (sic) and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

"Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem," Kury said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also praised Ecuador as the United States' most "aggressive" partner in its Western Hemisphere crackdown.

World.title: Trump admin opens civil rights probes into 15 colleges over DEI grants
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The U.S. Department of Education announced Monday that it has opened federal civil rights investigations into several teacher preparation programs following complaints alleging race and sex-based discrimination.

According to a department press release, the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) formally opened the probes on Friday, Nov. 13, targeting programs "designed to recruit, retain, and support future educators" that allegedly "provide sex or race-specific recruitment, support, and financial opportunities for candidates in violation of civil rights laws."

The initial four entities under investigation are the City University of New York (CUNY), the University of Maryland College of Education, the Minnesota Department of Education, and the Minnesota Office of Higher Education. The department noted that OCR is also opening investigations into 11 additional universities over similar allegations.

DEPT OF ED PUSHES AHEAD WITH EFFORTS TO DISMANTLE FEDERAL BUREAUCRACY AFTER BLUE WAVE

The department said OCR will examine whether the programs violate Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin, or Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, which prohibits sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programs.

Specifically, federal investigators are examining:

* City University of New York (CUNY): Under investigation over its NYC Men Teach program for alleged discrimination on the basis of both race and sex.

* University of Maryland: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination in its administration of the Maryland Higher Education Commission Teacher Quality and Diversity Grant Program and the EdTerps CARES Network.

* Minnesota Department of Education: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination through its Education Tuition Assistance Program, which provides scholarships and stipends to students in teacher preparation programs.

* Minnesota Office of Higher Education: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination in its administration of the Minnesota Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship Pilot Program and the Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant.

A NEW YORK UNIVERSITY FACES JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INVESTIGATION OVER 'BLACK MALE INITIATIVE'

A spokesperson from the Minnesota Office of Higher Education told Fox News Digital: "The Minnesota Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant (USTG) was established by the Minnesota Legislature in 2021. OHE is implementing this program in accordance with State law,"

"The Minnesota Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship was a pilot program also established by the Minnesota Legislature in 2021. This scholarship is no longer available to Minnesotans as funding ended after the 2024-25 academic year," the spokesperson added.

The investigations stem from complaints filed by the Equal Protection Project (EPP), a legal advocacy group founded by Cornell Law School professor William Jacobson as part of the Legal Insurrection Foundation.

"The Equal Protection Project welcomes the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights' decision to open investigations into complaints alleging violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964," Jacobson told Fox News Digital, adding that his organization will cooperate fully with the investigations.

"The opening of these investigations reflects OCR's determination that the allegations warrant further review and underscores the importance of ensuring that all students have access to educational environments free from discrimination based on race, color, or national origin," Jacobson added.

MINNESOTA YANKS RACE-BASED GRANT AFTER DOJ INITIATED CIVIL RIGHTS REVIEW, DOJ REVEALS

EPP chief counsel Maureen S. Riordan echoed that sentiment, calling the decision "an important step toward addressing serious concerns regarding compliance with federal civil rights protections and ensuring that educational institutions uphold their obligations under Title VI."

A Department of Education spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The Department will open investigations across the nation based on credible reports that universities with education programs withhold opportunities for recruitment and financial support from candidates based solely on race," adding, "Teachers are the heartbeat of our schools, and the Trump Administration will ensure a future where students are [judged] based on their merit and grit, not the color of their skin."

The enforcement push aligns with President Donald Trump’s effort to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives since he returned to office in January 2025. Shortly after his inauguration, Trump signed executive orders aimed at ending DEI programs across the federal workforce and federal contracting, directing agencies to enforce civil rights laws in alignment with the Supreme Court’s 2023 Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard ruling, which struck down race-based affirmative action in college admissions.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS

Department officials previously told Fox News Digital that the administration, led by Education Secretary Linda McMahon, plans to intensify efforts to dismantle federal bureaucracy, strengthen parental rights, and enforce federal civil rights laws against higher education institutions following Democratic victories in key midterm elections earlier this month.

A CUNY spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "CUNY is proud of its role educating the teachers of tomorrow and our programs are open to all students regardless of race, gender or national origin."

The University of Maryland declined to comment. The Minnesota Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Democratic judge under fire for releasing violent offenders calls bail law a ‘direct assault’ on rights

A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release violent offenders is criticizing a state law that allows defendants charged with certain violent crimes to be denied bail.

Circuit Court Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a direct assault on constitutional rights, arguing that defendants should not be held indefinitely based solely on criminal charges, citing the constitutional presumption of innocence.

In a social media post, Carpenter argued that critics of government overreach involving license plate cameras, such as Flock cameras, are not equally concerned about expanded pretrial detention laws.

"Can someone explain to me why the people who are so alarmed that a flock camera might spot their car on a public road, and they call that government overreach, are silent on the fact that voters across the country keep overwhelmingly passing new laws to empower the government to hold you in jail indefinitely on the basis of a charge only," Carpenter said.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

"These laws, like Alabama’s Aniah’s Law, are a direct assault on the Constitutional guarantee of the presumption of innocence. But no one is talking about this at all, much less expressing the hysteria associated with having a camera see a license plate," he said.

Although Aniah’s Law was originally passed in 2022, Alabama voters approved a major constitutional amendment this year expanding the law to cover additional offenses. The expansion added attempted murder, solicitation or conspiracy to commit murder, and discharging a firearm or explosives into an occupied dwelling, building or vehicle.

"We are all one accusation away from being a criminal defendant," Carpenter said in a post on Facebook.

WHITE HOUSE CALLS DC POLICIES 'INSANITY' AFTER 19-YEAR-OLD GUNMAN GETS PROBATION IN SHOOTING

Carpenter has faced controversy over several judicial decisions over the years. Local outlet 1819 News reported that he previously described himself online as a "far left, liberal, progressive, democratic socialist."

In April 2023, Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, who was arrested in 2019 for shooting two people in a car when he was 17 years old, 1819 News reported. After being released from jail, McDaniel allegedly went on a 14-month shooting spree across Alabama, killing 18 people and injuring more than 30 others.

Carpenter also granted bond to Raukeem Cunningham in connection with the 2022 shooting death of a teenage girl, the outlet reported. While out on bond, Cunningham was arrested and charged with fatally shooting three people at a Bessemer gas station in 2024, prompting the revocation of his original bond.

In addition, Carpenter reportedly dismissed a 2015 rape charge against Fredrick Terrenda Hampton in 2019, according to reports. The dismissal came just two days before Hampton met Paighton Houston, who later disappeared. Her body was found buried behind a home after she died of an accidental overdose.

CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE

Hampton pleaded guilty to abuse of a corpse in connection with Houston’s death, and Carpenter gave him a 20-year split sentence with only three years to serve in custody, the outlet said.

During his campaign for judicial office, Carpenter said one of his major goals was to "reform the criminal justice system in Alabama."

"If elected, I will work to reduce the number of repeat offenders while addressing the expensive problem of prison overcrowding in Alabama," he said.

DHS officials stated that Delon Raymond Jaundoo was arrested in Brooklyn on charges including attempted murder, first- and second-degree assault, criminal use of a firearm, and multiple counts of criminal possession of a loaded weapon.

His prior criminal record also includes an arrest for third-degree assault.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged an immigration detainer for Jaundoo on April 29, which the New York City Department of Correction declined to honor, allowing him to be released from Rikers Island.

MANHUNT UNDERWAY FOR VIOLENT ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO WAS RELEASED UNDER NYC SANCTUARY POLICIES

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized New York’s sanctuary policies following the release, arguing that state and local laws prevent cooperation with federal immigration authorities even in cases involving violent offenses.

DHS SECRETARY BASHES NEW YORK LEADERSHIP AFTER ANNOUNCING THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS IN SWEEPING OPERATION

HOCHUL BOASTS 'I JUST BANNED IT' AS NEW YORK OUTLAWS LOCAL POLICE PARTNERSHIPS WITH ICE

President Donald Trump’s flight to Asia took a detour Monday as extreme weather forced Air Force One to change its Alaska refueling stop before continuing to the Philippines.

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

TRUMP LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO KIM JONG UN JOINING HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH XI, PUTIN

World.title: Chase says transactions back to normal after outage online and at some branches
World.content:
Chase Bank said transactions were posting normally Monday evening after a nationwide outage that had some customers reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds.

“Transactions are now posting normally,” a Chase spokesperson said around 6:30 p.m.

The outage began Monday morning, according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.

Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions.

Chase said at around 4 p.m. on X that “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware system” and that it was working to resolve it.

The issues had been affecting both online and in-person branch transactions.

The issue was not “cyber-related,” the bank said, and did not impact the entire banking system. “Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.”

The bank said that customers still had access to their accounts and funds, but some transactions were taking longer than normal.

Regulators were in touch with the big banks affected “immediately,” a person familiar with the situation said earlier Monday. They “quickly determined this was contained and service was already in process of restoration,” the person said then.

The issues at Chase were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week that have shaken public confidence in systems that tens of millions of Americans use every day. However, there is no evidence that these incidents are connected to one another.

Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade.

On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.

It was not immediately clear how many Chase accounts were affected by the glitch. The bank counts approximately 94 million customer relationships in the United States, with 5,000 physical branches and 15,000 ATMs.

By late afternoon Monday, several Chase bank branches in Manhattan appeared to be operating normally. Customers leaving a branch at 6th Avenue and W. 51st Street told NBC News they didn’t know there had been a problem until they arrived at the branch, where they were told by employees that they’d gotten there at just the right time.

“This is really retail banking,” and not tied to the rest of JPMorgan Chase, said a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.

The issues with Chase accounts also appeared to be preventing customers from transferring money via Zelle. A representative for the company said that the technical issues on its platform originated with Chase.

“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” the company told NBC News. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly.”

JPMorgan Chase operates around 15,000 ATMs in the United States alone. Michael Kappeler / dpa / picture alliance via Getty Images file

A representative for U.S. Bank confirmed that Zelle customers were experiencing issues.

“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted,” the spokesman said. “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

A spokesperson for PNC Bank said it was “not experiencing any direct impact. We are aware of reports of transaction delays outside of the bank, but those appear to be resolving.”

Truist bank said its services “are operating normally,We continue to closely monitor our systems and are not aware of any broad service disruptions at this time.”

Customers at Wells Fargo also experienced delays, but the company did not provide a statement.

Citibank likewise declined to comment.

A spokesperson for Capital One said the bank “has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time.”

— WMAQ’s Lauren Stauffer and Leigh Lesniak contributed reporting from Chicago.

World.title: United Airlines says it has resolved a ‘widespread system outage’
World.content:
United Airlines on Monday said a widespread system outage that delayed flight departures is over.

In a statement early Monday evening, the airline said it had resolved a technology issue linked to the problem, which came on the heels of a nationwide FAA ground stop.

While some flights were delayed, the company said, there was no impact on flights in progress or on United Express flights.

United announced the outage roughly an hour earlier, just before 5 p.m.

The union representing United pilots said in a statement that the outage had affected multiple pilot-facing applications, including crew communications and messaging systems, as well as the airline’s ability to provide final aircraft weight information for departing flights.

The union said it was working with management to better understand the scope of the disruption. Pilots had been advised to follow procedures in the flight operations manual, according to the statement.

A passenger on a United flight bound for Hong Kong told NBC News that a pilot announced that they’d been unable to get performance data for takeoff because of an IT issue. The pilot said they planned on doing “old school” calculations so they could take off, according to the passenger, Halina Eth.

In another announcement, the pilot said that systems were back online and there was a “very narrow window of opportunity to get this flight in the air,” according to a video shared with NBC News.

The issue did not appear to be related to technical issues that prompted the ground stop that halted air travel across the United States for more than four hours Friday evening.

Other airlines did not appear to be affected by Monday’s United issue.

It’s the latest system relied on by millions of Americans to falter. Earlier Monday, JPMorganChase said a technical issue was causing some banking transactions to be delayed for both its own customers and others.

Late Friday, the FAA was forced to issue a nationwide ground stop after a fiber upgrade crashed a critical communication system. By Monday, air travel in the U.S. was largely returning to normal after a chaotic weekend for travelers, crews and airlines.

And last week, Microsoft Outlook went down due to what the tech giant said was a “bug” and overwhelmed servers.

While there is no evidence that any of the issues are related, they seem to be fulfilling concerns about America’s overreliance on aging infrastructure. They’re also occurring against a backdrop of warnings about AI risks and cyberattacks, stoking fears that wider problems may be afoot.

World.title: The FAA ground stop left them stranded, so they bought a car and drove it home
World.content:
Tara Harding and her employees were at the airport trying to get home from a work trip when a nationwide ground stop left them stranded in Charlotte, North Carolina — roughly 1,600 miles from home in Bismarck, North Dakota.

She found a $48,000 solution in the form of a new Ford Bronco.

Travelers across the U.S. were left scrambling Friday when the Federal Aviation Administration announced that it was grounding all flights as it saw inconsistencies in radar data and communications. Officials said that 20,000 flights were affected in the hourslong ground stop, with 12,000 “unable to recover” after the order lifted. Thousands more flights were either delayed or canceled the next day as airlines scrambled to recover service.

Harding, a nurse practitioner who owns a clinic, was ready to get home Friday after being in town for a training with two of her employees. Her group had been at the airport for about 30 minutes when the ground stop occurred.

All three women started out trying to find options through Delta Air Lines, but flights were delayed and rebooked until they gave up the idea of getting in the air altogether, Harding said.

“In the midst of all of that, though, we’re like, ‘We should probably look at trying to get a rental car,’” Harding said. “So we were trying to look, all three of us at one time, trying to get a rental car. There was zero available rental cars within a four-hour radius.”

Greyhound? Sold out.

Amtrak? No luck.

Uber? No rides to Bismarck.

Overwhelmed and out of ideas, Harding called her husband to ask what she should do. He relayed to her an idea from his mom.

“She said, ‘Why don’t you guys go buy a car?’” Harding recalled.

Harding and her employees at the airport. Tara Harding

At that point, the women had been trying unsuccessfully to rebook their flights or find alternatives for more than an hour.

So they started texting with a sales agent at a Ford dealership who promised to stay open while they waited 30 minutes for an Uber out of the Charlotte Douglas International Airport. They arrived at 7:45 p.m. and left with a new Bronco less than two hours later.

Harding said the process gave her an adrenaline rush.

“When we were leaving the airport, I was three-way calling with my husband, the car dealer and my employees, and we were looking at each other like, ‘Is this really happening right now?’” she said.

Harding said she knows it sounds “insane,” but she did what she had to do, relying on a problem-solving instinct she tied to being both an entrepreneur and a nurse.

“If it was just me, it would have probably been different,” she said. “But I had two employees that needed to get home to their children, and we had patients on Monday morning.”
