World.title: Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing

toggle caption i Greg Derr/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children. The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027.

There had been speculation that the mistrial of her first trial might spur prosecutors to consider lesser charges that wouldn't require a jury, such as manslaughter or second-degree murder. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.

"Given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Mass.

In response, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated, "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."

Sponsor Message

Judge Sullivan is expected to preside over the new trial. He oversaw Clancy's murder trial that ended in a mistrial two months ago.

The decision to retry Clancy emerges after the judge denied a request from Clancy's defense team to dismiss the criminal charges against her on double jeopardy grounds.

Clancy's defense has argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her young children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

Clancy was initially tried on three charges of first-degree murder, one for each of her children. Her case has drawn intense media interest, due to the shocking killings of her young children. And as WBUR has reported, the trial has also sparked conspiracy theories online.

Read WBUR's coverage of this case here.

Mistrial sparked defense motion to dismiss

Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4, after five weeks of testimony and seven days of jury deliberations. The jurors, nine women and three men, repeatedly told Sullivan they were deadlocked, unable to reach a unanimous decision. Jurors said a lone juror refused to join 11 others in finding Clancy not guilty of murder.

Clancy's defense filed several motions after the mistrial. The first asked the court to issue a "required finding of not guilty," a Massachusetts state law term for instances where judges determine there's insufficient evidence to sustain a conviction. Another focused on the holdout juror, asking the court for an inquiry and to examine their responses to a juror questionnaire and other records. Sullivan denied both of those motions.

When deliberations were dragging out at the end of the trial, Reddington had asked the judge to remove the holdout juror, saying the jury foreperson reported one juror refused to follow the law in regards to reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to dismiss the juror, saying he reaffirmed his instructions with all the jurors about the law.

Sponsor Message

Tragic case highlights postpartum mental health

Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. But her attorneys didn't deny that she killed her three children in January of 2023. Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were found strangled in the basement of the home Clancy shared with her then-husband Patrick in Duxbury, Mass., south of Boston.

In court, Clancy's defense argued that she can't be held criminally liable because of her mental state at the time of the killings. Her attorney said Clancy was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis, and didn't get adequate mental health help when she sought it out.

"I'm appalled and disgusted," Reddington said of Clancy's medical care, as NPR and WBUR reported. "It's repulsive what happened here."

But prosecutors argued Clancy was mentally capable of committing a premeditated crime, accusing her of sending her husband out on errands so she would be alone with their children. And they raised doubts about Clancy's claims that a voice told her to kill them.

"This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said in her closing statement. "That's a distraction to get you angry and passionate about an important issue, but an issue that's not on trial here."

During the trial, the jury visited the house where the Clancy children died. Their bus route also took them past two places Patrick Clancy visited that evening — a CVS and a takeout restaurant -- before returning home to a horrific scene. Sullivan told the jurors that the visit, called a "view" under Massachusetts state law, was meant to "help you better understand the evidence" by seeing the locations and the house's layout.

Clancy remains in the custody of a state psychiatric hospital where she's been held for more than three years. She was severely injured by attempts to end her own life, and she used a wheelchair during the trial.

Sponsor Message

Massachusetts' highest court recently reversed a conviction in a separate case involving a mother killing her children – a case that both Cruz, the prosecutor, and Sullivan, the judge, also worked on.

In August, the state Supreme Judicial Court ordered a new trial for Latarsha Sanders, saying Sullivan committed an error in not allowing the jury to see medical records documenting Sanders' mental illness after she was arrested. Sanders was convicted of murder in 2022; she had argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she suffered a psychotic episode.

If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or be in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

World.title: FAA ground stop still affecting thousands of flights. And, Trump meets Xi, Putin in Asia
World.content:
FAA ground stop still affecting thousands of flights. And, Trump meets Xi, Putin in Asia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Travelers are expected to face continued disruptions at airports as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide ground stop. As of Sunday evening, more than 2,300 flights have been canceled, and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed, according to FlightAware.com. Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta airports saw the most disruptions, with over 250 delayed flights each. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, was doing routine maintenance in at least one remote location, changing copper wire to fiber optics.

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

🎧 The U.S. air traffic system remains safe, and this recent incident is considered an unusual meltdown, NPR's Joel Rose tells Up First. The Federal Aviation Administration believes it has identified the issue, and airlines will be ready for the holiday travel rush. Rose says the nation's air traffic system has suffered from decades of underinvestment by Congress and administrations from both parties. Before the ground stop, Duffy had requested $30 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. Now he seems to be asking for $50 billion by the end of the year, on top of the $12.5 billion for air traffic equipment that the Trump administration secured from Congress last year. Democrats, who will control Congress in January, are not responding positively to Duffy's latest request. Rose expects Democrats to seek more clarity on the administration's spending and the causes of the ground stop.

Sponsor Message

As Democrats gear up for substantial majorities in Congress, one question looms: who will take the helm? So far, no one has challenged Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for the House speaker role. Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is setting his sights on unseating longtime leader Chuck Schumer in the Senate.



🎧 A wave of incoming senators has spent months hearing voters demand change in Washington. NPR's Eric McDaniel says this presents a real opportunity for Van Hollen and a potential risk for Schumer, especially after the recent election results. Van Hollen needs 30 Democrats to secure a simple majority. He has support he needs from popular progressives like Bernie Sanders, and incoming members like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, McDaniel says. Since votes are cast by secret ballot, it's uncertain how many will back each leader when they convene in a few weeks, and McDaniel says anything could happen.

President Trump is traveling to the Philippines and China this morning for a high-profile trip, which includes a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This marks Trump's second visit to China this year. The trip to Asia comes as the administration faces scrutiny following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman linked to China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. He traveled to China with Trump earlier this year; this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is accompanying Trump to Shenzhen.



Sponsor Message

🎧 It's not unusual for presidents who face midterm election defeats to shift their focus to foreign policy, NPR's Mara Liasson says. But Trump's recent foreign policy efforts, including tariffs and the war in Iran, have been widely unpopular and seen as reasons why his party lost in the midterms, Liasson says. The White House said that Trump isn't expected to address pressing issues like the war in Ukraine or tensions with China during this trip. Instead, he plans to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons. Trump will also skip mentioning Huang's affair. Bringing up the Nvidia situation could serve as a reminder that many in Congress believe the U.S. should restrict access to advanced chips in China. Trump disagrees with Congress on the matter, likely due to his ties with Huang, who committed millions of dollars for Trump's ballroom, Liasson says.

Living better

toggle caption i Mono/Getty Images

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Sleep plays a crucial role in weight management. Studies have found that poor sleep can increase appetite and lead to overeating, making it harder to shed pounds. On the flip side, quality sleep might actually enhance your weight-loss efforts. One study found that participants in a year-long weight-loss program who enjoyed better sleep lost more weight and fat. So, prioritizing sleep could be your secret weapon in the journey to a healthy weight. Here's what researchers say:

😴 While evidence linking more sleep to weight loss is limited, there is consistent science connecting insufficient sleep to weight gain.

😴 Lack of sleep increases activity in brain regions associated with pleasure and reward, making it harder to make good food choices.

😴 Not having enough sleep can disrupt circadian rhythms and reduce insulin sensitivity, encouraging fat storage and weight gain.

😴 The relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. Eating added sugars and saturated fats disrupts sleep and reduces deep sleep, while consuming fruits, vegetables and fiber improves sleep quality and decreases nighttime awakenings.

Sponsor Message

Picture show

toggle caption i Eric Baradat/

AFP via Getty Images





Route 66 is celebrating an incredible century as America's most iconic highway. Stretching across eight states — from the vibrant streets of Chicago to the sun-soaked shores of Santa Monica, Calif. — this legendary route invites you to embrace the spirit of adventure on the open road. Imagine cruising through vast plains, rolling prairies, stunning canyons and shimmering deserts. Along the way, you'll discover a mix of big cities, charming cow towns and ghost towns. Over the decades, Route 66 has inspired countless songs, been captured in books, been seen in artwork and been celebrated in Pixar's 2006 animated movie Cars. So hop in, buckle up and experience the magic of Route 66 through these photos.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i AP/NASA

NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any human-launched object and is about to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that's one light-day away from Earth. New Orleans port officials have filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River. They are seeking at least $1 million in damages. Mauricio Pochettino, who guided the U.S. men's national soccer team to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, is leaving to become the head coach of Manchester United in the English Premier League.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case
World.content:
Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case

toggle caption i Mark Makela/Getty Images

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that he is gaining momentum in his bid to unseat longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, taking a traditionally private Senate leadership contest into public view.

"Well, I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here," Van Hollen told NPR's Steve Inskeep on Morning Edition.

Over the weekend, he appeared on CNN, ABC and Fox News to make his case for new Democratic leadership after his party's sweeping midterm victories. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, says he has enough votes to remain leader.

Sponsor Message

Van Hollen is hardly a Washington outsider. The progressive Democrat has spent nearly 25 years on Capitol Hill, served as a deputy to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and led Democratic campaign efforts in both chambers. He has been a vocal opponent of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development, and he has called for investigations into the administration's foreign aid cuts.

Schumer has continued to support U.S. military assistance to Israel despite his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Van Hollen, by contrast, has pushed to restrict weapons sales and military aid to the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, while pressing for more humanitarian aid to Palestinians.

"I certainly oppose the idea of an American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel, regardless of its actions," Van Hollen said.

Van Hollen also wants Democratic leaders to stay out of contested primaries. He pointed to the victories of incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

"We have two senators-elect who would not be there if the current majority leader had his way," he said.

He described the midterm victories as a populist rejection of President Trump, rather than an election orchestrated by Washington Democrats.

Sponsor Message

Van Hollen also cited legislation to strengthen labor unions, which never received a vote on the Senate floor. On the war in Iran, he called for an end to further funding.

"We should not be voting for one penny in mid-December to continue this war," he said.

Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win. The election will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, making it difficult to know how many votes either candidate secured.

Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

The digital version of this live interview was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Regulating AI will being a top priority for congressional Democrats in the new year
World.content:
Regulating AI will being a top priority for congressional Democrats in the new year

A big priority for the incoming Congress will be regulating artificial intelligence. Democrats will face stiff opposition from the Trump administration and its hands-off policy towards AI.

Transcript

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

How to handle artificial intelligence is one of the big questions facing the new Democratic-led Congress beginning in January. As NPR's Katie McQue reports, lawmakers have ambitious plans, but the Trump administration may not like them.

KATIE MCQUE, BYLINE: President Trump has repeatedly said he wants the U.S. to beat China in the race to develop AI and that regulations could slow things down. Here's Trump at an event with tech CEOs in September.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: You're going to have a winner, or you're going to have a loser. We're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way.

MCQUE: Trump has rolled back Biden-era AI policies and has tried to stop states from making their own laws about AI. Yet there are concerns about the risks of increasingly powerful AI. Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, told NPR he plans to introduce multiple AI bills next year.

BERNIE SANDERS: People are worried that AI will take their jobs, invade their privacy, impact the mental well-being of their children, impact our democratic foundations.

MCQUE: Sanders says he also wants a ban on developing super-intelligent forms of AI. Another issue is privacy. Democratic New York Congresswoman Yvette Clarke says she wants rules on how people's data can be used by AI companies.

YVETTE CLARKE: A lot of the challenges that we face is the invasive ways in which our data is being used without permission.

MCQUE: She hopes some Republicans will sign on to these bills.

CLARKE: I'm just hoping that when the dust settles, we have enough open-minded and fair-minded colleagues on the other side of the aisle to make our efforts bipartisan.

MCQUE: President Trump can veto any bills that Congress passes. While Sanders has doubts about Trump's fitness as a leader, he is optimistic that Trump may still be persuadable when it comes to AI safety.

SANDERS: He is not stupid, and he actually is a good politician. And he changes his mind every day.

MCQUE: Sanders says the public wants AI safeguards, and it's Congress' job to act.

Katie McQue, NPR News, New York.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

World.title: Father calls for apology after son target of racist taunts at Kitchener, Ont., hockey tournament
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The father of a 16-year-old hockey player says he wants a public apology and cultural-competency training for the league after his son was the target of racist taunts at a tournament in Kitchener, Ont., on Nov. 8.

In a video provided to CBC Indigenous, a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers can be heard telling Brantford 99ers player Ryder Doxtator "Go back to the rez."

Aaron Doxtator, Ryder's father, from Oneida Nation of the Thames, was at his son's game Nov. 8. He said his son told him that he'd also been called a "dirty Indian" by the same player. Although Aaron Doxtator said he was unable to hear it from the stands, he said other players and staff on Ryder's team and parents told him they also heard the slur.

As a former athlete in hockey and lacrosse who experienced this type of racism throughout his playing career, Aaron Doxtator said he can't believe it's still happening.

Ryder Doxtator of the Brantford 99ers was told to 'go back to the rez' by a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers. (Submitted by Aaron Doxtator)

"It's always the same words, 'Go back to where you came from. Go back to the rez, you dirty Indian, or go back to your teepees.' Those are all different words I've heard growing up … My older son, happened to him all the way up," Aaron Doxtator said.

"You just get a gross feeling in your stomach when you hear those words."

He said despite being proud of his home, "They're making you feel like you're lower, 'Get out of here. You know you don't belong here.'"

Doxtator said there was a brawl just after Ryder scored a goal with one minute left in the game. The referees broke it up and Ryder was put in the penalty box along with two teammates and three Kitchener Jr. Rangers players.

Doxtator said they were arguing back and forth and a Brantford 99ers trainer went over to the box "to try to defuse the situation and tell our player to calm down."

He said she and a couple of the other parents heard the Kitchener players saying 'go back to the rez' and 'go back to where you came from.'

He was told by officials that the video was under review.

Doxtator said this isn't the first time his son's dealt with racist taunts from opponents.

"It angered him because he's heard that before and it's discriminatory … We should be equal with people," he said.

He said he's lodged formal complaints with leagues before, but they just get "brushed under the rug" and "nothing comes of it."

2 pending investigations into incident

The Kitchener Minor Hockey Association (KMHA) said it received several emails regarding the incident and there are two investigations looking into the incident.

Roland Cyr, general manager for KMHA, said in an emailed statement to CBC Indigenous that KMHA "is aware of allegations involving the use of a racial slur during a game conducted under the jurisdiction of the association."

The statement continued that KMHA is also aware that the matter was reported to the on-ice officials during the game, who documented the allegations and submitted the report to the Minor Hockey Alliance of Ontario (ALLIANCE Hockey) for review.

The statement said KMHA takes the allegations seriously "and is committed to ensuring a safe, respectful, and inclusive environment for all participants in our sport."

It said in accordance with its policies, KMHA will be undertaking a review of the incident and ALLIANCE Hockey, the governing body for both teams, will conduct its own investigation.

Brantford 99ers general manager Kevin Murray declined to comment as the investigation is ongoing.

ALLIANCE Hockey said in an emailed statement it is aware “of an alleged incident that occurred on Nov. 8 at the Kitchener Blueline Tournament" and is taking it seriously.

Previously in 2022, one of KMHA's U-13 Kitchener Lady Rangers players used a racial slur against an opponent and the team had to issue an apology and take part in diversity training.

Racial slurs pop out as they're 'still part of their lexicon,' says academic

Janelle Joseph, Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University in St. Catharines, Ont., said incidents like this are sad but not surprising.

Joseph said there's been a lot of work around racial and gender justice in hockey which "continues to be run predominantly by that white majority."

"We are in the midst of a culture shift, but we're not on the other side of it," she said.

Joseph said players understand there are phrases they shouldn't say, "but if it's still part of their lexicon … when they get into the heat of a conflict, it spurts out."

Janelle Joseph is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University and associate professor. She's also the founder and director of Canada's first research laboratory devoted to issues of race and movement cultures, the Indigeneity, Diaspora, Equity and Anti-racism in Sport (IDEAS) Research Lab. (Submitted by Janelle Joseph)

"That means that it was just always there. They were learning ways to cover it up or ways to communicate that would be more socially acceptable. But the anti-Indigenous racism, anti-Black racism, anti-immigrant and xenophobia is underlying in many, many of our communities."

Beyond superficial anti-racism training, Joseph said all teams would benefit from open dialogue about history and "what those expressions mean."

"When someone says 'go back to the rez,' what are they really saying there?" she said.

"I think we need to surface those kinds of conversations across every locker room, every team, so that we can start to make racism not something that happens over there, with those other people."

She said then we can start to see how some of those ideologies and understandings about who belongs and who doesn't are part of the dominant culture.

World.title: Exodus in Poilievre's office as 5 staffers plan departures
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit, according to emails obtained by CBC News.

Aaron Wudrick, Poilievre's deputy chief of staff and director of policy, emailed caucus last week with news of his departure.

Director of communications and issues management Micah Green and director of media relations Sam Lilly confirmed to CBC News on Monday that they are leaving to work with the newly elected British Columbia Conservative government.

Senior policy adviser Andrew Evans and Poilievre's executive assistant Hayley Quipp have also informed the leader of plans to depart.

Two Conservative sources say more departures could be coming, but only five staffers have given their notice at this time.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to share details about the internal workings of Poilievre's office.

These departures will leave big gaps in the Opposition leader's office (OLO), particularly in communications and policy.

Two senior staffers in Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre's office, Sam Lilly, left, and Micah Green, right, are both leaving for jobs in the newly elected B.C. Conservative government. (Sam Lilly/LinkedIn, Micah Green/LinkedIn)

Wudrick is a longtime Conservative and respected by caucus, previously serving as director of domestic policy at the right-leaning Macdonald-Laurier Institute. Before that, he was the federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.

He was one of the architects of the party's platform in the 2025 election campaign and has served in OLO for two-and-a-half years.

He was recently promoted to deputy chief of staff. His resignation follows other high-level departures from Poilievre's office earlier this year, including former chief of staff Ian Todd and former director of communications Katy Merrifield.

Wudrick wrote to caucus that he would be leaving his role effective Nov. 27 for a job in the private sector in a bid to spend more time with his family.

"It has been an honour and a privilege to serve our leader and this team the last 2.5 years," he wrote, adding that he believes the goal of electing Poilievre to be prime minister "remains achievable in the next election."

Evans has been senior policy adviser since 2024, and previously held roles as a staffer in the Ford government. He was assigned to the immigration file, which has been a focus of the Opposition.

Green and Lilly are Poilievre's office's most senior communications staff. Green replaced Merrifield in April, but has been at OLO in a communications role since December 2022.

His LinkedIn page says he's been working for the Conservatives, either at OLO, the party or through an MP's office, since 2019.

Green is married to Quipp, and they are expecting a baby.

"With our first child on the way, my wife and I are returning home to British Columbia, where I’ve accepted an exciting new opportunity with the provincial government," said Green in a statement.

"Working for Pierre Poilievre has been the honour of my career. The first door I ever knocked on was for Pierre, and I met my wife knocking doors for him. I owe him an enormous amount, both personally and professionally."

Lilly is a longtime figure on Parliament Hill. He's been in communications with OLO since April 2021, starting as a press secretary and rising to director of media relations. In the 2019 election, he was a candidate for the Conservatives in Edmonton Strathcona.

"Parting ways is never easy, but I leave with tremendous gratitude and thanks in my heart," said Lilly in a statement.

"I especially want to thank Pierre Poilievre for the opportunity of a lifetime serving as his director of media relations. Pierre has made a difference to this country, he continues to have my support and I know that our team will continue the work of ensuring he is the next prime minister of Canada."

In an internal letter sent Monday obtained by CBC News, Poilievre's chief of staff Steve Outhouse announced the changes and wished the departing staff well.

6 byelections 3 weeks away

These departures come as Poilievre faces pressure to keep seats in upcoming byelections after losing nine MPs since the 2025 election.

So far, he has lost four MPs to floor-crossing and four others have either announced plans to resign or have already resigned. Another MP, Quebec's Richard Martel, was appointed to the Senate. He still serves in the Conservative caucus.

There are six byelections on Dec. 7. The Conservatives are incumbents in two: Ontario's Brantford-Brant South and Saskatchewan's Yorkton-Melville.

Both seats were previously considered safe for the Conservatives, but the Carney Liberals' high polling in Ontario could see a fight in Brantford-Brant South, which was vacated by former justice critic Larry Brock.

Brock endorsed a local pastor, Dave Carrol, to succeed him — but the party chose Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis. Carrol later chose to run as an Independent, which risks splitting the Conservative vote.

Online posts and local news reports show Poilievre has been spending time in the riding, including this weekend, in a bid to shore up support.

Conservative sources who have spoken to CBC News in the past say, despite challenging polls, there is no plan to try to remove Poilievre and that he has the support of caucus.

Poilievre sailed through his last leadership review in January with 87.4 per cent of the vote from delegates at the party's national convention.

World.title: Meta would 'consider' pulling services from Canada if lawful access bill passes as is
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Representatives from Meta say the social media company would have to "consider" pulling encryption services from Canada if the government's proposed lawful access bill passes without further changes.

Bill C-22 would force tech companies to adapt their systems so they all have the ability to hand over information to investigators with a warrant.

The legislation is currently being studied in the Senate, where Meta representatives said the bill leaves encrypted information — meant only to be viewed by users sharing the information — vulnerable to malicious actors.

"Ultimately, the Canadian government would be enforcing and imposing a law that it is not technically feasible to comply with and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services to Canadians," Robyn Greene, Meta's director of privacy and public policy, told senators on the national security committee on Monday evening.

Meta services include Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp.

When asked if the legislation would mean the compan y would p ull some of its services from Canada, Meta's head of public poli cy for Canada Rachel Curran said the company would have to "review all of our options."

But she said it is something the company would have to "consider."

Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree proposed amendments to the lawful access legislation, but critics say they don't go far enough. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Bill C-22 also grants the minister the authority to issue confidential ministerial orders to electronic service providers (ESPs) operating in Canada, requiring them to build surveillance and monitoring capabilities into their systems. Orders would first be reviewed by the intelligence commissioner — an independent quasi-judicial official.

Before the bill was sent to the Senate in June, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree brought in amendments that put limits on when companies would be required to decrypt information.

Another change reduces the length of time that tech companies would have to retain metadata to six months from up to a year, after cybersecurity experts warned that data would be an attractive target for hackers.

Curran told the Senate committee that the government's amendments don't go far enough to protect encrypted data.

"They have protected just the core and not the outside layers that are an integral part of the encryption process," she said.

World.title: Police unsure how 120-year-old church bell weighing 300 pounds was stolen
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The case of the stolen church bell has police sounding an alarm — and scratching their heads.

A bell estimated to weigh 300 pounds (about 136 kilograms) was somehow removed from a wooden belfry at the Sacred Heart of Jesus Ukrainian Catholic Church , about 80 kilometres north of Winnipeg near Fraserwood, Man.

RCMP don't know how or when it was removed.

"It's still a bit of a mystery," RCMP Const. Merry Ploeg told CBC Monday, adding the bell is unique.

"It's brass, [and] it's got some ornate designs, including a rosary," she said, adding it also has an image of the sacred heart surrounded by a crown of thorns, crucifix and an anchor.

"We would really appreciate the public being kind of aware of it and on the lookout."

The theft was reported Saturday, RCMP said in a Monday news release.

Rev. Andriy Rabiy, auxiliary bishop of the Archeparchy of Winnipeg — which oversees Ukrainian Catholic churches in Manitoba — said he felt "great disbelief and shock" when he heard what happened.

"Sometimes we hear about break-ins into those kind of abandoned churches … [with] some small things being taken," he said.

"But not to that degree."

Rabiy said Sacred Heart of Jesus is one of two Ukrainian Catholic parishes in the Fraserwood area, with a history that goes back to when the first Ukrainians arrived in Manitoba.

Damage can be seen at the top of the wooden belfry. (Submitted by RCMP)

The number of parishioners has dwindled as people have left farming communities, he said, and the church is now mainly used for special occasions like funerals or annual liturgy services.

But those who remain in the community care deeply about the building, said Rabiy.

"Many of those churches actually kind of … stand as a witness to the past history that they had," Rabiy said.

"I can only imagine what kind of ache, of pain people experience," he said, adding that there is at least one person offering a $500 reward for any information that could help get the bell back.

Scrap dealers notified to watch for bell: RCMP

The wood-clad belfry is about 1½ storeys tall and stands on its own at the back of the church in Manitoba's Interlake region, about 12 kilometres northwest of Gimli.

The RCMP officers who investigated the theft found noticeable damage to the top of the belfry, police said in Monday's news release.

Ploeg didn't want to speculate on why someone would take the bell, but said the only thing RCMP can think of is that someone might try selling it for scrap metal.

"We've actually contacted all the scrap metal and recycling businesses in the area, including in Winnipeg, and notified them to be on the lookout for this bell specifically," Ploeg said.

The Manitoba Historical Society says the belfry was imported from Switzerland when the original church was built in 1906. That church was destroyed by fire in 1940, and the present church was built in 1942.

The bell is also from Switzerland and came at the same time, RCMP said.

The small church is a mission of the much larger Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in Gimli.

Ploeg said the parishioners are extremely concerned, as is she, by the fact someone went to such lengths to take the bell.

"Should the other churches be maybe … [be] looking at getting security footage or more regularly checking their properties?" she said.

"Everybody involved is very invested in seeing the bell returned. I'm really hoping that we can get it back and that it isn't scrap."

RCMP are asking anyone who has any information about the theft or noticed anything suspicious in the area over the last week to contact them at 204-642-5106.

World.title: Gordie Howe bridge surpasses 1M vehicle crossings while other bridges, tunnel lose traffic
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Gordie Howe International Bridge has seen more than a million crossings since it officially opened to vehicle traffic on July 27, according to new numbers from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators Association.

Meanwhile, vehicle traffic over the Ambassador and Blue Water bridges and through the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel has declined.

The numbers cover the first three full months since the Gordie Howe opened.

They show the bridge averaging around 248,000 passenger vehicle crossings per month and slightly fewer than 85,000 truck crossings.

In a statement, the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority said, too, that more than 48,000 pedestrians and cyclists had used the bridge's multi-use path.

"The Gordie Howe International Bridge supports the efficient and effective movement of traffic in the Windsor-Detroit gateway by providing additional capacity, crossing choice and highway-to-highway connectivity for travellers and commercial operators crossing the border," the statement read.

"We are encouraged by the continued interest in the bridge and the growth in traffic volumes as more users become familiar with the crossing."

Windsor-Detroit Tunnel crossings were down just shy of 19 per cent between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31, while crossings at the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia were down approximately 12.5 per cent.

The Ambassador Bridge saw the biggest decline in total crossings — down nearly 32 per cent compared with the same period last year.

Tunnel CEO not surprised by numbers

Most of that decline was in passenger vehicle traffic, not truck traffic.

Truck crossings were off just 8.75 per cent since the same August-through-October period last year, despite hopes among some residents of Sandwich Town that the new bridge would ease traffic congestion on Huron Church Road .

Truck crossings at the Blue Water Bridge were down just over 30 per cent.

Windsor-Detroit Tunnel CEO Tal Czudner said he’s not surprised by the numbers.

Tunnel CEO Tal Czudner said he is happy to see the tunnel, which is jointly owned by the cities of Windsor and Detroit, remain the most popular passenger vehicle crossing. (CBC)

“[The Ambassador Bridge] had a very long runway to negotiate some very favorable deals with different … trucking companies. And obviously they own a decent amount of trucking infrastructure themselves.”

Truck crossings at the Ambassador Bridge remain up 3.85 per cent for the period running from Jan. 1 to the end of October, compared with the same period last year, while overall bridge traffic is down 6.82 per cent over the same time period.

Czudner said he is happy to see the tunnel, which is jointly owned by the cities of Windsor and Detroit, remain the most popular passenger vehicle crossing.

He also said the Windsor side of the operation has lost less traffic than the Detroit side.

“I think what you're finding is there's a lot of the people who work in automotive, manufacturing, healthcare, live in Windsor-Essex, take the tunnel to work, and then they take the Gordie Howe home,” he said.

World.title: Volunteers back in Manitoba after grounding of U.S. flights set them on long road trip home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A group of Manitobans doing volunteer work are back home after Friday's closure of U.S. airspace forced them on a long journey across that country.

Doug Brown was returning from Nicaragua with about 40 other volunteers with Operation Walk Manitoba, a charity that provides surgical treatments to people in developing countries.

The former Winnipeg Blue Bombers player works for a medical device company. He was aboard a flight from Managua to Houston, Texas, when he learned U.S. authorities had grounded flights nationwide, causing tens of thousands of flight cancellations over the weekend.

"We were literally just about an hour and a half out of Houston, and we all found out via the internet," Brown said Monday.

"I thought it was some sort of AI-fabricated joke."

The nationwide stop, the longest in 25 years, was in place for about four hours Friday.

U.S. officials said a contractor was replacing a copper wire with fibre optic cable when an unknown issue triggered an air traffic control system outage.

Brown's plane landed in Houston, but the outage delayed a connecting flight that would take the cohort of volunteers he was with to Denver.

With cancellations rolling over into Saturday morning, the charity chartered a bus driving the volunteers back to Winnipeg instead.

The trip was about 28 hours long, Brown said.

"First stop, we went to Walmart just so we could get supplies," he said.

He bought pillows, a blanket, electrolyte water and a couple of apples.

Two Americans would alternate driving the bus, one taking over while the other slept.

"We didn't stop for dinner. We didn't stop overnight. We just essentially stopped when the bus needed fuel," Brown said.

"When we finally got to Winnipeg…, I almost laid down on the ground," he said.

"We hadn't showered or whatever in 24 hours. I was able to brush my teeth twice, but [it was the] first time I've done that at truck stops, right?…. It was a different world."

Sense of perspective

A team of nearly 70 volunteers was in Nicaragua for more than a week as part of the mission, with medical professionals performing hip replacement surgery to patients with severe joint disease who can't access that kind of care in the Central American country.

Medical lead Eric Bohm was in a cohort that managed to avoid disruptions while getting back to Manitoba.

Eric Bohm welcomed the volunteers who were left stranded in Texas after the U.S. ground stop. (Submitted by Doug Brown)

Bohm said those who made it home as planned wanted to make the other volunteers feel special. He was there to receive them at the end of their trip in Winnipeg.

"I thought … these guys are going to be tired and hungry and a little bit bummed out," Bohm said.

"Let's try to welcome them back home with some posters and some people showing up and some gift bags.… Just remind them, you know, how much the people in Nicaragua appreciate what they're doing."

Brown said he used to take a bus with the Bombers to Regina for the Labour Day Classic, but those trips were only about a quarter of the length of the 28-hour journey over the weekend.

He said nobody wanted anyone else to be in charge of the music. Everyone also wanted to avoid using the one tiny bathroom that was available.

At six feet eight inches tall, sitting in the bus was uncomfortable enough for the former professional athlete.

But Brown said the trip to Nicaragua gave him a sense of perspective.

"One of the surgeons on the bus ride said, you know, Nicaragua was one of the poorest nations in the entire Western Hemisphere.…

"This is still nothing compared to what the vast majority of those people go through on a daily basis."

Senior officials in U.S. President Donald Trump's administration blamed the grounding on aging air traffic control infrastructure and Congress underfunding.
