World.title: Data centres in the U.S. put out more carbon emissions in a year than Denmark, says Harvard study
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The 400 largest data centres in the United States put more heat-trapping gases into the atmosphere in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday.

Researchers found that more than half of the electricity powering hyperscale data centres in the U.S. was generated using fossil fuels, contributing to a significant increase in emissions.

The study results come as negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, which the U.S. skipped this year, launched a voluntary pledge Monday calling on companies and countries to power the world's data centres with clean energy and be more transparent about their power and water consumption and emissions.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse."

As public opposition to data centres continues to mount, the political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections for new sites.

In Canada, plans for massive data centres have triggered protests in communities across the country, including this fall over a proposed data centre for AI giant Anthropic in Nova Scotia and a $52-billion data centre near Regina, Saskatchewan.

Inside the climate toll of data centres

Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centres between May 2024 and April 2025, using available data and modelling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity used by the centres produced around 28.3 million tons (25.7 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide, according to the study in Monday's Nature Sustainability.

The Dave Johnson coal-fired power plant is silhouetted against the morning sun in Glenrock, Wyo. in this 2018 file photo. (J. David Ake/ The Associated Press)

More than half their 82 terawatt-hours of electricity use, enough to power nearly seven million homes for a year, came from fossil fuels, the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found. Coal, widely considered the most environmentally damaging fossil fuel, generated 15 per cent of the electricity used.

The emissions estimate is two to three times higher than previous studies had shown, said Francesca Dominici, the study's senior author and a Harvard biostatistics professor.

WATCH | 'Big emitters' putting profits over people, UN secretary-general says: Big emitters 'profiting' from the planet's destruction: UN chief | Duration 0:46 United Nations Secretary General António Guterres took aim at 'big emitters' and the fossil fuel lobby at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31), calling for drastic emissions cuts to keep global warming below the 1.5 C limit set by the Paris Agreement by the end of the century.

"It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country," Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centres make that quantity more worrisome for the future. "We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions."

Researchers noted that data centre construction has only expanded since the study period, meaning emissions from this industry are probably even higher now.

"What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," lead author Gianluca Guidi, postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics, said in a press release.

WATCH | Nova Scotians protest construction of AI data centre: Nova Scotians rally against planned $10B AI facility | Duration closed caption 2:12 Crowds across the province gathered to protest EverWind Fuels’ proposed Cape Breton data centre for AI giant Anthropic. CBC's Ben Dornan reports.

Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday's study reached realistic conclusions and that its use of modelling was reasonable because companies disclose little about their power consumption and pollution.

"We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure," said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn't involved in the study. "Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centres, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity."

'Selling us hope while hiding the harms'

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge, launched by COP31 host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centres should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems.

WATCH | Canada's data centre guidelines aren't strong enough, critics say: Canada's new data centre guidelines lack teeth, critics say | Duration closed caption 2:04 Alberta has become ground zero in Canada's plan to build hundreds of AI data centres, but locals are pushing back over concerns about energy demands and environmental impacts. Ottawa has issued new guidelines for responsible development, but critics say they lack teeth.

The pledge says the environmental impacts of data centres should be assessed and disclosed, but it also calls for harnessing artificial intelligence to help address climate change, which some climate experts see as a contradiction given AI's growing environmental footprint.

The explosion of new and planned data centres has driven demand for new sources of power generation and contributed to some of the biggest tech companies missing their climate goals, according to a report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation.

The report, published earlier this month, found that electricity consumption by Amazon, Microsoft and Google had risen 240 per cent between 2022 and 2025 amid the AI race. Its authors accused Big Tech of " greenwashing" AI by obscuring its current environmental impact behind claims of future climate gains.

WATCH | Digging into claims that AI can help the planet: Can AI save the planet before it wrecks it | Duration closed caption 3:31 The debate over artificial intelligence is raging. Some say it’s our best hope for solving the climate crisis. Others warn it might just wipe out humanity. Between those two extreme futures is a much less hypothetical reality – AI’s huge impact on our environment, and on emissions, now. Analyst and advocate Ketan Joshi helps us unpack what’s at stake for the climate as the AI buildout ramps up, and how much progress this technology has made so far when it comes to emissions cuts.

Former U.S. vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said that while it is essential for data centres to be powered by carbon-free energy, he is hopeful their computing power could help find new ways to fight climate change.

In an interview with The Associated Press, Gore cited research by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern, who predicted that by 2030 "we will see 6 to 9 per cent reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy."

Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said, "AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centres face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centres, but the fears may be overblown."

But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical.

"We have hope in one hand and then harms in the other," Newell said. "They're selling us hope while hiding the harms from us."

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Being Deposed as a Governor in Cuba with No Details Made Public
World.content:
The deposed governor of Camaguey, Cuba, Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia

By Amado Viera

HAVANA TIMES – On Saturday, November 14, during the debut of a radio program he will appear on every two weeks to “establish direct communication with the people,” Walter Simon Noris, the Communist Party’s first secretary in Camagüey, was so intent on focusing on his achievements at the helm of the province that he ended up with almost 20 minutes of airtime to spare.

He could have used precisely that time to reveal the “errors incompatible with his responsibilities” that had cost Governor Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia his position four days earlier. The accusations against the latter were so serious that the official announcement of his dismissal described it merely as a “resignation at his own request,” rather than softening it with terms such as “release from duties” or “assignment to other responsibilities,” which Cuban bureaucratic language typically uses in cases involving disgraced officials who have not been implicated in corruption or other similarly serious offenses.

Sutil had been “elected” governor of Camagüey in May 2023. At the time, the position of first secretary of the Communist Party was held by Federico Hernandez a party official from Granma province who would be dismissed two years later so that his involvement in a beef-trafficking network extending all the way to Havana could be investigated. The last information about him, several months later, was that he was in the capital awaiting legal proceedings in which several farm owners, private business owners, and a sizable group of Agriculture Ministry officials would also stand trial.

To get an idea of the magnitude of Sutil’s blunder, it is enough to note that, even under those circumstances, Hernandez’s removal had been described in official statements as a “release from duties as part of a renewal process.” That was far more lenient language than the wording used now.

“And What Do You Expect Me to Do?”

Sutil had arrived at Quinta San Zenon—the seat of the Camagüey provincial government—to replace Yoseily Gongora Lopez, a young politician who had taken advantage of her position to undergo a marathon series of cosmetic surgeries in Havana between 2021 and 2022. Thanks to those procedures, she managed to lose nearly 50 kilograms (110 pounds) and overcome her obesity. The problem was that she did so at the most critical point of the pandemic, when the province was on the verge of collapse. Gongora not only neglected the crisis but also clung to her office, aware that the preferential treatment she was receiving was due to her status as governor.

“If you ask me, it wasn’t an improvised decision but one based on pure calculation. Faced with a choice between improving her health and sacrificing herself to fulfill the responsibilities for which she had been elected, she chose the former. She must have known it would cost her career as a government official. That’s why, when she returned to lead the province, she didn’t make the slightest effort. You could see her at meetings and during official visits and realize she was there simply to go through the motions,” explained an official with the Camagüey provincial government.

Despite the controversies surrounding her, when Gongora was removed from office, she received “recognition for the effort, work, and dedication devoted to government service.” She was also appointed to a comfortable administrative position at Artex, a state-owned company that markets cultural performances and products.

Sutil’s final weeks as governor are reminiscent of that period under his predecessor. In fact, the only photograph published by the state press of the meeting at which he was dismissed shows him sitting in the second row of the officials presiding over the meeting, staring blankly into space and almost leaning against the wall. It was much the same way Gongora could sometimes be seen during her final official appearances.

There has been considerable speculation on social media about the reasons behind Sutil’s dismissal. More than one online content creator has claimed credit for bringing it about through alleged revelations concerning fuel trafficking, influence peddling, and other economic crimes. But the truth is that no one has been able to provide evidence beyond the testimony of sources who requested anonymity. Not a single incriminating document has come to light.

What is beyond dispute is that during the weeks preceding the former official’s “resignation”—when he had already been effectively excluded from major decision-making—some changes did occur in the way the province was run.

For example, the previous weekend, a massive cleanup campaign was launched in the city of Camagüey. The fuel needed to carry it out, which had been unavailable for weeks, suddenly appeared. State-operated minibuses also resumed service, transporting thousands of people daily at fares far lower than those charged by private operators. And several people connected to the Ministry of Public Health confirmed that the fleet of electric vehicles delivered to the province just a few months earlier to support healthcare services had been reorganized. These were the same vehicles that could often be found just about anywhere except at hospitals.

“It would be unfair to accuse Sutil of being directly responsible for so many things going wrong, but it’s equally true that he allowed them to happen. Even when problems were reported directly to him or were so obvious that there was no way to ignore them. I remember that about a year ago, a highly respected doctor approached him to denounce the shady dealings surrounding fuel sales in dollars. One specific example was the Sputnik gas station, where people who controlled places in line charged customers for their turns, and the regulations limiting the number of liters each customer could purchase were blatantly violated. ‘And what do you expect me to do?’ was Sutil’s response. That’s no way to run a province,” the official interviewed pointed out.

The former governor was not even capable of making simple decisions that would have been widely applauded by his fellow citizens, such as restoring order to Agramonte Park and Republica Street, the two busiest public spaces in the provincial capital, now overrun by skateboarders, beggars, and vehicles moving about as they please.

By the time rumors of his possible dismissal began to spread, Sutil had virtually no supporters left. In three years, he had exhausted the political capital he brought to office. Faced with that obvious reality, the government’s efforts have focused on preventing the details of his downfall from becoming public. There is little more they can hope to accomplish.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Nicaragua and The Fear of Dignity
World.content:
Carlos Brenes and Salvadora Martínez have now spent 15 months in detention, with the authorities providing no information regarding their whereabouts.

How terrified the Nicaraguan dictatorship is of the dignity of a 71-year-old man and his 69-year-old wife.

By Thelma Brenes Muñoz (Confidencial)

HAVANA TIMES – My father, Carlos Brenes Sanchez, was arrested on August 14, 2025, along with Salvadora Martinez. As of November 15th of this year, it has been 15 months without any news of them. Both suffer from high blood pressure. My father is insulin-dependent. Salvadora was scheduled to undergo gallbladder surgery the week after her disappearance, 15 months ago. Every day without medication and adequate medical care puts their lives at risk. That is why the Nicaraguan state is responsible for whatever happens to them.

I have called the prison system from abroad to ask whether they are being held there. I do not make these calls expecting an answer. I make them to demonstrate that I am still searching for them, to document my efforts, and to expose the silence of the Nicaraguan state.

My father had already been unjustly detained in August 2018. He was prosecuted and put on trial despite being innocent. He was released from prison in June 2019 under a general amnesty that the government was forced to grant political prisoners because of international pressure. The state itself issued a judicial order under the Amnesty Law, ordering his “immediate release,” directing that his “criminal records be expunged,” and expressly ruling that “the conditions associated with the precautionary measures are hereby rendered null and void.” However, the regime lied. They never left him in peace.

Since his release in 2019, police officers in Carazo regularly visited his home to monitor him. They also imposed the arbitrary requirement that he send daily photographs via WhatsApp to report to the police. Despite the illegality of these measures, he complied with the rules imposed by the dictatorship and demonstrated his integrity. The government failed to honor the provisions of the amnesty it had granted.

Why, if my father was a free citizen, did he have to keep reporting to the police and remain under surveillance through visits by police patrols? My father was not arrested and forcibly disappeared for committing a crime. They are holding him captive and isolated out of revenge: for thinking differently, for remaining true to his ideals, and for maintaining a dignity that the regime cannot break.

We will not stop searching for him and Salvadora. We will not stop demanding their unconditional release, and we will not allow them to be erased in the darkness of the cells of La Modelo and La Esperanza prisons.

First published in Spanish by Confidencial and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Nicaragua here on Havana Times.

World.title: What I’ve Learned in My Home Barbershop
World.content:
My first customers were my friends.

By Erick Hernandez

HAVANA TIMES – I come from a journalism background, as I’ve already mentioned in this space. I wasn’t an early reader, but from the age of fourteen, when someone sent me a folder full of ebooks, I read every night until my phone fell out of my hands.

The next morning, the device would be completely drained after spending the night displaying a page that no one would read. Back then, before buying my first books, I read exclusively on my phone, but I did so with a voracious appetite that I hope to recover.

That didn’t prevent me from socializing with other kids my age or having friends, both boys and girls, at school. Nevertheless, the barbershop gave me a crash course in practical knowledge and pragmatism. Suddenly, I found myself talking to strangers who had all kinds of stories to tell.

Once, I even cut the hair of a drunk man who said his father had died two days earlier and that he had gotten a tattoo in his honor. When he showed it to me, the tattoo turned out to be nothing more than the Real Madrid emblem, which looked more like a melted piece of candy.

I learned to communicate and to understand, above all, to understand. Not to understand the big problems, which I may already have explored through journalism, but to understand why a man gets a haircut before leaving for a week of work, and why a mother brings her child in, and sometimes it’s the grandmother who comes instead.

I learned a great deal about fatherhood and watched different kinds of fathers deal with their children’s restlessness. I didn’t learn about failures of the National Electric Power System, water shortages, or the lack of medicines. My customers faced all those problems, but I was already familiar with them myself. The lessons all those men taught me went much deeper and lay in the small details of their lives, in their motivations. They were there in the young man who wanted to raise fighting roosters and went to Uruguay, only to return because he couldn’t bear the loneliness.

I also learned a great deal about myself. On those mornings when no one came in, when I had grown tired of reading and listening to music, there was nothing left for me to do but think. And little by little, a quiet kind of understanding began to settle in. I thought about my work projects and household matters, but those subjects barely filled a day. If the following morning found me idle again, I had no choice but to venture into more uncertain territory.

My thoughts ranged from imagining the lives of people walking by, to fictional scenarios I invented for amusement, to observing the grass and plants in the garden. Every morning, I checked on the condition of those green stems that kept me company.

Sometimes I was in that introspective state when a customer arrived, and then I found it difficult to snap out of it. It was easier if the person was a regular, but if he was a stranger, with no previous conversation to pick up, sometimes we wouldn’t speak at all, and I would simply continue thinking about whatever was on my mind.

I didn’t realize it then, but now, looking back, I understand that I was discovering myself during that period. I reflected on many things and resolved questions that had lingered in my mind. I was able to think so deeply about subjects that interested me that I eventually felt confident enough to take a position on them. Out of that process came several professional decisions that I’m glad I made.

Those periods of reflection and conversations with customers made me, if not a more mature person, at least a more humane one, someone more directly connected to other human beings. And whenever I have to make a difficult decision, I remember that young man, the one who came back to be with his family.

Read more from the diary of Erick Hernandez here on Havana Times.

World.title: Dignity Still Survives in Guamuta, Cuba
World.content:
Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano. FREEDOM

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – In contemporary Cuba, protesting is not merely a public expression of discontent: it is also an act of personal exposure. Those who raise their voices against those in power face not only the possibility of arrest but also a system of surveillance, discrediting, isolation, and punishment that can turn a social demand into a personal tragedy.

It is in this context that the name Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano emerges. He is a resident of Guamuta, a community in Cuba’s Santiago de Cuba province, marked—like all the others—by the economic and political tensions that permeate everyday life on the island.

This young man became well known in late 2025 for confronting President Miguel Diaz-Canel during one of those carefully planned visits that the “handpicked president” makes to mingle with the crowds, although those gatherings are generally thoroughly screened to prevent uncomfortable situations.

In this case, however, Hurricane Melissa had just swept through eastern Cuba, and apparently the screening apparatus had not been fully activated. Somehow, Yoel Alejandro managed to reach the president and tell him some hard truths about how badly his fellow citizens in the eastern region were suffering. As usual, the responses were evasive, and everything seemed to end there—until the young man decided to take matters into his own hands.

First, he decided to write a book so that silence would not be the final outcome of his concerns, although he never made its title or publication date public, to avoid reprisals.

With the support of prominent dissident Jose Daniel Ferrer, the young man took small steps to improve his neighbors’ quality of life. But he committed the sin of saying that none of it had been accomplished with government assistance.

As though that were a grave offense rather than an undeniable truth, the regime’s henchmen arrested him and sent him to jail at the Versailles Police Operations Unit in Santiago de Cuba.

When someone is imprisoned after participating in a protest, the essential question is not simply which legal provision is invoked, but whether that provision is applied in a manner consistent with freedom of expression and assembly. Laws can become instruments of justice or mechanisms of intimidation. It all depends on whether they protect citizens from abuse or end up protecting those in power from the citizenry.

Protest in Guamuta, Cuba over Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano’s arrest.

Perez Serrano’s case is not an exception

As with other protesters against the regime whom we have discussed in recent months, Perez Serrano’s case should not be viewed merely as an individual case, but as a window into the broader problem of the criminalization of protest.

In Guamuta, as in so many Cuban communities outside the major urban centers, scarcity is felt more personally, and support networks are limited. Complaints circulate by word of mouth, through private messages, in family backyards, and in discreet conversations. When a protest erupts, it does not come out of nowhere: it represents months or years of accumulated frustration.

In this setting, the figure of the political prisoner—or the citizen detained for participating in a protest—takes on symbolic significance. Their body becomes the battleground between two opposing interpretations. For the authorities, the person may be a violator of public order, someone accused of contempt, disobedience, assaulting authorities, or public disorder.

For their relatives and supporters, however, that person is being punished for demanding rights or expressing legitimate grievances. In Perez Serrano’s case, he also tried to do something about the problems he denounced, contributing what little he could to alleviate the difficult circumstances facing his fellow citizens.

Unlike on other occasions, this time the person who stood up against tyranny was not met with indifference. Several videos are circulating on social media showing Guamuta residents demanding his release.

In Cuba, protests in recent years have revealed a profound transformation in social discontent. It is no longer simply a matter of organized opposition groups or voices from exile. Demonstrations have involved neighbors, workers, young people, mothers, and individuals who may never have considered themselves political.

Many take to the streets not with a fully developed ideological platform, but with immediate demands: “food,” “freedom,” “electricity,” and “medicine.” That spontaneity makes any power structure uncomfortable because it reveals that discontent can emerge outside official channels.

The state’s response to these expressions of discontent has included arrests, interrogations, prison sentences, and subsequent restrictions intended to silence certain individuals temporarily. Yet these measures simultaneously deepen social resentment.

A community may learn to remain silent, but that does not necessarily mean it stops thinking. Imposed silence is not the same as consensus, and sometimes it is merely a pause filled with fear.

The fundamental solution is not simply to release one person, although freedom for those unjustly imprisoned is an immediate demand. It is also necessary to review the laws that allow protests to be punished disproportionately, guarantee public and impartial trials, permit the presence of independent observers, and recognize citizens’ right to assemble peacefully.

A country does not grow stronger by punishing every dissenting voice. It grows stronger when it can listen to those voices without feeling that its very existence is constantly under threat.

Guamuta reminds us that Cuba’s political history is not written solely through official speeches or in major capitals, but also in small towns, on anonymous streets, and through the voices of those who, tired of waiting, decide to speak out.

Dignity remains in Guamuta, because a society that forgets its prisoners ends up normalizing injustice, and a society that turns protest into a crime gradually loses its ability to correct itself.

True stability does not arise from fear, but from the ability to voice grievances without facing persecution. And that distinction determines not only the fate of one man—in this case, Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano—but also the public dignity of an entire country.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Monday, November 16, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Monday, November 16, 2026.

U.S. Air Travelers Continue to Face Canceled or Delayed Flights After Nationwide Ground Stop Order

Nov 16, 2026

U.S. air travelers continue to face canceled or delayed flights today after a weekend of travel chaos sparked by a nationwide ground-stop order that halted domestic flights for about four hours on Friday. It was the biggest disruption to U.S. air travel since the September 11, 2001, attacks. More than 12,000 flights were canceled throughout the weekend; thousands more faced delays. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy refused to apologize for the cancellations during several public appearances. Duffy blamed a contractor doing maintenance to upgrade old copper wire to fiber-optic cable, and also blamed the travel chaos on prior presidential administrations and called on Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to modernize air traffic control systems. Democrats pointed to $12.5 billion already approved by the Republican-controlled Congress for Department of Transportation upgrades and said the Trump administration had only spent about $1 billion of those funds. Meanwhile, two people were injured on Saturday night when two planes collided on the tarmac while taxiing at Miami International Airport.

Iran Launches Attack on Bahrain, Targeting Radar Positions

Nov 16, 2026

Iran launched an attack on Bahrain early Sunday, the latest strike on the kingdom, as clashes between Iran and the U.S. continue while peace talks remain stalled. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it targeted radar positions at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base with six drones. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. Bahrain is officially home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, though the Pentagon largely abandoned its base there after it was heavily damaged by Iranian attacks in the opening days of the U.S. war on Iran. In recent weeks, U.S. forces have quietly hit several Iranian targets, among them Qeshm Island, which houses a major Revolutionary Guard naval facility. This is Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson.

Esmail Baghaei: “We will not leave any attack unanswered. No military aggression against Iran by the United States or others will go unanswered. We have demonstrated this in practice, and we will continue to act in the future in whatever manner and by whatever means Iran’s powerful armed forces deem appropriate.”

Yemeni Government Forces Retreat to Defend Aden from Houthis

Nov 16, 2026

In Yemen, forces aligned with the internationally recognized government announced Sunday they were retreating from areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait in order to focus on defending their interim capital, Aden. It’s a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against fighters with the Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis. The retreat came as Houthi forces pushed to within 40 miles of Aden. Meanwhile, the International Committee of the Red Cross said Sunday the Houthis had unilaterally released hundreds of prisoners. This is the head of the Houthis’ prisoner affairs committee.

Abdul Qader al-Murtada: “The largest and most extensive amnesty and release operation has been carried out. This operation includes 600 detainees who were captured over the past years, all of whom were captured on the frontlines, particularly along the border battle fronts. Most of them have been in captivity for several years, and some are individuals with humanitarian needs, including the ill and the elderly.”

Mass Funeral Held in Gaza for Dozens of Palestinians Killed by Israeli Forces

Nov 16, 2026

In Gaza, a mass funeral was held Sunday for dozens of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces and whose remains had been trapped in the rubble for years. Palestinian officials in Gaza say 70 skeletal remains were found beneath what were once homes and underneath the ruins of destroyed buildings in Gaza’s north. At least 10 of them were children. The remains of an estimated 8,000 Palestinians are believed to still be trapped in the rubble after more than three years of Israel’s war, and as Israeli forces block the entrance of heavy equipment needed to properly search for the missing in Gaza.

Gaza has been described as the “world’s largest mass grave.”

This comes as a senior Hamas commander, Samir Abu Younis, was killed in an Israeli strike on Khan Younis Saturday. Dozens of Palestinians attended his funeral Sunday.

Iyad Awadallah: “Now we, as the Palestinian people, affirm to the occupation that we remain steadfast and that it will not achieve its goals, because our people are determined to remain on their land.”

NYT: Israel Abducted Two Iranian Generals in Effort to Locate Missing Israeli Air Force Navigator

Nov 16, 2026

A New York Times investigation has found that Israel abducted two Iranian generals in recent years in a bid to gather intelligence about the 1986 disappearance of Israeli Air Force navigator Ron Arad in Lebanon. Both generals were secretly interrogated by Israel’s spy service Mossad. One of them, Alireza Asgari, was abducted in Turkey in 2006 and killed after his interrogation. The other general, Abdullah Saberi, was kidnapped in Damascus, Syria, in 2021 and later released in Johannesburg, South Africa. He said he had been tortured by his Israeli captors. The kidnappings came despite multiple Israeli intelligence reports that concluded Iran had not been involved in the missing airman’s disappearance.

Dozens Rally in Support of Democratic Sen. Van Hollen to Serve as Senate Majority Leader

Nov 16, 2026

In Maryland, dozens of protesters rallied Saturday outside the Baltimore office of Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, urging Democrats to elect him Senate majority leader instead of New York Senator Chuck Schumer when the party takes control of both chambers of Congress in January. Organizers from the Baltimore Rapid Response Network, Charm City Indivisible, Allies for Democracy and IfNotNow Baltimore said the midterm blue wave shows voters are demanding transformational change. Senator Van Hollen has been an outspoken critic of corporate money in politics, the war on Iran and U.S. weapons shipments to Israel, and has called on Democrats to break with AIPAC. This is Ashley Esposito, an elected school board member in Baltimore.

Ashley Esposito: “I’m out here supporting Chris Van Hollen because after the election, I did not want people to go to sleep, and, you know, I was focused on, like, how do we maintain this momentum that we have. And we can’t just go and look at, like, 2028 and the next election cycle.”

Democrats Win Governor’s Race in Alaska

Nov 16, 2026

Democrats have won Alaska’s governorship for the first time since 1998. Former state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins beat three Republicans, one of them endorsed by Donald Trump. His win gives Democrats control of 30 governorships nationwide. Meanwhile, in Alaska’s Senate race, Democrat and former Congressmember Mary Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 3.7 percentage points, or just over 10,000 votes.

Death Toll from U.S. Measles Outbreak Rises to 10

Nov 16, 2026

The death toll from the measles outbreak in the U.S. has jumped to at least 10, as more infections erupt across several states. Wisconsin health officials reported the death of a child Friday, marking the second measles-related death in the state so far this year. On the same day, officials in Pennsylvania said an unvaccinated resident had died of measles. This comes as the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization revoked the designation amid an unprecedented measles outbreak nationwide with more than 5,400 confirmed measles cases this year. The rapid spread of measles cases comes as Trump’s Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has backed anti-vaccine policies.

People’s Climate March Demands Urgent Action by Leaders at COP31 Climate Summit

Nov 16, 2026

Here in Antalya, Turkey, about 10,000 people marched through pouring rain on Saturday on the sidelines of the COP31 United Nations climate conference. They’re demanding an immediate phaseout of fossil fuels, support for impacted communities and to make polluters pay for climate damage, loss and destruction. The march included Indigenous campaigners, antiwar groups, trade unionists and environmentalists. It was led by LGBTQ+ protesters who have faced increased persecution in recent months by Turkish authorities, who have raided the homes and offices of NGOs that advocate for their rights. This is Brian Misiati, an organizer with the multifaith environmental movement Greenfaith Africa.

Brian Odhiambo Misiati: “Why we are not doing this protest at the COP venue is because not everyone is allowed into the COP venue, and we feel that we should take this to the people, who might not have the privilege of also accessing the COP venue. So, it’s a matter of the people; it’s not a matter of the delegates.”

After headlines, we’ll hear more voices from the People’s Climate March and spend the rest of the hour on the COP31 climate talks underway here in Antalya, Turkey.

Protesters Mobilize in Manila Ahead of Trump’s Visit to ASEAN Summit

Nov 16, 2026

In the Philippines, hundreds of protesters clashed with police in Manila on Sunday while marching toward the ASEAN summit to oppose President Trump’s expected visit on Tuesday. The protesters were also demonstrating against a planned American-led artificial intelligence hub in the Philippines under a new initiative called Pax Silica. This is a protester.

Teddy Casino: “The issues that we are here, of course, because Donald Trump will be arriving, is our opposition to the war on Iran, because this has caused so much hardship for the Filipino people in terms of rising prices and the economic crisis.”

Hundreds of Thousands Rally in Prague to Defend Public Broadcasting from Andrej Babiš’s Overhaul

Nov 16, 2026

In the Czech Republic, 350,000 people rallied in Prague on Sunday to defend the license fees that fund the country’s public broadcasters. Organizers called it one of the largest protests in the country’s history. It follows weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities and a strike by staff at Czech TV and Czech Radio. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’s right-wing government wants to scrap the license fees and pay for public TV and radio from the state budget. Critics say the change would give the government more control over content. This is a student protester.

Pavel Blazek: “I hope the government will finally understand that there are enough people here to be able to change it somehow and that the government will finally let it go. Will that happen? It’s hard to say, but we’ll meet here again sometime.”

Humpback Whale Spotted in Hudson River as New York Marks Progress in Combating Pollution

Nov 16, 2026

Last month, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani opened a 50-year-old time capsule on Staten Island that had been buried back on October 21, 1976. Inside was a letter from former Mayor Abraham Beame, who hoped that upgrading the city’s wastewater plants would eventually make New York’s polluted rivers clean again. So when a humpback whale showed up in the Hudson River last week, New Yorkers immediately connected the sighting to Mayor Mamdani and Beame’s 50-year-old wish. Here’s Mayor Mamdani reading former Mayor Beame’s letter last month.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani: “’We are doing all we can, despite a current period of governmental austerity, to leave you a legacy of a clean and beautiful environment. We hope you and your young people will be able to swim, fish and recreate in any part of the Hudson River, the East River, the Harlem River, the Long Island Sound, the Upper Bay and the beaches of Staten Island, Brooklyn and Queens.’”

Mamdani to Dismantle NYPD Unit That Spied on Protesters

Nov 16, 2026

Mayor Mamdani announced this morning that he’s disbanding the NYPD’s controversial Strategic Response Group, which was surveilling protests around the city. In a statement, Mamdani said, “New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat. We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation.”

Trump, Xi and Putin to Hold Unprecedented Trilateral Summit in Shenzhen

Nov 16, 2026

U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are scheduled to hold their first-ever trilateral summit later this week on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: Havana Times 2026 Photo Contest Finalists
World.content:
This photo by Sergio Leyva was a Special Mention in the 12th HT Photo Contest in 2023.

By Circles Robinson

HAVANA TIMES – The judging of our 15th Photo Contest is now in the final stage. We started with 328 pictures from 39 participants. A total of 150 photos from 31 photographers made the first cut in the six categories. In the second cut, 68 photos made it to the finals from 27 photographers.

To make it to the finals a photo had to have at least four of the 12 jurors selecting it in round two.

The finals are made up by: Colores / Colors (11 photos), Comida / Food (9), Compañia / Company (11), Movimiento / Movement (12), Resistencia / Resistance (14) and Transporte / Transportation (11).

In this final round, as in other years, the 12 judges are asked to select a 1st place, 2nd Place 3rd Place and 4th Place.

When we tabulate their selections we will be assigning the photos points (10 to first, 5 to second, 3 to third and 1 to fourth). Then we add them all up to find the winners and special mentions.

The jury this year is made up by 12 judges residing in four countries. Most of the jurors have taken part in judging all, or nearly all, of the previous 14 contests.

Prizes: The winners of each category will receive a prize of US $100.

Here are the HT 15th Photo Contest Finalists:

Note: since there are a lot of photos it may take a couple minutes for all to be visible.

FOOD / COMIDA

COMPANY / COMPAÑIA
