World.title: Venezuela: Changing Everything So That Nothing Changes?
World.content:
The return of Maria Corina Machado and the appointment of new Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco suggest that a political transition is taking shape in Venezuela. How much influence will the results of the US elections have on the South American country’s immediate future?

By Suhelis Tejero Puntes (Connectas.org)

HAVANA TIMES – Washington is aiming for presidential elections in Venezuela in 2027, while analysts say this would require reforms to the electoral and judicial branches.

The new US Congress could demand transparency regarding oil agreements and the management of revenues from oil sales, but without changing the terms favorable to the United States.

Investigations have been announced into attacks in Venezuelan waters against alleged drug-trafficking boats, which have left hundreds dead without any judicial proceedings.

Delcy Rodríguez may try to wear down Machado politically, but Chavismo no longer controls the pace of negotiations as it once did.

In Venezuela, there are weeks when nothing happens and others when the entire political landscape shifts. Between October 25 and November 2, opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to the country after nearly ten months in exile, acting President Delcy Rodríguez appointed Oliver Blanco, a politician with a background in the opposition, as foreign minister, and four days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio received him in Washington.

All this would suggest that Venezuela’s transition toward a democratically elected government has begun. But now that Democrats have won the US midterm elections and will control both chambers of Congress beginning in January 2027, some are wondering whether that victory could alter a Venezuelan process whose fate is being decided not in Caracas, but in the White House.

For political consultant Eugenio Martínez, the starting point is clear: the United States is promoting and overseeing talks between the government and the opposition, meaning it will also serve as guarantor of any agreements eventually reached. It follows that whatever is negotiated will respond both to Washington’s foreign policy needs and to the dynamics of the Trump administration as the 2028 election campaign approaches.

There is a clear reason for this. As Martínez explains, “Congress, generally speaking, has no power or authority to change foreign policy. What is clear, however, is that Venezuela will be among the issues on which the new Congress will demand transparency.”

Congressional Priorities

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee, has already announced four investigations: the enrichment of the Trump family, abuses by the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), corporate corruption, and the Epstein files. This does not mean these will be the only subjects investigated, but they will be the priorities.

Beyond these issues, Laura Dib, director of the Venezuela Program at the Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA), also expects Congress to demand accountability regarding oil and mining agreements between the United States and Venezuela.

Congress will also raise the need for greater transparency regarding the audit reportedly conducted by KPMG of the US Treasury account holding Venezuelan oil revenues managed by Washington, as well as joint military operations in the states of Apure and Bolívar and attacks on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean.

“However, one possible risk of increased tensions between the legislative and executive branches is that attention will shift to domestic issues and Venezuela will cease to be a priority,” Dib said in a thread posted on her X account.

Another factor is that Venezuela’s transition enjoys bipartisan support. Experts agree that both Democrats and Republicans support the return of democracy. Moreover, both parties share similar positions when it comes to economic interests.

“There may be investigations, but they won’t challenge the basic premise of the negotiated oil agreements,” says political analyst Carmen Beatriz Fernandez.

This raises the possibility of a less dramatic outcome. Rather than a break by Democrats with Trump’s policies toward Venezuela, there could simply be a realignment. In other words, beyond the details, the broader relationship — the oil business and the energy and mining alliance — could remain essentially unchanged.

“I believe the broad agreements concerning the relationship between Venezuela and the United States enjoy consensus between both parties, and much of Venezuela’s political leadership also sees it that way,” Fernandez emphasizes.

Elections in 2027?

After considerable back-and-forth, Rubio said this week that elections should “ideally” be held in 2027. But to conduct them with all the necessary legal formalities, reforms to the judicial and electoral branches are still needed.

The process of renewing the Supreme Court of Justice (TSJ) is already underway, while a call to renew the National Electoral Council (CNE) is expected in the coming weeks.

Regarding the latter, Rubio said that Venezuela “needs a new electoral council that is administrative rather than political in nature.”

“I think we’ve made good progress. We just have to stay on top of everything and make sure we meet these deadlines, because once the electoral council is established, the necessary elements will be in place,” he explained at a press conference.

For his part, new Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, while avoiding setting a date for the elections, assured that all political forces would be guaranteed the opportunity to participate.

Although he did not say so explicitly, he was referring to the fact that, over the past several decades, Chavismo has disqualified opposition leaders to prevent them from running for office, as it did with Mari Corina Machado in the 2024 elections.

In fact, this is one of the issues being addressed at the political guarantees negotiating table, where Chavismo and the opposition are currently negotiating the transition under White House leadership.

The analysts consulted agree that it would be possible to organize elections under acceptable conditions within no more than two months, provided the necessary reforms to the judicial and electoral branches are carried out.

But Martínez warns that any additional discussions would cause delays.

“It is impossible for the first electoral process of Venezuela’s transition to resolve all the shortcomings of the past two decades. In this regard, the opposition must be quite pragmatic when demanding conditions and guarantees,” the analyst concludes.

Signs of a Transition?

Oliver Blanco’s appointment as foreign minister under Chavismo lends itself to two interpretations that are not mutually exclusive.

On the one hand, Fernandez describes him as “a bridge between two systems,” someone “extremely skilled” who was trained in the political school of diplomat Diego Arria and former opposition lawmaker Henry Ramos Allup.

On the other hand, the analyst believes the acting president would hardly have appointed him without the influence of the US State Department.

Martínez, meanwhile, highlights Blanco’s political path. Blanco first came to public attention through his ties to a sector of the opposition but gradually distanced himself from it and moved closer to the circle surrounding Delcy and Jorge Rodriguez.

Martinez says Blanco became foreign minister because the acting president wanted to appoint officials with whom Washington felt comfortable.

The other significant sign is the return of María Corina Machado. “She could not have returned to Venezuela if there weren’t already talks underway,” Fernandez says.

“There has been a trade-off, an exchange of important things for other important things,” she adds.

Martinez, meanwhile, offers a more measured assessment of the significance of her return. It could serve as a catalyst, but “neither the opposition nor Maria Corina Machado alone controls the timing of the negotiations,” something that rests entirely in the hands of the White House.

Nevertheless, the situation is not without risks.

According to Fernandez, Delcy Rodríguez and her brother Jorge Rodriguez, president of the National Assembly, are betting that an improving economy will provide them with at least a minimum degree of legitimacy.

They also hope Machado will begin to lose political momentum because she lacks a clear electoral timetable and the opportunity to conduct a formal campaign, all while the country’s problems remain unresolved.

But unlike on previous occasions, Chavismo no longer has the option of buying time through endless negotiations. With the United States as a third party at the negotiating table, the ruling party now faces the same uncertainty as the opposition.

Thus, the developments of recent weeks can be interpreted in two ways. They may represent the opening chapter of a transition with a clear timetable, or merely a reshuffling of the players without changing anything fundamental.

As in the famous line from The Leopard, the novel by Lampedusa, this would amount to “changing everything so that nothing changes.”

Read more feature articles here on Havana Times.

World.title: Orsi praises “excellent” ties with Milei and Lula’s re-election ahead of the Mercosur summit
World.content:
Orsi praises “excellent” ties with Milei and Lula’s re-election ahead of the Mercosur summit

16th Monday, November 2026 - 20:47 UTC Full article

Orsi also praised Lula’s regional role and described his October 25 re-election as “fundamental”

Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi described his government’s relationship with Javier Milei’s administration in Argentina as “excellent” and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election in Brazil as “fundamental”, in a Mercosur assessment given in Madrid less than three weeks before the bloc’s summit of heads of state in Montevideo on December 4.

“The relationship is excellent,” Orsi said of Argentina at a breakfast forum organised by Nueva Economía Fórum, according to Europa Press. “Things we had never achieved, we did achieve with this government.” The Uruguayan president, of the left-wing Broad Front, attributed the good ties with Milei’s government to fluid contact even from “different philosophies and positions”, citing as examples progress on dredging the access channel to the port of Montevideo and the resolution of tensions over HIF Global’s green hydrogen plant project in Paysandú. Both countries also agree on the need to make Mercosur more flexible and modern.

Orsi also praised Lula’s regional role and described his October 25 re-election as “fundamental”. “It is good news because of the positions both candidates took on integration,” he said.

The remarks come at a time of strong tensions within the bloc. Relations between Argentina and Brazil are at their lowest point following Milei’s repeated attacks on Lula and the departure of defeated candidate Flávio Bolsonaro from Brazil via Argentine territory. Paraguay is also going through an institutional crisis after the removal and arrest of President Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, with his successor, Pedro Alliana, sworn in ten days ago.

The Montevideo summit, which will close Uruguay’s pro tempore presidency, is expected to address the debate on making the bloc more flexible and ongoing trade negotiations with Canada, the United Arab Emirates, Vietnam and Japan. The trade agreement with the European Union has applied provisionally since May 1.

World.title: Venezuela accuses Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi of “interference” over call for free elections
World.content:
Venezuela accuses Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi of “interference” over call for free elections

16th Monday, November 2026 - 20:42 UTC Full article

Uruguay and Venezuela broke off diplomatic relations in 2024, after the Uruguayan government refused to recognise Nicolás Maduro’s proclamation as winner of the presidential election

Venezuela’s government on Monday rejected as “interference” remarks by Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi, who had said hours earlier in Madrid that he cannot recognise a democratic government in Venezuela until free elections are held. Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco replied that the country’s future “belongs to the sovereign will of Venezuelans”.

Orsi, of the left-wing Broad Front and Uruguay’s president since March 2025, was speaking at a breakfast forum organised by Nueva Economía Fórum in the Spanish capital, during a visit in which he also met Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. “Let’s call things by their name. Since my election campaign and before, Venezuela did not function as a democracy. What needs to happen in Venezuela is a roadmap that culminates in free and transparent elections,” he said. He added that “until there are free elections” he cannot “recognise a democratic republican regime”, but that this does not prevent restoring relations. “Uruguay does not only have relations with democratic countries or with our style of democracy. Countries relate as countries, not as friends,” he said.

Blanco replied on X that a president’s agenda “should be marked by attention to the affairs of his population and the development of his country”. “Mutual respect, sovereign equality and cooperation between our countries are the basis for a constructive dialogue that contributes to peace, stability and Latin American integration,” he wrote. Blanco, a former opposition aide, was appointed foreign minister in late October by acting President Delcy Rodríguez.

Uruguay and Venezuela broke off diplomatic relations in 2024, after the Uruguayan government refused to recognise Nicolás Maduro’s proclamation as winner of the presidential election, which the opposition says was won by Edmundo González Urrutia. In June 2025, the two countries reactivated consular services in Montevideo and Caracas, although Uruguay maintained its political position. Rodríguez has governed as acting president since January, after Maduro’s removal from power in a US military operation, and on October 29 promised elections organised by a “renewed” electoral authority, though without setting a date.

World.title: British polar ship Sir David Attenborough sails from Montevideo for Antarctica
World.content:
British polar ship Sir David Attenborough sails from Montevideo for Antarctica

16th Monday, November 2026 - 18:57 UTC Full article

A call at the Falklands is scheduled for December 8 to 13, before returning to Rothera

The British polar ship RRS Sir David Attenborough sailed from the port of Montevideo on Saturday bound for Signy Island in the South Orkneys to continue the British Antarctic Survey’s (BAS) 2026/27 Antarctic season, in a year in which the United Kingdom is without its military polar patrol ship, HMS Protector.

The vessel left the Uruguayan capital at around 9.20 a.m. on November 14, according to ship-tracking records. According to the official BAS schedule, it will remain at Signy station from November 20 to 24 and then operate at Rothera station, on Adelaide Island, from November 28 to December 4. A call at the Falklands is scheduled for December 8 to 13, before returning to Rothera. BAS has not detailed what tasks the ship will carry out during its stop in the islands.

At about 129 metres long and able to break ice a metre thick, the Sir David Attenborough carries personnel, scientific equipment and supplies to British research stations and conducts oceanographic studies in polar waters. It is the main vessel of the season BAS began in late October, which includes the largest penguin census ever carried out in Antarctica. The ship is registered in the islands’ maritime register, which Argentina does not recognise and has protested in the past, according to Escenario Mundial.

The season is taking place without HMS Protector, the Royal Navy’s polar patrol ship. The UK Ministry of Defence confirmed on October 26 that the vessel would not take part in the 2026/27 season due to “unforeseen circumstances” and that it is working with other government bodies to find alternatives. According to the website, the patrol ship was towed to Devonport after a breakdown, and London is assessing whether it is worth continuing to repair it. The Sir David Attenborough, a scientific and logistics vessel, is not a direct replacement for the Protector, which also carried out patrol and hydrographic survey duties.

World.title: Milei’s government races to suspend primaries and pass the budget before year-end
World.content:
Milei’s government races to suspend primaries and pass the budget before year-end

16th Monday, November 2026 - 18:54 UTC Full article

The stated aim of suspending the PASO is to cut public spending

Javier Milei’s Argentine government is accelerating a legislative agenda in the final weeks of the year whose priority is the suspension of the open primary elections, known as PASO, along with approval of the 2027 budget, reform of the Central Bank’s charter and the sovereignty defence bill, which toughens sanctions on companies operating in the Falklands without Argentine authorisation and has been cleared by committee in the Chamber of Deputies since late October.

The stated aim of suspending the PASO is to cut public spending. According to El País, the measure could also give Milei an advantage in the October 2027 presidential election: the Peronist opposition has no common candidate and, without primaries, is more likely to run divided across several lists. Abolishing them would also complicate a possible candidacy by Senator Patricia Bullrich should she decide to run outside La Libertad Avanza, amid tensions with Milei and his sister, presidential chief of staff Karina Milei.

Bullrich, the ruling party’s Senate leader, is tasked with securing the votes. According to local media, the ruling party has 33 senators willing to suspend the primaries and needs at least four more. Committee debate begins this week.

The 2027 budget will also be debated in committee on Tuesday, and the Chamber of Deputies plans to vote on it on Wednesday, November 25. Allied governors are demanding more funds for infrastructure in the provinces and payment of outstanding debts, while increases for universities, disability services and science, three areas hit by government cuts, remain without agreement. If approved, the bill will go to the Senate.

Two weeks of ordinary sessions remain, not enough for the whole agenda, so the government has already said it will call extraordinary sessions in December.

Political tensions resurfaced after the visit of Pope Leo XIV, which the president of the Argentine Bishops’ Conference, Marcelo Colombo, described as “an oasis in the desert”. The economy, with monthly inflation of around 2% according to El País and country risk at its highest level in a year, weighs on the government’s prospects.

World.title: Leo XIV denounces “market and exploitation logics” threatening the Amazon
World.content:
Leo XIV denounces “market and exploitation logics” threatening the Amazon

16th Monday, November 2026 - 13:50 UTC Full article

“In recent years, many Indigenous leaders have been killed for protecting their own territories. The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice from men,” the pontiff said

Pope Leo XIV on Sunday denounced in Pucallpa, in the Peruvian Amazon, the “logics of market and exploitation” threatening the rainforest and its peoples, and demanded justice for Indigenous leaders killed for defending their territories, in the most combative speech of his visit to Peru, which ends on Monday.

“The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor rise together, unmasking logics of market and exploitation that endanger the very balance of creation,” he told representatives of Amazonian peoples and missionaries, in a region that is also home to communities living in voluntary isolation. “It is not possible to separate the care of the Amazon rainforest from concern for the peoples who inhabit it,” he said after hearing testimonies from lawyer Susy Díaz and environmental leader Cecilio Soria, both of the Shipibo-Konibo people.

“In recent years, many Indigenous leaders have been killed for protecting their own territories. The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice from men,” the pontiff said. He also criticised institutional neglect of communities: “It is unacceptable that in many communities the right to access health and education is denied.” And, after Díaz spoke about the abuse suffered by girls and teenagers, he referred to “the searing pain of those who suffer violence and sexual abuse, which cause deep wounds, often with the silence of complicity and impunity”.

Julio Cusurichi, representing the Indigenous peoples of the Peruvian Amazon, handed the Pope a letter asking him to intercede with President Keiko Fujimori’s government. “We cannot allow economic interests to be placed above the lives and rights of these vulnerable peoples,” the text says, according to El País. Cusurichi put at 37 the number of environmental defenders killed in Peru over the past decade. According to El País, the government last week blocked recognition of a protected reserve in Madre de Dios for the Mashco Piro, one of the world’s largest communities living in voluntary isolation.

With his visit, Leo XIV takes up the defence of the Amazon and the “integral ecology” championed by Pope Francis. After the meeting, he celebrated Mass before some 70,000 people, according to El País. In the morning he had visited Cusco.

The Pope returns to Rome on Monday, at the end of an eleven-day tour that began on November 6 in Uruguay and continued in Argentina and Peru, the country where he lived for some twenty years and whose nationality he holds.

World.title: Uruguay among the region’s most productive countries, but with below-average growth
World.content:
Uruguay among the region’s most productive countries, but with below-average growth

16th Monday, November 2026 - 01:29 UTC Full article

At the current pace, the region would not regain its 2013 productivity and employment conditions until around 2029

Uruguay ranked fourth in Latin America and the Caribbean for labour productivity per hour worked in 2025, according to a report by the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), but the indicator grew by only 0.6% during the year, below the regional average of 0.7%.

The Panorama of Productive Development Policies in Latin America and the Caribbean 2026, which compares the value generated per hour worked across 28 economies in the region, places Uruguay behind only Guyana, the Bahamas and Barbados, and ahead of Panama, Costa Rica, Chile, Argentina and Brazil.

The trend in the indicator is less favourable. While Uruguayan productivity rose by 0.6%, other economies in the region recorded much higher increases, such as Paraguay (3.3%), Argentina (3.1%) and Chile (3%). The biggest gains were in Guyana, at 18.7%, St Vincent and the Grenadines, at 3.5%, and the Bahamas, at 3.4%. Across the region as a whole, labour productivity per hour grew by 0.7% in 2025, down from 0.8% in 2024.

ECLAC warns that Latin America and the Caribbean remains trapped in a low-growth dynamic linked to stagnant productivity and difficulties in transforming economic structures. At the current pace, the region would not regain its 2013 productivity and employment conditions until around 2029. To reverse this, the organisation recommends strengthening productive development policies, improving the adoption of technology by companies and aligning worker training with the needs of economic sectors.

In October, the International Monetary Fund cut its 2026 growth forecast for Uruguay to 1.3%.

World.title: Leo XIV rides in a Peruvian military helicopter cockpit and reaches Cusco
World.content:
Leo XIV rides in a Peruvian military helicopter cockpit and reaches Cusco

16th Monday, November 2026 - 01:11 UTC Full article

The Air Force shared a video of the pontiff with the pilots on social media

Pope Leo XIV shared the cockpit with Peruvian Air Force pilots during one of his helicopter journeys on Saturday, in the final stretch of his South American tour, and on Sunday arrived in Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, the BBC reported.

The Air Force shared a video of the pontiff with the pilots on social media, calling his presence “an honour and an unforgettable memory”.

Así ha entrado el papa León XIV en la cabina del helicóptero @fapperu https://t.co/wdQrIKm7Jd — ROME REPORTS (@romereportsesp) November 15, 2026

In Cusco, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by “divisions, wounds, mistrust”, stressing that faith should bring people together “in the light of faith and love”.

The Peruvian leg of the tour holds special significance for Leo XIV, who lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023, served as bishop of Chiclayo and became a Peruvian citizen in 2015. After Cusco and Pucallpa, in the Amazon, the Pope returns to Rome on Monday, November 16, after a tour that began on November 6 in Uruguay and continued in Argentina.

World.title: Milei and Bullrich: a rift becoming routine ahead of the 2027 election
World.content:
Milei and Bullrich: a rift becoming routine ahead of the 2027 election

16th Monday, November 2026 - 01:07 UTC Full article

Bullrich has a 46% favourable and 50% unfavourable rating, against 33% and 60% for Milei

The tension between Argentine President Javier Milei and the ruling party’s Senate leader, Patricia Bullrich, has become part of daily life in La Libertad Avanza less than a year before the 2027 presidential election, and over the weekend it reached the international press. The British newspaper Financial Times devoted an analysis to the dispute on Saturday, citing a poll that ranks Bullrich as the most popular figure in the ruling camp.

According to the survey, carried out in late October by Sergio Berensztein’s consultancy and researcher Eduardo D’Alessio and shared with the newspaper, Bullrich has a 46% favourable and 50% unfavourable rating, against 33% and 60% for Milei. The Financial Times described the former security minister as “a veteran lawmaker who brought crucial centrist voters to Milei in 2023” and, according to Ámbito, said some donors see her as an alternative should the president’s re-election prospects deteriorate. A person close to Bullrich denied to the British newspaper that the senator plans to leave the ruling party or run outside it.

Mixed signals are multiplying on social media. Milei posted an Instagram message without naming anyone: “There are people willing to sink the ship when they realise they cannot be the captain.” Shortly afterwards, he shared posts backing a Milei-Bullrich ticket capable of winning “in the first round”. According to Ámbito, the government includes both those who believe the limit has been reached with Bullrich and those who argue for offering her the vice-presidential candidacy as soon as possible. Presidential chief of staff Karina Milei has called a meeting of the government’s political council for Tuesday.

The dispute coincides with the ruling party’s legislative push, which on Tuesday begins committee debate on a political reform to suspend the open primaries, known as PASO. Cabinet chief Diego Santilli insists “the votes are already there”, although doubts persist in the Senate, according to Ámbito.

The reform has also run into an unexpected obstacle in Neuquén province, where Governor Rolando Figueroa has called provincial elections for February 14, 2027, with alliances to be registered by December 4. Some allied lawmakers are using the early vote as an argument against the reform. “They want to change the rules in the middle of the game. If Neuquén votes on February 14, that’s it. I won’t support it,” Congressman Oscar Zago, a former head of the libertarian bloc, told Ámbito.

The government also faces a difficult economic backdrop: country risk hit its highest level in a year in early November, and Pope Leo XIV criticised during his recent visit an economy not “at the service of the person”.

World.title: In a sign of wetlands recovery, 2 young wood storks are spotted at Lake Texcoco
World.content:
Two young wood storks have been formally documented for the first time at Lake Texcoco in a new sign of continued environmental recovery in the area that includes the canceled airport construction site near Mexico City.

A community monitoring brigade found the juveniles Nov. 5 near a ditch on communal farmland in San Salvador Atenco, México state, according to a Facebook post by managers of the Lake Texcoco protected area.

The species was not previously listed in the reserve’s management plan.

The sighting brings to 20 the number of bird species that have returned after periods of absence or been newly recorded, reserve director Jorge Daniel Fonseca Cando said.

He suggested the wetland could provide a temporary winter stopover for the storks.

🦩✨ ¡Nuevo registro en el Lago de Texcoco! La cigüeña americana llega por primera vez a este ecosistema del #Edomex. Con ella, ya son 20 las especies de aves que regresan tras años de desecación o que llegan por primera vez. Una señal de recuperación de la vida silvestre. #ExcélsiorDigital #LagoDeTexcoco #Conservación — Excélsior (@Excelsior) November 12, 2026

The species, Mycteria americana, is known in Spanish as cigüeña americana, literally “American stork.”

The discovery does not establish that the birds are permanent residents.

But it does add to signs of improving habitat in an ecosystem damaged by drainage and construction of an international airport that was canceled in 2018 — yet won an international architectural design award in 2021. The project was championed by President Enrique Peña Nieto and canceled by his successor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

Fonseca Cando attributed the wildlife gains to rehabilitation work and this year’s rainy season, which flooded more than 4,700 hectares, or 47 square kilometers. He said improved water quality and recovering bodies of water have encouraged greater species diversity.

The Lake Texcoco protected area in México state not a single continuous lake. Areas flooded this year include Lake Nabor Carrillo, San Juan Marsh, Xalapango Lagoon and parts of the former airport construction site.

Recovery extends below the surface, as well, Fonseca Cando said, noting that the mexclapique, a fish native to the region, expanded its presence across more than 1,200 hectares this year. The small, freshwater fish’s common name in English is Chapultepec splitfin.

Fonseca Cando reported more than 290,000 migratory and resident birds representing 285 species in the protected area.

Recovery was also evident in November 2025, when roughly 4,300 hectares were covered with water following abundant rain.

Restoration efforts have included replanting grass, reforestation and rehabilitating lakes and wetlands.

In November 2025, Fonseca Cando reported that more than 280,000 birds had arrived to winter in the reserve, compared with 60,000 in a related survey in 2021. Parts of the abandoned airport’s infrastructure have been repurposed to create wetlands, architect Iñaki Echeverría told Uno TV.

Mexico granted protected status to more than 14,000 hectares (54 square miles) in March 2022. The designation prohibits urban development and ecosystem destruction while allowing conservation, restoration and sustainable farming.

The Lake Texcoco protected area, which includes the 2-year-old Lake Texcoco Ecological Park, also helps regulate water around the capital. Fonseca Cando said the reserve collected more than 43 million cubic meters of water in 2025.

With reports from La Jornada, El País and Excélsior

World.title: Migrant caravan continues journey northward from Chiapas
World.content:
A migrant caravan made up of around 1,200 people arrived in Mapastepec, Chiapas, on Monday, after leaving the town of Escuintla on Sunday afternoon.

The migrants walked more than 30 kilometers from Escuintla to Mapastepec, where they began arriving in the early hours of Monday morning.

Jessica López, a Salvadoran woman, told the newspaper La Jornada that she and other members of the caravan were “very tired” and sore all over, especially their feet.

“But here we are with one goal in mind: to get to the United States,” she added.

The caravan mainly consists of Hondurans, but also includes migrants from various other countries, including El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti and Cuba. It includes men, women and children, and is traveling under the name “Dios con Nosotros, el Señor nos Protege (God with Us, the Lord Protects us).

The migrants set off from the city of Tapachula last Tuesday and have since walked more than 100 kilometers. Some 1,500 migrants were initially part of the caravan, but its numbers have declined as some people have left the group for reasons including fatigue.

Last Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if Mexico didn’t stop the caravan. In response, President Claudia Sheinbaum said that “no migrant caravan has reached the northern border” since Trump began his second term in January 2025.

What’s next for the caravan?

The migrants set up camp on a basketball court after arriving in Mapastepec on Monday. After resting there, they plan to walk to Pijijiapan, a town and municipality north of Mapastepec.

North of Pijijiapan is Arriaga, a town near Chiapas’ border with Oaxaca where a group of some 100 migrants is reportedly waiting for the migrant caravan to arrive.

Reuters reported last week that the caravan is first aiming to get to Mexico City “to seek assistance from the Mexican federal government and protection from being detained while traveling toward the U.S. border.”

The news agency also reported that the migrants “are hoping that the election ​victory by Democrats that gives the party control of Congress starting in January could open pathways for them to live and work in ​the United States.”

López, the Salvadoran migrant, told La Jornada that the migrants are seeking help from Mexico to achieve their goal of reaching the U.S., or at least the northern border.

“We ask Mexico to support us, to help us achieve our goal,” she said.

“We’re only seeking an opportunity to work. We didn’t come to cause problems; we want to work to get ahead,” López said.

Sheinbaum said last Thursday that Mexican authorities tell migrants that entering the United States is “very difficult” due to the Trump administration’s strict border policies.

“We tell the people in the caravan that it’s very difficult to get to the United States, that if their goal is to get to the United States, they won’t be able to achieve it,” she said.

“We seek a way for them to safely return to their countries. If someone wants to stay in Mexico under certain conditions in a certain place, they can. But the vast majority return to their countries of origin once they find out they won’t be able to cross Mexico’s border with the United States,” Sheinbaum said.

It is likely that some of the members of the migrant caravan currently in Chiapas will seek to work in Mexico, at least temporarily.

Sheinbaum said that the government wouldn’t use force against migrants traveling through the country, as has occurred in the past.

With reports from Diario del Sur, La Jornada and Latinus

World.title: In China, Mexico’s environment minister takes notes on its waste-to-energy circular economy
World.content:
Mexico is aiming to convert its waste management strategy to an energy-from-waste model and it’s looking to China, a world leader in the relevant technology, for the know-how needed to take a major step toward a circular economy.

Waste utilization would not only provide a new source of clean energy but also solve waste disposal problems and reclaim public spaces that would otherwise be used for landfills.

Toward that end, Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena visited several Chinese facilities over the weekend specializing in waste utilization and water restoration to understand how they work to restore ecosystems and clean waterways, and to assess their potential use in Mexico.

Her tour came in advance of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, where President Sheinbaum will stress deepening technological cooperation with China, including the development of solutions for the use of organic waste (including sargassum, the brown seaweed that plagues Mexico’s Caribbean shore) to produce energy and cut greenhouse gas emissions.

Bárcena traveled to the city of Zhuhai in China’s southern Guangdong province to visit the SUS Environment plant, which processes up to 3,000 tonnes of waste per day and produces up to 90 megawatts of electricity.

She also noted that China has tackled its waste problem by increasing the share of solid waste used for energy from 9.8% in 2005 to 84.6% in 2024. Meanwhile, China’s landfill disposal has decreased from 64% to 5%.

“Learning about this experience allows us to identify alternatives for waste management in Mexico,” Semarnat wrote on X on Saturday.

Many of China’s waste-to-energy plants use advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence, to enhance operations, something that could be incorporated into any new Mexican operation.

In Shenzhen, where the APEC summit will take place, Bárcena visited the Honghu underground plant, which can process up to 100,000 tonnes of wastewater a day. Above ground, Honghu houses a public park, demonstrating the potential for providing more clean public spaces.

“Shenzhen is… an example of how to reclaim rivers, restore ecosystems and transform formerly polluted spaces into meeting places and gathering spots for communities,” Bárcena said. “The Chinese experience demonstrates that it is possible to move beyond landfills and advance toward a circular economy model.”

With reports from La Jornada and XEU Noticias Veracruz

World.title: Guadalajara Cartel co-founder and convicted murderer Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies at 80
World.content:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a drug lord known as the “Boss of Bosses” who was convicted of the 1985 murder of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena, died in a hospital in Guadalajara, Jalisco, on Sunday. He was 80.

The Jalisco Security Ministry announced Félix Gallardo’s death, which came two days after he was transferred from the Puente Grande prison near Guadalajara to a private hospital in the state capital. The ministry said that “multiple organ failure” was the cause of his death. He was also suffering from pneumonia.

Félix Gallardo, the co-founder and erstwhile leader of the now-defunct Guadalajara Cartel, had been in poor health for years. He spent the last 37 years of his life in prison after he was arrested in Guadalajara in 1989.

DEA Administrator Terry Cole acknowledged Félix Gallardo’s death in a social media post on Sunday night.

“The cartel kingpin who built an empire of violence and orchestrated the brutal murder of DEA Special Agent Enrique ‘Kiki’ Camarena has died in custody after more than 37 years behind bars,” Cole wrote.

“Kiki’s sacrifice will never be forgotten — nor will the criminals and corruption behind his death. His courage lives on in every agent carrying out our mission, and our pursuit of truth and justice will never end.”

In 2017, Félix Gallardo was sentenced to 37 years in prison for the murders of Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar, who worked with Camarena. Before the murder conviction, he had received a 40-year sentence for drug trafficking, weapons offenses and bribery.

In 2022, a federal judge took Félix Gallardo’s advanced age and poor health into account when ruling that he could complete his 40-year sentence at a residence in Zapopan, Jalisco. However, the federal Attorney General’s Office challenged the ruling, preventing the release of the then 76-year-old Guadalajara Cartel co-founder.

Rafael Caro Quintero, another Guadalajara Cartel co-founder who was transferred from a Mexican prison to a U.S. prison in early 2025, was also convicted of the murder of Camarena, a Mexicali native who joined the DEA in 1973.

The early years

Félix Gallardo was born on Jan. 8, 1946, in Culiacán, Sinaloa, a city that has been plagued by Sinaloa Cartel infighting for the past two years.

His parents were farmers and exported legumes to the United States, according to the now-deceased drug lord.

Félix Gallardo, who left school after completing the second grade of primary school, told Noticias Telemundo in a 2021 interview from prison that he had “dedicated” himself to “agriculture and ranching” since he was a boy.

Before founding the Guadalajara Cartel with Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo in the 1970s, Félix Gallardo worked as a police officer and spent a period as a bodyguard for former Sinaloa Governor Leopoldo Sánchez Celis, who was in office from 1963 to 1968.

The New York Times reported that his employment as a police officer and bodyguard for Sánchez allowed him to forge “connections that helped him and his partners transform the Mexican drug trade in the 1970s and 1980s.”

A life of crime

Félix Gallardo, Caro Quintero and Fonseca Carrillo co-founded the Guadalajara Cartel in the late 1970s. Under their leadership, the Guadalajara Cartel became a major trafficker of narcotics, including cocaine and marijuana, to the United States.

Félix Gallardo, who was also known as “The Godfather” and “The Drug Czar,” forged alliances with criminal groups in Colombia — the world’s largest producer of cocaine — that helped the Guadalajara Cartel establish itself as Mexico’s dominant drug trafficking organization in the 1980s.

The BBC reported that he “led the organization which revolutionized drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly [Pablo] Escobar’s Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.”

“At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the U.S. came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organization played a major role in smuggling it in,” the BBC wrote.

“At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships,” reported the British broadcaster and media organization.

His nickname, “The Boss of Bosses” (El Jefe de Jefes), is a testament to the immense power he once wielded in Mexico’s criminal underworld.

CNN reported that “the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in ensuing decades.”

“… His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials and innovations like using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent.”

The Wall Street Journal reported that Pablo Escobar turned to Mexico — and Félix Gallardo — after “U.S. interdiction efforts began seizing his submarines, speedboats and freighters.”

“Through his government contacts, Félix Gallardo arranged protection for overland routes carrying cocaine from South America through Mexico to the U.S. border,” the Journal reported.

“For a fee, traffickers could move their product under the protection of the Mexican state. Rather than cash, Félix Gallardo demanded a percentage of each shipment — an innovation that made him one of the richest men in the hemisphere and altered the global narcotics business.”

In the 1980s, Félix Gallardo also worked with Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, the erstwhile Sinaloa Cartel leader who is now imprisoned in the United States.

The New York Times reported that Guzmán got his start in the drug trafficking business “working as an air logistics expert for Mr. Félix Gallardo.”

The murder of Camarena and Félix Gallardo’s capture

In 2017, Félix Gallardo was found guilty of involvement in the murders of both Camarena and Zavala. He was frequently described as the autor intelectual, or mastermind, of Camarena’s murder. Félix Gallardo always denied involvement in his killing.

The slain DEA agent angered the Guadalajara Cartel leadership due to his involvement in a 1984 raid on a large marijuana plantation in Chihuahua that belonged to the criminal group.

The BBC reported that the murder of Camarena in February 1985 “sparked one of the biggest manhunts the U.S. government has ever launched in North America,” and “the net started to tighten” around the leaders of the Guadalajara Cartel. The murder strained U.S.-Mexico relations for years and led to an intensification of the U.S. government’s war on drugs.

Caro Quintero and Fonseca were both arrested in April 1985, while Félix Gallardo was detained on April 8, 1989, ending his life of crime.

At the time of his arrest, Enrique Álvarez del Castillo, then Mexico’s attorney general, described Félix Gallardo as the “No. 1 narcotics trafficker in Mexico.”

The news outlet N+ reported that the Guadalajara Cartel “fragmented” after his capture, giving rise to the Sinaloa and Tijuana cartels.

Félix Gallardo gained international notoriety after the DEA accused him of the kidnapping, torture and murder of Camarena. His infamy grew when he was portrayed as a central figure in the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. Mexican actor Diego Luna played the role of Félix Gallardo in the hit series, whose first season began in late 2018.

Among Félix Gallardo’s surviving relatives are his children Miguel Ángel Félix and Abril Félix.

Jorge Eduardo Montiel, a spokesperson for the Jalisco Security Ministry, said on Sunday that relatives of Félix Gallardo would attend a small religious ceremony at the hospital where he died.

With reports from Animal Político, El Universal, Reforma, N+, BBC, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and CNN

World.title: Sheinbaum lands in Shenzhen on a commercial flight, then heads straight to tacos with Mexicans living in China
World.content:
Listen to this article

President Claudia Sheinbaum has arrived in Shenzhen, China, on a visit featuring a packed agenda of meetings with state leaders, diplomats and businesspeople at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

As with her previous travels to Brazil and Canada, the president elected to take a commercial flight — a symbol of government austerity, anti-elitism and a commitment to connecting with everyday citizens that started with her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who sold the presidential plane to Tajikistan for US $92 million in 2023.

Sheinbaum arrived at the Mexico City airport at 11 p.m. Saturday for a 12:35 a.m. flight to Tijuana before boarding China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 to Shenzhen, China.

While in Tijuana, Sheinbaum released this message:

“We’re going to a two-day event with business leaders from all the APEC countries. Afterward, we’ll have a Cabinet meeting and will participate in the APEC forum. I’ll keep you updated. Look for me during the morning press conference (in the National Palace); I’ll be connecting there.”

The Cabinet members in Sheinbaum’s entourage are Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, Energy Minister Luz Elena González, Health Minister David Kershenobich, Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena and Science Minister Rosaura Ruiz. A contingent of Mexican business leaders is also accompanying the president.

With the time change, the president arrived in the city hosting the APEC meeting at 11:30 a.m. Monday, before hustling to the Tequila Coyotes restaurant to meet with Mexican citizens residing in China.

Afterward, she praised “the extraordinary Mexicans who have decided to live their lives [in China],” adding that “we should find ways for them to stay connected with Mexico.”

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum will speak to the APEC Business Advisory Council, where she will outline her Plan México investment strategy to more than 1,000 business leaders.

She will then meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Her talk with Xi comes amid a backdrop of trade tensions after Mexico slapped tariffs of up to 50% on certain products from countries with which it does not have free trade agreements, including China. Sheinbaum said she’ll deliver a message of “cooperation for development and friendship” to Xi and will discuss projects related to smart hospitals, renewable energy, waste transformation and scientific development.

She will also meet with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.

Sheinbaum intends to return to Mexico by Friday morning, Nov. 20, in order to lead the commemorative activities for the 116th anniversary of the start of the Mexican Revolution.

With reports from Reforma, Latinus, SDP Noticias, Expansión and EFE

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Water deliveries set to rise, while new initiatives aim to clean the environment and protect threatened city cats
World.content:
With social media awash in stories of Guadalajara residents who have gone without water for a month or longer, city officials shifted into high gear. Last week, the city announced expanded water truck service to more than 35 affected neighborhoods.

Meanwhile, there is some good news on the environmental front. Various state agencies are cracking down on illegal waste disposal, clean technologies are slated for installation in Guadalajara’s historic center and a new program is in the works to combat animal cruelty.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Verónica Delgadillo G (@verodelgadillog)

Let’s dive in.

Water truck deliveries are increasing to address critical shortages

With numerous city neighborhoods enduring water outages lasting much longer than the advertised rationing schedule, Guadalajara expanded its water distribution program this past week.

Commenting on the changes to local media, Mayor Verónica Delgadillo said, “Our goal is to deliver 2.1 million liters of water to the most critical areas of the city, and we have set ourselves the goal of visiting (at least) 35 neighborhoods (daily).”

The new volume equates to roughly 210 standard 10,000-liter tanker trips daily and a tenfold increase over the 200,000-liter average daily volume delivered last month, when the water distribution program began.

Pipa deliveries are focused in particular on high-elevation areas and neighborhoods where severe low pressure keeps water from reaching rooftop tanks (tinacos). These neighborhoods are primarily located on the city’s east and south sides.

In addition to mobile deliveries, the government is also increasing its network of fixed community water cisterns from 19 to 33 across the affected neighborhoods to improve access to water.

The Jalisco state government is also supplying roughly 20 additional pipas daily to city hospitals, schools and emergency facilities to alleviate the burden the water crisis is having on myriad public service providers.

Residents can request free pipas or report low water pressure on WhatsApp using the Siapabot phone number, 33-5164-4440.

Solar energy and electric charging stations are coming to Guadalajara’s historic center

With an eye to lowering pollution levels and energy costs in Guadalajara’s historic center, the Association of Business Owners of the Historic Center of Guadalajara has developed a plan to install solar panels on rooftops across the neighborhood.

According to Diego Amorós Alfaro, the organization’s president, their green initiative involves generating electricity through photovoltaic systems that would allow businesses to recoup their investment in as little as three years.

The plan also calls for expanding infrastructure to support electric vehicles. To this end, the association looks to create partnerships with hotels and parking facilities to install more charging stations, making it easier for visitors who drive these low-polluting vehicles.

Finally, the project aims to promote other unspecified measures to optimize electricity consumption and reduce the carbon footprint of downtown businesses.

Local agencies step up efforts to improve environmental protection citywide

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Unidos por Jalisco (@unjalmx)

The Jalisco State Environmental Protection Agency (Proepa) recently shared several accomplishments that highlight the agency’s stepped-up commitment to environmental protection this year.

In a public statement, Proepa announced its staff has conducted 596 inspection visits, addressed 253 citizen complaints and imposed 233 temporary closures to remedy industrial pollution associated with manufacturing businesses and waste management and prevent further environmental damage.

Among the most significant actions is a new agreement with waste management operator Caabsa Eagle Guadalajara to comprehensively remediate environmental damage caused by the Los Laureles and Coyula-Matatlán landfills in Tonalá. The deal reportedly includes a bond posted by the company for 341 million pesos (US $18.37 million).

In another high-profile case, Proepa has temporarily closed a property near Technology Park Guadalajara and the University Center of Biological and Agricultural Sciences (CUCBA) in Zapopan due to improper hazardous waste disposal. In conjunction with the State Attorney General’s Office and Zapopan’s city government, Proepa also arrested several individuals responsible for the illegal dumping at this facility.

Separately, Proepa has been expanding its work focused on pollution prevention, with new training aimed at businesses involved in livestock farming, industrial activities and tequila production. In cooperation with the state Secretariat of Environment and Territorial Development (Semadet), it is also training city workers in methods to improve their inspection and oversight capabilities.

A new plan is announced to protect the cats of Alcalde Park

The shocking dog-poisoning incident in Parque España in Mexico City’s Condesa neighborhood last month received significant media coverage. Meanwhile, far less attention has gone to a similar incident affecting the feral cats living in Alcalde Park.

Alcalde Park, located immediately north of Guadalajara’s historic center, has long been known as a place where irresponsible pet owners dump their unwanted cats. Cleanup efforts have come and gone, but the cat abandonments have continued in recent years, albeit on a smaller scale than in decades past.

Tended by compassionate neighbors, the park’s feral cat colony rose to around 40 cats.

Late last month, caregivers discovered as many as 16 deceased cats due to suspected poisoning. Toxin-laced food packets were reportedly found scattered about the park grounds, prompting a public outcry.

Formal criminal complaints and public petitions followed. In response, city and state authorities launched an investigation, with analysis of both the dead specimens and laced food packets.

In recent days, the Metropolitan Agency for Urban Forests (AMBU) announced a formal plan to improve the well-being of the cats living in Alcalde Park and prevent more felines from being abandoned there.

Jesús Alexandro Félix Gastélum, director of AMBU, said the plan calls for a roughly 800-square-meter space to house the cats, with day and night surveillance to ensure their safety. The agency also plans a new adoption program for younger cats with the potential to be socialized, along with training for citizen volunteers assisting in the cats’ care.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Steel firms look to bolster investment in Mexico to fend off Chinese competition and US tariffs
World.content:
In an international market pressured by oversupply and competition from Chinese steel, the steelmaker Ternium is nearing completion of one of its largest industrial projects in Mexico — a US $7.51 billion expansion of its complex in Pesquería, Nuevo León.

Maximo Vedoya, president of the Latin American Steel Association (Alacero) and CEO of Ternium, said the completed project will add 2.6 million tonnes of steelmaking capacity starting in 2027.

At last week’s inauguration of the Alacero Summit 2026 in Mexico City, Vedoya said Ternium aims to enhance its ability to serve demand from the automotive, construction and energy sectors in Mexico while contending with stiff Chinese competition.

Vedoya said one solution is to increase the regional steel content in Asian cars.

“If Chinese cars continue to arrive without any regional content, it will be difficult to increase … investment in the industry and the value chain,” he added.

Vedoya said the Latin American steel industry is battling against the inroads Chinese companies have made, allocating US $22 billion in the last five years and, in an effort to defend local manufacturing, Alacero members intend to invest $13 billion more through 2030.

This includes investment in small and medium-sized enterprises to improve their added value and integration into supply chains.

At the same time, Mexico has taken steps to reduce Asian steel imports by imposing tariffs and control measures on the entry of steel from countries with which it does not have free trade agreements.

Speaking at the summit, Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez, Mexico’s undersecretary of foreign trade, said metal imports have decreased thanks to the required traceability of steel products. Tracing helped to reduce 80% of the steel imports from Vietnam, he said, putting a stop to 13 billion pesos (nearly US $700 million) in falsified imports that can now be supplied by the domestic industry.

La industria del acero es estratégica para México y para la integración productiva de Norteamérica. Trabajamos para fortalecer la cadena de valor, promover un comercio justo, garantizar que NO exista “transhipment” o triangulacion de importaciones de Asia-Exportaciones de México, y atraer más inversión y empleo con el Plan México. 🇲🇽 @CANACERO

@m_ebrard @Claudiashein @SE_mx — Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez (@LuisRosendo_) November 12, 2026

So while imports from China and other Asian countries fell by 30% since last year, Gutiérrez expressed hopefulness that U.S. tariffs on Mexican steel will soon be reduced from 50% to zero.

Vedoya said that although U.S. tariffs on steel products affect all Latin American countries, they have a greater impact on Mexican exports, claiming that the sector faces unfair trade in finished products and throughout the value chain.

Meanwhile, Vedoya said regional investment will focus on technological innovation, decarbonization and technical training for local talent.

With reports from El Economista, Informador, Expansión and Milenio

World.title: Interior Minister fills in for Sheinbaum, touting poverty data and approval ratings: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🎤 Rodríguez leads mañanera as Sheinbaum attends APEC summit: Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez presided over Monday’s press conference while Sheinbaum is in Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting, where she will hold bilateral meetings with leaders, including Xi Jinping. Sheinbaum returns to Mexico on Friday and will join Tuesday’s mañanera by video link. Rodríguez said Security Cabinet members were told to stay alert and work together, as they usually do.

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez presided over Monday’s press conference while Sheinbaum is in Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Leaders’ Meeting, where she will hold bilateral meetings with leaders, including Xi Jinping. Sheinbaum returns to Mexico on Friday and will join Tuesday’s mañanera by video link. Rodríguez said Security Cabinet members were told to stay alert and work together, as they usually do. 📉 World Bank: poverty rate projected to fall 15 points in 8 years: Deputy Science Minister Violeta Vázquez Rojas presented World Bank data showing that the share of Mexicans in monetary poverty fell from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025. The World Bank projects poverty rates of 20% in 2026 (a 15.3-point drop from 2018) and 18.7% in 2028. The threshold is US $8.30 per person per day, adjusted for purchasing power.

Deputy Science Minister Violeta Vázquez Rojas presented World Bank data showing that the share of Mexicans in monetary poverty fell from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025. The World Bank projects poverty rates of 20% in 2026 (a 15.3-point drop from 2018) and 18.7% in 2028. The threshold is US $8.30 per person per day, adjusted for purchasing power. 👥 17.3 million fewer people in poverty: Vázquez said 17.3 million fewer Mexicans are projected to be in monetary poverty at the end of 2026 than in 2018, equal to the population of México state. Rodríguez credited the poverty-reduction policy begun under López Obrador and continued by Sheinbaum.

Vázquez said 17.3 million fewer Mexicans are projected to be in monetary poverty at the end of 2026 than in 2018, equal to the population of México state. Rodríguez credited the poverty-reduction policy begun under López Obrador and continued by Sheinbaum. 🏆 Sheinbaum most popular leader in Latin America: Polls by CB Global Data in 18 countries in early November put Sheinbaum’s approval at 69.8%, narrowly ahead of El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele (69.5%). Rodríguez attributed the rating to “strong public support” and to a president who is “always thinking” about improving Mexicans’ living standards, pointing to minimum wage increases and social programs.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez presided over the federal government’s Monday morning press conference as President Claudia Sheinbaum is in Shenzhen, China, where she will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting, hold bilateral meetings with various world leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and address the APEC Business Advisory Council before returning to Mexico on Friday.

Rodríguez noted that Sheinbaum had already met with members of the Mexican community in China.

At the start of the press conference, the interior minister told reporters that the government would present “some very good news” from the World Bank.

That news, she said, is that “millions and millions of Mexicans were lifted out of poverty” between 2018 — the year Andrés Manuel López Obrador began his six-year term as president — and 2026.

“This is the result of the [poverty-reduction] policy that began with the President Andrés Manuel López Obrador and continues with the President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo,” Rodríguez said.

She said that the policy is known by the slogan, “Por el bien de todos, primero los pobres” (For the good of all, the poor come first).

Also of note at today’s mañanera was the presentation of poll results that showed that Sheinbaum is the most popular leader in Latin America.

Rodríguez outlines her responsibilities in Sheinbaum’s absence

Asked whether Sheinbaum had assigned her any specific tasks for this week, Rodríguez said that the president instructed her and other members of the government’s Security Cabinet to stay alert and work together at all times.

She said that was no different from their usual practice when the president is in the country. Rodríguez said that she and other government officials would be alert to “problems throughout the country,” as they always are.

She noted that Sheinbaum also asked her to lead her weekday morning press conference, known as la mañanera.

Rodríguez said that the president would join Tuesday’s mañanera via video link from China.

World Bank: Mexico’s poverty rate projected to fall 15 percentage points between 2018 and 2026

Violeta Vázquez Rojas, a deputy minister in the Ministry of Science, Humanities, Technology and Innovation, presented World Bank data that showed that the percentage of Mexicans living in “monetary poverty” declined from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025.

The World Bank’s monetary poverty threshold for upper-middle-income countries such as Mexico is US $8.30 per person per day, adjusted for local purchasing power.

According to the World Bank’s projections, Mexico’s monetary poverty rate will be 20% in 2026, a decline of 15.3 percentage points compared to 2018, and 18.7% in 2028.

The number of people living in monetary poverty in Mexico is projected to be 25.2 million in 2028, representing a reduction of 18.7 million people compared to 2018.

Vázquez noted that 17.3 million fewer people are projected to be living in monetary poverty in Mexico at the end of 2026 than in 2018. She highlighted that the number is equivalent to the population of México state, Mexico’s most populous state.

Vázquez said that the World Bank data “confirms” that the government’s stated ethos of putting the nation’s poorest people first is not just “discourse,” but “a tangible and measurable reality.”

The U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean reported late last year that Mexico was leading Latin America in poverty reduction, primarily due to recent increases in the minimum wage.

Why is Sheinbaum so popular? Rodríguez gives her take

A reporter asked Rodríguez about polls conducted by CB Global Data that found that Sheinbaum is the most popular president in Latin America.

According to the results of polls conducted by CB Global Data across 18 Latin American countries in early November, Sheinbaum has an approval rating of 69.8%. That was the highest approval rating among the leaders of the 18 countries.

Nayib Bukele, president of El Salvador, had the second-highest approval rating (69.5%), ahead of Laura Fernández of Costa Rica (52.3%), Luis Abinader of the Dominican Republic (51.2%), Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil (50.4%) and Daniel Noboa of Ecuador (47.8%).

Rodríguez said that “we think” that Sheinbaum’s high approval rating is due to “the strong public support” Sheinbaum enjoys. Moving beyond the self-evident, she said that Sheinbaum has ample support because she’s a president who is “always thinking” about how to improve Mexicans’ standard of living.

“The purchasing power of most people has improved,” Rodríguez said, pointing to increases in the minimum wage and the government’s social programs.

“This great economic effort directly reaches those who most need it,” she said.

“… We have a president who, because of her actions, her honesty and her work, … deserves to be in first place among Latin American leaders,” Rodríguez said.

“… We’re very proud of her,” she added.

World.title: Kenya Fuel Pipeline Board Shifts Before Vote
World.content:
File photo. Traffic on the Nairobi–Mombasa highway near the airport in Embakasi, 11 May 2019. Photo: Endesia94 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

KENYA · CORPORATE GOVERNANCE

Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) runs the fuel pipeline from the port of Mombasa that supplies Kenya and its neighbours. It will hold its first annual general meeting (AGM) since listing on Wednesday 2 December 2026.

The company’s notice, dated Wednesday 11 November, shows the National Social Security Fund (NSSF), Kenya’s state pension fund, losing its board seat. A new 24.9% shareholder, Greenview Oil Trading Corp, gains the right to nominate one director.

Key Facts What Board changes at Kenya Pipeline Company before its first annual meeting since listing.

When Meeting on Wednesday 2 December 2026 at 9.00 am Nairobi time, held virtually.

Who Pension fund loses its seat; new 24.9% holder Greenview Oil Trading Corp may nominate one.

Money KES (Kenyan shillings) 0.32 a share, about US$44.6 million in total, due about 8 January 2027.

Deadline Shareholder registration and the dividend register both close on Monday 30 November 2026.

Kenya’s fuel pipeline operator heads into its first shareholder meeting since listing with a changed board. The notice sets out who leaves, who may join and what investors receive.

The Big Picture

KPC listed its shares in 2026, and the notice of Wednesday 11 November calls this meeting the first AGM following the listing. It carries the name of company secretary Flora Okoth.

Our earlier reports on a 25% stake purchase by Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote and on the share price cover the ownership change. The notice of 11 November adds a board consequence: a 24.9% holder with the right to nominate one director.

Central Nairobi from the KICC rooftop, 2021 file photo. Rio Times photo library.

Who Leaves and Who May Join the Board

Item 2.3.5 of the notice says Ronald Nyamosi, nominated by the NSSF, has ceased to be a director. Article 24(7) of KPC’s articles of association ties that nomination right to being the largest institutional investor, and the NSSF no longer holds that position.

Item 2.3.6 says Greenview Oil Trading Corp bought 24.9% of the issued share capital on the secondary market and is entitled to nominate a director. The notice does not name the nominee.

In Plain English Secondary market: buying shares from other investors, not from the company itself.

Independent non-executive director: a board member who does not work for the company.

Retire by rotation: a rule that directors leave office on a set schedule.

Eng.: the title used for a registered engineer.

Government Directors and Retiring Appointees

Item 2.3.1 says Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for the National Treasury, the finance minister, appointed three directors and the Government of Uganda appointed two, Dr Ramathan Ggoobi and Eng. Irene Pauline Bateebe.

Their reserved shareholder rights mean they need not retire by rotation at this first meeting after listing. Item 2.3.3 says five directors the board appointed to fill vacancies retire at the end of the meeting, among them Joyce Emanikor and Irene Wachira.

Item 2.3.4 says independent non-executive directors will be appointed, with profiles to be made available to shareholders beforehand.

Dividend and Auditor

Item 2.2 lists a first and final dividend of KES 5.79 billion (about US$44.6 million), which is 50% of profit after tax for the year ended 30 June 2026. That equals KES 0.32 per share (about US$0.0025), converted at about KES 129.9 to the US dollar on 16 November 2026.

The share register closes at the end of business on Monday 30 November 2026, and payment is due on or about Friday 8 January 2027. Registration to attend closes the same day at 10.00 am.

Why the Board Mix Matters

On the notice’s figures, the governments of Kenya and Uganda appoint five directors, Greenview may nominate one, and independent directors are still to be named. The same board will oversee a payout of KES 5.79 billion (about US$44.6 million), half of profit after tax for the year to 30 June 2026.

What It Means for You

Investors should note Monday 30 November 2026, when the share register closes, and Wednesday 2 December, when shareholders meet online. The dividend follows on or about Friday 8 January 2027, the notice says.

A US reader has no direct stake unless a fund holds KPC shares, and the notice does not list the holders. The practical signal is governance: a pipeline that supplies Kenya and its neighbours may soon seat a nominee of a private buyer.

More: Kenya news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

What Is Not Known

The notice does not name Greenview’s nominee or say whether the independent directors will include anyone linked to Greenview. It also does not say who will be named independent directors.

The notice does not state what Greenview or the governments intend to do with their board positions. The notice does not say who owns Greenview.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Kenya Pipeline annual meeting?

Kenya Pipeline Company will hold its 46th annual general meeting virtually on Wednesday 2 December 2026 at 9.00 am Nairobi time. Shareholder registration closes on Monday 30 November at 10.00 am.

Why did the pension fund lose its board seat?

The National Social Security Fund is no longer the largest institutional investor in Kenya Pipeline Company. Under Article 24(7) of the articles, that status carried the right to nominate a director, so Ronald Nyamosi has ceased to be one.

What does Greenview Oil Trading Corp hold?

Greenview bought 24.9% of the company’s issued share capital on the secondary market, the notice says. That entitles it to nominate a director, but the notice does not name its nominee.

How much is the dividend and when is it paid?

The first and final dividend is KES 0.32 a share (about US$0.0025), KES 5.79 billion (about US$44.6 million) in all. Holders on the register on Monday 30 November 2026 are paid on or about Friday 8 January 2027.

Sources: Kenya Pipeline Company PLC, “Notice of the 46th Annual General Meeting”, dated 11 November 2026: https://www.kpc.co.ke/download/87/investor-relations/13765/notice-of-the-46th-annual-general-meeting.pdf. Exchange rate used: about KES 129.9 per US$ on 16 November 2026.

World.title: Argentine Oil Operating Earnings Up 72%
World.content:
Three Argentine oil and gas companies made US$7 billion in operating earnings (EBITDA, not profit) in nine months, up 72%, a brokerage says.

ARGENTINA · OIL AND GAS EARNINGS

Three Argentine oil and gas companies that trade in New York generated US$7,001 million (about US$7 billion) in EBITDA from oil and gas production in the first nine months of 2026. EBITDA means operating earnings before depreciation and amortisation, so it is not profit.

RICSA ALyC, an Argentine brokerage, said in a report on Monday 16 November that the figure is up 72% on a year earlier. The report compiles the results that the three companies published for January to September 2026.

All trade in New York as ADRs or ADSs (American depositary receipts, US-traded certificates that represent company shares), so the numbers matter to readers following Argentina news.

Key Facts What Combined EBITDA (operating earnings before depreciation, not profit) of the three producers: US$7,001 million.

Growth Up 72% on a year earlier; revenue US$11,616 million, capital spending US$4,731 million, up 10%.

YPF EBITDA US$4,449 million, up 70%; shale (rock-formation oil) output share rose from 63% to 78%.

Vista EBITDA US$2,098 million, up 82%, with a production EBITDA margin of 61.8%.

Pampa EBITDA US$455 million, up 53%; 78.8% of its output is still natural gas.

RICSA ALyC counts these as operating earnings of the production units, not profit, and the report does not say what caused the jump.

How the Shale Boom Shows Up

RICSA ALyC said on 16 November that YPF’s shale share of output rose from 63% to 78%, while total output slipped 1.2% to 533,800 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Old conventional fields were retired, and a barrel of oil equivalent (boe) counts oil and gas in one unit.

Vista’s third-quarter record was 169,000 barrels a day, and its nine-month output rose 41.2% to 153,300 boe per day, RICSA ALyC said. The brokerage ranks Vista first for profitability and efficiency per barrel.

What the Three Companies Reported

RICSA ALyC said YPF’s upstream revenue was US$7,298 million and its EBITDA US$4,449 million, up 70%. Its upstream EBITDA margin was 61.0%, against 61.8% at Vista.

Vista’s revenue was US$3,395 million and its EBITDA US$2,098 million, up 82%, the brokerage said on 16 November. That is US$50.1 of EBITDA per boe, with a lifting cost (the cost of bringing a barrel out of the ground) of about US$4.5 per boe.

Pampa’s oil and gas segment had revenue of US$923 million, up 40%, and EBITDA of US$455 million, up 53%, RICSA ALyC said. Its operating result nearly doubled, from US$95 million to US$185 million.

Why Lower Costs Matter

YPF’s underlying lifting cost, the cost of bringing each barrel out of the ground, fell 31% from US$12.1 to US$8.4 per barrel of oil equivalent, RICSA ALyC said on 16 November. The brokerage links the fall to the larger weight of shale and the exit from costly conventional fields.

Vista kept the lowest extraction cost of the three, the brokerage said. Pampa’s cost was US$7.4 per boe over nine months but US$8.3 in the third quarter, the brokerage said.

Spending Slowed in the Third Quarter

Combined capital spending was US$4,731 million, 10% above the same period of 2025, RICSA ALyC said on 16 November. Third-quarter spending fell from the second quarter by 13% at YPF, 8% at Pampa and 2% at Vista.

Pampa put 76% of its third-quarter capital spending into the Rincón de Aranda oil block in Vaca Muerta, which passed 26,000 barrels a day in September after a second treatment plant started. Even so, 78.8% of its output is still natural gas.

In Plain English EBITDA: operating earnings before depreciation and amortisation (the accounting write-down of assets). It is not profit.

Upstream: the oil and gas production side of a company, as opposed to refining or power.

Lifting cost: what it costs to bring a barrel of oil out of the ground.

ADR: a US-traded certificate that represents shares of a foreign company.

What It Means for You

A US reader holding or watching these ADRs should read the US$7 billion as operating earnings from production, before depreciation and amortisation, not as profit. The RICSA ALyC compilation covers only the production divisions of each group.

Lower lifting costs and rising shale volumes are the two figures to follow in the companies’ next results. They show whether Argentina’s shale growth is becoming cheaper to run.

What Is Not Known

RICSA ALyC does not say how it defines upstream EBITDA against each company’s own segment reporting. It also gives no oil price assumption and does not say whether the figures are adjusted.

The date of the companies’ next quarterly results is not confirmed. The figures are the brokerage’s compilation of published results, not a combined statement by the companies.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the US$7 billion measure?

It measures EBITDA, operating earnings before depreciation and amortisation, from the oil and gas production divisions of three companies. It is not net profit.

Which companies are included?

YPF, Vista Energy and Pampa Energía, three oil and gas companies that trade in New York. RICSA ALyC, an Argentine brokerage, compiled their January to September 2026 results on Monday 16 November.

How far did YPF cut its lifting cost?

YPF’s underlying lifting cost fell 31%, from US$12.1 to US$8.4 per barrel of oil equivalent, according to the RICSA ALyC report. Lifting cost is the cost of bringing oil out of the ground.

Can US investors trade these companies?

All three trade in New York as ADRs, American depositary receipts, which are US-traded certificates of Argentine shares. This article gives no price targets or investment advice.

World.title: Ghana Gold Mine Wins Social Investment Prize
World.content:
File photo, 2008. Photo: SteKrueBe / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

GHANA · GOLD MINING

The Obuasi Mine in Ghana’s Ashanti Region, an underground gold mine run by AngloGold Ashanti (a global gold miner), was named SSI Foundation Company of the Year at the 10th Sustainability and Social Investment (SSI) Awards, a Ghanaian programme that honours corporate community work. According to coverage of the ceremony published on Monday 16 November 2026, the mine also collected several individual honours.

World.title: Bolivia Probes State Telecom Ad Deal
