File photo. A street stall selling route signs for minibuses and other transport in La Paz, Bolivia, August 2018. Photo: Olga Lidia Paredes Alcoreza, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

BOLIVIA · STATE SPENDING

Bolivia’s Vice President Edmand Lara has ordered an immediate oversight of the directors of Entel, the state-owned telecom operator, over an advertising contract with TV presenter Anabel Angus. The Vice Presidency, the office of the vice president, said in a communiqué on Monday 16 November that the deal is worth more than 400,000 bolivianos (about US$34,300, at 11.67 bolivianos per US$, the central bank rate for 16 November 2026).

According to the communiqué, the contract was signed in May 2026 and is valid until 2027. It covers brand advertising and the production of two promotional videos a month.

A senior Bolivian official is asking whether a well-known state company should pay for a media campaign. His case rests on unmet needs in health care and basic services.

Why Lara Objects

The Vice Presidency said Lara’s objection is not a personal conflict with Angus but a question of whether the spending is appropriate. He argued that Entel is an established, nationally known company that does not need such a campaign in the current economic situation.

He compared the sum with unmet needs, naming kidney and cancer patients who need medicines and hospitals with shortages. He also pointed to communities without basic services or street lighting.

The communiqué says public money should go to improving services. It frames the review as a matter of priorities rather than a personal dispute.

What It Means for You

The review concerns how a state company spends public money on advertising, which matters most to Bolivian taxpayers and to Entel’s customers. Readers following Bolivia news should treat the communiqué as one side of the story.

Edmand Lara ordered oversight of the directors of Entel, the state telecom operator. The trigger is an advertising contract with TV presenter Anabel Angus worth more than about US$34,300.

It covers brand advertising and two promotional videos a month. The Vice Presidency says it was signed in May 2026 and is valid until 2027.

Has anyone been accused of wrongdoing?

No. The Vice Presidency warned of legal proceedings only if irregularities are found, and it says its objection is not personal.

World.content:
Banana plantation in Ecuador (undated); the photo does not show any company named in this guide. (Photo: Dave Lonsdale, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ECUADOR · MERGER APPROVAL

Ecuador’s antitrust regulator has cleared Grupo Nutresa, a Colombian food group, to own La Universal, a Guayaquil maker of chocolate, confectionery and biscuits. The Superintendencia de Competencia Económica (SCE), the national competition authority, made the approval official in Resolution SCE-CRPI-30-2026 on Monday 16 November 2026.

The SCE concluded that the deal will not substantially reduce competition or create or strengthen a dominant position. The finding follows a purchase that Nutresa announced as completed on Friday 30 October 2026, and we follow it in our Ecuador news.

A Colombian food group now owns a leading Ecuadorian chocolate brand, and the national competition authority has found no harm to rivals. The record leaves the price and the integration plan open.

The Big Picture

Nutresa and the seller, Bia Culinary and Snacks Investments, the previous owner of the shares, agreed in June 2026 on the sale of 100% of the shares of Universal Sweet Industries (USI), subject to regulatory approvals, according to Nutresa’s announcement that month. Nutresa then announced on Friday 30 October 2026 that it had completed the purchase, and the SCE resolution followed on Monday 16 November.

Nutresa’s announcement said regulators had approved the deal, and the sources do not explain the gap between the two dates. Jaime Gilinski, Nutresa’s chairman and president, said on 30 October that bringing La Universal into Nutresa’s chocolate business opens a new chapter.

He said the company will invest so that the brands keep growing, which is the company’s own stated aim. Our earlier reports covered Nutresa Buys Ecuador Chocolate Icon Despite Colombia Trade War and Grupo Nutresa Agrees to Buy Presto.

Those articles are background only, and the facts here come from the regulator and the company.

Why the Regulator Looked Closely

Nutresa already operates in Ecuador through Cordialsa, a subsidiary that imports and distributes chocolates, biscuits and cocoa powder drink mixes. Those products overlap with the ones USI makes, according to the SCE.

The SCE also examined USI’s production of cocoa paste, a key input for other cocoa products. It reviewed two markets: cocoa powder mixes for drinks, and the risk that the group could restrict cocoa paste supply to competing manufacturers.

In Plain English SCE: Ecuador’s national antitrust regulator, which reviews company mergers and purchases.

Cocoa paste: a key input that other cocoa products are made from.

Dominant position: a market strength that lets a firm act without regard to rivals.

What the SCE Concluded

In cocoa powder mixes, the SCE said other manufacturers and brands can compete fully, and new entrants can produce themselves or use third-party makers. Both Nutresa and USI sell their own brands there and will now sit in one corporate group.

In cocoa paste, the SCE said the other competitors have other suppliers, so the acquirer would lack the ability and incentive to limit access. On that basis it found that the deal will not substantially reduce competition.

What It Means for You

The parties most affected are Ecuadorian cocoa and chocolate competitors, and the cocoa growers who supply buyers of paste. The mechanism the SCE tested was whether rivals could lose access to paste, and it found they have other suppliers, though the record gives no US figure for the deal.

For investors and readers following Ecuador, the ruling is the regulator’s own finding that the purchase does not threaten competition. It does not tell us how Nutresa will run the business.

What Is Not Known

The price has not been disclosed. Nutresa says it will spend the coming months carrying out an integration plan, but it has not published the details.

It does not say whether the SCE attached any conditions to its approval. The next dated step is not set out in the sources we used.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ecuador’s regulator approve?

The SCE authorised Grupo Nutresa to acquire 100% of the shares of Universal Sweet Industries, known as La Universal. It made this official on Monday 16 November 2026.

Why did the regulator review the deal?

Nutresa already sells chocolates, biscuits and cocoa drink mixes in Ecuador through Cordialsa, and these overlap with USI’s products. The SCE also checked USI’s cocoa paste output.

What did the SCE conclude?

It found the deal will not substantially reduce competition or create or strengthen a dominant position. Rivals can compete in drink mixes and have other cocoa paste suppliers.

How much did Nutresa pay?

The price was not disclosed. Nutresa announced on Friday 30 October 2026 that it had completed the purchase.

Sources: Superintendencia de Competencia Económica (Ecuador), Resolution SCE-CRPI-30-2026 and statement, 16 November 2026; Grupo Nutresa announcements, June 2026 and 30 October 2026.

CHILE · ARGENTINA · FORESTRY

Empresas CMPC, a Chilean pulp, paper and forestry group linked to the Matte family, one of Chile’s largest business families, agreed to sell its entire forestry operation in Argentina for US$170 million. The company said on Monday 16 November that the buyer is Grupo Faro Verde, an Argentine conglomerate.

The deal covers about 94,000 hectares in the provinces of Corrientes and Misiones, CMPC said in its announcement of 16 November. It ends more than 30 years of CMPC forestry in Argentina and follows other disposals covered in our Chile news.

Who Is Buying

Faro Verde is a group based in Tandil, in Buenos Aires province, founded by businessman José María Larocca. It works in agriculture, livestock, forestry, hotels and real estate, according to local business reports on Monday 16 November.

The same reports say Faro Verde added about 24,000 hectares of farmland from the Pereda family, a local landowning family, at the start of 2026. They add that it bought the grain trader Ceres Tolvas in September 2026.

Local business reports on 16 November also say Faro Verde owns eucalyptus forestry in Uruguay that supplies the pulp industry. Larocca is an Olympic show jumper who rode for Argentina at five Games, from Beijing 2008 to Paris 2024.

In Plain English Hectare: a metric land unit of 10,000 square metres, about 2.5 acres.

Pulp: wood fibre that mills turn into paper and packaging.

Plantable land: ground suitable for planting trees, as opposed to the total area.

What It Means for You

Shareholders of CMPC are affected most directly, because the three sales announced since September add up to US$955.5 million by our addition. The two Argentine companies will have a new owner, Faro Verde, once the deal closes.

The price of US$170 million is the figure CMPC announced on 16 November for about 94,000 hectares. CMPC’s announcement gives no figure for the wood the two companies sell.

CMPC agreed to sell its entire Argentine forestry operation to Grupo Faro Verde for US$170 million, it said on 16 November. The land is about 94,000 hectares in Corrientes and Misiones.

It is an Argentine conglomerate based in Tandil, in Buenos Aires province, founded by businessman José María Larocca. It works in agriculture, livestock, forestry, hotels and real estate.

CMPC says the sale is part of a strategy to tidy up its businesses and focus resources where it has the strongest competitive advantages. It also says the forests were not integrated with its industrial operations.

How much has CMPC announced in sales recently?

Our addition of the three sales announced since September gives US$955.5 million. They are a US$420 million packaging sale, a US$365.5 million Chilean forest sale and this US$170 million deal.

World.title: Argentina Braces for Days of Heavy Rain
World.content:
A large low-pressure system is forecast to bring days of heavy rain to northeastern Argentina this week, on ground that is already waterlogged. Some forecasts put the five-day total near 200 millimetres (about 8 inches) in places.

That matters beyond Argentina because the affected Paraná River basin feeds the country’s grain-export corridor and a major travel region. Forecasts can still change, and the official picture is thinner than the headlines suggest.

Key Facts Forecast. Private forecasters see more than 180 mm in parts of the northeast and Litoral by Friday 20 November.

Peak day. Tuesday 17 November brings the strongest storms, with up to 70 mm and gusts in the northeast.

Storm zone. Forecasters see severe storms in five northern provinces on Tuesday, the worst-hit day.

Power Index Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 60.2 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. Monday 16 November 2026, 6:30 p.m. ET.

Argentina’s northeast faces a wet, stormy week as a low-pressure system moves across the country. The risk is highest where rivers are already high.

Big Picture

Argentina’s national weather agency, the Servicio Meteorológico Nacional (SMN), issued a three-month outlook on 30 September 2026 that pointed to above-normal rain for the Litoral, the river region of the northeast, during October to December. The outlook implies that El Niño, a warm Pacific pattern that often brings extra rain to the area, will persist in the coming months.

That backdrop explains why this system looks more dangerous than its rainfall alone suggests. Soils near the Paraná River, one of South America’s largest rivers, are already saturated and streams are high.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

According to forecasts published on Monday 16 November, the low-pressure centre crosses northern Patagonia first and then moves out over the Atlantic. On Wednesday 18 November the low-pressure centre is expected to sit over the Atlantic, east of Buenos Aires.

Cold air then pushes in from the south.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Argentina 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What We Know

A private forecasting service, Meteored, expects the strongest storms on Tuesday 17 November in northern Santiago del Estero, Chaco, Formosa, Corrientes and Misiones. It projects up to 70 mm, strong gusts and possible hail.

The same forecast puts more than 60 mm in 24 hours on Wednesday 18 November over northern Santa Fe, eastern Chaco, Formosa and western Corrientes. Weekly totals above 180 mm are possible in several northeastern areas.

On Thursday 19 November a further 50 to 60 mm is possible in Corrientes, parts of Chaco and northern Santa Fe. On Friday 20 November isolated points in eastern Chaco, Formosa, northeastern Corrientes and Misiones could see up to 80 mm.

Wind is a secondary risk. Southwest gusts of up to 60 km/h (about 37 mph) are forecast for Buenos Aires province on Wednesday 18 November, and above 50 km/h (31 mph) in the capital area that afternoon and evening.

Some towns near the Paraná have already seen residents leave their homes. A flood wave on the river is still moving south.

What Is Not Known

We could not read the SMN’s alert map directly on Monday evening, so any official alert colours for each province remain unconfirmed. The SMN, Argentina’s national weather agency, is the body that issues them.

The 200 mm figure is a forecast peak from private modelling, not a measurement or an official warning. Actual totals depend on where the heaviest bands settle, which can shift by tens of kilometres.

Nobody has yet published a reliable river-height forecast for the lower Paraná for this week. Damage, evacuations and any effect on transport are therefore still open questions.

What It Means for You

Travellers heading to the northeast, including Iguazú Falls in Misiones, should expect disrupted roads and flights this week. Check with airlines and tour operators for the latest, since storms can close airports at short notice.

For readers who follow commodities, the Paraná carries a large share of Argentina’s soybean and grain exports through the Rosario area. We have not seen an official warning of river-port delays, so any trade impact is a possibility rather than a finding.

Residents and expats in Buenos Aires should expect rain returning on Tuesday morning and a windy Wednesday. Heavy totals in the capital are not forecast.

What to Watch

The SMN’s alerts for Tuesday 17 November and Wednesday 18 November will show how seriously the national agency rates the storms. Those updates, published on its official alert page, are the first checkpoint.

The second is the low-pressure centre’s position on Wednesday 18 November and whether the northeast gets the second pulse of storms on Thursday 19 November. A shift of the low would change where the heaviest rain falls.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Argentina really expecting 200 mm of rain?

Private forecasters see weekly totals above 180 mm and peaks near 200 mm in parts of the northeast. The strongest single day is Tuesday 17 November, with up to 70 mm.

Which provinces are most at risk?

The northeast and Litoral, mainly Corrientes, Chaco, Formosa, Misiones and northern Santa Fe. Northern Santiago del Estero is also in the storm zone on Tuesday.

Should travellers cancel trips to Argentina?

Buenos Aires faces rain and wind, not extreme totals. Travellers to the northeast should check flights and roads with their carriers, as conditions may change.

Could the rain affect Argentine soybean exports?

The Paraná is a key export route, and the river is already high. We have found no official warning of port delays so far.

World.content:
File photo: the flags of Canada, the United States and Mexico at an opening ceremony of the FIFA World Cup. Photo: Omar David Sandoval Sida, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

United Airlines suffered a widespread system outage on Monday, 16 November 2026, that delayed departing flights. The airline said it later resolved the technology issue.

It struck only three days after a nationwide halt to U.S. flights on Friday, 13 November. For travellers heading to or from Latin America through American hubs, two failures in one week raise the cost of any tight connection.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. What. United Airlines, a major U.S. carrier, reported a widespread system outage on Monday, 16 November 2026.

Effect. Departing flights were delayed. Flights already in the air and United Express flights were unaffected.

Earlier. A U.S. air traffic control failure on Friday, 13 November grounded nearly 3,500 flights.

Cause. No cause has been confirmed. United says it has no indication of a cyberattack.

As of. Monday, 16 November 2026, 6:30 p.m. ET

Two unrelated failures in one weekend show how a single broken system can strand thousands of passengers. Neither failure has been tied to an attack.

Big Picture

On Friday, 13 November, a communications failure at air traffic control centres led the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the U.S. aviation regulator, to stop takeoffs nationwide for about four and a half hours. The FAA said instability hit 17 of its 22 en route centres, which guide aircraft between airports.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

File photo: File:Exterior of the United States Department of State Harry S. Truman Building, Washingto.

The stop held nearly 3,500 scheduled flights on the ground. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who runs the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), said a newly installed router at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, was the likely cause.

Duffy said that router was sending about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. That flood destabilised the FAA’s older network and disrupted communications with aircraft and radar feeds.

Friday’s halt disrupted schedules across the country. That is why a second failure on Monday drew so much attention.

United’s outage is a separate event on a private airline system. Reports so far do not link it to Friday’s air traffic control failure, so Friday’s cause does not explain Monday’s.

What We Know

United said on Monday it was aware of a widespread system outage and told passengers to check its app or website for flight status. The airline later said it had resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures.

United said there was no impact on flights in progress or on United Express regional flights. The airline said it had no indication the outage was related to cybersecurity.

The union representing United’s pilots told members in an internal memo that the airline could not provide final aircraft weights. Pilots need those figures for their pre-departure calculations.

The same memo said several pilot applications were hit, including crew communications. It told pilots to follow guidance from local airport staff on whether to leave the gate.

What Is Not Known

United has not named the cause of the outage or the exact time it began. The weight explanation comes from the pilots’ union, not from the airline.

No official link between Monday’s United failure and Friday’s FAA failure has been reported. The FAA says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers.

It is also unclear how many United flights were delayed or cancelled because of the outage. Friday’s final cause is not settled either, since the FAA and L3Harris are still investigating.

It is also open whether the fault lay in the router, its settings or the wider network. L3Harris, a defence contractor, is the FAA’s network service provider.

What It Means for You

If you fly between the United States and Latin America, a delay at a U.S. hub can break a connection to cities such as Bogotá, São Paulo or Mexico City. Evening departures matter most, because the last onward flights often leave within hours of arrival.

Passengers on a single ticket are normally rebooked by the airline, while separate tickets leave the traveller to pay for a missed leg. Checking the airline’s rebooking terms before departure is the practical step.

Travellers with a flexible ticket can often move to an earlier or later flight at no charge, but terms differ by fare. Reading the fare rules before a trip costs nothing and avoids surprises at the gate.

Business travellers face the same chain of dependencies. One grounded evening can push a meeting back by a full day.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to United Airlines on 16 November 2026?

United reported a widespread system outage on Monday that delayed departing flights. The airline later said it had resolved the technology issue.

Is the United outage linked to the nationwide FAA ground stop?

Reports so far do not tie it to Friday’s air traffic control failure. They describe United’s outage as a separate problem in the airline’s own systems.

Was it a cyberattack?

United said it had no indication of a cybersecurity link. Officials also reported no sign of a cyberattack in Friday’s ground stop.

Are United flights back to normal?

United said it had resolved the issue on Monday evening. Delays can linger overnight, so passengers should check flight status before leaving for the airport.
