World.title: 5 countries announce plan to deport failed asylum-seekers to Rwanda
World.content:
There are still some “technical things” that have to be “sorted out,” Frederiksen said. “But the framework, the idea and the partnership is now in place.”

A reform of EU legislation adopted earlier this year made it possible for countries to negotiate deals to set up such deportation centers — as long as they comply with fundamental rights obligations.

The five countries plan to transfer people to Rwanda who have already gone through full asylum proceedings and were ordered to leave the EU.

The countries said they intend to target adults without children, and specifically people who don’t cooperate — or whose home countries don’t collaborate — in the deportation process.

“For me, today marks a crucial step towards a new migration system; a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens. To put it very short, it needs to be a democratic decision who can enter and who can stay in our societies,” Frederiksen said.

Staying in Rwanda

The five countries want to set up a reception center with the capacity to register and process 100 people at a time. Rejected asylum seekers who decide to stay in Rwanda rather than return to their country of origin would be given a residence permit and support to find a job and learn the language.

World.title: Europeans court China’s help to keep climate action on track
World.content:
The dispute ensnares the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a body which produces scientific assessments every five to seven years, and whose advice is considered the ultimate authority on the state of knowledge on global warming — and how to fight it.

The IPCC’s scientists hope to release their next series of reports in 2028. But the timeline is set by consensus among world governments, and a small group of countries led by India and Saudi Arabia are seeking to postpone publication.

As part of the dispute, they’re also blocking the body’s budget, throwing the IPCC into a funding crisis that could impede its work.

Any delay to the next reports would deprive climate negotiators of fresh scientific input at the pivotal COP conference in 2028, when countries must assess their progress toward the Paris Agreement and take remedial action to fix shortfalls. (The exercise is known as the second global stocktake, or GST2).

“We have this issue with the IPCC — the alliance of Saudi Arabia and India that wants to postpone the reports,” said Corvaro. “Without the reports of the IPCC, it’s tough to have a good global stocktake. We need to know the details of how far we’re falling short if we want to respond.”

European countries see China as key to resolving the impasse. If they manage to pull Beijing onside, the diplomats said, the blocking countries may fold.

World.title: Google says Russian speakers pulled off first-ever fully automated AI cyberattack
World.content:
Hackers, who used Russian in technical documentation identified by Google, set up a series of AI agents to “continuously compare pre- and post-patch code, identify vulnerabilities, and automatically develop exploits without human intervention,” Google said.

That means the agents independently found software flaws and ways to use them. The attackers targeted French websites in the media, entertainment and education sectors, Google said.

Until now, even the most advanced AI models could not carry out cyberattacks entirely independently; they often required skilled hackers to guide them or fix mistakes. The key change instead was that AI models allow hackers to accelerate attacks and make them more targeted.

The development is likely to spook governments and critical infrastructure operators who are still reeling from this summer's hack by an OpenAI agent into the Hugging Face platform. Though acting autonomously, that hack didn't appear to be maliciously aimed at certain targets like the one being reported by Google. Fears are also running high after the recent discovery of major flaws in PHP, a programming language that underpins 70 percent of the web, and a series of hacks on supermarket fridges, which have been partially blamed on Iran.

This article has been updated.

World.title: Sánchez and Lula meet in Madrid to strengthen ties amid 'threat of the far right'
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez welcomed Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to the Moncloa Palace on Monday, where the pair discussed the importance of international law and multilateralism at a time when both pillars of the global order are facing what the Spanish government described as the "threat of the far right."

 

"The head of the executive has highlighted the defence of international law and multilateralism, in a meeting in which the two leaders addressed the future of the United Nations and the importance of defending democratic institutions and social cohesion," the government said in a statement.

The two leaders are also said to have discussed their "bilateral agenda" and reaffirmed their intention to continue strengthening cooperation between Spain and Brazil.

After the meeting at the Moncloa Palace, the duo held a second conversation focusing on the state of the Western left and the progressive political vision they share. They highlighted a model centred on improving working conditions and fair taxation as ways to promote prosperity.

"I had a productive meeting with the Spanish prime minister," Lula wrote in a post on X. "We emphasised the importance of combating hate speech and disinformation from the far right and of promoting an agenda of social inclusion that strengthens democracy worldwide."

"We emphasised our stance in defence of multilateralism and the need for reform of the UN Security Council, which has become even more evident given the body’s ineffectiveness in the face of the escalating armed conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East," he added.

Sánchez and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva shake hands during a meeting in Madrid, Spain, Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Lula's visit to Spain comes after he skipped the 30th Ibero-American summit, held in Madrid at the beginning of November.

The summit exposed the ideological differences across the region, with the absence of the Brazilian leader and the president of Mexico, Claudia Sheinbaum, leaving Sánchez as the most prominent left-wing leader in attendance.

One of the summit's most talked-about moments was Argentine President Javier Milei's frosty encounter with Sánchez. The two shared a notably cold greeting upon their arrival at the Royal Collections Gallery. It was the first meeting between the two leaders since the Argentine branded Sánchez a "disgraceful dictator" in October.

Lula has also been involved in numerous clashes with Milei, including during the recent Brazilian election campaign, when he unexpectedly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, one of the Argentine president's closest regional allies.

Sánchez, who is fighting to remain in power, called an early election in Spain after his government partners refused to back a series of measures proposed by his administration to tackle the country's housing crisis.

World.title: Europe Tonight: MEPs debate Rwanda deportation scheme announced by five EU countries
World.content:
In the first edition of Euronews' new flagship show, Europe Tonight, presenter Mared Gwyn Jones brought viewers the latest analysis of the stories making headlines over the weekend and on Monday.

 

Jones opened the programme with the latest EU developments on migration, as five countries - Greece, Denmark, Germany, Austria and the Netherlands - announced a partnership with Rwanda to establish deportation hubs for irregular migrants, with the first pilot centres expected to be operational by mid-2027.

Our correspondent Vincenzo Genovese, reporting from Vienna, said it marked an unprecedented move in EU migration policy, with the bloc sending irregular migrants to a country with which they have no previous connection - a move compared to Donald Trump's approach in the US.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the agreement a "game changer," saying it would help European countries regain control and remove incentives for illegal migrants.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, the first facility will accommodate around 100 people. The hub would consist of open facilities rather than closed deportation centres, and migrants would be free to move around the country. The goal is to give them the chance to integrate into local society and the labour market.

The EU law enabling return hubs outside the bloc states that only non-EU countries “where international human rights standards are respected” are eligible.

Rwanda has a questionable track record on human rights. However, Rwanda's minister of the interior, Vincent Biruta, said the country was ready, had good experience in dealing with migrants and would respect fundamental rights.

Legal challenges could emerge when deportations begin next year, as happened with the UK-Rwanda agreement.

On Monday, Frederiksen added that she had a strong feeling that other countries would join the scheme.

Nineteen of the twenty-seven EU governments support the deportation plan. Only France and Spain have made clear their opposition to it. Italy already has its own agreement with Albania.

THE DEBATE

MEPs Charlie Weimers and Abir Al-Sahlani discuss Rwanda

Jones hosted Swedish MEP Charlie Weimers, a Member of the European Parliament since 2019 and part of the European Conservatives and Reformists group, and Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of the Renew Europe Group, who has also been an MEP since 2019, to debate the Rwanda "Return Hub."

Weimers said he agreed with Frederiksen, adding that he thought the policy was a "game changer." Noting that "every system" starts small, he said it would be successful if it led to further steps in the future to address migration policy in the EU.

Al-Sahlani pondered the feasibility of Rwanda returning migrants to their countries of origin, questioning how Rwanda would be able to carry out such returns when European countries themselves had struggled to do so.

“If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked, citing concerns over Rwanda's dependence on development aid and security concerns, as well as other unanswered questions.

Weimers calls deal a 'deterrent'

Meanwhile, Jones challenged Weimers over the cost-effectiveness of the proposed centres, citing Italy’s Albania scheme, which is costing Italian taxpayers €670 million over five years while handling only 0.3% of illegal arrivals into Italy. But Weimers described the new deal as being intended as a "deterrent" to those considering illegally migrating to Europe.

Al-Sahlani also criticised the growing influence of far-right narratives on European migration policy, arguing that governments were failing to use existing legislation and tools effectively.

The Renew Europe Group MEP further accused political leaders of portraying refugees as a threat and making them scapegoats for wider societal problems. She also warned that migration debates were increasingly driven by emotion rather than facts, fuelled by the misuse of statistics, selective truths and fabricated stories that vilify people seeking refuge.

Don't forget to join us tomorrow at 6 p.m. for the latest analysis of Europe's top headlines.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV struck in eye by rosary during tour of South America
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV was struck in the eye by what appeared to be a rosary as his popemobile made its way through crowds of onlookers in Peru on Monday.

 

Video footage showed the 71-year-old pontiff rubbing his eye after the object was thrown towards him before a farewell mass at Las Palmas air base.

Chicago-born Leo was able to continue with his schedule and appeared to be uninjured.

"My journey is coming to an end, but the mission continues," Leo later told the crowd.

"At the conclusion of my Apostolic Journey, I too wish to confirm you in faith and charity and assure you that I will always carry you with me. Yes, the Peruvian people are my people too!" he added.

Pope Leo XIV waves as he boards a plane to depart from Callao Naval Air Base on the outskirts Lima, Peru, Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Leo's tour of South America has also seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina and came just weeks after he underwent lung cancer surgery in Rome.

The Vatican said in October that the pope's "lower lobe of the right lung was removed" during the procedure, while also confirming a diagnosis of a "pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests."

Doctors later said a chest X-ray had shown "good recovery" of the affected lung, but the operation had nevertheless cast some doubt over Leo's South America trip.

His performance on the tour will have done much to ease fears about his recovery.

Leo was also able to return to his former hometown of Chiclayo during the trip, presiding over an open-air mass for around 500,000 people in the northern Peruvian city. He previously worked as a missionary and then bishop in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship.

World.title: Video shows rocket failure that destroys 40 Amazon satellites
World.content:
A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday, but the mission ended in failure after an anomaly occurred around 10 minutes into the flight.

 

The rocket failed to deliver its payload of 40 Amazon internet satellites into orbit, the company said. The satellites were part of Amazon's planned network to provide broadband internet services.

The launch was one of several dozen flights Amazon has purchased from ULA to deploy satellites for the project.

World.title: France can no longer support Kyiv 'financially,' Le Pen tells Ukrainian ambassador
World.content:
France's hard-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen confirmed on Monday that she planned to end financial aid to Ukraine if she is elected as president next year, following a meeting with Kyiv's ambassador in Paris.

 

Le Pen said she "regretted" that France's public finances would not allow it to provide further financial support but that a number of existing commitments would be maintained.

Le Pen is currently topping the polls at around 32% ahead of France's 2027 presidential elections, according to a survey published on 14 November by pollster Elabe. The hard-left France Unbowed party's Jean-Luc Mélenchon is trailing behind at roughly 17%.

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine draws closer, a statement issued by the National Rally said that while France could not continue to provide financial assistance to Ukraine, it would honour its "existing commitments" - citing the European Union's €90 billion support loan to Ukraine as well as "material donations, humanitarian aid, and more active diplomacy."

Le Pen described the talks with Ukraine's ambassador to France, Vadym Omelchenko, as "cordial" and an opportunity for her to reiterate her "unwavering support for Ukraine."

Le Pen has faced criticism over her past ties to Russia, which included a 2017 meeting in the Kremlin with President Vladimir Putin and her party taking a loan from a Russian bank that it paid off in full in 2023.

The statement also said the pair had held a "frank discussion" on the future of the conflict, with Le Pen emphasising that "the pursuit of peace - though a difficult goal to achieve - must remain a priority for all."

Le Pen's opponents have warned that by emphasising the importance of ending the war swiftly, she could force Ukraine to accept unfavourable terms.

"If Russia imposes its will on a European nation through brutality, all of Europe is weakened," Macron wrote on Facebook at the weekend.

Taking aim at Le Pen, he added: "Let us be clear: those who seek to limit the resources available to Ukraine are, in effect, pushing for an unjust peace - one that would leave Ukraine permanently vulnerable, and, by extension, leave Europe vulnerable as well."

During their meeting, Le Pen asked the Ukrainian ambassador to tell President Volodymyr Zelensky that she was ready to meet in "either Paris or Brussels."

However, there was no mention of her making the journey to Kyiv, where Zelensky has invited her.

World.title: Germany's 'bratwurst tax' sparks backlash as community groups face new VAT rules
World.content:
Controversy is brewing in Germany over the country's so-called "bratwurst tax."

 

From 1 January, new VAT rules are set to apply across all German municipalities, potentially meaning that key local community groups such as volunteer fire brigades could have to pay tax on sales of things such as bratwursts at village festivals and other local events.

The changes stem from section 2b of Germany's VAT Act, which has been repeatedly delayed but which is now expected to come into force. Under the rules, public bodies such as municipalities and towns are to be generally liable for VAT when they engage in commercial activities.

That means if a volunteer fire brigade operates as part of the municipality and not as an independent association, VAT would have to be paid on sales at local events.

Since 1 January 2026, a reduced tax rate of 7% has applied to food sold at snack bars or in restaurants. However, those affected have to keep detailed records of their sales and issue receipts.

On the website "Kommunal.de," Christian Erhardt-Maciejewski has taken a satirical swipe at the tax in a piece titled "Hurrah, the tax office is grilling the fire brigade."

He writes: "I can already imagine what will happen now: the most resourceful brigades will set up a support association so that they can carry on selling sausages. The fire brigade festival becomes an association festival, the grill master turns into a treasurer, mustard becomes a question for the statutes. A whole new form of volunteering is born in Germany: finding ways to dodge the tax authorities."

Grilled sausage desert in Germany: New tax triggers criticism Creative Commons / Schlurcher

In the Schleswig-Holstein state parliament, the CDU, Greens and FDP are calling for the new rules to be put on hold or for additional exemptions to be introduced.

"If the bratwurst at the Easter bonfire becomes a case for the tax office, something has gone seriously wrong," Christopher Vogt, the chair of the FDP parliamentary group, said, per NDR.

Vogt urged the state government in Kiel to "urgently provide support for local volunteers."

There has already been some movement in North Rhine-Westphalia, where the state's finance minister, Marcus Optendrenk, reportedly issued a decree clarifying that bratwurst sales by volunteer fire brigades are to be exempt from VAT.

"Anyone who volunteers with the local fire brigade deserves a tailwind rather than paperwork," Optendrenk said.

World.title: Qatar Sustainability Week explores ways to cut food waste, track carbon emissions and support wellbeing
World.content:
Qatar Sustainability Week explored what households and businesses could do differently, from shopping habits to managing waste. At LuLu, shoppers were encouraged to use reusable bags and return empty bottles and old electronics for recycling. Schoolchildren have also helped spread the message by speaking to customers about replacing single-use bags.

 

At Qatar Foundation’s Green Island in Education City, sustainability programmes for schools and companies run throughout the year. Enbat’s permanent food waste exhibition shows the resources needed to get a meal onto the table and what is lost when food is thrown away. It also demonstrates how discarded ingredients can be used again, with banana peels turned into taco filling, potato skins into crisps and carrot tops into pesto.

At Qatar University, researchers explained how digital tools could help organisations measure carbon emissions and report their environmental impact. Youth Fest also explored the social side of sustainability, with young organisers combining environmental activities with a space focused on physical and mental wellbeing.

World.title: Italian schools hit by new wave of bomb and poison threats
World.content:
At least 100 Italian schools received emailed bomb and poison threats on Monday, triggering a new security protocol introduced by the government following similar threats last week.

 

The email arrived at around 10:50 am, signed with the initials MA, warning of two imminent dangers.

"I have just been tasked with placing and activating an explosive device in your building. The explosion will take place in 40 minutes," it said, while also claiming that "an employee in your canteen has mixed a toxic substance including sodium azide and potassium cyanide into the food and supplies."

"You have ignored our demands," it added.

On this occasion, the threats prompted just a handful of evacuations. Checks on food served in school canteens did not reveal any anomalies.

Under new security guidelines, Italian schools are no longer automatically evacuated in response to such vague, mass-distributed threats, with the decision left to the discretion of law enforcement and security officials.

Monday's messages came from the email account of a Vietnamese institution, which is believed to have been hacked. The address academic.affairs3@vnuk.udn is linked to a research centre in the city of Da Nang.

Investigation launched

Italy's postal police have since launched an investigation into the incident.

"We are facing an investigative challenge: the simpler the operation, the harder it is to identify an error by the person who carried out the attack," Ivano Gabrielli, director of the cyber police service, told SkyTg24. "These days, retrieving an email from the dark web and using it anonymously is unfortunately very easy from a technical point of view."

But he added that whoever set up the infrastructure to send such a large number of emails may still have made a mistake that investigators can find and pursue.

Speaking in Brussels, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said there was a "shared vision and desire to be increasingly united in responding to attacks and preventing different types of threats by email, cyber or hacking."

World.title: Germany beat Netherlands 5-0 to win Nations League group
World.content:
Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany cruised to a comfortable 5-0 win over the Netherlands to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals on Monday.

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

World.title: United Airlines resolves tech outage that delayed flights
World.content:
United Airlines said a system outage that delayed departures has been resolved. The disruption came on the heels of a stoppage that halted all flights to and across the US for five hours last week.

United Airlines said it has resolved a "widespread system outage" that affected hundreds of departing flights on Monday.

Flight tracker FlightAware said 418 United flights were delayed on Monday afternoon.

The issue comes three days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network grounded flights across the US on Friday.

What did United Airlines say about Monday's tech issues?

United Airlines said there was "no indication" that Monday's outage was the result of a cyberattack.

There was also no indication that the issues affecting United Airlines on Monday were related to Friday's nationwide shutdown.

US lifts nationwide air travel ground stop, but disruptions continue To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

United Airlines said later on Monday that it had "resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures."

The airline added that airborne flights, as well as those operated by its regional brand United Express, were not affected.

The disruption on Friday and Monday highlights how vulnerable air travel is to tech failures.

Disruption follows other recent major tech meltdowns

United Airlines' computer problem comes amid other recent similar high-profile technology meltdowns, including Friday's nationwide grounding.

Thousands of people in the US said they were unable to access their online banking accounts at several large US banks after JPMorgan Chase reported a technical issue.

On Thursday, Microsoft saw a major disruption to its services, including its Outlook email and Teams messenger.

The tech company said Saturday that its services had been fully restored.

World.title: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
World.content:
Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Gianni Infantino seeks another term as FIFA president Image: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/picture alliance

Son of boxer, head of French football

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was appointed the federation's president in 2023 after being elected with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

FIFA will hold the vote for its next president in March Image: Ennio Leanza/EPA/dpa/picture alliance

Embattled Infantino

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. The criticisms were led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round of 16 game against Belgium despite being shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

World.title: EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia's richest woman
World.content:
Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from travel to the bloc.

The European Union added Russia's wealthiest woman, online retailer Wildberries' CEO and owner Tatyana Kim, to its Russian sanctions list on Monday.

Kim's EU assets will be frozen as a result and she is barred from making financial transactions in or traveling to the bloc.

Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce retailer.

Kim, born in Grozny, Chechnya, to ethnic Korean parents, has an estimated net worth of $8.1 billion (€7.4 billion).

The sanctions were part of a larger regime targeting some 50 banks and oil export enablers and nearly 100 business leaders, propagandists and a major pro-Russian hacking group.

EU authorities say they targeted ​Kim due to the fact that Wildberries is "one of the largest taxpayers" in Russia and "operates as a supply network ​for the Russian military by facilitating the sale of military and ​dual-use ‌goods."

An EU statement went on to say that "Kim is supporting, materially or financially, and benefiting from Russia's military and industrial complex."

Why is the EU targeting an online retailer?

In its defense against invading Russian forces, Ukraine expanded its military target list this summer to include Wildberries warehouses inside Russia, saying the company's product list — which includes night-vision goggles, ammunition pouches and helmets alongside ‌regular clothing, cosmetics and electronics — is supporting Russia's illegal war.

Kim defended her company at the time, saying its offerings were no different than other online retailers like Amazon in the US and Alibaba in China.

The Kremlin, too, denied that the company and its warehouses were involved in the war effort.

Why Ukraine is targeting Russia's biggest online retailer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who else is on the EU's newest sanctions list?

In a statement, Wildberries said Brussels' sanctions would have no impact on the company since it has no assets in the bloc nor does it conduct business there.

Other entities on Monday's sanctions list include firms in China, Oman, the Seychelles and the United Arab Emirates linked to the sale of oil from Russia's so-called shadow fleet of illicit tankers.

The sale of that oil also fuels Russia's invasion, which the EU is seeking to hamper through sanctions as well as direct financial and military assistance for Kyiv.

Brussels has imposed more than 20 sanctions packages in response to Russia's February 24, 2022, invasion of Ukraine, targeting thousands of individuals and companies to pressure President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the assault.

The 27-nation bloc intends to introduce another sweeping sanctions package by year's end.

World.title: Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care
World.content:
Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed to the country's Supreme Court in a bid to receive urgent medical attention for himself and his wife.

According to an open letter conveyed to the court through Khan's lawyer, the former leader's doctors had warned him of a risk for brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest and that his blood pressure had risen sharply.

He also said his wife Bushra Bibi required further eye operation, and that she is at risk of losing her eyesight should she not be granted the surgery.

The letter was released to the public by Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar.

"Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” the letter reads, asking the judges to give him "justice" before it was too late.

"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," Khan wrote.

Government contests account

An earlier court order ordered Khan's transfer to a hospital in Pakistani capital Islamabad, with Khan alleging that the authorities had not implemented it.

However, cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said Khan was receiving medical care, while also receiving food and books of his liking.

According to Chaudhry, the former leader has been taken to medical examinations at a hospital in Islamabad eight times, with his health and blood pressure being found to be in order.

Still a popular figure

Despite being in prison since 2023 for corruption offenses, Khan is still considered a popular figure in Pakistan, with his party demanding his release. His wife is alo serving jail time for graft offenses.

Khan argues the charges against him are politically motivated, which the government denies.

The government, led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, also denied Khan was in solitary confinement. More than 900 visits to Khan have been registered since he started his jail time in 2023, according to the authorities.

Imran Khan is still a popular figure in Pakistan Image: PPI/ZUMA/picture alliance

In a previous case, Khan's attorney told the court that his client had lost about 85% of his right eye's vision. However, his sister later said his situation was improving.

World.title: Grammy Awards: Raye and Rosalia lead nominations
World.content:
The nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards are in and women dominated the top categories for the highest accolade in the music industry.

British singer Raye, with the genre mixing hit "Where Is My Husband!," landed at the top of the list of Grammy Award nominees on Monday, followed by Spanish musician Rosalia and "Choosin" Texas" artist Ella ‌Langley.

Raye earned 11 ⁠Grammy ⁠nominations including nods for song and record of the year for "Husband," and for album of the year for "This Music May Contain Hope."

She now ties Beyonce's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.

For her part, Rosalia received nine nominations, just days after sweeping the Latin Grammys with ​her album "Lux."

Rosalia mixes genres such as flamenco and pop Image: Julie Sebadelha/AFP

First-time nominee Langley secured seven, as did Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers.

Megastar Taylor Swift received five nominations.

Only one male artist nominated for Best Album

Besides Raye, competitors in the album race include Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl," Langley's "Dandelion," Rosalia's "Lux," Bridgers' "Lost Weekend," Olivia Dean's "The Art of Loving," and Rodrigo's "you ​seem pretty sad for a girl so in love." Bruno Mars was the only male artist nominated in the category, for his album "The Romantic."

Taylor Swift, has taken the album of the year trophy a record four times Image: Caroline Brehman/REUTERS

The record of the year category is made up of Dean's “Man I Need,” Langley's “Choosin' Texas,” Mars' “I Just Might,” Raye's “Where Is My Husband!”, Rodrigo's “The Cure,” Rosalía’s “Berghain” featuring Björk and Yves Tumor, Swift's “The Fate of Ophelia” and Tame Impala and Jennie's “Dracula.”

K-pop sensation ⁠BTS declined to submit any ​music for consideration in protest over a new Asian pop music category. Members of the South Korean band said they did not believe music should be categorized by region.

K-pop powerhouse BTS said in July they are not interested in winning a new Asian music category Image: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

Dolly Parton, the country legend who died in August, received three posthumous nominations.

Winners will be announced on February

The final Grammy voting round will run from December 10 to January 7, with winners selected by around 16,000 Recording Academy members.

Winners will be announced at a red-carpet ceremony in downtown Los Angeles ‌on ​February 7.

The event will be broadcast live on Walt Disney's ABC and streamed on Disney+ and Hulu.

World.title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
World.content:
When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

How did Voyager 1 get so far and where is it going?

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

There were two Golden Records, one on Voyager 1 and another on Voyager 2, a second spacecraft on the same 1970s mission. They were protected with this gold aluminum cover. Image: United Archives/picture alliance

Voyager 1 is an ongoing scientific experiment

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

Something you didn't already know about Voyager 1

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

World.title: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
World.content:
In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

How it all started

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Bond girls were typically portrayed as ditzy blondes with little to say Image: IFTN/United Archives/IMAGO

A machismo problem

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

The first bond girl was named Honey Ryder, a name which would likely be considered sexist by today's standards Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Questionable lifestyle choices

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

Even such artwork associated with the original Bond film would never be deemed appropriate in this day and age Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Why are all secretaries women?

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

It wasn't until the 2012 film that we finally learn something about Bond's boss's secretary, Moneypenny Image: CAP/MFS Image/Capital Pictures/picture alliance

Inappropriate casting

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

White actor Joseph Wiseman was made to look Asian with makeup Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Pattinson as a modern 007?

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

World.title: El Gobierno aprobará este martes la subida del 4,5% de los salarios de los funcionarios para 2027
World.content:
El Gobierno aprobará este martes la subida salarial del 4,5% para los empleados públicos correspondiente a 2027, según ha anunciado este lunes Pedro Sánchez en una entrevista en Informativos Telecinco. El incremento, anunciado en plena campaña electoral, tendrá efectos desde el 1 de enero y se abonará en las nóminas de ese ejercicio. A esta mejora se sumará, durante el primer trimestre de 2027, otro 0,5% correspondiente a la desviación de la inflación del año pasado, una compensación que ya estaba prevista en el acuerdo con los sindicatos y que dejaría la revisión en el 5% anunciado en octubre de este año.

El incremento salarial de los empleados públicos forma parte del acuerdo plurianual que el Gobierno cerró en noviembre de 2025 con CC OO, UGT y CSIF para actualizar las nóminas de más de tres millones de trabajadores de las Administraciones públicas hasta 2028. Y el medio punto adicional responde a una cláusula de garantía de poder adquisitivo incluida en el pacto. El Gobierno condicionó su abono a que la inflación interanual de diciembre de 2026 alcanzase al menos el 1,5%, un umbral que se supera ampliamente pese a que hay que esperar a que el INE publique el dato definitivo de diciembre.

“Mañana, en el Consejo de Ministros, aprobarán la subida del sueldo de los trabajadores públicos”, ha dicho el presidente del Gobierno. “Y si a eso le unimos la reconstrucción del Pacto de Toledo y la obligación por ley de la revalorización de las pensiones, hablamos de blindar la capacidad adquisitiva de 15 millones de personas en un momento que coincide con las tensiones con Irán”, ha indicado el jefe del Ejecutivo.

El pacto estableció una subida acumulada del 11% en cuatro años, con el objetivo de compensar la pérdida de poder adquisitivo del colectivo y dar continuidad a las mejoras salariales tras un 2025 en el que los funcionarios pasaron prácticamente todo el ejercicio sin actualizar sus retribuciones. La aplicación de las mejoras se ha ido produciendo de forma escalonada. El Gobierno aprobó en diciembre de 2025 un incremento del 2,5% para ese ejercicio, con efectos retroactivos desde enero, y otro del 1,5% fijo para 2026. El acuerdo contemplaba, además, medio punto adicional condicionado a que el IPC interanual de diciembre de 2026 alcanzase al menos el 1,5%, lo que elevaría la subida de ese año al 2%. La mayor parte de las comunidades autónomas abonaron los atrasos pendientes de 2025 en las nóminas de diciembre y enero, de modo que sus empleados comenzaron el año con una mejora acumulada del 4%.

Con la nueva revisión salarial del 4,5%, el Gobierno habrá aplicado ya alrededor del 80% del incremento salarial pactado con los sindicatos. CSIF había reclamado que la subida correspondiente a 2027 se aprobara antes de las elecciones para evitar retrasos derivados de las limitaciones que afronta el Ejecutivo cuando se encuentra en funciones. El sindicato también advirtió del encarecimiento de los precios al cierre del año y pidió que las distintas Administraciones —estatal, autonómicas y locales— pudieran presupuestar y preparar las nóminas con criterios homogéneos. Además, el sindicato reclama que las indemnizaciones por residencia y por razón de servicio se actualicen antes de que termine 2026, tal y como recoge el acuerdo. El sindicato advierte de que el coste de la vivienda está llevando a algunos empleados públicos a renunciar a sus plazas porque no pueden permitirse vivir en los destinos asignados. Según CSIF, el Ministerio le ha trasladado su intención de cumplir el plazo y aprobar la revisión antes de que acabe el año.

En efecto, más allá de las retribuciones, el pacto alcanzado con los sindicatos incorporaba compromisos para reformar la Administración y mejorar las condiciones laborales de sus plantillas. Entre ellos figura la eliminación progresiva de la tasa de reposición, que es el mecanismo que limita la creación de plazas públicas en función de las bajas producidas, principalmente por jubilación. El objetivo es facilitar la renovación de las plantillas y cubrir las necesidades de personal de los distintos servicios públicos.

UGT, por su parte, ha señalado que “con esta subida se cumple lo pactado en materia salarial con las organizaciones sindicales firmantes del acuerdo y supone un paso en la dignificación de los salarios que perciben los empleados públicos”, aunque a la vez el sindicato precisa que “aún queda por concretar medidas como las cuantías de las indemnizaciones por razones de residencia en territorios de Canarias, Ceuta, Melilla y Valle de Aran”. El sindicato reconoce que había exigido al Ministerio de Función Pública que agilizase los trámites para que “el abono se formalizase de inmediato, a pesar de la disolución del Parlamento y la convocatoria de elecciones generales para el 29 de noviembre”.

Miriam Pinillos, responsable de políticas públicas de CC OO, también ha valorado positivamente el anuncio hecho por el presidente, pero recuerda al Gobierno “que hay que seguir trabajando para cumplir con el resto de materias recogidas en el Acuerdo Marco”.

World.title: Dutch progress in Nations League despite 5-0 drubbing in Germany
World.content:
The Netherlands came crashing down to earth after hammering Greece as they were outclassed and outmuscled by Germany in Berlin.

Oranje went into the final match of the Nations League group stage with high hopes of recording their first win over their old rivals in seven matches stretching back to 2019.

Instead they suffered their second worst defeat ever at the hands of Germany, but still progressed to the knockout stages thanks to their thumping 7-0 win in Amsterdam on Friday.

Coach Xavi Hernandez was forced to make one change in midfield as Jurriën Timber replaced Barcelona’s Frenkie de Jong, who pulled out with an obturator muscle strain.

Germany shaded the first half and went ahead five minutes before the break when Freiburg striker Derry Scherhant cut in from the left hand side and beat Bart Verbruggen with a curling strike into the top corner.

Scherhant had struck the post minutes earlier, while the Dutch might have taken the lead earlier when Crysencio Summerville slipped in the penalty area as he tried to control a cross by Cody Gakpo.

But in the second half the Dutch fell apart. In the 60th minute Florian Wirtz shoved Denzel Dumfries off the ball and had space to tee up a left-footed shot from the edge of the area that gave Verbruggen no chance.

Nico Schlotterbeck added a third from a free-kick five minutes later, before Wirtz drifted past Gakpo on the right side of the penalty area to score his second.

The humiliation was complete when Brajan Gruda capped a fine attacking performance by firing in a rebound.

Dumfries made no excuses afterwards for what he admitted was a “terrible performance”. “We gave the ball away too easily, left too much space and were too weak in the challenges,” he told NOS. “We can’t let that happen.”

World.title: Outcry over “cruel” plan to send failed asylum seekers to Rwanda
World.content:
Some 46 human rights, civil society and trade union organisations have signed a letter objecting to the “cruel” plan presented by the Netherlands and four other EU member states on Monday to begin sending asylum seekers whose applications have been rejected to Rwanda.

The plan, presented in Vienna on Monday, will pave the way for people to be sent to “deportation hubs” in Rwanda, on the idea that it will help secure national borders and break apart human trafficking networks. The reality, the signatories say, is that this is just a euphemism for forced deportation and will deteriorate security.

Dutch foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen joined counterparts from Austria, Denmark, Germany and Greece at the conference. The letter of objection notes that the vulnerable people will be sent to a place that they have never been to, have no connection to, and which has a serious ongoing record of human rights violations.

“It signals that member states accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalised groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach. Such cruel measures drive people into further insecurity, and risk making migration routes more dangerous,” the letter states.

Berendsen said at the press conference after the event that “effective return is important” and that through the deal the Netherlands is “taking a concrete step towards a better migration system by establishing a return hub in Rwanda.”

He also spoke of the need for economic development in Rwanda, though how the deal will work is unclear. According to broadcaster NOS, Rwanda wants economic support in return, and the five countries will share the costs, which have not been made public. Rwanda will initially offer around 100 places, and only single men will be sent at first.

A spokesperson from asylum foundation Stichting Vluchteling told Dutch News: “We are against this concept as a humanitarian organisation. Member states are responsible for these people. We’re very concerned about the situation in Rwanda. We see human rights abuses on press freedom. We don’t believe there will be the possibility for independent monitoring from member states.”

The spokesperson said the talk of improving human rights through this agreement was nothing but “pretty words”.

They said that the move sends a signal that Europe does not want to accept its responsibility for asylum seekers. “This is super dangerous. Even if one person is sent over the next couple of years, it sends a signal that we don’t want you here and that we’re willing to go quite far to remove you.”

There is a critical shortage of asylum beds in the Netherlands, with many taken by people whose applications have been rejected but are stuck in legal limbo. But the spokesperson said “this is not a numbers crisis, it’s a political crisis. The focus should be on obligations that member states have, which is that we’re responsible for people who are rejected.”

The letter also warns that the EU’s proposed new rules for border agency Frontex would allow it to support returns to non-EU countries, including a possible role in running “return hubs”. Frontex already operates with “a de facto lack of accountability”, the organisations say, and the proposal would remove the obligation to assign at least one fundamental rights monitor to each operation.

The Dutch foreign ministry’s own country report on Rwanda, which the immigration service IND uses to assess asylum claims, records extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and torture in unofficial detention centres.

The letter also warned that “by relying on third countries to take on its protection obligations, the EU makes itself dependent on non-EU states, enabling third countries to leverage migration in line with their own political agenda.”

World.title: King raises history of slavery at ceremony to mark First Salute
World.content:
King Willem-Alexander has acknowledged the role of the Dutch Caribbean islands in the transatlantic slave trade during a ceremony to mark the 250th anniversary of the Netherlands’ recognition of the United States.

The king was speaking on Statia Day, a national holiday on the island of Sint Eustatius to mark the First Salute, when a Dutch cannon was fired from Fort Orange to return a salute from the American ship Andrew Doria.

The event on November 16, 1776, is seen as the first formal recognition of the USA by a foreign power after the Declaration of Independence in July that year.

At the time the island was a Dutch colony with around 70 slave plantations. Today it is a special municipality of the Netherlands with a population of around 3,300.

During his speech on Monday, the king referred to the recently published study into the royal family’s role in slavery, which concluded that the house of Oranje-Nassau earned more than €500 million from the colonies since the 17th century.

Prime minister Rob Jetten had also been due to attend the ceremony, but he was forced to stay in the Netherlands for crisis talks with his coalition partners after last week’s budget vote brought his cabinet to the brink of collapse.

Common history

“The First Salute is a milestone in history, but our common history goes far wider,” the king said. “There is also the story of Statia as a place to commemorate slavery.

“In the 17th and 18th centuries several thousand people from west Africa landed here. After an inhumane journey of two months, packed into the bowels of ships with no more than two square metres per person, there was no salute for them on their arrival.”

He said that he had been moved by the results of four years of research into slavery, led by Leiden university professor of colonial history, Geert Oostindië, which he commissioned and paid for.

“I know that life on this isolated island is not easy for many people,” he said. “Groceries are expensive, there are few jobs to be had and healthcare is limited.” He added he would continue to work for “fair opportunities and a good life for everyone.”

World.title: More than 14,000 bogus police officers recorded this year so far
World.content:
The number of cases of people being approached by bogus police officers is continuing to rise despite efforts to warn elderly residents to watch out for doorstep conmen.

In 2023 police received just over 500 reports of people being tricked by criminals posing as officers who tried to persuade them to hand over cash and valuables, but in the last three years the number has exploded.

Police suspect that organised gangs are behind the trend, which saw the number rise to 13,000 last year and 14,176 in the first 10 months of 2026. Nearly 3,300 official crime reports have been filed of theft by bogus police officers, suggesting around a quarter of attempts are successful. The oldest victim was 103.

Criminals typically appear on the victim’s doorstep and tell them that thieves are operating in the area. They then offer to take in cash and other valuable items such as jewellery for safekeeping.

Some offenders dress in clothes resembling police uniforms, while others wear casual clothing and tell their victims they are working with CID.

Police said genuine officers will never offer to take away items from householders and anyone with doubts about an officer on the doorstep should call 112 to find out if police are making enquiries in their neighbourhood.

Information campaign

Last year police and Omroep MAX, which broadcasts daytime TV programmes on NPO, ran an information campaign highlighting the doorstep techniques used by bogus officers.

“We do a lot of work to prevent and detect these offences,” said Sybren van der Velden Walda, national co-ordinator for high impact crime. “But it’s evidently so lucrative that criminals keep posing as police officers to rob people.”

So far this year 783 people have been arrested on suspicion of pretending to be police officers, one of whom was a 13-year-old boy who stole a bank card and €20,000 worth of jewellery. Police say it is likely he was working for gangsters.

“We see it is a vulnerable group who are recruited by organised criminals to do things like this,” said Van der Velden Walda.

He added that the prevalence of bogus officers was making it harder for his colleagues to carry out genuine police work.

“Elderly people won’t open the door any more because they don’t trust police at the door,” he said.

World.title: Preventative health made accessible for internationals
World.content:
For many new internationals, going to a Dutch doctor, or huisarts, takes a bit of time getting used to. With a more hands-off approach to healthcare than in many other countries, you often don’t get to your huisarts until you have symptoms you want checked.

But what if you want to understand your health before symptoms appear? Knowing what to check, and which lifestyle changes could make a difference, isn’t always straightforward.

Enter Blue Health Intelligence, a health-tech startup that offers a 360-health check, providing insight into cardiovascular health, metabolism and liver and kidney functions within an hour, sharing results immediately in a consultation with a doctor.

“In countries such as Japan, Germany and the UK, periodic health checks are already embedded in the healthcare system, but that is not yet the case in the Netherlands,” says Onno Huyghe, CEO and co-founder of Blue Health Intelligence. “By gaining earlier insight into their health, people can stay healthy for longer and health issues can be prevented. We aim to make prevention more accessible to many people.”

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 1.8 million deaths from noncommunicable diseases are avoidable each year in Europe. About 60% are linked to changeable risk factors – such as tobacco and alcohol use, high blood pressure, unhealthy diets, obesity and physical inactivity – while the remaining 40% could be prevented or delayed through timely diagnosis and high-quality health care.

For €299, you get a 360-degree health check that uses hundreds of data points, the results of which are discussed immediately on-site with a doctor and uploaded to the Blue app. The 10 tests administered include an ECG, 3D body scan, blood analysis and an ultrasound.

“You don’t always realise how much your health risks increase as you get older,” says customer Petra. “For me, the health check at Blue Health was a real eye-opener. Under professional guidance, you’re efficiently taken through all the tests in a short time.”

If something is discovered, Blue Health Intelligence offers a free follow-up before passing that information on to your huisarts.

As common as an annual dental check-up

“Our participants gain a comprehensive understanding of their health and potential health risks,” says Leanne Verdonck, physician and co-founder of Blue Health Intelligence. “Our goal is for a regular health check to become just as common as going to the dentist.”

At its modern, state-of-the-art facility on Amsterdam’s Prinsengracht, Blue Health Intelligence has made preventative healthcare affordable. It follows the growing trend in the health and wellness sector of getting insight into people’s potential health risks, advising them on healthy lifestyle changes in a personalized plan that is then shared in the app.

Having recently secured €3.4 million in funding, Blue Health Intelligence plans to expand its capacity in Amsterdam and even internationally, including in Paris and Milan, while continuing to develop its preventative health platform.

More than 2,500 people have already booked a health check with Blue Health Intelligence. Due to high demand, bookings are now offered through a waitlist. If you choose to join, Blue will contact you when it’s your turn to book, with appointments a few days away.

Click on the link if you want to join.

World.title: Dutch influencer still held by ICE with no reason given, family
World.content:
Dutch influencer and OnlyFans model Vera Dijkmans, who was arrested five days ago by US ICE agents, remains in custody without any reason given for her detention, according to her family, who also say she is being held in dire conditions.

Dijkmans has millions of social media followers and often does promotional work with UFC fighters. She was arrested at Newark airport where she’d travelled to from Miami for an event.

Her details don’t show up on the ICE database and no details have been made public as to why she was detained. Her mother, who has travelled there to protest for her release, said “we fear for her life”, adding that “she is in a room with twelve other women, receives little food and drink, and there is barely any fresh air. The conditions are inhumane,” AD reported.

Dijkmans is staying in the US on a B2 visa that allows you to be in the country without working for up to six months. She had applied for a permanent residency there and may have missed an appointment for that application procedure, her mother speculated to AD.

The US government warned people this year that using social media for commercial purposes was not allowed on a tourist visa.

ICE, which was expanded by the Trump administration to round up and deport people from the country who do not have the correct paperwork, often targets people who have failed to comply with visa rules.

Delaney Hall, the immigration detention centre in Newark where Dijkmans is being held, is run by private prison company GEO Group, which was awarded a 15-year, $1 billion contract by ICE in 2025 to detain up to 1,000 people there. It is notorious for its harsh conditions.

The Dutch foreign affairs ministry told AD it is aware of Dijkmans’ situation and is providing consular assistance, though it did not say what that entails.

World.title: Man recovered after operation to remove 10kg tumour from stomach
World.content:
Surgeons in Groningen have removed a tumour weighing more than 10 kilograms from the intestines of a man in a ground-breaking operation.

The benign tumour, described as being the size of a large basketball, had been growing slowly in the patient’s stomach for around 25 years and almost entirely filled his stomach cavity.

It was discovered by accident when the man, 68-year-old Ronald van de Kimmenade, went to hospital with a lung infection. Further investigations revealed he had been gaining weight since 2000 without suspecting the cause.

“He had no symptoms at that time that indicated the huge aberration in his stomach,” said surgeon Sijbrand Hofker.

Hofker initially decided not to operate because the tumour was not malignant, but changed his mind a year later when it became so large that it threatened to cause massive blood loss.

The 10-hour operation involved removing Van de Kimmenade’s intestines with the tumour, keeping them refrigerated and replacing them afterwards. It is the first time in Europe that a so-called “autotransplant” has been performed successfully.

No donor organ

Hofker explained on the university hospital’s website that Van de Kimmenade was not eligible for a regular transplant with a donor organ and a standard operation would have left him dependent on tube feeding for the rest of his life.

“I spent a lot of time beforehand studying images of his intestines and the tumour. I had to work out exactly what route we would follow during the operation so that we could remove the tumour and reconnect the major arteries.

“What you don’t know beforehand is what it will actually look like when you come to perform the operation. You have to estimate based on your experience if it is technically possible and if the patient can endure the operation.

“Our aim was to remove the tumour without the patient losing his intestines so that he could lead a normal life.”

Van de Kimmenade, who underwent the operation a year ago, said the operation had been lifesaving.

“Before the operation I had to undergo a huge number of blood transfusions. I had 35 bags of blood in a year,” he said.

“I was frequently tired, had little energy and threw up when the temperature changed.

“Now I have occasional check-ups and that’s all. I’m back at work and am going to keep working for longer. Beforehand I was glad to have retired. Now I think: if I sit still I’m just going to get old and I’m still much too young for that.”

World.title: Heirs seek to stop $180m Van Gogh sale, citing Nazi-era duress
World.content:
The heirs of a German Jewish publisher have asked Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting from auction in New York this week. They say their family was forced to sell it in Amsterdam in 1936 under the pressure of Nazi persecution, and it should be withdrawn from the auction.

Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees), which Van Gogh painted in May 1890, weeks before his death, is the top piece in Sotheby’s sale of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection on Wednesday, according to the Volkskrant.

The auction house has put an unofficial estimate of around $180 million (€156 million) on the work, which would beat the artist’s auction record of $117.2 million (€106 million), set at Christie’s in 2022.

Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher in Berlin, bought the painting in 1909, according to Sotheby’s catalogue. In the early 1930s it was placed with an art dealer in Amsterdam.

The heirs say the family fled Berlin for Vienna in 1936 and that the painting was sold three months later, after their publishing house had suffered heavy losses under Nazi rule.

In an email seen by The New York Times, the heirs’ lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, asked Sotheby’s to prove that the painting was sold at market value and that the sale would have happened without Nazi pressure. Otherwise, he wrote, “no auction may take place.”

Sotheby’s says its research has not shown that the painting was sold under duress, and that it is in talks with the heirs. It told ARTnews that the painting sold for 68,000 Swiss francs in June 1936, which it considers a good price.

International guidelines backed by the Netherlands and the United States say that sales made under financial pressure from Nazi persecution can count as involuntary, but the guidelines are not legally binding.

The Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier bought the painting in 1975. It has not been shown in public since 1964. As of Monday, Sotheby’s had not said whether it would stay in Wednesday’s sale.

World.title: Kraków church holds mass for perpetrator of deadly attack just metres from where he shot victims
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! The historic St Mary’s Basilica in Kraków has hosted a holy mass for Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out the recent attack in the city and later died of injuries sustained in a shootout with police. The six people who died in the attack and more than a dozen who were injured were shot by Oskiński on the square where the church stands, some of them just a few metres from its doors. St Mary’s Basilica says that the mass is “an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime”. On the afternoon of 7 November, Oksiński launched his attack on Kraków’s famous market square, which was packed with locals and tourists. He shot at random from his car while driving through the square and surrounding streets before police managed to bring his rampage to an end. Later that same day, the dead bodies of Oksiński’s parents and sister were found in his home. They had each been shot in the head while sleeping. Two days after the attack, Oskiński himself died in hospital. On Sunday, Łukasz Wantuch, a former city councillor, shared a photograph of an announcement that there would be “a holy mass for the late Michał Oksiński and the deceased members of his family” at the Roman Catholic St Mary’s Basilica on Monday morning. The church, built in the 14th century, is one of the most famous in Poland and dominates the skyline in Kraków’s historic, UNESCO-listed city centre. It stands on one corner of the market square, just a few steps from where some of Oksiński’s victims were shot. “I won’t hide the fact that I find this somewhat shocking,” wrote Wantuch. He noted that the announcement referred to the “blessed memory” (świętej pamięci) of Oksiński. However, that phrase is standard usage in Polish to refer to someone who has died (the equivalent ot the English “late”). “But perhaps that is what faith is about: praying even for a murderer,” added Wantuch. Among the more than 1,000 comments under his Facebook post, many agreed with that sentiment. “The whole of Christianity is based on forgiving the unforgivable,” wrote one. “I don’t think anyone needs God’s mercy more [than Oksiński],” said another. However, some others were critical of the fact that the mass was being held in that particular church among the dozens in Kraków. “It is the height of impudence that they’ll celebrate mass for him in the very church he murdered in front of,” wrote one commenter. Later on Sunday, St Mary’s Basilica issued a statement, signed by parish administrator Father Mariusz Słonina, saying that the holy mass “is a private initiative of one of the priests, not of St Mary’s Parish”. However, Słonina added that “praying for the deceased is an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime, a lessening of the perpetrator’s responsibility, or a trivialisation of the suffering of the victims”. Local news service KR24 reported that uniformed police officers were posted outside the church for today’s mass while plainclothes officers were inside, with one of them right next to the altar. Three priests were present, including Słonina, who presided over the mass. Only around a dozen faithful were in attendance, with KR24 suggesting that many did not even seem aware for whom mass was being held. Separate private funeral ceremonies will take place for Oksiński, his parents and sister, who lived in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 160 km from Krakow. On Sunday, their family issued a statement asking the media to “respect the privacy, dignity and mourning of our family and loved ones”. Meanwhile, police and prosecutors continue to investigate the possible motive behind Oksiński’s attack, which they are treating as a terrorist offence. Last week, the justice minister said that there were “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the perpetrator’s online activity. Two police officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who were seriously injured in the shootout that debilitated Okisński, have been recovering in hospital after undergoing emergency surgery. World.title: Poland detains neo-Nazi teens accused of terrorist plot
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
