Poland has detained and charged three teenagers who are allegedly linked to “an international neo-Nazi network” and had been planning terrorist attacks, including with the use of homemade explosives. The arrests were announced on Monday morning by Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, who revealed that the suspects are Polish citizens. Two are aged 17 and one is 16. “The teenagers not only promoted Nazi and fascist ideology but had also already taken steps toward committing terrorist offences,” wrote Siemoniak. Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 3 obywateli RP, 16-latka i dwóch 17-latków, związanych z międzynarodowym środowiskiem neonazistowskim. ▶️ Nastolatkowie nie tylko propagowali ideologię nazistowską i faszystowską, ale podejmowali już działania zmierzające do popełniania… — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 16, 2026 The National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that the trio were “fascinated by the activities of an international neo-Nazi terrorist organisation…[that] has an ideology based on hatred against people of Jewish descent, immigrants, black people, the LGBT community, politicians and state security officials”. Though prosecutors did not name the organisation, they said that members of it have been involved in planning terrorist attacks in the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom. In some countries, including the UK, Canada and Australia, it has been outlawed and designated a terrorist group. Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) had found that the three suspects’ online communication indicated “an interest in constructing explosive devices, modifying weapons and using such items to carry out terrorist activities”. During a search of the home of one of the 17-year-olds (named only as “suspect 1”), officers found chemicals that are precursors for the production of explosives. That suspect has also been charged with possession of a so-called pipe bomb, which prosecutors say he wanted to “transfer to a neo-Nazi terrorist group”. Suspect 1 was found to have discussed with the other 17-year-old, named as suspect 2, how to construct an explosive device and detonate it in a specific residential building where someone they knew lived. Suspect 1 had also “incited extremist behaviour and hate-motivated violence” in his online activity, while the 16-year-old, named as suspect 3, had “promoted fascist content” (a crime in Poland) and encouraged someone to assault another person based on their race. Each suspect has been charged with three crimes, relating variously to terrorist offences, possession or attempted production of explosives and weapons, promoting Nazism, fascism and racial hatred, and inciting others to commit violence based on racial differences. Prosecutors note that Polish law generally allows people to face full criminal liability from the age of 17. The two 17-year-olds have therefore been placed in adult pretrial detention, while the 16-year-old is being held in a juvenile facility. Śledztwo w sprawie neonazistów i planowanych aktów terroru kryminalnego Szczegóły w komunikacie: ⬇️https://t.co/dQpdgiTYJD — Prokuratura Regionalna w Gdańsku (@Prok_Regio_GDA) November 16, 2026 The arrests come in the context of recent concerns over radicalisation of young people in Poland. Earlier this month, a 24-year-old carried out a terrorist attack in the city of Kraków, killing six people by firing a rifle from his car. He had earlier killed his parents and sister in their home. In the aftermath of the attack, justice minister Waldemar Żurek revealed that investigators had found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the attacker’s online activity, though he emphasised that the motive was yet to be determined. In the space of a few days last month, three knife attacks took place in Polish schools, resulting in one case in the death of a member of staff. Dozens of young people were arrested in the aftermath for making threats and/or possessing weapons. In September, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them has been charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. World.title: Ukraine blames Russia for graffiti glorifying WWII Ukrainian nationalists on Polish monuments
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around a dozen public monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two nationalist partisan group that was responsible for the massacre of Poles and Jews. Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia, which has previously been accused by the Polish authorities of orchestrating provocative graffiti on monuments. W sobotę, 14 listopada, w Warszawie doszło do kolejnych dwóch dewastacji pomników. Napisy „Slava UPA” pojawiły się na Pomniku Bohaterów Getta przed Muzeum Historii Żydów Polskich POLIN oraz na Pomniku Żołnierzy 1 Armii Wojska Polskiego przy ulicy Andersa 13. To kolejna odsłona… pic.twitter.com/Y7NDsfpjxn — Miejski Reporter (@MiejskiReporter) November 14, 2026 The latest spate of vandalism was first reported in early November in the western city of Poznań, where three World War two memorials were painted with graffiti saying “Glory to the UPA” (Slawa UPA). While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Local police in Poznań told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily that they were searching for a young man dressed in black who is believed to be the culprit, but have so far not been able to identify him. Similar graffiti was subsequently reported on seven monuments, including ones dedicated to Polish World War Two heroes and anti-communist protests that took place in 1970, in Gdańsk and Gdynia, neighbouring cities on Poland’s northern Baltic coast. On Friday, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian on suspicion of “painting offensive slogans propagating hatred”. They shared blurred-out images of the suspect as well as cans of spray paint. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. If convicted, he could face up to three years in prison. Previously, on Tuesday this week, MOST, a Polish-based Belarusian independent media outlet, published findings that an anonymous person on messaging service Telegram, which is popular among Russians, Ukrainians and Belarusians, had been offering $500 plus travel expenses for a job in Poznań. When an undercover MOST journalist responded to the advert, he was told that the job would involve spray painting “Glory to the UPA” on monuments. The recruiter confirmed that the job was illegal, “but if you cover your face and do everything quickly, they won’t find you”. They also revealed that similar jobs were available in other Polish cities, including Warsaw, Wrocław and Lublin. Subsequently, similar inscriptions appeared in Warsaw on the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, which honours the Jews who rose up against their German-Nazi oppressors in 1943; a monument commemorating the Polish First Army, which fought in World War Two; and a monument to sappers who served in the war. The vandalism was condemned by Poland’s Jewish Historical Institute (ŻIH), which called it a “disgraceful attack on the memory of the victims of the Holocaust and the heroes of Jewish resistance”. Noting MOST’s findings and the vandalism of other monuments, ŻIH said that “this points to the possibility of an organised provocation intended to incite hatred and divide society”. Warsaw police told PAP that they are investigating and seeking to identify the perpetrator. An unnamed police source also told Gazeta Wyborcza they see the incidents in all four cities as related to one another, pointing to the similar style of the inscriptions. On Sunday afternoon, Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, condemned the vandalism and shared images of the municipal authorities cleaning the graffiti off the Ghetto Heroes Monument. “Given the scale of similar incidents in other cities, we must consider the possibility that this is a planned provocation,” added the mayor. “Let us not let ourselves be divided – the authorities are working to identify both those who carried out these acts and those who ordered them.” Nie ma zgody na wandalizm w Warszawie. Minionej nocy służby miejskie wyczyściły pomniki oszpecone przez wandali – między innymi Pomnik Bohaterów Getta. Sprawców szuka policja. Patrząc na skalę podobnych incydentów w innych miastach, musimy brać pod uwagę, że mamy do czynienia… pic.twitter.com/5xMgPhnHf8 — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) November 15, 2026 A day earlier, on Saturday, the Ukrainian embassy had also condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation”. “In our view, these unlawful acts are a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states, and in Poland in particular,” wrote the embassy. “The objective is clear: to incite hostility between Poles and Ukrainians, undermine mutual trust, and weaken support for Ukraine.” Writing in both Polish and Ukrainian, the embassy appealed to Ukrainians “not to be tempted by offers of ‘easy money’ in exchange for painting graffiti, damaging property, or carrying out other illegal tasks” and to report any such offers to the Polish police. “Let us respect the laws of the country in which we reside, as well as historical memory and each other’s dignity,” they added. “Polish-Ukrainian solidarity is our shared strength. Let us not allow the enemy to destroy it.” Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians. Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases. In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 There have long been tensions between Poland and Ukraine over the massacres, which Poland recognises as a genocide. Ukraine rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting for independence. The issue has recently flared up again this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That sparked widespread anger in Poland and prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of his country’s highest honour. World.title: Polish president vetoes law on removing harmful online content, warning of “censorship”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has vetoed a government bill creating new powers to block harmful online content. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, argued that the measures were too far-reaching and could be abused to introduce “censorship”. Government figures have strongly criticised the president’s decision, arguing that it will leave young people in particular more exposed to dangerous content. It also means that Poland still has not fully implemented the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA). ❌ Nie dla cenzury Internetu! pic.twitter.com/WusnK7LImD — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Previously, in January this year, Nawrocki had vetoed an earlier bill intended to implement the DSA, describing the measures as “Owellian”. That prompted the government to split the legislation in two. In September, Nawrocki agreed to sign one of those bills, which appointed the president of the Office of Electronic Communications (UKE) as Poland’s digital services coordinator, responsible for overseeing enforcement of the DSA. A second bill was then needed to introduce the actual powers to block harmful online content. In October, it was approved in parliament by the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The right-wing and far-right opposition either voted against it or abstained. Among the new powers included in the legislation were authorisation for the heads of UKE and the National Broadcasting Council (KRRiT) to order the blocking of online content containing violence or threats based on race, nationality, ethnicity, religion or political affiliation. It also allowed the immediate blocking, at the request of a prosecutor or the police, of content involving the acceptance of a contract to commit murder or inciting or assisting in suicide or self-harm. “Perpetrators of serious crimes should not be allowed to use the internet to spread violence and threats,” said digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. “The state must have effective tools to quickly respond to such threats. The safety of internet users must transcend political divisions.” The government also argued that last month’s series of stabbings in schools and this month’s deadly terrorist attack in Kraków – which have raised concern about the online radicalisation of young people – have emphasised the importance of tough controls over digital content. There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister. His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 However, on Friday, the final day by which the president had to make a decision on the bill, Nawrocki announced that he was vetoing it. He argued that “the government has clearly mixed up European obligations with its own political interests”. The measures in the bill threaten to create a “censorship official” and “essentially give the government arbitrary control and the ability to decide what we can and cannot say, write or publish, said the president. Decisions on whether content is permitted or not should be “the exclusive competence of the justice system and independent judges”, he argued. Nawrocki also said that the powers in the vetoed bill were “disproportionate”, allowing an entire domain to be blocked due to a single example of illegal content. “The security of citizens cannot be a pretext for weakening their freedoms,” said Nawrocki. “We must not create a false choice: either the security or the freedom of its citizens. A responsible state must ensure and balance both.” Dlaczego Prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki zawetował ustawę o DSA? ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/1BUJVFEftl — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) November 13, 2026 Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski, however, said that the president was “not defending free speech” but instead “once again siding with global [digital] platforms and allowing them to decide what users see”. “The vetoed provisions concerned illegal content, not opinions or views expressed online,” added the ministry, which also noted that all decisions on blocking content were subject to appeals and judicial review. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, accused Nawrocki of “waging war on the government at the expense of Polish children and Polish security”, which would both be threatened by the absence of the vetoed measures. Z prezydenckiego weta zadowoleni są hejterzy, rosyjskie farmy trolli, pedofile, ekstremalni nihiliści i lobbyści. Ofiarami tego weta są polskie dzieci, rodzice, bezpieczeństwo wszystkich obywateli. Tego nie da się w żaden sposób usprawiedliwić. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) November 14, 2026 Aleksandra Wójtowicz, an analyst on new technologies at the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), told the Fakt newspaper that the measures do “not in any way relate to alleged censorship”. They are intended to force digital platforms to remove illegal content, she explained. Wójtowicz added that the measures would actually have protected free speech by giving Polish users whose accounts were unjustly deleted by social media platforms the right to appeal against those decisions outside of the platform itself. However, Nawrocki’s veto was praised by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party. Czarnek told TV Trwam that the proposed measures had been intended to “fight the opposition” rather than actual hate speech. A new hub has opened at the University of Oxford to support research cooperation with Poland, offering grants for academic projects, visits, training and workshops. The Oxford Poland Hub, which its organisers describe as Poland’s first initiative of its kind anywhere in the world, will also hold public events exploring Polish history, language and culture. We’re proud to have worked on the Oxford-Poland Hub & helped make it a reality together with great partners 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Huge thanks to: 🔹 @UniofOxford & @JesusOxford, esp. Prof Paulina Kewes & Dr Marek Naczyk 🔹 Ministry of Science and Higher Education & Minister @MarcinKulasek 🧵 pic.twitter.com/LghfpOhptC — Polish Embassy UK 🇵🇱 (@PolishEmbassyUK) November 12, 2026 “The launch of the Oxford-Poland Hub is an exciting new chapter in Oxford’s longstanding relationship with Poland,” said the University of Oxford’s vice-chancellor, Irene Tracey. “[It] will create new opportunities for academic exchange, collaborative research and partnership between Oxford and Poland.” The centre is initially funded for three years by Poland’s National Agency for Academic Exchange (NAWA), with support from the science and higher education ministry. It will operate within The Oxford Research Centre in the Humanities (TORCH). “The Oxford Poland Hub…gives us a permanent institutional presence at one of the world’s leading academic centres,” said Wojciech Karczewski, NAWA’s director general. “We see it as an investment in long-term partnerships that will enable researchers from Poland and Oxford to tackle increasingly ambitious research challenges together.” The University of Oxford is the oldest university in the English-speaking world and one of the most prestigious. It ranked first globally in the latest Times Higher Education World University Rankings. The new centre will offer grants of up to £5,000 (26,400 zloty) to support research projects or academic visits and up to £10,000 for academic workshops. Training scholarships are due to be introduced from the hub’s second year. All researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford will be eligible to apply for funding if their work involves collaboration with researchers based in Poland. The hub will focus on humanities and social sciences as well as cooperation with Oxford’s libraries and museums. The hub will also organise public lectures, exhibitions and events related to Polish history, language and culture for the academic community and Oxford’s residents, including its Polish community. 🇵🇱🇬🇧 Oxford-Poland Hub oficjalnie otwarty! Polska nauka zyskuje nowe możliwości współpracy z Uniwersytetem Oksfordzkim. W uroczystym otwarciu wziął udział minister nauki i szkolnictwa wyższego Marcin Kulasek. Centrum powstało dzięki współpracy Ministerstwa Nauki i Szkolnictwa… pic.twitter.com/bZaCdM3Y53 — Ministerstwo Nauki i Szkolnictwa Wyższego (@MNiSW_GOV__PL) November 10, 2026 The hub was inaugurated on Monday at Jesus College, one of Oxford University’s colleges, with Poland’s science and higher education minister, Marcin Kulasek, and Rafał Wiśniewski, chargé d’affaires at the Polish Embassy in London, among those attending. “Poland and the United Kingdom have for many years developed strong cooperation in science and higher education through joint research projects, academic mobility programmes and institutional partnerships,” Kulasek said. “The Oxford–Poland Hub opens a new chapter in this cooperation.” The centre is directed by Paulina Kewes, a professor of English literature at Oxford who was born in Poland. Professor Norman Davies, the renowned historian of Poland and an honorary fellow at St Antony’s College, Oxford, attended the launch. The inaugural lecture, given by Dariusz Wójcik, a professor at the National University of Singapore and honorary research associate at the University of Oxford, discussed Maria Czaplicka, the renowned Polish academic who in 1916 became Oxford’s first female lecturer of anthropology. A Belgian court has overturned an order to seize funds from Poland’s air-traffic control agency, PANSA, as part of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer’s efforts to enforce a €1.3 billion claim for COVID-19 vaccines Poland ordered but later refused to receive and pay for. The ruling, issued on Thursday, followed a legal challenge by PANSA to the freezing of its funds. It argued that it was not a party to the dispute between Pfizer and the Polish state. ❗️Dziś Francuskojęzyczny Sąd Pierwszej Instancji w Brukseli wydał korzystny dla strony polskiej wyrok w sprawie zajęcia opłat trasowych należnych @PANSA_PL , pobieranych za pośrednictwem EUROCONTROL. Sąd uznał zajęcie za bezzasadne i uchylił postanowienie, na podstawie którego… pic.twitter.com/EHvHZnL6ab — Ministerstwo Zdrowia (@MZ_GOV_PL) November 12, 2026 In July this year, PANSA announced that it had been cut off from the fees paid to it by the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol), which manages air traffic in Europe. Around 80% of PANSA’s revenue comes from those fees. Eurocontrol is based in Belgium, which is where Pfizer has been fighting its legal battle against Poland over the unpaid vaccines. The move to freeze PANSA’s funds was part of Pfizer’s efforts to claim money it had been awarded from Poland by a Belgian court in April this year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk pledged government support to ensure PANSA had sufficient funds to maintain its operations and assured that air safety would not be compromised. Poland’s air-traffic control agency has been cut off from most of its revenue as part of efforts by pharmaceutical giant Pfizer to enforce a Belgian court ruling requiring Poland to pay €1.3bn for Covid vaccines it ordered but then refused to receive https://t.co/Nd9IyLqmmf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 11, 2026 On Thursday this week, PANSA announced that its legal challenge to the seizure of its assets by bailiffs had been successful, though it noted that the ruling can still be appealed. Poland’s health ministry, which has been involved in overseeing the legal battle with Pfizer, said that the Belgian court had confirmed that PANSA’s funds belong to the agency itself, not to the State treasury. “The agency is a separate legal entity; it possesses its own assets and manages its own finances independently. It is not liable for the obligations of the State treasury; therefore, its funds cannot be used to satisfy Pfizer’s claims against Poland,” wrote the ministry. In comments to Polish Radio, PANSA chief Magdalena Jaworska-Maćkowiak said the agency had become a hostage in a case “that did not, in fact, concern us”. “It stemmed from an entirely separate dispute,” she noted. “This created extreme difficulties, as we were relying on a ‘bridge’ financing arrangement that, under current law, could not provide us with long-term stability.” Pfizer, meanwhile, said Thursday’s court decision affected only one avenue of its efforts to enforce payment of the April ruling. “We are taking ​appropriate steps through ​established legal ⁠and contractual mechanisms to ensure compliance with the court’s [April] decision,” it added, quoted by Reuters. Sąd w Brukseli uznał sprzeciw PAŻP wobec zajęcia komorniczego dokonanego na wniosek Pfizer za zasadny i uchylił postanowienie z 25 czerwca 2026 r., stanowiące podstawę zajęcia komorniczego. Rozstrzygnięcie jest zatem korzystne dla PAŻP, ale wyrok nie jest jeszcze prawomocny. — PANSA (@PANSA_PL) November 12, 2026 The dispute stems from Poland’s refusal in 2022 to accept and pay for COVID-19 vaccine doses ordered from Pfizer under European Union procurement agreements. In April 2022, the then health minister, Adam Niedzielski, invoked a force majeure clause following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 Poland, which by then had already sold or donated some of its surplus vaccines, argued the mass influx of Ukrainian refugees strained its public finances, while its cases of Covid infections had dropped. Romania later made a similar decision to not comply with the contract. In 2023, Pfizer sued both countries in Belgium, the country where the contracts were signed. Over the course of the case, Poland also argued that Pfizer had potentially abused its market position. A Belgian court has ordered Poland to pay US pharmaceutical giant Pfizer around €1.3 billion for Covid vaccines ordered by the European Commission on behalf of member states during the pandemic but which the Polish government later refused to receive https://t.co/1ZtPgl8Y3o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 But in April, a Belgian court rejected those arguments and ruled in Pfizer’s favour, ordering Poland to accept approximately 64 million vaccine doses and pay more than 5.6 billion zloty, plus interest and legal costs. Poland appealed against the judgment in August 2026. The health ministry said on Thursday it would not disclose details of its legal arguments or planned procedural steps while the proceedings remain ongoing. World.title: Temporary no longer: Ukrainian refugees in Poland confront the long term
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Leo Greenberg Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back. “We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said. Zelensky: We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu — Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026 Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return. A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority. This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty. A new reality sets in When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year. When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.” Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.” In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023 For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland. The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens. So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes. Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022 For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad. Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers. Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026. “Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited. Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return. Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May. ⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin. "This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0 — The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025 So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.” Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools. Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return. Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration. However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs. Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.” So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back. From welcome to wariness in Poland Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland. Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees. The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits. Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced. Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added. Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment. She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps. Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay. Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners. Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026 This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency. Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status. Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.” The citizenship question At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections. An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier. In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry. The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values. Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day. Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”. The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply. Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”. Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.” Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for. At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that. For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says. For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”. At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland dismisses Russia’s claim of breaking up Polish spy network as “disinformation”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. After Russia announced that it had dismantled a Polish spy network and arrested two alleged agents, Poland has dismissed the claims as “disinformation” and a “provocation”. On Wednesday, while Poland was celebrating its national Independence Day, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) announced that it had “disrupted the activities of an intelligence network of the Polish special services operating in Kaliningrad”, a Russian exclave that borders Poland. It claimed to have detained two “agents”- one working for Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW), the other for the Internal Security Agency (ABW) – who had been “collecting and transmitting information about military personnel and facilities” and “the socio-economic situation in the Kaliningrad region”. The FSB added that seven Polish citizens and three Russians who had had contact with Polish intelligence agencies had been “officially warned”, and that the Polish citizens had been banned from entering Russia. The agency also published a film containing images of alleged suspects being detained and various documents and telephone messages in Polish. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the arrests would not further worsen relations with Poland given ties between the two countries “essentially do not exist right now,” reported the RIA news agency. In a statement on Wednesday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for Poland’s security services, said that he regarded the Russian announcement “as yet another provocation and act of disinformation”, especially as it had been released on Polish Independence Day. He added that he would not comment further and “appealed to everyone not to amplify hostile narratives or play into Russian propaganda”. Speaking to news website Wirtualna Polska, Maciej Wewiór, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, said that Poland was working to verify the information announced by the FSB. However, he urged “extreme caution” when dealing with such claims from Russia. “Let’s not fall for Russian propaganda and become pawns in this game,” he said. Jako rzecznik ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych nie komentuję materiałów zamieszczanych w sieci przez rosyjskie służby. 🛑 W dniu Narodowego Święta Niepodległości traktuję je szczególnie jako kolejną prowokację i dezinformację. 🛑 Apeluję o niepowielanie wrogiej narracji i… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) November 11, 2026 Polish fact-checking and investigative journalism service OKO.press also raised doubts about the material shared by Russia. It notes that the alleged Polish-language phone messages released by the FSB have unnatural wording and appear to have been translated from Russian. It also points out that the footage showing the alleged detentions appears to have been recorded much earlier, judging by the green folliage on trees. This assessment was echoed by Stanisław Żaryn, who served as spokesman for the security services from 2016 to 2022. He said that “fabricated propaganda materials” were clearly “prepared in advance” and “fit the Russian security services’ ongoing campaign against Poland”. “It should be assumed that, in its operation against Poland, Moscow will resort to fabricated evidence, and today’s FSB statement will be used to legitimise earlier accusations against Poland of preparing an attack on Kaliningrad,” he added. #InfoAlert. Kolejna rosyjska prowokacja. FSB twierdzi, że rozbiła polską siatkę szpiegowską pracującą w Obwodzie Królewieckim. Analiza komunikacji rosyjskiej wskazuje, że mamy do czynienia z zaplanowaną sekwencją działań informacyjnych. Wpisuje się ona w stałe oddziaływanie… pic.twitter.com/s6bTV9pIK8 — Stanisław Żaryn (@StZaryn) November 11, 2026 The FSB’s announcement came a week after Poland announced that it had detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components, which were smuggled over the border into Kaliningrad. Poland also sent additional security personnel to its regions along the Russian border this month following intelligence reports suggesting a planned act of sabotage or other provocation there. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later claimed that “individuals with flashlights” had been spotted at the border but “we very quickly mobilised the appropriate forces and managed to prevent a provocation”. Poland recently launched a special operation along the Russian border after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. For more, see our report from yesterday:https://t.co/RVaXb6SQJI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2026 Poland has seen a sharp rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Moscow in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates on its territory, prompting Russia to do the same with Polish consulates in a tit-for-tat move. World.title: Now in English! Experience 17 November 1989 in Prague With a Free Audio Walk
World.content:
As Prague marks the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution on November 17, visitors and international residents can follow the route of the 1989 student demonstration through a free English-language audio walk.

Created by SmartGuide in cooperation with Korzo Národní, the walk follows the students’ journey from Albertov, through Vyšehrad and along the Vltava River to Národní třída, where the demonstration was violently suppressed by communist police on November 17, 1989.



The newly released English edition allows those who do not speak Czech to explore one of the defining moments in modern Czech history through eyewitness accounts, historical recordings and stories connected to the locations along the route.

The audio walk uses the original recordings made during the events, including accounts from people who witnessed the demonstrations.

Its English version also includes dubbed radio communications between agents of StB, the communist secret police, giving listeners an insight into how security forces monitored and prepared for the student demonstration.

Unlike a traditional guided tour, the walk can be completed independently, at any time and at the participant’s own pace. It requires no booking or app download. Visitors only need a smartphone and headphones to follow the route and listen to the recordings at the relevant locations.

The starting point is Albertov, where students gathered on November 17, 1989, for a demonstration commemorating the 1939 Nazi crackdown on Czech universities and marking International Students’ Day. What began as a permitted march later developed into a turning point in the country’s history.

After the demonstration was blocked by police on Národní třída, news of the crackdown spread across the country, helping trigger a wave of protests that eventually brought down the communist regime. Within weeks, Czechoslovakia had begun its transition to democracy, in what became known as the Velvet Revolution.

World.title: INTERVIEW: “We Chose the Riskier Option”: From Nashville to Prague, With No Regrets
World.content:
Seven years ago, Joshua Hayden swapped a secure career in Nashville for Prague, drawn by his research on Václav Havel and Charter 77. Today he teaches leadership at Anglo-American University, where Václav Havel, poetry and the spirit of 1989 are part of the curriculum.



Joshua Hayden, EdD, holds a doctorate in leadership from Vanderbilt University and taught at three universities around Nashville, Tennessee, before moving his family to Prague. At Anglo-American University (AAU), the country’s oldest private university founded in 1990, he is the Department Chair of Social Sciences, teaches the psychology of leadership, ethics and leadership, and a summer course on the Czech dissident tradition.

Ahead of November 17, we talked to him about teaching far from home, why small classes matter more than ever in the age of AI, and why Havel’s words still resonate with students today.

You built your career in Nashville. Why did you leave it for Prague?

Before my family and I moved to Prague, I worked at three universities in and just outside Nashville, Tennessee. I earned my doctoral degree in leadership at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, and my wife and I really loved the city. After a lot of discernment and prayer, we decided to live a bigger story for our family and move to Prague, partly because of my research on Václav Havel and Charter 77.

During that year of transition, I was offered a job running a leadership program at a liberal arts college. It was in a small town in the US, so we had a choice between the risk of moving internationally in the hope of teaching leadership and the “sure thing” of running a program in the US. We chose the riskier option. What I remember most about that time is the assurance that we were making the right decision, come what may.

Teaching Far From Home

What’s it like to teach in a country that isn’t your own, to students who are often far from home too?

It’s just the kind of challenge I was looking for. I’ve learned so much in dialogue with students, and in many classes we end up talking about cross-cultural differences. The adjustment for me meant trading many of my American examples for international ones. I often ask students to share their cultural perspectives and interpretations of the research and data I share in class. On the other hand, for all the cultural differences, I am struck by the commonalities between cultures and the connections that can be made if we are open to them.

For example, I include poems in my class on the psychology of leadership. Poems and leadership? Yes! Poems have a way of expressing the human condition and the dynamics of change, power, resistance and critical engagement that are really at the heart of leadership. I include poems from different cultures around the world, and one day we used a Polish poem. A Polish student looked it up in her own language after reading it in English and showed us how the author used political and subversive terms. Our class had a great discussion about how language shapes our own and other people’s reality. She brought a cultural perspective that I did not anticipate, and it added so much to our class.

Small Classes, Big Difference

What happens in a small class that you’d never see in a big lecture hall?

Students learn at a much deeper and more active level. There are experimental studies showing that students in active-learning classes learn more than those in traditional lectures, even if they don’t feel they learned more. I’ve found that when I get students into groups working on problems and applying the course materials, they correct each other’s misunderstandings and get immediate feedback.

Written and verbal feedback is another thing that sets small classes apart from large ones, and the more frequent feedback students get on how they explain, apply and synthesize information, the more higher-order learning takes place. I think one misconception old-school professors tend to have is that if students enjoy discussing and working actively in the classroom, there must be less learning going on, because you aren’t covering as much material. But the evidence does not support this.

Especially in the AI-saturated world we all live in, practicing social and argumentative skills, problem-solving and critical thinking in the classroom is more important than ever. In my classes we have case studies, role plays, simulations and hands-on experiments, we go on field trips, and we have small-group discussions. Students are rarely distracted by technology if they are immersed in a problem, a group task or a deep discussion. I have the same challenges all professors do in the classroom, but the small, diverse classes we have are great environments for deeper learning.

If you could take one AAU class as a student, which would it be and why?

Take a colleague’s class? I would take Professor Ondřej Pilný’s course Theatre and Politics or Pavla Jonssonová’s Czech Culture in Film and Literature. They are both great teachers!

Do you stay in touch with former students? Is there one whose story surprised you?

Yes, I do stay in touch with former students, and I love to follow their lives and careers. One of my thesis advisees had a profound experience taking a course in South Africa, went on to write a great thesis, graduated and then pursued her passion for pottery. I gave her a copy of one of my favorite books, Let Your Life Speak by Parker Palmer, and she read it while working in a pottery studio in California. She wrote to me about it, and later she came to Prague and told me she was in the process of opening her own pottery studio.

Some of us take the necessary path of getting a job that works for the lifestyle we want, but I love it when former students take risks and go for something they are passionate about that also serves others.

Havel in the Classroom

You’ve spent years studying Václav Havel. How does he show up in your classes?

I teach a summer leadership course on the Czech dissident tradition. It starts with Jan Hus and ends with Václav Havel: his early life and absurdist theatre – we see his plays performed – and the context of communist Czechoslovakia in the 1950s and 1960s, his emergence as a “dissident” in the 1970s and 1980s, and finally his presidency. I am much more interested in taking a critical approach, discussing Havel in his social, economic and political context and in relation to artists, writers, former communists, rock bands and philosophers.

Havel also shows up in my Ethics and Leadership course, where we use ethical theories to examine the leadership of various historical and contemporary figures. I use Gabriel Marcel’s ethics of hope to look at Havel and others and their collaboration in starting Charter 77, VONS (the Committee for the Defense of the Unjustly Prosecuted) and other human rights groups. We read his Letter to Husák, The Power of the Powerless and the speech he gave as president when he received the Sonning Prize.

I’ve found Havel’s 1990 New Year’s Address helpful in other leadership courses I teach, such as Leadership and the Self. We look at the context of the speech and how he called on his listeners to take responsibility for their society after communism fell, instead of seeing themselves only as victims.

The Spirit of 1989

AAU was founded in 1990, right after the Velvet Revolution. Does that history still feel present at the university today?

It does, thanks to the initiative of our faculty and their desire for students to catch the spirit of the revolution: a love of freedom, democracy and dialogue – all great outcomes of a university education. My colleague Monika MacDonagh-Pajerová was literally one of the student leaders of ’89. She teaches a very popular course and weaves her experience and relationships into it.

About six years ago, I created a walking tour of the Velvet Revolution for our students and staff, which takes place every November 17. Colleagues who remember the communist days usually join us, and some of them were actually there on Národní třída on November 17, 1989. Other colleagues teach courses that involve Havel and other Czech artists and dissidents.

We regularly have events and special guests that bring that history alive. A few colleagues and I are “screening” a radio play Havel wrote, Guardian Angel, and then discussing it with our students and faculty. This play captures so many themes highly relevant to us today: technology and humanity, the nature of trust, listening, and how the powerful understand the needs of others. Of course, it was written under communism in the 1960s – it’s history – but it also has a timeless quality to it.

Why Prague?

If a student were choosing whether to study in Prague, what would you tell them?

I hope that a student would choose Prague to get immersed in its culture and history, not to live in a bubble. The Czech Republic has so much to offer. It is rich in history and beautiful, in and outside of Prague. It is also in the heart of Europe, so you can jump on a train and visit so many cultures and people. The city is safe and walkable, and it has a nice pace of life. After seven years, I never get tired of the sights, the streets to roam and the places to get good beer.

I think many students find it refreshing, especially those coming from large schools, that AAU is small and a close community. It is quite an intellectual place, so I see many students having deeper conversations in groups than I had ever seen in the places I’ve worked before. If you are coming from far away, it is a transformative experience to be a foreigner and live in such a different culture. You’ll never be the same. In a good way.

About Anglo-American University

Founded in 1990, Anglo-American University (AAU) is the oldest private university in the Czech Republic and offers bachelor’s and master’s programs taught entirely in English. It holds both Czech and US (WSCUC) accreditation, and its campus is located in the Thurn-Taxis Palace just below Prague Castle. More information at aauni.edu.

World.title: Love Sausages? Prague Has a New Bistro Serving Berlin-Style Currywurst
World.content:
Prague has a new fast-food spot dedicated to one of Germany’s best-known street dishes.

Currywurst11 opened on Palackého Street on November 11, serving German sausages with a selection of traditional and locally inspired sauces.

The project took nine months to prepare. Its menu features several types of German sausage, including traditional grilled bratwurst, Bauernwurst with herbs and steamed Bockwurst.

A vegetarian option made from peas is also available.

The sausages are served with tomato-based curry sauce, but customers can choose from several alternatives. These include an American-style version made with Coca-Cola, a Czech-inspired sauce combining plum butter, caraway seeds and beer, and a honey-mustard option.

Side dishes include French fries, bread, sauerkraut, pickled vegetables and kimchi.

The drinks menu features German bottled beers, homemade lemonades and Spezi, a popular German mix of cola and orange soda. Seasonal specials are also planned, with Pizza-Fleischkäse, a meatloaf-style sausage with cheese and red peppers, among the current offerings.

A currywurst with sauce costs CZK 150, with side dishes available for an additional CZK 20.

Currywurst11 is the latest venture from Ondřej Bednář, Tomáš Huml and Martin Červenka, the three entrepreneurs behind Dim Sum Spot.

They opened their first restaurant in Prague’s Letná district in 2019 and have since expanded to several locations in Prague and one in Liberec.

The partners initially considered opening an Asian noodle shop in the space next to their existing restaurant on Palackého Street. They eventually opted for German street food instead.

World.title: Apple’s New Christmas Short Film Features Prague and Czech Landmarks
World.content:
Apple has released its latest Christmas commercial, a four-minute short film featuring several locations across Prague, including a metro carriage, a housing estate and one of the city’s best-known landmarks.

Titled The Dreamer, the film follows a boy with a talent for drawing who faces difficulties at school and in his personal life but continues pursuing his ambition of becoming an artist.



The story centres on the support of someone who believes in his abilities. The commercial also promotes Apple’s latest MacBook laptops.

Several scenes were filmed in Prague, with locations from different parts of the city appearing throughout the film.

One sequence features a Soviet-era 81-71 metro carriage, a model still used by the Prague Public Transit Company for special retro services.

The production also visited Vršovice, where scenes were shot in the courtyard of the Sídliště Vlasta housing estate.

Another recognisable location appears towards the end of the film, when the main character, now an adult, walks home past Strahov Stadium.

K Topírně Street provided the backdrop for two further scenes. In one, a Czech Railways Pendolino train passes through the frame. In another, the protagonist runs alongside the railway tracks after a fight. The steel lattice road bridge on Moskevská Street can be seen in the background.

The school scenes were filmed at Hanspaulka Elementary School (Základní škola Hanspaulka). It is here that the young protagonist receives a marked maths test with the teacher’s handwritten instruction to “focus”.

Apple has a long history of filming advertising campaigns in the Czech Republic, regularly choosing the country and Prague in particular as locations for international productions.

World.title: Will Žabka Become Albert? 113 Stores Change Hands in Czech Republic
World.content:
The future of the Žabka convenience store chain in the Czech Republic is uncertain after its acquisition by Ahold Delhaize, the international retail group behind Albert supermarkets.

The deal covers all 113 Žabka locations in the country, but it remains unclear whether the stores will keep their existing name or eventually become part of the Albert network.



Ahold Delhaize agreed to acquire Tesco’s operations in the Czech Republic and Slovakia in late October. The transaction includes Tesco’s hypermarkets and supermarkets, as well as the Žabka chain, which operates through Tesco’s subsidiary, Tesco Franchise Stores ČR.

Customers and franchise operators should not expect immediate changes. The transaction is not expected to close before the fourth quarter of 2027. Until then, Tesco will remain responsible for managing the business.

In its announcement, Ahold Delhaize said it planned to modernise the acquired stores and bring their product ranges and loyalty programmes closer to those offered by Albert. However, the company has not confirmed whether Žabka will retain its brand or be gradually rebranded.

Žabka entered the Czech Republic in 2008, when investment group Penta brought the Polish convenience store concept to the country. Three years later, Tesco acquired the chain together with the Koruna network.

Ahold, meanwhile, has repeatedly brought acquired retail chains under the Albert brand. Its previous portfolio included Mana, Sezam, Prima and Hypernova, as well as stores operated by Julius Meinl.

Tesco Franchise Stores ČR, the company operating Žabka, reported a profit of CZK 16.6 million for the financial year ending in February 2026. A year earlier, it had recorded a loss of CZK 13 million.

The figures have prompted questions about whether all existing locations will remain open.

World.title: From Rugby Pitch to Prague Bistro: The Story Behind SAFFA MASO
World.content:
Founded by former rugby player Nicolaas Uys, the business has grown from a small biltong venture into a bistro celebrating South African cuisine.

We spoke with Uys about his journey to Prague, the Saffa Maso story and his plans for the future.

Uys’ Journey to Prague

Nicolaas Uys initially came to Prague to pursue an opportunity to continue his rugby career. He eventually joined the Czech national rugby team.

After 11 years in the sport, Uys decided to step away from rugby and devote more time to his biltong business before opening a bistro to expand the concept.

His first impression of Prague was unlike anything he had experienced before.



“I was more used to a safari,” he says, laughing. “In South Africa, the environment around me was flat compared to Prague. There was no public transport and no big buildings in sight. I almost felt claustrophobic.”

Today, Uys has adapted well to life in Prague and enjoys living in the city with his family.

Prague’s Growing Interest in South African Food

When Uys first arrived in Prague in 2017, South African cuisine was largely unknown in the Czech capital.

“It was a niche market, which is why it was difficult for me to introduce it to local people,” he says.

That has gradually changed. Interest in South African food has grown, and SAFFA MASO now attracts both curious newcomers and returning customers.

The bistro has also become a place for sports fans, particularly during rugby matches. Uys uses a projector to show major sporting events on the wall, while a television allows people sitting outside to follow the action as well.

“During the FIFA World Cup this summer, many people watched from outside. It was crazy,” he says with a smile.

What Makes South African Cuisine Different?

For Uys, one of the defining features of South African cuisine is its distinctive use of spices.

“The most unique thing about South African food is the strong use of spices. Many visitors come in specifically to try them and even buy our spices,” he says.

He also believes the freshness and handmade nature of many South African dishes appeal to customers in Prague.

“Most of the food from my home country is handmade and very fresh, and that attracts people here. It makes me happy to see the appreciation for the food growing,” he adds.

Plans for the Future

Today, Uys and his family have settled in Prague. However, when the Czech winter arrives, he occasionally returns to South Africa to “chase the sun” until the weather in Prague becomes warmer again.

Looking ahead, he is working on a new project: a bar combining his love of rugby with his passion for South African food and music.

“The upper part is planned as a restaurant where people can also watch sports events, while the lower part could be used as a club playing Afrobeats,” he explains. “However, it is still a work in progress.”

For now, SAFFA MASO continues to introduce Prague to the flavours of South Africa — one plate of biltong, spice and home-style cooking at a time.

World.title: Bohemian Burlesque Festival Returns to Prague for Its 10th Anniversary
World.content:
The Bohemian Burlesque Festival returns for its 10th anniversary, bringing four nights of international performances and a daytime market to Ostrava (already sold out), Brno, and Prague.

The festival, the largest burlesque event in the Czech Republic, will welcome a record 100 performers from 20 countries for this year’s edition. The programme combines classic burlesque, cabaret, contemporary performances, and vintage glamour.



This year’s theme is French-inspired, with three of the festival’s guest performers and headliners coming from France. Artists from Finland, Lithuania, and Estonia will also join performers from across Europe and beyond, alongside Czech talent.

Two major international names lead the programme. Medianoche, originally from New York and raised in Spain, is one of the industry’s best-known performers and won the prestigious Miss Exotic World title in 2017. Representing France, Chanelle de Mai is an acclaimed performer and costume designer known for her elaborate acts and precise choreography.

They will be joined by French special guests Vicomte Harbourg and drag performer Chantaaaal.

Prague will host three festival events over two days, all taking place at Hotel Belvedere in Prague 7.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bohemian Burlesque Festival (@bohemianburlesquefestival)

The programme opens on Friday, November 20, with Bohemian Cabaret Prague, a gala evening featuring international headliners, professional performers, and local artists. The show starts at 20:00, with doors opening at 19:15.

On Saturday, November 21, the festival continues with the Bohemian Market, running from 12:00 to 18:00. Visitors can browse vintage clothing, accessories, jewellery, lingerie, and burlesque-inspired fashion.

It is also a great opportunity to enjoy plenty of burlesque at an affordable price: tickets cost just CZK 350, making it a good alternative for those who miss out on the evening shows.

The programme also includes fashion shows, retro hair and makeup services, photo sessions, discussions about body image, interviews with festival guests, and performances by 24 emerging burlesque artists. A pin-up competition, live singer, and magician are also planned.

The weekend concludes with Bohemian Queen Night, the festival’s closing gala, starting at 20:30. Twelve performers from around the world will compete for the titles of Bohemian Queen and Bohemian Princess, as well as the Best Costume Award.

A new feature for 2026 will give audience members the opportunity to vote for their favourite performer in an Audience Choice Award. Festival headliners and special guests will serve as judges and perform during the second half of the evening.

Both evening shows will feature a raffle and a Best Dressed Audience competition, with prizes for visitors who arrive in their finest outfits.

World.title: Prague Adds Special Trams and More Metro Services for Letná Demonstration
World.content:
Prague is preparing for a large demonstration at Letná on Sunday, November 15, with additional public transport services planned to accommodate the expected crowds.

The city will increase the frequency of trains on all three metro lines and introduce two temporary tram routes, numbered 40 and 44, to help transport participants to and from the demonstration.



Organized by the Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek) movement, the event is expected to attract thousands of people from across the Czech Republic. Organizers are anticipating a record turnout.

The additional tram services are intended to ease pressure on regular routes, particularly around Letná and neighbouring districts.

Metro services will run more frequently between 11:30 a.m. and 7 p.m. on Sunday.

Tram 40 will operate from approximately noon until 7 p.m., running every five minutes. It will connect Letná with all three metro lines, travelling from Palmovka through Florenc, Vltavská, Hradčanská and Dejvická before terminating at Červený Vrch.

Tram 44 will also run at five-minute intervals, but only from noon until approximately 3 p.m. Starting at Špejchar, the route will pass through Strossmayerovo náměstí and Výstaviště towards Nádraží Holešovice. It will then continue around Holešovická tržnice, pass Vltavská and return to Letná.

The second route is intended primarily for passengers arriving on Metro Line C.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Milion chvilek pro demokracii (@milionchvilek)

Despite the additional services, transport authorities warn that overcrowding and delays are likely, particularly at Hradčanská, Vltavská and Nádraží Holešovice stations and on connecting tram routes.

According to Prague 7 authorities, the busiest periods are expected shortly before the demonstration starts and immediately after it ends. The greatest pressure on public transport is anticipated before 2 p.m. and at around 4 p.m.

Tram Disruptions Elsewhere in Prague

Passengers should also expect changes to regular tram services in central Prague.

From approximately 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., trams will be temporarily suspended in the area between Palackého náměstí, Národní divadlo, Jiráskovo náměstí and Myslíkova Street.

Tram lines 5 and 17 will be diverted via Karlovo náměstí during this period.

Road Restrictions and Changes to Letná Ice Rink

Drivers heading towards Letná should also expect traffic restrictions and temporary road closures in the surrounding area. The city recommends avoiding car travel to the demonstration and allowing extra time for journeys.

World.title: Budapest faces new rival in race to host the 2036 Olympic Games
World.content:
Hungary’s capital has a new competitor in the race to host the 2036 Summer Olympics, as South Korea’s North Jeolla Province has decided to submit an independent bid after talks with Seoul collapsed.

North Jeolla Province announced on Monday that it would pursue a solo bid to host the 2036 Summer Olympics after failing to reach an agreement with South Korea’s capital over a potential joint application, The Korea Times reported.

The province’s governor, Lee Won-taeg, and Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon met last Thursday and agreed to abandon the joint bid, citing differences in their respective circumstances and positions.

“We will now make a concerted push to host the Olympics alone,” the provincial government said in a statement.

Seoul raises concerns over infrastructure

North Jeolla had previously moved towards a joint bid with Seoul after acknowledging that it lacked the infrastructure needed to host an event of this scale independently. The shortcomings included accommodation, transport links and sports venues.

Seoul initially appeared open to the idea. On 7 October, Mayor Oh said he had “no reason to reject” the province’s proposal, but also called on it to present concrete construction plans for the venues.

However, the two sides ultimately decided not to proceed together.

Hungary among seven Olympic hopefuls

North Jeolla’s announcement comes as the international race to host the 2036 Games gathers pace. On 3 November, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) included South Korea among seven countries interested in hosting the event.

The other candidates are Germany, Hungary – with Budapest as its proposed host city – India, Qatar, South Africa and Türkiye.

The candidates are expected to deliver virtual presentations to the IOC’s Future Host Commission later in November. The IOC Executive Board is scheduled to open a strategic dialogue with the prospective hosts in March 2027.

South Korea has previously hosted two Olympic Games: the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul and the 2018 Winter Olympics in PyeongChang.

Budapest entered the race earlier this year

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) confirmed in October that Hungary is one of seven interested parties currently in continuous dialogue over the 2036 Olympics.

The selection process will take several years. The current interested parties will present their projects to the Future Host Commission in November 2026. By March 2027, the IOC is expected to complete feasibility assessments and open a more detailed Strategic Dialogue with the candidates.

The 2036 Olympic host is expected to be elected by IOC members in mid-2029.

World.title: Hungary blocks the EU’s EUR 45 billion funding for Ukraine, but what will the consequences be?
World.content:
Hungary is among four European Union member states opposing a proposed EUR 45 billion joint loan to help finance Ukraine, putting the bloc’s plans to secure Kyiv’s funding at risk. The dispute could also become entangled with negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget, as Germany considers using its veto power to pressure reluctant governments.

Magyar government to block Ukraine’s funding

The European Commission is preparing to propose borrowing EUR 45 billion against the EU budget to cover a substantial part of Ukraine’s expected financing needs next year, the Financial Times reported. Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria have indicated that they do not wish to take part in the arrangement.

Ukraine faces an estimated EUR 70 billion funding shortfall as it prepares for what is expected to be its toughest winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. The proposed loan would follow a model used last year, when the EU arranged EUR 90 billion in financing. Hungary secured an exemption from participating in that package.
