Ms. Ruma Saha was protesting against an incident where a businessman was beaten up on Saturday (November 14, 2026) when she was subjected to verbal abuse by a fellow party worker. When Mr. Arup Saha — who was also an active BJP worker — intervened, a scuffle broke out in which he sustained injuries.

He was admitted to a State-run hospital on Saturday (November 14, 2026), but succumbed to his injuries on Sunday (November 15, 2026).

Ms. Debnath, who was also seen grieving with wife of the deceased, alleged that party workers who joined the ruling party after May 4, 2026 — when the West Bengal State Assembly election results were announced — were responsible for the crime.

“District president (BJP president) has appointed conveners of his choice in various wards of Panihati. Most of them have joined the BJP from Trinamool,” Ms. Debnath said.

The mother of Abhaya (a doctor at RG Kar Hospital, who was raped and killed on August 9, 2024), who also joined the BJP just before the 2026 Assembly polls, said that ward coordinators have been placed unofficially in all 29 wards of Panihati Municipality. All of them are Trinamool supporters.

Political observers say that the majority of the BJP leadership, including Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, had joined the party about five to six years ago.

The factional feud between BJP leaders came to the fore at Barrackpore, in the same district, on Sunday (November 15, 2026), where slogans of “go back” were raised against BJP MLA Kaustav Bagchi, allegedly by supporters from his own party.

According to reports, Mr. Bagchi has raised allegations that illegal businesses are being operated in his constituency.

Those protesting against him alleged that the MLA had gone out to distribute Chhath Puja sarees with the accused in the murder of a BJP leader.

World.title: Dar says Pakistan to host next Makkah alliance summit later this month
World.content:
Pakistan will host the next meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance’s apex committee, likely later this month, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Monday.

He made the remarks while answering a query during a press briefing regarding a ministerial meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) held in Islamabad.

Asked about regional security architecture, Dar recalled the Aug 7 signing of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. The pact empowers the three states to treat an attack on any one of them as an attack on all.

Providing details on the alliance’s progress, Dar noted that its apex committee, called the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC), “will actually be meeting, hopefully [at the] end of this month, in Islamabad”.

“We offered in our inaugural meeting that our next formal meeting will be held in Islamabad and everybody accepted,” he said, noting that an emergency meeting of the SPDC was held in Riyadh last month amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The SPDC comprises the foreign and defence ministers of the three countries, as well as their top military officials.

In response to the question about a possible new security architecture for the region, Dar said: “Well, let me be very honest with you. I think time and again, different regions, including this region, have witnessed that the need and the best way to have regional security is to have some sort of security at the local or domestic architecture.

“In other words, this region should have its own security architecture. Maybe this is a beginning.”

He remarked that the “global institutions who claim to be masters of having the security arrangement globally were not created in one day”, adding that the Makkah pact was signed for self-defence.

The foreign minister highlighted that the pact does not violate Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, which allows individual and collective defence.

“Now, it is not restricted that these three countries will have a monopoly and will not have, will not entertain ever [any] other membership,” he said.

DPM Dar said there was a “transition time of setting up the infrastructure” of the alliance, as part of which various decisions were made, including related to the secretary general’s office and the permanent secretariat in Riyadh.

He added that a working committee has also been formed, comprising one person each from the foreign, defence and military offices of the three countries.

“That committee has been working; it has had a few sessions. And the last meeting, hopefully, will be in November, where they will work out all the nitty-gritty regarding detailed SOPs etc,” he said.

“I’m very hopeful that, God willing, this is not going to benefit just these three countries. New membership will be entertained after we are established in about one year,” Dar further said, adding that membership requests of those who will agree to the alliance’s principles will be entertained.

ECO Secretary General Asad Majeed Khan and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar were also present at the media briefing.

Islamabad has ‘not given up’ on US-Iran peace efforts

DPM Dar also reaffirmed that Islamabad has not given up on its diplomatic efforts for a peaceful resolution to the US-Iran war.

Replying to a query, Dar said he had “very candid, very frank, very brotherly, very comprehensive discussions” with Iran’s FM Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the ECO meeting, which they both attended.

Noting that the two discussed the latest regional situation, the deputy premier said Iran had “fast-tracked” its seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to a two-day plan.

“So, the response from the United States is pending. We have not given up hope or efforts. We are still doing our best [so] that the situation gets sorted out,” DPM Dar stated.

He also expressed hope that, now that Washington was no longer busy with its midterm elections, it would respond to the proposal “very soon”.

Asked how ECO planned to navigate the US sanctions on Iran, considering that the organisation’s secretariat was based in Tehran, Dar said, “Sanctions are not going to be there forever.

“And once sanctions are over, the whole world will just land there; I can guarantee,” he maintained, recalling that a British prime minister was the first person to visit Tripoli when sanctions against Libya were withdrawn.

“I think the legal side, the sanctions, international abiding of the sanctions … Pakistan has always, you know, followed international law, UN Charter and followed whatever resolutions have been decided and adopted in the UN Security Council,” Dar affirmed.

He expressed his hope that the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding signed between Iran and the US on June 18 was implemented.

Dar remarked that the seven-day and two-day Hormuz proposals were “actually extracted” from the Islamabad MoU.

“There’s nothing new. It’s only fast-tracking things here and there, showing confidence-building measures, taking actions by one side and opening of the Hormuz by the other.

“So I think let’s hope for the best. We haven’t given up hope,” the foreign minister reiterated.

In their meeting on the sidelines, Dar and Araghchi reviewed bilateral relations and exchanged views on regional and international developments of mutual interest, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

“They reaffirmed the strong and brotherly ties between Pakistan and Iran and reiterated their commitment to further strengthening bilateral cooperation through sustained high-level engagement.”

According to FO, Araghchi congratulated Pakistan on the successful hosting of the ECO ministers’ meeting and “appreciated the productive deliberations, warm hospitality and excellent arrangements”.

Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to advancing ECO’s priorities, particularly regional cooperation and connectivity, the statement added.

On his part, Dar emphasised that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means of addressing outstanding issues, preventing escalation and achieving lasting peace and stability”.

Stressing the value of continued engagement and consultations, both sides agreed to maintain close contact on matters of mutual interest.

Months of diplomacy have failed to resolve the war, which began with surprise US-Israeli strikes on Tehran that assassinated Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

During more than eight months of war, Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — a key oil trade route — and struck infrastructure and US assets across the Middle East.

On Sunday, Bahrain was rattled by the second Iranian drone attack in three days, ending a long lull in strikes during the war.

World.title: 'I may not return alive': In open letter to top judges, Imran pleads for medical treatment for him and Bushra Bibi
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Incarcerated PTI founder and former prime minister Imran Khan on Monday appealed for medical treatment for himself and his wife Bushra Bibi in an open letter to the chief justices of the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), the Supreme Court (SC) and the Islamabad High Court (IHC).

The letter was shared on the social media platform X by Imran’s lawyer Barrister Salman Safdar, who had met the ex-premier at Adiala jail on Nov 2 and Nov 11. The letter said that during the Nov 11 meeting, Imran had directed Safdar to “carry his words to your lordships”.

“I have conveyed this letter faithfully and solely on these instructions. The words that follow are his [Imran’s],” the letter said, which also bore Safdar’s signature.

In the letter, Imran detailed his own deteriorating health condition as well as his wife’s, pleading with the courts to grant them access to medical treatment.

“I spent my life building hospitals so that those who could not afford treatment would receive it free of cost. Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” he said.

Imran said that he was writing from a “solitary cell”, as that was now “the only way my voice can leave these walls”.

“I do not write as a former prime minister, nor as the head of a political party. I have given my life to Pakistan. I served this nation on the cricket field, in social work and philanthropy and as its 22nd prime minister. For seventy years, not a single criminal case stood against my name,” he said.

“Then, after the age of 70, came an unprecedented and ruthless campaign of political victimisation: countless prosecutions, more than a hundred appearances before the courts, pre-arrest bail sought again and again, and an assassination attempt which, by the grace of Allah, I survived. Through all of it, I chose the path of law. I decided that I would fight every one of these politically motivated cases in the courts and I never stopped,” he said.

He said that from “time to time” he was granted relief from the courts that “renewed my faith that justice would prevail”.

“After the constitutional amendments, however, that relief became narrow, and then it closed off altogether. It grieves me deeply to say that, when I needed it most, the system I had placed my trust in did not come to my aid. Within the walls of Adiala, my wife and I have faced criminal trials one after the other, and our appeals still await decision. Yet I have never once sought relief on medical grounds, nor used illness as a tactic. I fought on the merits, with confidence, and I still do,” he said.

Imran went on to say that “everything changed” after the judgement in the Toshakhana-2 case.

The ex-premier and his wife were sentenced to 17 years in jail in the case, which pertained to the purchase of an expensive Bulgari jewellery set, gifted to Imran by the Saudi crown prince during an official visit in May 2021, at a throwaway price.

“I was totally isolated, disconnected and held incommunicado from the outside world, in torturous solitary confinement for up to twenty-two hours a day, in disregard of every constitutional right and every entitlement the Prison Rules guarantee a prisoner: no family, no lawyers, no call to my sons, no books and no television,” Imran said in his letter.

He said that after months without access to his lawyer, Safdar was allowed to meet him on Feb 10 after the SC appointed him amicus curiae.

“He found that I had lost 85 per cent of the vision in my right eye and that neither my family nor my counsel had been told. After that visit, the disconnect returned, and the jail administration, acting vindictively, isolated me once again,” he said.

Imran said that he had only been allowed to meet his lawyer four times during the year, while Bushra Bibi had only been allowed to meet her counsel once. He asserted that this was a violation of the rules and the basic rights of every prisoner, adding that it had left them “unable to defend ourselves in the very cases we are fighting”.

“Prolonged solitary confinement and the absence of any meaningful human interaction have taken a heavy toll on my mental health. This is not my claim alone: the jail’s own medical board has recorded my anxiety and advised more frequent contact with my wife and family, reading material and television. That advice has not been followed,” he said.

Imran alleged that his weekly meeting with his wife was skipped by jail authorities “without reason or explanation”. He said that he had also learnt that his sisters were in custody, adding that he was not allowed to meet them. He said his sons, Kasim and Sulaiman, were also not allowed to call in contradiction of court orders.

“No one in the jail is permitted to respond to me or speak to me, not when I offer them salaam and not when I recite a verse of the Holy Quran. The purpose, I can only conclude, is to make me ill and to break my will,” he said.

Imran said that despite this, he was more concerned about Bushra Bibi’s conditions. He said that in April, she suffered a retinal detachment and underwent a “complicated eye surgery in secrecy” and was sent back to solitary confinement.

“When I saw her this month, she could neither bear the light nor open her eyes, and without another surgery she may lose her sight permanently. Her records are withheld, her doctors denied, her suspension of sentence unheard, despite the law’s compassion for women prisoners,” he said.

Imran said that on Aug 18, the SC directed that he be shifted to Shifa International Hospital within two days, a medical board be constituted to examine him and that he be allowed interactions with his family.

“That order has not been implemented. My case now rests on the docket of the FCC, awaiting a hearing,” he said. He said that his appeal in the Al-Qadir trust case was being taken up ahead of older ones concerning the health of the couple and unimplemented court orders.

“It is my wife’s failing sight, and that unimplemented order of the honourable SC, that compel me to write. In solitary confinement, my blood pressure has become uncontrolled: 130, then 150, then 170, and last week 192 and 193 on Nov 10. The doctors now tell me that I am highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest and that my heart has already suffered damage. At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive,” he said.

“I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice,” he lamented.

“I do not ask your Lordships for any favour. All I request as justice is the implementation of the orders of the honourable SC and proper treatment for our medical conditions. I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive. I appeal to your Lordships, on the most basic grounds of human compassion: give me justice before it is too late,” he concluded.

Meanwhile, Imran’s son Kasim said in a post on X that it was “devastating to read this letter from my father”.

His other son, Sulaiman, described the letter as “incredibly harrowing”.

“My father’s appeal to receive proper medical care is in no way a request for special treatment. It is the absolute bare minimum required to comply with internationally recognised standards for human rights,” he said. He called on authorities to shift Imran to Shifa International hospital for treatment “before it is too late”.

The leaders of the opposition in the National Assembly and the Senate, Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas expressed “grave concern, sorrow and regret” over the conditions and treatment described in Imran’s letter, calling it a “test for our entire justice system”.

“It is deeply regrettable that a former prime minister who has consistently approached the courts to face the cases against him and fight his legal battles is now compelled to appeal to the higher judiciary through an open letter merely to secure his basic human needs, medical care and the right to meet his family,” they said in a joint statement.

“The fundamental responsibility of the state and the relevant authorities is to ensure the protection of every person in custody’s life, health and human dignity, not to add to their difficulties and suffering,” they said.

The joint statement also termed the concerns regarding Bushra Bibi “profoundly regrettable”.

“We strongly urge the higher judiciary to take immediate notice of all the matters raised in Imran’s letter and take effective judicial action to protect his life, health, liberty and fundamental rights,” the opposition leaders said.

They clarified that their demand was “not for any special concession or extraordinary facility, but for compliance with the Constitution, the law and court orders”.

Speaking to Dawn, PTI Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram called on the courts to take notice of Imran’s letter.

“His case should also be seen on humanitarian grounds and medical treatment for him and Bushra Bibi should commence immediately,” he said.

We urge the court to take notice and provide legal rights to Imran without further delay,” he said.

‘Claims contrary to facts’

Meanwhile, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said that claims regarding the “denial of medical facilities, treatment and other basic amenities in prison are contrary to the facts”.

“Imran being provided with the necessary facilities, including meals of his choice, books and television. In fact, he is currently among the most privileged prisoners in Pakistan,” the minister said.

“His health is reviewed and monitored weekly by qualified medical specialists. Whenever required, he is also examined at leading medical facilities outside the prison,” he said.

Chaudhry added that Imran had been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences “eight times for medical examinations, where doctors declared his health satisfactory”.

“A doctor from London, who also practises in Pakistan, was specifically called to examine his blood pressure. According to the medical assessments, his blood pressure is satisfactory,” he said.

“It is the government’s responsibility to ensure proper healthcare, medical supervision and protection of the legal rights of Imran, just as it is for every other prisoner. The government has neither neglected his medical care in the past nor will it allow any negligence in the future,” he said.

The minister said that the PTI should refrain from turning a “sensitive matter like Imran’s health into a political propaganda campaign and should instead present facts responsibly”.

“Political narratives cannot overturn legal proceedings or provide anyone with an escape from legal accountability,” he said.

Imran and Bushra Bibi’s health

Imran has been in prison since August 5, 2023 , while his wife was arrested on January 17, 2025, in a separate case in which the couple were sentenced.

The IHC has allowed Imran twice-a-week meetings — on Tuesdays and Thursdays — with his family, lawyers and other associates. Despite multiple court directives , Imran’s meetings with his family and party leaders have been largely restricted .

Imran’s eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion — came to light in late January, following which he has been taken to hospital multiple times.

On Aug 18, the SS directed the government to shift the jailed ex-premier to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad, a day after the superintendent of the Adiala jail — where Imran is imprisoned — submitted a report to the court on the ex-premier’s health condition.

However, the government took the PTI founder to Pims and subsequently transported him back to prison. At the time, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar had blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside” the hospital for the diversion. The PTI has denied the allegations and accused the government of deliberately flouting the court’s orders.

Meanwhile, Bushra Bibi suffered a retinal detachment in April and was taken to the hospital for surgery. She has since approached the courts seeking an immediate medical examination by an ophthalmologist and permission to receive treatment from doctors of her choice at her own expense amid concerns over her deteriorating eyesight.

According to the former first lady, doctors who examined her had diagnosed her condition as a “mature cataract” and advised that another eye surgery would be required.

World.title: We know how to hurt India, says Pakistan coach Solano ahead of SAFF Championship final
World.content:
Pakistan head coach Nolberto Solano believes his side has what it takes to trouble India in the SAFF Championship final, insisting that his players must focus on their own strengths rather than become preoccupied with their opponents as the two arch-rivals prepare for a historic showdown on Tuesday.

Pakistan will face defending champions India at the National Stadium in Dhaka, Bangladesh, with the Green Shirts chasing their maiden SAFF Championship title and a landmark first appearance in the tournament’s final.

Speaking at the pre-match press conference on Monday, Solano acknowledged India’s quality but maintained that Pakistan had studied their opponents and understood where they could make an impact.

“We all prepare. It’s a final match, and we respect India. We are always checking and looking, but in football there are no more secrets,” Solano said.

“You know how they play. The most important thing is to focus on ourselves, on what we want to do, because we know our strengths and how we can hurt India.”

The Peruvian coach described the encounter as a special occasion and a derby, recognising the significance of a Pakistan-India contest, particularly with silverware at stake.

However, he stressed that his team’s attention must remain on executing its own game plan rather than allowing the occasion or the opposition to dictate its approach.

‘Football history’

For Pakistan, Tuesday’s final represents an opportunity to turn an encouraging tournament campaign into one of the most significant achievements in the country’s football history.

The Green Shirts booked their place in the showpiece match with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over hosts Bangladesh in Saturday’s semi-final. Abdul Samad Arshad scored the decisive goal in the closing stages to send Pakistan into their first-ever SAFF Championship final.

Their progress has been particularly noteworthy given the limited preparation time and the difficulties surrounding the availability of several overseas-based players during the group stage.

Pakistan’s final opponents, meanwhile, are pursuing a historic achievement of their own. India have won the SAFF Championship nine times and will be looking to secure an unprecedented third consecutive title, having lifted the trophy in the previous two editions.

The final will be a rematch of the Group ‘B’ encounter between the two sides on Nov 5, when India secured a 3-2 victory after establishing a commanding three-goal advantage.

Suhail Ahmad Bhat scored twice, while Manglenthang Kipgen added India’s third as Pakistan struggled to find their rhythm during the opening half.

The Green Shirts responded with two goals in stoppage time, including a spectacular overhead kick from Alamgir Ghazi, but their late rally proved insufficient to prevent defeat.

Solano admitted that Pakistan’s slow start and lack of concentration had contributed to the result, while also pointing to the difficult journey and inadequate preparation time before their opening fixture.

“I don’t like to make excuses, but we had a very bad journey before we arrived, and we faced them without two days of training. In the first 45 minutes, we weren’t focused. We were quite slow, so they took their chances and scored,” he said.

The coach, however, was encouraged by his side’s response after the interval, believing Pakistan had shown enough improvement to suggest they could compete more effectively in the rematch.

“In the second half, we improved and played much better. We could have come back into the match, but we did it a little bit late. That’s why we lost 3-2. But it’s another game, a different game,” Solano added.

Pakistan’s squad has since received a significant boost with the arrival of several overseas-based players who were unavailable during the group stage because the tournament fell outside the FIFA international window.

Captain Abdullah Iqbal, Easah Suliman, Adil Nabi, Ali Akbar Khan and Abdul Samad Arshad were among the players who joined the squad ahead of the knockout stages, giving Solano additional options and greater depth.

The impact of their arrival has been evident in Pakistan’s subsequent performances, particularly their defensive organisation and ability to manage difficult moments against Bangladesh.

India coach Naushad Moosa has also acknowledged that Pakistan present a different challenge from the team his side defeated in the group stage, pointing to the arrival of additional players and the tactical adjustments expected for the final.

Abdullah acknowledged the importance of the occasion but insisted that the players would not approach the final any differently from their other matches.

Rather than allowing the pressure of a historic opportunity to affect their performance, the defender wants his teammates to remain disciplined, support one another and follow the instructions of the coaching staff.

“It’s a final, a big game, but we have to take it like any other game. Focus on the plan the coach has set for us, help each other out on the pitch and perform as usual. Nothing extra,” Abdullah said.

He admitted that the pressure of competing for a major regional title was unavoidable, particularly given what victory would mean for Pakistan football, but insisted that it would serve as additional motivation.

“Of course, there is pressure to win a final. It’s a big thing for our country, creating history, and it only motivates us to do better,” he added.

Abdullah also described Pakistan’s qualification for the final as a historic achievement, saying a tournament triumph would take the country’s footballing progress to another level.

“On the footballing side, it is the biggest achievement that we’re here in the final, and if we can go all the way, it will be even bigger,” the captain said.

With Pakistan having played a demanding schedule during the tournament, Solano was also asked whether fatigue could become a concern ahead of the final.

The coach dismissed the suggestion, insisting that his players were mentally prepared for the challenge and would not use the schedule as an excuse.

“Nobody is tired, my friend. We all focus. We all have a strong mentality,” he said. “When you play a final, my friends, the last thing you can be is tired. We are ready for fighting. No excuse. We want to give you everything.”

World.title: Govt reduces petrol, diesel prices by Rs2 per litre
World.content:
The government on Monday reduced the price of both petrol and high-speed diesel by Rs2 per litre, marking the tenth consecutive decrease in the rates.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs328 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs358 on Nov 17 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation.

The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: Trump says 'would not mind' Huang being reinstated at Nvidia
World.content:
United States President Donald Trump on Monday signalled that he would welcome Jensen Huang being reinstated as chief of the AI chip giant Nvidia, after Huang resigned last week amid a spy scandal.

“I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told reporters as he headed on a trip to China when asked if he thought Huang should return at Nvidia.

“I think he learned a big lesson.”

Trump also referred to a campaign to bring back Huang, with tech tycoon Elon Musk and an Uber co-founder among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter.

“A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said.

Trump also raised fresh doubts over allegations that Alice Huang, a woman with whom Huang had an affair, was spying for China after all.

“I don’t know that she is a spy. Usually what happens with that is that, any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she is a spy,” Trump said.

“China plays games with us and we play games with them,” he said.

Trump dismissed reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had flagged intelligence to him indicating that Alice Huang was a spy, saying: “I haven’t heard that.”

Huang was a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which US investigators suspect of illegally channeling Nvidia’s technology to China.

The Nvidia scandal has caused tensions in the White House over the sale of advanced American AI chips to China.

US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department has been accused by voices led by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent of failing to properly enforce export controls on the most powerful chips.

The Commerce Department on Monday closed a loophole on Chinese access, issuing a rule aimed at stopping Chinese companies from using advanced American AI chips housed in data centres in other countries.

Trump said that Lutnick and Bessent “have two different views. One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.

“The other view is just go down and dirty and do what you have to do. You can’t say either is wrong or right, we’ll let you know.”

But Trump appeared once again to defend Huang, a frequent guest at the White House who accompanied the US leader on his trip to China in May, over the chip sales.

“Jensen obviously has two things going: he has a family situation which is a rough deal, and what he wants to do is to sell chips,” Trump said.

“We prohibited him from selling the important chips, the modern day chips.

But frankly, selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing.”

World.title: In tit-for-tat move, Chaudhry Salik sends CM Maryam, Azma Bokhari defamation notices
World.content:
In a tit-for-tat move, PML-Q leader and Overseas Pakistanis Minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain said on Monday he has also sent a defamation notice to Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz.

After the PML-Q leader levelled allegations of corruption against the incumbent Punjab government, CM Maryam sent a Rs5 billion defamation notice to him, demanding he retract his remarks.

Alongside furnishing a reply to that notice, Salik said on Monday that he had also sent two legal notices for defamation to Maryam and Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari.

“A formal reply to the legal notice has been duly sent,” Salik said in a post on X.

“Attempts to intimidate through legal notices will neither silence nor deter me from raising concerns on matters of public interest and their well-being,” he reaffirmed.

The minister went on to reiterate the allegations: “The province continues to suffer from gross mismanagement and rampant corruption, issues that demand a ‘little’ self-reflection and accountability, not intimidation.”

The PML-Q leader also reiterated the “commitment to transparency in the interest of Punjab and Pakistan”.

In a separate X post, Salik announced, “Further, I have also sent through my legal counsel two legal notices for defamation. One to Mrs Maryam Nawaz Sharif and the other one to Mrs Azma Zahid Bokhari.”

In an interview last week, Salik stated that he stood by his earlier remarks regarding corruption in Punjab and also termed Maryam’s statements in response to him as “below the belt”.

The PML-Q minister also regretted that fiery statements by Bokhari had worsened the row.

Salik’s defamation notice to Maryam, seen by Dawn and filed via Advocate Waleed Khalid, was sent over “false, baseless and defamatory” statements made by her during a public speech in Attock on Nov 3, 2026.

The statements constituted an “unwarranted attack” on reputation, and had been made and propagated without any lawful justification, the notice said, citing Sections 2(h) & 3 of the Punjab Defamation Act 2024.

The notice demanded that within seven days of its receipt, Maryam withdraw the said allegations against Salik and tender an “unconditional apology with prominence comparable to that of the original publications”.

It also urged the chief minister to remove the statements from the accounts and channels within her control, warning of seeking proceedings and relief as per law, including costs and damages, if Maryam failed to provide a satisfactory response.

The notice recalled that during the Nov 3 speech, the Punjab chief minister specifically named Salik and sought to portray his remarks concerning corruption in Punjab as nothing more than a reaction to his alleged failure to secure the posting of a DC of his choice in Gujrat.

In the notice, the lawyer clarified that Salik’s interview to ARY News was recorded on Sept 25, and certain parts of it were aired by the channel on Nov 2 “as per its own editorial policies”.

Reiterating the explanation provided earlier by Salik, the lawyer said the Gujrat DC was reported to have been transferred by the Punjab government on Oct 31, and another officer was posted in her place.

The notice asserted that, in effect, Maryam’s statement falsely insinuated that Salik wanted to have a DC in Gujrat of his choice and that, upon failing to secure his preferred appointment, he resorted to making false allegations of corruption against the Punjab government.

“As the incumbent chief minister of Punjab, the most populous province of Pakistan, you are expected to appreciate the weight and responsibility that attaches to your words and public statements. A person occupying such high office ought to be more cognisant of adversely affecting the rights and reputations of other persons.

“Instead, you have abused your public platform to publicise statements which have injured the reputation of Salik, and exposed him to unjust criticism, contempt and hatred,” said the notice to Maryam.

It termed the chief minister’s statement as having no “legal or ethical basis”.

Reply to CM’s defamation notice

Salik’s response to CM Maryam’s notice, a copy of which is available with Dawn, stated that the minister’s remarks were “an expression of opinion on a matter that is fair and in the public interest”.

“Even otherwise, and without prejudice to the foregoing, the remarks would not have fallen within the scope of ‘defamation’ at all,” it contended. It said that the notice from CM Maryam wrongly portrayed Salik’s remarks as “assertions of fact”.

“Even assuming, for the sake of argument, that the remarks were statements of fact (which they were not), they would not amount to defamation because, by definition, defamation can only occur by a ‘false or untrue statement’, whereas the remarks, even if they were assertions of facts, would not have been false or untrue,” it said.

The response also cited several public statements by CM Maryam in which she acknowledged the existence of corruption in the province. It argued that the chief minister’s own statements supported Salik’s position that corruption existed in Punjab and that discussing the issue was a matter of legitimate public interest.

In his response, the PML-Q leader termed CM Maryam’s notice “an attempt to weaponise the law of defamation to stifle legitimate discussion and criticism on matters of public interest and importance”.

“It is well established across common law jurisdictions that governments, government bodies and public authorities, particularly those that are democratically elected, cannot maintain an action for defamation,” it stated.

“The demand for five billion rupees is, in any event, wholly baseless. It bears no relation to any genuine claim for compensation,” the response said, adding that the objective was to “intimidate public representatives and to warn others, including the press, against speaking about corruption in Punjab”.

“The notice is legally misconceived, untenable and, in several respects, verges on the absurd,” the response went on to say, adding that it appeared to be a calculated attempt to “intimidate and exert undue pressure” on Salik with the “ulterior objective of stifling legitimate discourse on the serious and important issue of corruption”.

Rejecting the demands made in the notice, the PML-Q leader declared that he would not withdraw the statements made in the interview, apologise, publish any retraction or pay any sum.

Notice to Bokhari

Meanwhile, the minister also sent a defamation notice to Bokhari over “the false, baseless and defamatory” remarks by the Punjab information minister on her X account on Nov 2, wherein she had termed Salik’s criticism as the consequence of not having his choice be appointed the deputy commissioner (DC) of Gujrat.

The said statements constitute an “unwarranted attack” on reputation and had been made and propagated without any lawful justification, the defamation notice said.

It said that Bokhari’s statement, which insinuated that the remarks made in the interview were a consequence of the change of the Gujrat DC, was “clearly false and untrue”.

The notice called upon Bokhari to withdraw the allegation that Salik sought the appointment of a DC and tender an unconditional apology within seven days.

It also demanded the removal of the alleged defamatory statements within seven days from the accounts and channels within Bokhari’s control.

The notice said that if the Punjab information minister failed to provide a satisfactory response within the stated period, Salik reserved the right to institute appropriate proceedings and to seek the relief available under the law, including damages and costs.

What did Salik say?

During a talk show on a private television channel, the PML-Q leader praised the performance of his uncle Chaudhry Pervez Elahi as a former Punjab chief minister.

He further criticised the incumbent provincial administration headed by CM Maryam, alleging that he regularly heard complaints of corruption.

He also questioned lavish government spending , particularly the use of an official aircraft , arguing that public representatives should remain mindful of the country’s economic difficulties.

Incensed by Salik’s allegations of corruption, Maryam sent a Rs5bn defamation notice to him.

She challenged him to provide evidence for his corruption claims, threatening legal action if he failed to do so. She also questioned why he remained a minister in a government he considered corrupt.

Both CM Maryam and the Punjab information minister alleged that Salik’s displeasure stemmed from his request to appoint a DC of his choice in Gujrat being turned down.

Salik later clarified that his interview was recorded on Sept 25, before the new DC was appointed, suggesting CM Maryam’s information was incorrect.

He also regretted the withdrawal of his security by the provincial government after the incident.

Additional input by Waseem Ashraf Butt

World.title: At ECO moot, Dar calls for translating 'collective commitments into concrete action'
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar closed out the 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers (COM) in Islamabad on Monday with a call for countries to translate their commitments into action.

Pakistan, which holds the ECO chairmanship for 2026-27, hosted the meeting under the theme “Reviving Regionalism for a Resilient ECO”.

The deputy premier, who chaired the meeting, expressed his “sincere appreciation to all delegations” for their constructive engagement during the meeting.

“The deliberations today have reaffirmed our shared commitment to regional economic cooperation and integration,” Dar said.

He termed the adoption of the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035 an “important milestone in charting the future course of our organisation over the next decade”, saying that it provided a shared framework to advance regional priorities alongside the Islamabad Communiqué.

“Our task now is to translate our collective commitments into concrete action,” he added. “This will require clear priorities, realistic timelines, and effective follow-up mechanisms.”

He highlighted regional cooperation as a central pillar of Pakistan’s foreign policy and noted that the country had consistently advocated a “stronger, more effective and responsive” ECO that harnessed “geographical proximity, historical bonds and economic complementarities”.

Dar underscored Pakistan’s commitment to advancing the ECO agenda as the chair of the organisation and to working with all institutions and member states to strengthen regional connectivity, facilitate intra-regional trade and promote mutually beneficial economic cooperation.

He looked forward to welcoming the countries back for the 31st COM meeting in 2027, saying, “Let us build on the momentum generated here so that our next meeting can take stock of tangible progress in advancing our shared priorities.”

In addition, he wished Iran success in hosting the upcoming 18th ECO summit on Dec 3-4.

The deputy premier thanked all member states, as well as the secretary general and his team, ECO permanent representatives, and senior officials for their support.

Later in the day, Dar held a media briefing on the meeting alongside ECO Secretary General Asad Majeed Khan and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar.

Joint communiqué

The COM meeting concluded with the adoption of two documents, including the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035 and the Islamabad Communiqué.

Pakistan’s mediation efforts hailed

In the Islamabad Communiqué, ECO member states expressed concern over the “challenging geopolitical environment in the region, emphasising the importance of restraint, dialogue and diplomatic engagement, and recognising the important role” of Iran as a founding member of ECO.

They expressed support for the mediation efforts undertaken by Pakistan and Qatar, as well as for the recent initiative put forward by Iran “aimed at achieving a dignified resolution of the conflict and ensuring the complete and permanent termination of the current war”.

The ECO states commended Pakistan’s “consistent and constructive diplomatic support for ECO Member States and its mediation efforts towards de-escalation during the recent Iran-United States crisis”.

They reaffirmed the importance of dialogue, diplomacy, respect for international law and promoting mutual trust. stability and the peaceful resolution of disputes, and calling for continued cooperation within the ECO framework towards lasting peace and stability in the region.

The communiqué also highly appreciated Qatar’s “important role as a trusted facilitator of international diplomacy, most notably demonstrated by its mediation efforts at the 81st United Nations General Assembly”.

The members commended ECO for “demonstrating that regionalism can remain effective and operational even under conditions of acute geopolitical stress”.

The communiqué expressed concern over the humanitarian situation in Gaza after flooding on Nov 6 as winter begins. It urges priority delivery of food, medicine, fuel, heating equipment, tents, shelters, blankets and winter clothing. It also called for an immediate end to “policies of forced displacement and the deliberate deprivation of food” and full implementation of the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire agreement.

The organisation rejected “unilateral coercive measures, sanctions and economic pressures and their extraterritorial economic, technological, financial or trade impacts”.

It said they are contrary to the UN Charter and international law, adversely affect international peace and security, and undermine the provision of supply chains for food, pharmaceutical, energy and humanitarian assistance.

The joint statement also mentioned Afghanistan, a member of the ECO, though seemingly not present at the meeting.

ECO acknowledged the need for “continued consultation with member states to address the issues of Afghanistan’s engagement with the organisation in relevant areas, with a view to achieving the country’s full and effective participation once circumstances permit”.

They stressed the need for “achieving meaningful progress on concerns of member states for fostering regional cooperation and laying the basis for Afghanistan’s participation in any ECO activities and processes”.

Economy and trade

The meeting expressed support for various documents adopted in the past, including ECO Vision 2025 and the 2021 Ashgabat Consensus for Action. They also welcomed various UN resolutions and initiatives.

Members were urged to speed up amendment and implementation of the ECO Trade Agreement (ECOTA), with non-parties to the pact invited to consultations.

The communique called for timely implementation of Turkmenistan’s feasibility study on the establishment of joint trade zones within the ECO region. They pointed to the Turkmenistan–Uzbekistan zone as a model and to a proposed trade market at the Altyn Asyr–Incheh Boroun border crossing between Iran and Turkmenistan.

It urged joint measures on foreign direct investment, free economic zones, joint manufacturing, e-commerce and digitised customs “single window” systems.

The ECO further stressed “expeditious conclusion” of the draft ECO Trade Facilitation Agreement and tasked the Joint Working Group with intensifying its technical negotiations toward the pact’s early finalisation. Pakistan has offered to host the 4th JWG meeting in the third quarter of 2026.

The ministers called for more diversified financing, including through the ECO Trade and Development Bank (ECOTDB), whose membership they want expanded.

Members were urged to fully implement the ECO Transit Transport Framework Agreement to “unlock the region’s full potential and enhance regional connectivity, trade, and economic development”.

The ministers highlighted the ECO Sustainable and Resilient Transport Strategy 2026–2035 as a flagship framework. They also called for transport and transit corridors and better seaport access for landlocked members.

The ECO members welcomed Shusha as ECO Tourism Capital 2026 and noted the schedule of future capitals: Lahore (2027), Mary (2028), Karakol (2029) and Aktau (2030).

They also welcomed the operationalisation of the ECO Clean Energy Centre in Baku, as well as the “ECO Five-Year Roadmap on minerals cooperation for 2026–2030”, described as the first overarching framework for regional cooperation on minerals, including critical minerals.

AI and technology

The Islamabad Communiqué acknowledged UN actions on AI, including the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva on July 6–7.

It underlined the need to bridge the AI capacity gap and promote “safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems in the non-military domain for sustainable development”.

The statement also recognised the “transformative potential of emerging technologies”, such as AI, blockchain, quantum computing, 5G and robotics. It called for harnessing these technologies for regional prosperity, while noting the need to share experience on mitigating associated risks.

Members were encouraged to cooperate on AI through exchanges of best practices, joint capacity-building and training under the ECO Science Foundation, aiming at bridging the “digital and artificial intelligence divide”.

The ministers also noted the significance of the ECO Regional ICT Strategy 2026–2030, stressed the security of critical digital infrastructure, and called for cooperation among members in ICT security.

They emphasised the “importance of ensuring equal, fair, transparent and non-discriminatory access, particularly for developing countries, to global markets for ICT security products, technologies and services, as a confidence-building measure”.

The ECO members encouraged exploring cooperation on the peaceful uses of outer space, including satellite services, and space-based services in support of regional connectivity, disaster risk reduction and environmental monitoring.

Araghchi calls for sustainable energy mechanism

At the ECO meeting, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stressed the need for a reliable and sustainable regional energy mechanism during his address.

The Iranian FM spoke about the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has also resulted in the choking of key fuel supply routes — the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.

“Our region needs not only an independent security framework but also a reliable and sustainable regional energy mechanism to safeguard energy flows, ensure stable supplies, reduce external vulnerabilities and enhance collective resilience against geopolitical shocks and disruptions,” Araghchi said, according to a transcript of his speech provided by the Iranian embassy in Pakistan.

Araghchi said ECO was moving “beyond its traditional role towards becoming an effective platform for collective action, strengthened cooperation and joint efforts”. He said the shift would enable member states “to address emerging challenges and contribute to an inclusive and equitable global economic order”.

He stressed the need for a “modern, new-generation, more inclusive, effective and operational trade agreement” that would benefit the region.

Referring to the US war on Iran, Araghchi said, “Iran has remained committed to diplomatic engagement and peaceful solutions.”

He added, however, that the US had opted for a different course of action, which was “marked by aggression, threats, targeted assassinations, economic coercion, and blockades, in flagrant violation of international law and the UN Charter”.

He underscored that Iran had “no inherent dispute” with countries in the region, adding that “the territories, airspace and facilities of the regional countries must not be used as platforms for launching attacks against each other”.

“Iran’s legitimate defensive measures are directed exclusively at the targets and military bases of the aggressors and should in no way be construed as actions against the peoples or governments of the neighbouring countries,” Araghchi said.

He also called attention to Palestine, describing the genocide in Gaza as “the most pressing international crisis”.

Condemning the destruction and killings at the hands of Israeli forces in Palestine, he said, “We are witnessing the intensification of expansionist policies by the Israeli regime in the West Bank and occupied Al-Quds.”

“This is a moment that calls for concrete action, collective responsibility, and an end to silence and indifference.”

He concluded his speech by reiterating that Iran’s stability and prosperity were “intrinsically linked” to those of other ECO members.

ECO delegation heads call on PM Shehbaz

Separately, the foreign ministers and delegation heads of ECO member states paid a joint call on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, according to a handout issued by the PM’s Office.

The premier thanked them for their participation in the meeting and reaffirmed Pakistan’s “strong commitment” to ECO objectives. He reiterated his government’s resolve to promote regional cooperation, connectivity and economic integration within the ECO member states.

The premier appreciated the meeting’s successful conclusion and welcomed the adoption of the Islamabad Communique and the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035, describing them as “important steps” towards strengthening the organisation and advancing shared regional priorities.

The premier highlighted Pakistan’s ECO chairmanship and emphasised the need to translate the organisation’s collective vision into concrete, result-oriented initiatives that deliver “tangible benefits” to the region’s people.

Furthermore, the handout said that the premier called for enhanced cooperation in trade and investment, transport and transit connectivity, energy, information and communication technology, and sustainable development.

“He stressed the importance of effective implementation of existing ECO agreements and strengthening institutional mechanisms to accelerate regional economic integration,” the statement said.

PM Shehbaz highlighted the country’s strategic geographical location. He reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to enhancing regional connectivity through road, rail and multimodal transport corridors, including linkages with the ports of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar, to facilitate access to regional and international markets, particularly for landlocked ECO member states.

“Underlining Pakistan’s commitment to dialogue and diplomacy for the peaceful resolution of disputes, the premier stressed the importance of collective efforts to address threats to regional security,” the statement added.

He also expressed Pakistan’s resolve to work closely with all member states and the ECO secretariat to further strengthen the organisation during its chairmanship.

“The prime minister reaffirmed that Pakistan looked forward to welcoming ECO member states again in 2027 for the next Council of Ministers Meeting and the ECO summit,” the handout concluded.

Dar holds sideline meetings with participating dignitaries

The deputy premier also held separate meetings with ministers from several countries attending the ECO moot.

With FM Araghchi, Dar emphasised that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means of addressing outstanding issues, preventing escalation and achieving lasting peace and stability, the Foreign Office said.

Meanwhile, Tajikistan’s FM Sirojiddin Muhriddin and Dar reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation within ECO and advancing its regional priorities.

According to FO, the Tajik minister appreciated Pakistan’s warm hospitality.

The two leaders “underscored the importance of realising the full potential of bilateral trade” and also discussed advancing energy cooperation, particularly through the early operationalisation of CASA-1000.

Dar and Turkiye’s Deputy FM Musa Kulaklikaya reaffirmed their “commitment to further strengthening the longstanding bonds of friendship and brotherhood” between their countries, FO said.

Dar thanked Türkiye for its active participation in the Council of Ministers meeting, while Kulaklikaya thanked Pakistan for the warm hospitality and arrangements for the meeting.

In his meeting with Dar, Kyrgyz Republic’s Deputy FM Kairat Tursunkulov delivered a letter from Foreign Minister Zheenbek Kulubaev, “reaffirming the close bonds of friendship and commitment to advancing bilateral ties”, FO said.

The two sides discussed strengthening bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and connectivity, and emphasised the importance of continued cooperation under ECO.

Pakistan calls on Afghanistan to address terror concerns

In his opening speech at the meeting, Dar said Pakistan desired a peaceful, prosperous and stable Afghanistan, but meaningful progress towards regional cooperation required the Afghan authorities to address the legitimate security concerns of neighbouring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism.

He added that a stable Afghanistan, at peace with itself and all its neighbours and fully integrated into the ECO framework, would benefit the Afghan people as well as the wider region by opening up avenues for trade, transit and economic cooperation.

“At the same time, meaningful progress requires the Afghan authorities to address the legitimate security concerns of the neighbouring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism,” Dar said.

He stressed that a secure and stable environment was essential for sustained regional economic partnerships, adding that these considerations remained central to Pakistan’s broader connectivity agenda.

“Regional connectivity rests on more than the routes that link us. It depends upon trust between states and confidence that international commitments will be honoured. Unresolved disputes and the non-fulfilment of international obligations can erode that trust and impede economic progress,” said Dar.

The foreign minister emphasised that respect for international law and treaties is essential to enduring economic partnerships between countries.

Outlining Pakistan’s priorities during its chairmanship of the ECO, Dar identified five key areas of focus, including expanding trade and investment, strengthening regional connectivity, advancing the ECO Trade Agreement, building regional resilience and promoting human development.

The foreign minister said the region’s natural resources, energy reserves, agricultural potential and strategic location offered considerable opportunities for economic cooperation, but realising that potential required functioning transport corridors, efficient border procedures and predictable transit arrangements.

He said Pakistan would work towards wider market access, stronger regional value chains and greater private sector participation, particularly by small and medium-sized enterprises, to boost trade and investment among member states.

“Closer interaction among our business communities can help translate commercial potential into greater trade and investment.”

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in a cordial exchange with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Tajikistan Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin, OIC Secretary General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed and ECO Secretary General Dr. Asad Majeed Khan on the sidelines of the 30th ECO Council of Ministers Meeting in Islamabad on Nov 16. — ForeignOfficePk/X

On connectivity, Dar said Pakistan would seek to improve transport and transit links between Central Asia, South Asia and Pakistani ports on the Arabian Sea. Harmonised customs procedures, efficient border management and predictable transit arrangements were essential to making regional trade routes commercially viable, he added.

The foreign minister also highlighted the need to advance the ECO Trade Agreement, saying the negotiating strategy and roadmap approved by ECO trade ministers in November 2025 provided a basis for modernising the agreement. Pakistan would support efforts to develop a more effective, inclusive and digitally enabled regional trade framework, he said.

On regional resilience, Dar called for closer cooperation in disaster preparedness, early warning systems, sustainable water management and climate-resilient infrastructure, noting that climate change and growing pressure on water and energy resources posed serious challenges to regional economies.

He also underscored the importance of human development, particularly in education, research, innovation and vocational training, saying greater opportunities in these areas could equip young people with skills needed by changing economies. Promoting entrepreneurship and professional exchanges would further strengthen regional integration, he added.

The foreign minister maintained that the five priorities were interconnected and their success would depend on collective efforts by member states. He expressed Pakistan’s readiness to work with ECO members and the organisation’s secretariat on initiatives relating to trade facilitation, transit connectivity and disaster preparedness.

Regional peace and diplomatic efforts

Dar cautioned that peace and stability were essential for economic development, warning that conflict and insecurity in the region could disrupt trade routes, energy supplies, investment and economic projects.

“Peace and development reinforce each other,” he said.

He added that Pakistan remained “deeply concerned about conflict and instability” in the region.

“Their consequences extend beyond national boundaries, disrupting trade routes, energy supplies, investment, and the economic projects of our peoples.”

He said that Pakistan has consistently advocated for “the peaceful resolution of disputes through dialogue and diplomacy in accordance with international law and the United Nations Charter”.

Referring to Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in the US-Israeli war on Iran, Dar said, “Pakistan will continue these diplomatic efforts in support of dialogue, de-escalation, and lasting regional stability.”

He said that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir “remained closely engaged with brotherly countries and international partners to facilitate peaceful outcomes”.

Senior officials meet to finalise agenda

Senior officials of the ECO finalised the agenda and draft Islamabad Communiqué on Sunday, ahead of the organisation’s COM meeting.

According to a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA), the Senior Officials Meeting (SOM) was held on Nov 15 under the chairmanship of Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad.

The meeting was attended by senior officials from ECO member states, representatives of the ECO Secretariat, and delegates from the organisation’s specialised agencies and regional institutions.

The officials reviewed preparations for the ministerial meeting and finalised its agenda and the draft Islamabad Communiqué for consideration by the foreign ministers.

They also reviewed the activities undertaken by the ECO Secretariat during the year, including ongoing programmes and initiatives, outcomes of sectoral ministerial meetings, and the work of subsidiary bodies and specialised institutions, the ministry said.

Administrative and financial matters of the organisation also came under discussion, with participants exchanging views on measures to improve its effectiveness.

The SOM serves as a preparatory forum for the ECO COM, enabling member states to assess progress, discuss issues of mutual interest and build consensus on proposals and draft documents ahead of ministerial-level deliberations.

World.title: IHC directs petitioner to prove ownership of Bari Imam House to CDA
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Monday disposed of a writ petition challenging the sealing of Bari Imam House in Nurpur Shahan, directing the petitioner to approach the Capital Development Authority (CDA) with documented proof of ownership, while leaving the authority free to proceed in accordance with law if he failed to do so.

Justice Ayyaz Shaukat, in a judgment authored on the petition filed by Muhammad Akmal, caretaker of the premises located opposite the shrine of Bari Imam Sarkar, declined to grant the declaratory relief sought.

He observed that the core dispute — whether the structure stands on exempted shrine land or on land acquired by the CDA in 1963 — turned on contested questions of fact that could not be resolved in constitutional jurisdiction on bare assertions.

The court noted that the petitioner had produced no ownership documents, and that his counsel had candidly conceded that the relevant record lay with the CDA and the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) administration.

The CDA had sealed the premises on Oct 30 in a joint operation with the district administration, maintaining that the property is an unauthorised encroachment on government land acquired under Award No. 4/DC CDA/1963, with compensation paid to the landowners.

According to CDA, the land comprising Khasras No. 435, 582, 591, 592 and 593 formed part of that acquisition and contains no building by the name of “Bari Imam House” in the official record. Meanwhile, the shrine’s land is recorded on entirely different Khasra numbers — 277, 665, 677, 678, 679 and 680 — across the road.

The petitioner, by contrast, had claimed that the premises comprise a mosque, a langar khana and wuzu (ablution) facilities, and that the land was exempted shrine property never acquired by the CDA.

He also alleged that the sealing took place without any notice or opportunity of hearing, in violation of several constitutional provisions.

The court, however, refrained from a pronouncement on the merits of either claim.

Noting that the petitioner’s grievance regarding the absence of notice and the CDA’s objection to his locus standi could both be addressed through a fair and expeditious determination based on documents, the court directed the petitioner to submit his ownership documents, if any, before the CDA within five days.

The CDA was then required to afford him a hearing, consider the documents alongside its own record, and decide the matter by a speaking order within two days thereafter.

The court clarified that if the petitioner does not submit the documents or does not wish to do so, the CDA will be at liberty to proceed in accordance with the law.

During the hearing, the petitioner’s counsel conceded that the property was not his own and that he was merely a caretaker of the shrine, while also stating that he did not possess the relevant documents and that they were held by the CDA.

The CDA’s counsel, Kashif Ali Malik, argued that the petition was not maintainable and that the occupation amounted to encroachment on CDA land.

The interim order dated Nov 3, which had directed the de-sealing of the premises, stands merged in the final order. The court had restrained the officials from carrying out any “demolition” until the next hearing.

Any person aggrieved by the CDA’s decision may avail the remedy available under the law, and the court expressly stated that nothing in its order shall be construed as an expression of opinion on the merits of title or possession.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years.
