To survive, detainees and staff rely on informal coping strategies. Families supply outside medications, while medically trained inmates assist infirmary staff. Wealthier families sometimes pay inmate caregivers or contribute to shared dormitory funds to cover basic health needs for destitute prisoners. Though unauthorized by formal rules, these practices are tacitly tolerated to prevent institutional collapse.

However, reliance on informal arrangements creates wide disparities in care. Inmates with financial means or personal influence receive timely medical intervention, whereas impoverished detainees face severe neglect, fostering systemic favoritism and corruption.

Distinguishing between necessary humanitarian accommodation and corrupt favoritism is vital. While preserving life is a state duty, conditioning care on wealth or political standing degrades fundamental rights into privileges. Strictly enforcing rules without resolving resource shortages will only exacerbate inmate suffering.

The Sandiganbayan must look beyond the controversy

Correctional administrators face a double bind: strictly enforcing inadequate rules risks detainee deaths and public outrage, while permitting external family assistance risks accusations of political favoritism and corruption. Investigations must distinguish illicit financial exchanges from reasonable efforts to prevent fatalities due to staffing shortages.

The judiciary and oversight bodies must address systemic deficiencies rather than singling out individual officers. Reducing overcrowding, expanding non-custodial options for low-risk or ill detainees, and standardizing medical access are essential steps to ensure correctional health measures depend on medical need rather than status.

Eliminating preferential treatment requires establishing a uniform, basic standard of care across all facilities. True equality in the justice system means expanding humane health protections for underprivileged detainees, ensuring that basic human rights are upheld for all persons in state custody. – Rappler.com

Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.

The author originally posted a longer version of this \to Facebook on November 11, 2026.

World.title: Spy scandal, US midterm defeat heat up Trump’s Asia visit
World.content:
PROTEST. Activists protest at Liwasang Bonifacio on November 16, 2026, against US President Donald Trump's participation in the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila.

Trump will first visit Manila for meetings with Southeast Asian and other regional leaders on Tuesday before jetting to Shenzhen for the APEC forum, where he will meet the Chinese president and hold three-way discussions with Xi and Russia's Vladimir Putin

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump headed to Manila on Monday, November 16, after a midterm election drubbing and allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy that have raised the stakes for his latest meeting with Beijing’s powerful leader, Xi Jinping.

As he left the White House, Trump said he might also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, a surprise announcement that could reshape his swing through the region if it in fact occurs.

Trump will first visit Manila for meetings with Southeast Asian and other regional leaders on Tuesday before jetting to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where he will meet the Chinese president and hold three-way discussions with Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

Trump said he would discuss denuclearization, Iran and Ukraine in the meeting with Putin and Xi, as well as trade and the economy.

“We may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said, adding: “He may come. I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”

The president met the North Korean leader several times during his 2017-2021 term and has repeatedly expressed interest in another meeting, but has also previewed meetings that never took place, including during a trip to Asia last year.

North Korea, whose mission to the United Nations did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has publicly indicated it has no intention of meeting with the US president at this time.

With a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China extended to early next year, and more Trump-Xi talks due in December at the G20 in Miami, some analysts had initially billed the Shenzhen meeting as a low-stakes summit.

But a backlash against Trump’s Republican Party in this month’s midterms and criticism that his administration failed to act on intelligence that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has close ties to Trump, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy have muddied those expectations.

Chinese analysts say there are concerns in China that allegations that restricted semiconductors were diverted to Chinese customers could harden US attitudes toward China.

“With less reason to worry about market reactions or electoral fallout, (Trump) may be more willing to consider disruptive measures,” said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser on China at the Tony Blair Institute, a London-based think tank.

Washington has already signaled such willingness ahead of the meeting, urging China to live up to its commitments made under the truce agreed between Trump and Xi a year ago.

And on Monday, the Trump administration issued a rule that will restrict chip exports to overseas data centers in countries like Malaysia and Thailand and hurt Chinese companies that use these to access advanced AI chips to train their artificial intelligence models.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson said last week there was growing consensus in Congress on further limiting Chinese access to advanced chips after the scandal, and Democrats are expected to press hard on the issue when they take over the House and Senate majorities in January.

Zhu Feng, director of the Institute of International Studies at Nanjing University, said the spat could also speed up “the decoupling of AI” between the world’s two superpowers even as they try to cooperate on mitigating the technology’s risks.

Legacy building

China has said the US has fabricated the spy narrative to justify a technological blockade. One senior US administration official said the Nvidia situation “should not really have any bearing on the trip,” on which analysts say Trump may want to focus on legacy-building.

Trump said on Monday he would not mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO and that he did not believe his relationship with the tech executive had put national security at risk.

Trump sees the unprecedented summit with Xi and Putin as possibly providing movement toward an agreement on nuclear arms control. But that is a non-starter for China, which has far fewer warheads than the others, Chinese analysts said.

The proposed three-way meeting has drawn comparisons, particularly in Russia, with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.

Such a framing is particularly worrisome for Ukraine, which is engaged in a four-year war with Russia.

The Kremlin said on Monday that the meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi would have a major impact on global affairs.

Some analysts say Xi could seek to take advantage of Trump’s political weakness after his election humbling.

Top of Beijing’s wish list is ensuring the US president doesn’t approve a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Trump has said he is holding the arms back as a “negotiating chip” with China.

“Xi just needs Trump to remain reluctant to revert toward a more competitive posture toward China for as long as possible,” said Jonathan Czin, a foreign policy analyst at the Brookings Institution, a US-based think tank, and a former director for China at the US National Security Council.

He said Beijing will be acutely aware that whoever succeeds Trump when his term ends in two years may be less accommodating and “will take whatever time it can get to fortify itself for the next round in the contest.”

Despite the frustration the US has voiced over Chinese implementation of the terms of a truce in a trade war that threatened the global economy last year, analysts like Kurt Tong, a former senior State Department official now with the Asia Group think tank, expect that deal to be further extended beyond its January 10 expiration.

“The two sides are quite incentivized to maintain this fragile stability … despite also having some disagreements,” said senior China analyst Chim Lee at the Economist Intelligence Unit. “They both have quite a lot to lose.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Trump says he might meet with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un in China
World.content:
HANDSHAKE. US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un shake hands before their one-on-one chat during the second US-North Korea summit at the Metropole Hotel in Hanoi, Vietnam February 27, 2019.

Trump says while departing the White House en route to the Philippines and China that any meeting would occur in China, and that the North Korean leader's presence was ultimately up to Chinese President Xi Jinping

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump said on Monday, November 16, he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China this week, an announcement that could dramatically reshape his trip through East Asia.

The president met the North Korean leader several times during his 2017-2021 first term in unprecedented direct diplomacy that failed to persuade Kim to give up his nuclear weapons.

Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in another meeting during his current term, but also previously previewed meetings with Kim that never took place, including during a trip to Asia last year.

Senior US officials have previously said he has no immediate plans for another meeting, while North Korea has said it sees no need for talks at this time and denounced hostile US policies.

Trump told reporters while departing the White House en route to the Philippines and China that any meeting would occur in China, and that the North Korean leader’s presence was ultimately up to Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“(Xi) was here … and we’re also going to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said.

“So that’ll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot.”

Trump added in reference to Kim: “He may come. I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”

North Korea’s mission to the United Nations did not respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks.

The Kremlin said on Monday a planned meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi on the sidelines of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in China would have a major impact on global affairs.

Trump said he would discuss denuclearization, Iran and Ukraine with Xi and Putin, as well as trade and the economy, but US officials and analysts have played down the possibility of a meaningful agreement emerging.

Russia’s Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying later on Monday that Putin could meet Kim if he comes to China.

North Korea has sent about 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion.

Victor Cha, head of the Korea program at Washington’s Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank, said Trump’s comments made clear he had asked Xi to bring Kim to China for a meeting.

“One could see a huge diplomatic victory for Kim if he were to share a stage with the US, Russia, China … the three other nuclear powers in Asia – in addition to any bilateral with Trump,” he said.

“The common narrative is that China would not want to distract from their hosting APEC but I think Xi’s global diplomacy offensive would probably be enhanced, in his mind, if he were bringing together all of the leaders for this extraordinary meeting,” Cha said.

Trump’s interest in renewed engagement with Kim comes seven years after their last summit ended without agreement when they failed to bridge differences over North Korea’s nuclear weapons and sanctions relief.

Since then, North Korea has significantly expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities while strengthening ties with Russia and China, and any willingness by Trump to make major concessions to Pyongyang risks creating friction with regional allies.

Trump has referred to North Korea as a nuclear power, a status allies in the region and the West have refused to recognize despite the dozens of nuclear warheads experts believe Pyongyang has built. – Rappler.com

World.title: Making P-pop history: SB19, BINI nominated for 2027 Grammys

The two P-pop groups are nominated under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category

MANILA, Philippines – History is made as P-pop groups SB19 and BINI are nominated for the 69th Grammy Awards.

The Recording Academy announced on Monday, November 16 (Manila time), that the two Filipino music acts were nominated under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category.

SB19 received a nomination for the song “VISA,” while BINI was nominated for “Unang Kilig.”

“From the Philippines to the world, thank you for believing in SB19 and standing with us as we carry Filipino music to the global stage!” SB19 said about its nomination.

“A historic moment for OPM, for Filipino music, and for everyone who believes in them. The girls are making history, and we couldn’t be prouder! Thank you to everyone who continues to support us!” BINI wrote.

Under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, SB19 and BINI are joined by fellow nominees, K-pop girl groups IVE (“BANG BANG”) and KiiiKiii (“404 (New Era)”), Japanese soloist LiSA (“Yes”), and Japanese kawaii metal band BABYMETAL and American rock outfit Polyphia (“Sunset Kiss”).

SB19 and BINI’s nominations come at a time when the two groups have achieved several major milestones all year.

BINI became the first-ever homegrown Filipino music act to perform at the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in April, while SB19 later achieved the same feat in July at Lollapalooza in Chicago.

SB19 will also be heading to Coachella in April 2027. Their inclusion in the lineup was just announced on November 11.

BINI, meanwhile, just wrapped up their 2026 BINI Signals World Tour in Taiwan on November 15. – Rappler.com

World.title: Climate advocates at COP31 urge probe into mass arrests at ASEAN protests
World.content:
PAX SILICA PROTEST. Militants gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on November 15, 2026, to protest the proposed Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump's visit to the 49th ASEAN Summit.

(1st UPDATE) Pax Silica, a key issue in the ASEAN protests, is opposed by many environmental and climate groups as well

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino climate justice and environmental advocates present at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, are urging an independent probe into the mass arrests of people who joined the protests against the ASEAN Summit back in Manila.

“Whether at COP31 or the ASEAN Summit, the government cannot speak of a peoples-centered future while treating their voices as a security threat,” read the groups’ statement released Monday, November 16.

They demanded “an independent, transparent and immediate investigation into the arbitrary mass arrests and illegal detention.”

Climate justice activists underscored the link between the fight for the planet and for human rights and democratic freedoms.

“We stand in solidarity with the victims of this police brutality, their families, and the communities demanding accountability,” they said.

A key issue in the ASEAN protests is the Philippines’ participation in the United States’ initiative Pax Silica

— a red flag for environmental groups for its components of building data centers and processing critical minerals.

The groups called on the government to “reject the Pax Silica initiative and all related projects affecting ancestral domains, respecting the right of affected indigenous peoples to free, prior, and informed consent.”

Some of the climate organizations listed as signatories in the statement have members or allies who were arrested in the protests in Manila.

The 49th ASEAN Summit, hosted by the Philippines, opened on Sunday, November 15. Hundreds who massed up for the protests in Metro Manila on Sunday were arrested. Nearly 300 people, delegates of Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan opposing the expected visit of US President Donald Trump, were arrested in Muntinlupa.

There were also arrests in Bulacan, Liwasang Bonifacio, Malate Church, and Welcome Rotonda in Quezon City, according to various local environmental and human rights groups.

“This is one of the largest mass arrests by the PNP (Philippine National Police) in recent years,” the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines noted. The network has started a donation drive for legal funds to support those arrested.

Even before the opening of the ASEAN Summit, thousands of students had already walked out and marched on the streets.

Meanwhile, Bishop Gerry Alminaza, climate champion of the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines, called on the government to “stop criminalizing the poor.”

“It is unconscionable that the poor are met with police violence when they should be met with justice, protection and action,” Alminaza, who was also in Turkey for the climate summit, said in a separate statement on Monday.

The statement was signed by the Klima Center of the Manila Observatory, Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, the Philippine Movement for Climate Justice, IBON International and other groups.

Among the fears surrounding Pax Silica is the threat of displacement of indigenous peoples. Human Rights Watch expressed concern over the displacement risk and noted that available information indicated that the Bases Conversion and Development Authority “never secured the free, prior, and informed consent of Aeta community members.”

“The Philippine government shouldn’t be trampling the rights of indigenous peoples and farmers in its haste to attract foreign technology investment,” Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch said on Monday.

“Development officials should provide information to people who will be affected and genuinely consult them before proceeding with the hub.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Lawmakers, groups slam November 15 arrests: Where is maximum tolerance?
World.content:
ASEAN PROTEST. Police arrest a protester in Liwasang Bonifacio during the opening of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, on November 15, 2026.

'Where is the maximum tolerance expected of police officers and their respect for freedom of speech and expression in these arrests?' asks Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima

MANILA, Philippines – Several personalities and groups raised concerns over the massive arrests of activists and media workers during Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Pax Silica-related protests in Metro Manila on Sunday, November 15.

Progressive group Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) condemned the arrests, saying that they contradict the statement of Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Nartatez Jr.’s claim that the summit’s opening was “generally peaceful.”

“It is the police who were caught on camera kicking down arrested protesters in Manila, manhandling Lakbayan delegates in Sucat, and torturing the detainees by threatening to handcuff those who refuse to have their mugshots taken. They acted like criminal thugs who ordered the throwing of human waste at the Liwasang Bonifacio to discourage people from gathering in the park,” BAYAN said on Monday, November 16.

“The police should also explain the use of deadly weapons such as nails and ice picks in puncturing the tires of the truck to be used for the protest in Manila,” the group added.

As of Sunday, the Manila Police District said at least 11 protesters were arrested by the police in Liwasang Bonifacio.

Most of the arrests in Metro Manila happened in Muntinlupa, where PNP nabbed 276 individuals. They were from Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan, who were heading to Liwasang Bonifacio to join other groups that protested against Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump’s expected arrival.

Some student journalists were also among those arrested.

Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima questioned the PNP’s supposed observance of maximum tolerance and respect for freedom of expression. She called for an investigation into the reported violence and alleged denial of detainees’ access to lawyers and family members.

“Where is the maximum tolerance expected of police officers and their respect for freedom of speech and expression in these arrests?” said De Lima.

“We strongly condemn these arrests and the disregard for protesters’ rights. We demand a thorough investigation into the reported unlawful acts committed by the arresting officers and that those responsible be held accountable. All protesters who have been illegally detained must be released immediately!” she added.

On Sunday, several progressive groups gathered outside Camp Bagong Diwa, Taguig City, to denounce the arrests.

“Pinapakita ng pag-aresto sa humigit-kumulang tatlong daang Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan kung kaninong interes ba talaga nagsisilbi ang rehimeng US-Marcos. Sa pagbisita ni Trump, pinapakita talaga na nasa interes ng mga dayuhang bansa ang interes nila,” human rights advocate Charm Maranan said.

(The arrest of almost 300 people of Lakbayani ng Timog Katagulan shows where the interest of the US-Marcos regime truly lies. With Trump’s visit, it just shows that their interest lies in a foreign country.)

The Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan protest march kicked off in Los Baños, Laguna, on November 12, with progressive groups led by BAYAN Timog Katagalugan.

Throughout the march, activist groups and alternative media outlets reported multiple instances of harassment from the police. This included blocking the march’s path, allegedly sabotaging the protest vehicles’ tires, alleged violent manhandling of arrested protesters, and denial of the Commission on Human Rights and lawyers’ entry to police stations.

Call for accountability

“Malinaw na ginagarantiya ng Saligang Batas ang kalayaan nating magpahayag at mapayapang magtipon. Ang kakayahan ng mamamayang pumuna at manawagan ng pagbabago ang patunay na buhay ang ating demokrasya,” said Akbayan Representative Chel Diokno.

(It’s clear that the Constitution guarantees our freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The ability of the citizens to redress their grievances and call for change is proof that our democracy is alive.)

Meanwhile, the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) demanded the immediate release of individuals detained for participating in or covering the protests. The group also appealed to fellow lawyers to provide legal assistance to those arrested, calling on them to “help secure the freedom of the arrestees.”

“While we have already dispatched quick reaction teams to assist the detainees, we need more lawyers to assist them. And we are calling [on] our people’s lawyers to once again rise to the occasion. Our brave clients need brave lawyers,” said NUPL president Ephraim Cortez.

Karapatan secretary general Cristina Palabay also pushed for accountability from police personnel and officers involved in the reported assaults.

“Protestors must be immediately released,” Palabay asserted, urging authorities to guarantee the arrested’s access to legal counsel, relatives, and medical assistance while in custody.

On a similar note, the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines also pressed authorities to stop the violence against media workers, noting the importance of peaceful assembly and press freedom.

“Journalists must be allowed to exercise their duty to cover public events, document abuses, and report the stories of those who take to the streets,” the union stated. – Ren Enano and Rhen Peñada/Rappler.com

Rena Eñano and Rhen Peñada are Rappler volunteers. Eñano is a senior literature student from Ateneo de Manila University, while Peñada is a third-year information technology student from Polytechnic University of the Philippines Sta. Rosa, Laguna Campus.

World.title: Dangerous heat index forecast in 3 PH areas on Nov. 17
World.content:
INQUIRER file image

MANILA, Philippines — Three areas in the country are expected to experience dangerous heat indices of up to 42°C on Tuesday, Nov. 17, the state weather bureau reported.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) identified these areas as Puerto Princesa City, Palawan; Borongan, Eastern Samar; and Zamboanga City, Zamboanga del Sur.

READ: Fair weather expected in PH on Nov. 17

Article continues after this 

According to Pagasa, the heat index refers to the level of discomfort a person experiences due to the combined effects of temperature and air humidity.

Heat indices from 42°C to 51°C fall under the “danger” threshold, as prolonged sun exposure can cause heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and even heat stroke.

In Metro Manila, Pagasa forecast a heat index of 38°C at the weather station in Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Pasay City and 37°C at the Science Garden in Quezon City.

These fall under the “extreme caution” category, which covers heat indices from 33°C to 41°C.

Under this threshold, heat cramps and heat exhaustion may occur, while continued activity in the heat can also lead to heat stroke.

Article continues after this 

READ: No LPA, cyclone expected to form in PH in 3 days

To avoid health complications, the public is advised to limit time outdoors; drink plenty of water; avoid tea, coffee, soft drinks, and alcohol; use an umbrella, hat, and clothing with sleeves; and perform strenuous activities during the cooler hours of the day. /mcm

World.title: Magsaysay awardee backs Chin survivors’ quest for justice in PH courts
World.content:
Bo Kyi —RMAF PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines —A Ramon Magsaysay Awardee has voiced solidarity with Chin survivors seeking justice before local courts in the Philippines against what was described as “continuing Myanmar military atrocities.”

Bo Kyi, a human rights defender and former political prisoner in Myanmar, called on Philippine officials on Sunday, Nov. 15, to uphold the rule of law and prosecute the junta for war crimes.

“I stand in solidarity with the Chin Human Rights Organization (CHRO) and Chin survivors,” he said as he accepted the award, which is widely considered as Asia’s response to the Nobel Peace Prize.

Article continues after this 

“Their unflinching courage reminds us that justice knows no borders,” he said, pointing out that “Southeast Asia must not become a safe haven for perpetrators of serious violations of international law.”

READ: Myanmar ex-political prisoner Bo Kyi receives Ramon Magsaysay Award

His appeal came after five Chin complainants asked the Court of Appeals on Nov. 3 to compel the Department of Justice (DOJ) to formally docket and investigate a war crimes complaint against Myanmar junta chief Senior Gen. Min Aung Hlaing and nine other military officers.

Filed on Oct. 25, 2023, under the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity, the complaint has remained undocketed for three years.

Bo Kyi was imprisoned twice for his role in Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement and spent more than seven years behind bars.

Article continues after this 

After his release in 1998, he fled across the border to Thailand, where, in March 2000, he and fellow former political prisoners co-founded the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners.

Bo Kyi expressed hope that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the rest of the international community will help restore democracy, human rights and justice in Myanmar and secure the release of all political prisoners, including State Counsellor Daw Aung San Suu Kyi./dp

World.title: Sara Duterte camp links alleged threat to ex-staff to Marcos admin
World.content:
Atty. Paolo Panelo Jr. – Screengrab from video of the Office of the Vice President

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s camp on Tuesday raised concerns over an alleged threat to the life of her former household staff, saying it may be part of another “relentless campaign” by the Marcos administration against her.

Her legal counsel, Atty. Paolo Panelo, said Duterte received a message at 11:19 p.m. on Nov. 16 from her former household staff member, who asked for help and rescue in Manila.

He said the unnamed staff member was in the custody of certain individuals who threatened their life and asked them to sign a document, which they refused to do.

Article continues after this 

READ: Duterte: NBI tried to ‘forcibly’ bring ex-Davao info officer to Manila

Panelo likened the incident to what happened to Jefry Tupas, former Davao City chief information officer. Former police officer Rodulfo Gracioso earlier alleged that he had handed over suitcases of money to Tupas for Duterte.

“What makes this incident particularly concerning is its striking similarity to what happened to Jefry Tupas, who was previously told by agents of the National Bureau of Investigation on September 29, 2026, that there were threats to his life and was subsequently subjected to an attempt to bring him to Manila,” Panelo said in a statement.

Panelo also expressed concern over the government’s “efforts” to coerce individuals into becoming “false witnesses” against Duterte, “weaponize state agencies, and undermine the rule of law for political ends.”

“We are deeply concerned that this incident may be part of what we believe to be a relentless campaign by the Marcos administration, utilizing state institutions like the NBI, against the Vice President,” Panelo added.

Article continues after this 

Panelo also said the whereabouts of the former household staff member remained unknown and that their safety and well-being had yet to be verified.

READ: NBI recommends obstruction of justice raps vs Jefry Tupas

Article continues after this 

Tupas was summoned by the NBI to shed light on Gracioso’s allegations but submitted a counter-affidavit through his lawyer.

Tupas then alleged that the bureau “initiated efforts” to bring him to Manila after agents who went to his house supposedly offered him security, saying they had received information that he would be abducted by the Dutertes.

Matibag earlier said it was Tupas who disclosed that there were threats to his life, not the bureau’s agents.

Matibag’s response

Responding to Panelo’s statement, Matibag said he would check the alleged threats raised by Duterte’s camp.

“Maybe they should file a formal complaint, [and not show it on social media],” Matibag told the INQUIRER in a Viber message.

“And they have to show the message and have it authenticated and validated,” he added.

World.title: Baguio folk urged to avoid panic buying, water hoarding
World.content:
Residents in Baguio City are urged to practice responsible water consumption and avoid unnecessary wastage as authorities prepare for the possible effects of Super El Niño. Photo by Maureen Matayew

BAGUIO CITY—The Baguio Water District (BWD) on Monday urged residents to avoid panic buying and hoarding water amid concerns over the possible effects of Super El Niño, warning that unnecessary stockpiling could put additional pressure on available water resources.

According to BWD General Manager Engr. Salvador Royeca, a sudden increase in water consumption could make it more difficult to distribute available supply equitably, particularly during the dry months.

Royeca acknowledged public concerns over a possible water shortage but urged households and business establishments to conserve water instead of stockpiling it out of fear.

Article continues after this 

READ: Food stockpiling eyed amid El Niño other crises

He said rainfall brought by the southwest monsoon in August helped replenish the district’s underground and open water sources, improving water availability and providing additional reserves ahead of the possible effects of El Niño.

However, he stressed that the improved water supply should not lead to complacency, as the district still needs to manage its resources carefully in preparation for the dry season.

BWD continues to implement measures to protect and manage its water resources while reminding consumers to avoid unnecessary consumption and wastage, particularly of potable water.

Customers experiencing water supply concerns are also encouraged to report them through the district’s official communication channels for assessment and appropriate action.

Royeca noted that water conservation should remain a daily practice regardless of weather conditions. /dp

World.title: Food stockpiling eyed amid El Niño, other crises
World.content:
STAPLE SUPPLY Workers stock bags of rice at the National Food Authority warehouse in Valenzuela City in this photo taken in February. The Philippines is proposing a regional mechanism for Asean member states to stockpile food to prepare for El Niño and other crises. —Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines plans to propose a regional mechanism for stockpiling food and staple grains, as Southeast Asia braces for the impact of crises, including a potentially severe El Niño episode.

So far, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) has agreed to strengthen cooperation on agricultural productivity, including the exchange of best practices in farming technologies.

While the proposed food stockpile has yet to be formally discussed, Trade Secretary Cristina Roque said the Philippines intends to raise the idea with other Asean member states.

Article continues after this 

“Definitely, we will suggest that concept,” Roque said on Monday during a briefing on the results of the final Asean economic ministers’ meeting under the Philippines’ chairship. “That has not been discussed, but we can bring it to the table.”

READ: DA: El Niño puts food supply under pressure

She emphasized that existing Asean commitments could already help stabilize food supplies across member states and prevent prices from surging.

Such cooperation becomes particularly crucial during periods of crisis, Roque said.

One pressing concern is El Niño, which threatens to disrupt agricultural production across Southeast Asia through prolonged drought, extreme heat and changing rainfall patterns.

Article continues after this 

In its September 2026 Asian Development Outlook, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) warned that the ongoing El Niño could become one of the strongest on record, with its effects expected to peak around this month and the greatest economic impact likely to be felt in 2027.

READ: Why Philippine agriculture matters, even when budgets are tight

Article continues after this 

The report identified the southern Philippines, Brunei and Singapore as among the areas facing the most immediate rainfall risks, alongside parts of Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam.

According to the ADB, El Niño-related dry spells during planting seasons have historically reduced rainfed rice yields in the Philippines and Vietnam’s Mekong River Delta, while disruptions to agricultural output could drive up food prices across import-dependent economies.

Data from the Department of Agriculture (DA), on the other hand, said that as of Nov. 11, damage and losses caused by El Niño on rice, corn, cassava, high value crops, and livestock and poultry was at P9.99 billion, with 324,327 farmers and 323,419 hectares of agricultural areas affected.

The information was based on the field assessment conducted by DA regional field offices in Cordillera, Ilocos, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, Bicol, Western Visayas, Negros Island, Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Davao Region, Soccsksargen and Caraga.

Oil reserve

On the energy front, Roque reiterated that four Asean member states have already signed on to the oil stockpiling plan initiated by the Philippines. (See related story on this page.)

Joining the Philippines are Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia. The United Arab Emirates, while not an Asean member, has also agreed to make some of its oil reserves available for storage in a participating country.

In a briefing last month, Roque said that six countries had expressed support for the plan. Not mentioned in Monday’s briefing were Thailand and Vietnam.

Roque said that not every Asean member state had to 

The bloc will now review the study conducted by the Economic Research Institute for Asean and East Asia before the plan can be activated.

“This will enable Asean member states to manage supply disruptions and reduce risks to businesses and consumers during periods of global uncertainties,” she added.

Roque also said that all 11 members of the regional bloc had agreed on the Asean Power Grid memorandum of understanding (MOU), which lays down the framework for cross-border electricity projects and trade.

In a statement, the Department of Energy said the MOU would provide a strengthened framework for developing power interconnections and progressively advancing multilateral electricity trade.

World.title: SC strikes down portions of Magna Carta of seafarers
World.content:
Inquirer photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has struck down as unconstitutional the provisions of the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers requiring workers to post a bond pending resolution of labor cases, as well as restricting legal remedies, as these violate due process.

The high tribunal, in an en banc session on Nov. 11, partially granted five consolidated petitions filed by various seafarers’ groups. The decision has yet to be made public.

Among the petitioners were labor leader Sonny Matula and maritime and labor organizations Philippine Association of Maritime Institutions, Inc., Concerned Seafarers of the Philippines (CSP) and Association of Marine Officers & Ratings Inc.

Article continues after this 

In a statement, Xavier Bayoneta, CSP chair, welcomed the Supreme Court ruling, saying “It demonstrates the strength of the unity among Filipino seafarers, their families, and the entire nation, that will pave the way for us to achieve victory in our fight for our rights.”

According to the high court, Section 59 of Republic Act No. 12021 violated the equal protection clauses of the Constitution. It said this added a financial burden on seafarers awaiting judgment of labor disputes and subjected them to a “disadvantage not similarly imposed on other workers.”

READ: Marcos signs Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers into law

Also declared unconstitutional and void was Sec. 60 as it imposed limits to legal representation of seafarers, including a 10-percent ceiling on fees.

The high court, however, upheld the constitutionality of Sections 75, 76 and 78, which were also challenged by the petitioners, noting that they do not violate the right to academic freedom under the Charter.

RA 12021 was signed into law by President Marcos in 2024 after being on the back burner for years. Some seafarers’ groups, however, criticized it for containing “antiseafarer” provisions. /cb

World.title: Probe arrests in Asean rally, bishop urges CHR
World.content:
During protests surrounding the Asean Summit on Nov. 15, 2026, a police barricade led to an altercation between protesters and police officers, with both sides violently pushing and shoving each other. —Photo by Zacarian Sarao

MANILA, Philippines — Bishop Gerardo Alminaza of San Carlos, Negros Occidental, on Monday urged the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) to investigate the arrest of more than 200 persons in rallies in Muntinlupa City and Manila on the opening of the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) the day before.

On Sunday night, lawyers were barred from speaking with the 211 individuals at Police’s Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City, where they were brought following their arrest at the People’s Park in Muntinlupa for reportedly holding a rally without a permit.

They were set to march toward Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila and join mass protests against the controversial Pax Silica project and US President Donald Trump, who is arriving on the summit’s last day on Wednesday.

Article continues after this 

READ: Over 300 protesters vs Asean meet held

“I urge the Commission on Human Rights and other competent, independent bodies to investigate the arrests and all reported abuses, including those involving journalists and Church property,” Alminaza said. Police said minors were rescued from the rally.

The CHR told the Inquirer that it had opened an investigation of the incidents, including the arrest of nine other protesters following a scuffle with policemen in Manila on Sunday.

READ: Protesters, police clash in Manila during Asean Summit protest

The Conveners Against Tyranny and the August Twenty-One Movement said the arrests were reminiscent of the martial law years.

Article continues after this 

On Monday, protests against the proposed establishment of a Pax Silica hub in New Clark City continued in Manila, but were notably calmer as all programs were only within the grounds of Liwasang Bonifacio.

“The reason I am here is that we are opposing the foreigners because of their project in our area,’’ Nelson de Guzman, an elder from Sitio Kalangitan in Capas, Tarlac and leader of the Ayta Hung-ey, told reporters. —With reports from Kurt dela Peña and Cristina Baclig

World.title: Yangon Condo Raid Reveals Myanmar’s Cyber Scam Sector Thriving in Commercial Capital
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has arrested 106 suspected online scammers in Yangon, signaling the country’s cyber-fraud epidemic has spread from the lawless borderlands to its largest city.

The regime announced Saturday that its forces raided Golden River Residence Condo in Yangon’s Thaketa Township on November 12, arresting 52 Chinese naionals, eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar citizens from multiple apartments.

The arrests come as Naypyitaw and Beijing trumpet crackdowns on cyber-fraud syndicates in notorious border scam hubs.

Those reportedly detained included a high-profile target of China’s Public Security Ministry — the first arrest of a warranted Chinese scammer in Myanmar in months. Also seized from the condo were over 120 computers and laptops and nearly 200 mobile phones.

Authorities said the gang ran online investment fraud schemes targeting Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian citizens, while separate Telegram-based operations targeted victims in Brazil and Colombia through fake e-commerce platforms.

The raid came shortly after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi pressed Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe to intensify efforts to combat scams and prevent a “resurgence of chaos” in Karen State’s Myawaddy crime hub on the Thai border.

Analysts say the Yangon bust signals a growing shift of Myanmar’s online scam industry from border enclaves to urban centers.

After the 2024 collapse of notorious fraud compounds in northern Shan State’s Laukkai and crackdowns along the Chinese and Thai borders, many scam syndicates dispersed in small, mobile operations through remote eastern and southern Shan, according to regime arrest reports and independent monitors.

However, many that had fled to Myawaddy have since moved deeper into the country under the protection of regime-aligned militias and other armed groups.

In September, 28 foreign and Myanmar nationals were arrested in Mandalay — the country’s second city — over an online gemstone scam involving Chinese, Indonesian and Malaysian suspects. The gang was charged with selling fake jade products via livestream and transferring the profits to accounts in Indonesia and Malaysia.

While the Nov. 12 raid was the first of its kind reported in Yangon, former fraudsters told The Irrawaddy that scam operations have long established a foothold in the commercial capital, targeting overseas victims through operations based in condominiums, housing estates and companies registered as legitimate businesses.

Analysts say enforcement efforts target low-level operators while overlooking the networks and militias behind the multibillion-dollar industry. Among them is the regime-aligned Karen Border Guard Force, whose Western-sanctioned leaders remain untouched even as the regime hails the demolition of scam compounds in Myawaddy.

World.title: ASEAN Seeks ‘Calibrated Engagement’ With Myanmar: Statement
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—Southeast Asian leaders agreed Sunday on pursuing a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar’s post-coup government, according to a joint statement, as the regional bloc seeks a path towards normalization.

Myanmar is still a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but it has been frozen out of high-level meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar in an effort to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC) plan aimed at ending the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila adopted that language in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground,” according to the joint statement.

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the statement said.

The five-point plan has yielded little in the half-decade since it was agreed to, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos conceding at a May summit he had not seen “any progress in Myanmar.”

On Sunday, in opening remarks at an ASEAN leaders’ retreat in Manila, he repeated a question he had posed to the group six months earlier: “What more can we do for Myanmar?”

“I hope our session leads to practical and forward-looking discussions on how we can further advance the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, make our efforts more responsive to the realities on the ground, and support a peaceful, inclusive, Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process,” he said.

The ASEAN bloc’s rotating chair will pass at the end of this year from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalizing ties with Myanmar.

In 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.

“We believe it’s crucial to have someone at the table who can really talk on policy issues because engagement requires that they have someone who can really convey to us the position of Myanmar,” Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told AFP in Singapore on November 5.

“This is not about… recognizing… upgrading their position. But I think in reality, what is important is that we need someone at the table who can speak on behalf of Myanmar.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.

Three years after the first drone bombs fell on Hopang, the town has changed beyond recognition for longtime residents.

During Operation 1027, the MNDAA and TNLA went on to seize almost the whole of northern Shan State including the capital Lashio and all vital trade routes with China.

However, under strong Chinese pressure, in 2025 the ethnic armies were forced to halt fighting the Myanmar military and hand back several liberated towns to the regime.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: Tokayev Meets Central Election Commission Chairman Ahead of Nov. 29 Maslikhat Elections
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Chairman of the Central Election Commission Nurlan Abdirov to discuss preparations for early elections of deputies to maslikhats at all levels, scheduled for Nov. 29, according to the presidential press service.

Abdirov briefed Tokayev on the work of election authorities ahead of the vote. Tokayev stressed the importance of conducting the elections in line with the constitutional principle of Law and Order and ensuring equal conditions for all candidates and political parties.

He also noted that the upcoming renewal of the deputy corps would significantly strengthen the work of local representative bodies.

Earlier, while inspecting polling stations across the country’s regions, Abdirov also said Kazakhstan has 228 maslikhats at various levels, with more than 9,000 candidates competing for 3,447 seats.

He highlighted efforts to prepare members of district election commissions, including training seminars and two rounds of testing designed to assess both the quality of training organised by territorial election commissions and the effectiveness of the seminars themselves.

“I instructed territorial election commissions to continue training election commission members in the remaining time before the elections. This is important to ensure that the electoral campaign is conducted in strict compliance with the law, with openness and transparency,” Abdirov said.

He added that the Central Election Commission was paying particular attention to organizing training seminars during visits to the regions.

World.title: Kazakhstan Seeks to Develop Middle Corridor as Green Trade Route Between Asia and Europe
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to strengthen the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, as a key trade link between Asia and Europe, focusing on increasing freight volumes, digitalizing logistics and introducing environmental standards.

These priorities were discussed at a Nov. 16 special session organized by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration and QazTrade during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

The Middle Corridor is becoming an increasingly important route for international trade. Stretching nearly 7,000 kilometers, it passes through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea and the countries of the South Caucasus, providing access to European markets. Cargo delivery along the route takes an average of 15 to 20 days, making it a competitive alternative to traditional maritime shipping.

Freight volumes have increased significantly in recent years. In 2020, the route carried 800,000 tons of cargo, compared with 4.5 million tons in 2024, representing more than a fivefold increase.

Container traffic has also continued to grow. In 2025, approximately 77,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) were transported along the route, a 36% increase compared with the previous year. During the first eight months of 2026, container traffic reached 44,200 TEUs. Meanwhile, 419 container trains departed from China, an 84% increase compared with the same period in 2025.

However, the route’s development is no longer measured solely by delivery times and freight volumes. As environmental requirements in international trade become more stringent, the sustainability of transport and logistics operations is gaining importance.

Speaking at the session, Vice Minister of Trade and Integration Zhanel Kushukova said Kazakhstan’s export competitiveness depended not only on the environmental characteristics of its products but also on the efficiency of international logistics.

“The competitiveness of our exports depends not only on how environmentally friendly the production process is. It is also determined by how efficiently, quickly and sustainably we can deliver goods to international markets,” Kushukova said.

According to Kushukova, Kazakhstan views the Trans-Caspian route not merely as an alternative transport direction, but as an emerging green corridor that should meet the evolving requirements of international trade.

One example is the Port of Kuryk on Kazakhstan’s Caspian coast. The port has received EcoPorts certification, confirming the implementation of European approaches to environmental management in port operations. It has also been certified under the international ISO 14001 environmental management standard.

For Kazakh exporters, the development of such infrastructure has practical implications. Environmental standards are increasingly taken into account when organizing international supply chains, making it important for transport routes to combine reliability and efficiency with environmental responsibility.

Digitalization is another priority for the Middle Corridor. Efforts include aligning procedures among participating countries, improving transport transparency and establishing a unified digital environment. These measures are expected to help businesses track cargo movements, plan delivery times and reduce administrative obstacles at border crossings.

Participants in the session also discussed increasing the route’s capacity, introducing environmentally friendly solutions and strengthening cooperation between transport and trade organisations. Kushukova emphasised that further development of the TITR would require coordinated efforts from all countries involved in transportation along the route.

World.title: Kazakhstan Discusses Healthcare Investment, Pharmaceutical Production With International Businesses
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov discussed investment opportunities and pharmaceutical industry development with international businesses during a Nov. 16 meeting of the Council for Improving the Investment Climate, according to the Prime Minister’s press service.

The meeting focused on attracting investment, introducing innovations in healthcare, expanding pharmaceutical production, improving access to modern treatment methods and creating more favourable conditions for investors.

Bektenov noted that protecting public health had been enshrined in Kazakhstan’s Constitution for the first time.

“In his recent state-of-the-nation address, the Head of State also set the task of accelerating the construction of medical facilities with the involvement of private capital. To achieve these goals, the government is implementing the Healthcare Development Concept through 2029 and the Healthcare Infrastructure Development Concept for 2024-2030. These strategic documents provide for improving medical care, introducing innovative technologies and strengthening the pharmaceutical supply system,” Bektenov said.

Healthcare infrastructure and pharmaceutical investment

According to the Prime Minister’s press service, Kazakhstan’s life expectancy has approached 76 years. The Rural Healthcare Modernization project has helped make medical services available to approximately one million people.
