World.title: WA Labor MP faces police scrutiny amid US lawsuit over $1m loan
World.content:
WA Police are assessing a complaint related to embattled Labor MP Jags Krishnan’s financial affairs, including an allegation of fraud.

Questions about the business dealings of the Riverton MP and his disclosures to parliament about his debts have been growing since it emerged he was being sued in the United States over a million-dollar loan.

He has vowed to "vigorously defend" his position and has launched a defamation case in response.

WA Labor MP vows to 'vigorously defend' US lawsuit A Western Australian MP embroiled in a legal dispute over a million-dollar loan in the United States insists everything he did was above board.

Yesterday, Premier Roger Cook defended the government's reluctance to let parliament's Procedure and Privileges Committee conduct an inquiry into Dr Krishnan's affairs, saying there was no evidence to justify such an investigation.

Now WA Police have confirmed they are looking into his financial dealings dating back to 2023.

"On Saturday, 14 November 2026, police received a report alleging fraudulent conduct relating to financial matters between 2023 and 2026," a police spokesperson said.

"Police have commenced an assessment of materials provided."

Police are looking into Jags Krishnan's financial dealings back to 2023. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

Dr Krishnan's lawyer Martin Bennett has been contacted for comment. The ABC does not suggest that Dr Jags is guilty of any criminal offence.

Dr Krishnan last week told state parliament he was in the final process of selling a network of doctors' surgeries he had built and that "all outstanding matters will be resolved upon settlement".

Jags Krishnan has been the Labor MP for the southern suburbs seat of Riverton since 2021. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"I have taken legal advice about my parliamentary declarations and I am confident that these are in order," he said.

Colleagues shield Labor MP Jags Krishnan from media Journalists trying to ask questions about the business dealings of Riverton MP Jags Krishnan are blocked by a group of his colleagues outside state parliament.

Mr Cook has said he did not believe Dr Krishnan had any obligation to provide an explanation of his business dealings to parliament.

"Members of parliament, through their own private undertakings, have these issues all the time," the premier said.

"And Dr [Krishnan] has undertaken to meet all the requirements … for members of parliament to one, be transparent, and two, to assure the people of Western Australia that these issues do not interfere with their obligations and duties."

World.title: Breaking: David Jones creditors owed almost half a billion dollars
World.content:
It's been revealed that David Jones is deeply in debt, with its liabilities tallied so far reaching almost half a billion dollars.

The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff.

The debts are being revealed right now at the first creditors' meeting for the embattled department store, which was placed into voluntary administration earlier this month.

It's already been announced that about half of its stores nationally will close.

Administrators are now trying to find a buyer for David Jones to keep the legacy brand alive.

David Jones was placed in voluntary administration on November 5.

The 188-year-old department store's collapse came after negotiations broke down with the owner of key shopping centre chain Westfield, Scentre Group, which confirmed David Jones was behind on its rent since September.

Store suppliers have also told ABC News about how they had been struggling to get invoices paid for months. Some have debts owed of more than $100,000.

McGrath Nicol's role as voluntary administrator is now to tally the company's debts and possibly find a buyer to recoup cash for entities owed money, such as suppliers and landlords.

The retailer's key secured lender, Hilco, will be first in line to claw back money. It has appointed a receiver, FTI Consulting, to David Jones and now controls its day-to-day operations.

Last week, the receiver confirmed it is closing 19 of the retailer's 38 stores by the end of 2027.

David Jones stores set to close The retailer, which has 38 stores nationally, was placed in voluntary administration less than a week ago.

FTI has not confirmed how many jobs will go as a result of the store closures, with the main retail union estimating it could be 2,000.

David Jones has more than 6,000 staff in total.

McGrath Nicol has previously talked up interest in the business, with its partner describing interest from buyers as "extraordinary".

Expressions of interest closed on Friday, with it expected to take at least a month for a buyer to be formally announced.

World.title: Breaking: Sam Wood's lawyers to argue most recent bail denial was 'plainly unjust'
World.content:
Former reality star Sam Wood's fight for bail is now being heard in Queensland's Court of Appeal as his lawyers are expected to argue the most recent denial was "plainly unjust".

The fitness influencer is charged with assaulting and strangling his wife on the Sunshine Coast in October.

Mr Wood intends to contest the allegations.

After two failed bail bids Mr Wood's legal team filed an appeal to challenge the most recent denial by a Supreme Court judge earlier this month.

Today his lawyers are expected to say that Justice Patrick McCafferty's decision to refuse bail was "unreasonable".

They will also argue the judge failed to consider whether the bail conditions proposed would reduce the risk of further offending to an acceptable level.

Mr Wood, who normally resides in Melbourne, was staying at a Noosa apartment complex last month, when he was arrested.

At his bail application, the court heard he allegedly became involved in an argument with his wife and 21-year-old stepdaughter about packing after consuming "several drinks".

During this confrontation, the court heard it is alleged he told the pair they can "both die".

He then allegedly grabbed his wife by the throat, and pushed her against a wall, then onto the floor, and banged her head on the way down.

World.title: Dusty the dog's days as Hobart's 'deputy mayor' could be numbered
World.content:
Hobart's new council may have chosen its deputy lord mayor, but the role's unofficial holder, a dog named Dusty, may no longer be welcome in the council chambers.

During his campaign, newly elected lord mayor Charles Wooley regularly referred to his kelpie-bulldog-shar pei cross as his "deputy".

Charles Wooley regularly referred to Dusty as his "deputy" during his election campaign. (Facebook: Charles Wooley)

The dog was wandering around the chamber during the Hobart City Council's first meeting on Monday night, when councillor Mike Dutta interrupted proceedings.

"Excuse me, I have a bit of a problem with dogs because I was bitten once and I feel very uncomfortable," Cr Dutta said.

Mike Dutta said Dusty's presence in the chamber was unsettling him, as he had once been bitten by another dog. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Cr Wooley then spent some time trying to call over Dusty and make him sit and stay, describing his behaviour as "unusual".

"I won't bring him in again if you have a problem with dogs," the lord mayor said.

The interaction took place after the council decided on who would be the actual deputy lord mayor, with independent John Kelly securing the spot over Greens candidate Bill Harvey, five votes to four.

John Kelly, former owner of the State Cinema in Hobart, is the new deputy lord mayor. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Cr Kelly, a fifth-generation Hobartian, campaigned on a platform of protecting heritage, preserving the natural environment, supporting small businesses and the economy, fair rates, and a united and financially disciplined council.

He was also vocal about improved transport and access, including through a light rail.

"Rail or fail, I'm thinking," he posted during his campaign.

Hobart City councillors swearing in ceremony, (left to right) Zelinda Sherlock, Ryan Posselt, Simon Behrakis, Harvey Lennon (part obscured), John Kelly, Mike Dutta, Bill Harvey, Charles Wooley, Louise Elliot. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Speaking on 936 Radio Hobart Drive, Cr Kelly said he felt good about the future of the city, and looked forward to "jumping in the seat and getting on with business".

"Hobart, we're really at the crossroads here, now. We've got a big future ahead of us," he said.

"I'm very known for being frugal, and I look forward to bringing that more into the council."

Cr Kelly 'on the same song sheet' as lord mayor

Former Hobart councillor Ben Lohberger was chosen as deputy lord mayor at the local government elections but did not secure enough votes to earn a seat on the council, making him ineligible — a rare occurrence in recent elections.

Hobart avoids all-male council but deputy mayor-elect fails to win seat Two women, Louise Elliot and Zelinda Sherlock, are elected to Hobart City Council, while the deputy mayor-elect, Ben Lohberger, has failed to win a council seat and will not be able to serve.

The previous council was marred by in-fighting, code of donduct complaints and social media stand-offs, a tone that carried into the recent elections.

Cr Kelly said people needed to grow up. He believed the council now slimming down from 12 elected members to nine would help.

"There's less talking heads in the chamber, which will make things more efficient," he said.

"Sure, I encourage robust debate, and that's all part of politics, but underlying all that … we've just got to have some mutual respect and listen to all opinions."

Charles Wooley at the swearing-in ceremony for the new city council. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Cr Kelly has never worked with incoming Lord Mayor Charles Wooley, but said provided there was good intent and sound judgement, he looked forward to it.

"We're on the same song sheet," he said.

"He's got an appetite for seeing the city progress and [to] not be too ideological in any particular area and just have a balanced approach to the opportunities we've got."

Both Cr Kelly and Cr Harvey were given three minutes to address their fellow councillors before the votes were anonymously cast.

Cr Harvey drew on his experience as a councillor and chair since first being elected in 2007, as well as his background in the not-for-profit sector, and qualifications in town planning, politics, geography and environmental management.

Hobart City councillor Bill Harvey was unsuccessful for the deputy lord mayor position. (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers )

"I'm reliable, I have a good reputation for what I do, no-one's criticised me very much at all over these years for how I operate," he said.

" I also remind people that I have had no codes of conduct against me. "

Cr Kelly, meanwhile, referred to his achievements in business and community connections.

"[It] gives me a deep understanding of the city, its challenges and what we need to do to move forward as a team," he said.

After Cr Kelly's appointment was announced, Cr Harvey stood up, joking that he dissented, before congratulating him.

"It was a fair vote round the table. I can't say the best person won, because that's not necessarily the way I roll," he said.

"However, well done. Congratulations on being elected deputy lord mayor of Hobart."

The new planning committee includes the lord mayor and deputy, and councillors Simon Behrakis, Louise Elliot and Harvey Lennon, with the remaining four members serving as nominees, making for a more conservative line-up than the previous term.

World.title: Live: Victorian Premier Ben Carroll grilled over Labor's poor polling results
World.content:
Vision Australia is calling on the next Victorian government to become the first state in the country to fund an autonomous accessible taxi pilot program.

Under current laws, an automated driving system (ADS) permit is required to operate an automated vehicle in automated mode for testing or development purposes.

But Vision Australia’s Chris Edwards says a dedicated driverless taxi pilot would test the practical benefits for all people who cannot drive and provide evidence to guide future transport planning.

“Whether someone is travelling to work, going to a medical appointment or visiting family and friends, the ability to travel independently is pivotal,” said Mr Edwards. “We can see from the national data that only around half of people with disability are currently able to use all forms of public transport without difficulty, so there is certainly room for improvement. "As Victorians we want to see how this technology could support and build upon existing transport options for people with low vision or who are blind."

Self-driving taxis are currently in use in several cities internationally. (Unsplash: Aamy Dugiere)

Self-driving robotaxis are already in use internationally on the streets of London, San Francisco and Beijing as rideshare companies expand into driverless transport.

World.title: Mayor pushes for inquiry into mining licence approvals
World.content:
A regional Victorian council is pushing for an inquiry into the granting of mining licences for projects across Western Victoria.

Multiple licences have been granted for controversial projects to mine rare earth minerals in the Wimmera and Mallee across the next few decades.

These include the VHM Minerals Sands project in the small farming town of Lalbert, Astron's Donald Rare Earth and Minerals Sands project and WIM Resource's Avonbank Mineral Sands project.

Horsham Rural City Council Mayor Brian Klowss said the community was concerned and asking a lot of questions about the Avonbank mine, which could begin construction next year pending final approvals.

"I think it's getting to the point where we nearly need an inquiry into the granting of these mining licences and what's going on," Cr Klowss said.

" It's beyond a joke. "

The mine site is near Dooen, a rural village in the Wimmera region. (Supplied: WIM Resource)

Last month, Resource Victoria granted a 20-year mining licence to the Avonbank mine set to be located in Dooen, 15 kilometres north-east of Horsham, including approvals to mine heavy mineral sands such as zircon, titanium and rare earth elements.

The site will cover about 3,400 hectares, with the Chinese-backed company planning to mine around the clock for 36 years for materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy infrastructure.

Horsham Rural City Council had previously raised concerns about the mine, including dust issues, use of the nearby intermodal freight hub and rehabilitation prospects for agricultural land.

Cr Klowss said the community felt their voices had not been heard and urged whichever party forms government after the state election to start listening to locals.

"That's what we want and that's what's not happening," he said.

"It's like these things are being pushed on our community and we're not getting a say and we're not even getting consulted about it."

Brian Klowss says the situation is "beyond a joke". (ABC News: Gillian Aeria)

Planning scheme changes

These concerns were exacerbated when council discovered Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny had changed the Horsham Planning Scheme for the Avonbank project without consultation.

WIM Resource requested an amendment to allow for provisions to help with mineral sands processing and other infrastructure required to support the project.

As part of the amendment, the government issued a new map doubling the size of the base mining area, a move described by Cr Klowss as "a serious mapping error".



He said the increase could impact other projects and businesses hoping to invest in the region and has written to the minister requesting an immediate correction.

Horsham Rural City Council says the area is double the size of the area listed in the Environment Effects Statement in 2023. (Supplied: Horsham Rural City Council)

Council said the planning authority decision was made on October 28, a few days before the state election caretaker period, but it was only made aware of the change on November 12 after the amendment was advertised in a government gazette.

"Yet again, council has not been consulted and has been kept at arms-distance from the process," Cr Klowss said.

"Had we have been given an opportunity to review the maps we would have likely picked up the error, helping the state government avoid embarrassment.

The proposed Avonbank mine site back in 2022. (Supplied: Horsham Rural City Council)

"I am concerned that mistakes that have occurred with this mapping anomaly, send the wrong message to project proponents and the community."



The state government has been contacted for comment.



It is not the first time Ms Kilkenny has amended a local government planning scheme without consultation.

Not an anomaly

Only last month, she used her powers to amend Yarriambiack Shire Council's planning scheme to approve the Warracknabeal Energy Park — a wind turbine facility that will be the largest in Australia.

The project has proven deeply controversial among the local community and has been the target of numerous protests.

At the time, council chief executive Tammy Smith told the ABC she felt blindsided by Ms Kilkenny's move.

"We thought we would have another opportunity to make a submission and we thought it would go through a planning permit process," she said.

"The community and council now have no recourse — we have no ability to make further submissions — effectively the minister has used her powers to waiver the usual notice and exhibition requirements that would otherwise apply for a planning scheme amendment."

The proposed site for the Warracknabeal Energy Park. (Supplied: WestWind Energy)

Ms Smith said local government should not have been shut out of the amendment to its own planning scheme.

"It makes it difficult for council staff, because we're having to implement or deal with decisions made at a state or federal level, and we're the ones on the ground having to work with our community," she said.

In a statement at the time, the government did not answer questions from the ABC, only referring to an earlier press release.

World.title: How an Australian became the newest face of The Hunger Games
World.content:
Welcome to Cheat Sheet, where we give you all the intel you need about iconic franchises! In honour of its fifth instalment heading to cinemas, this month we're looking at the beloved dystopian series The Hunger Games.

Almost 20 years since The Hunger Games and Suzanne Collins's series about resistance against a tyrannical government has sold more than 100 million copies worldwide.

The books gave birth to five movies, a stage play, a theme park ride and mountains of merch to become one of the highest grossing franchises of all time.

The franchise has been so resonant that its trademark three-finger salute has become shorthand for pro-democracy action across the globe.

Now an Australian is the newest face of the behemoth.

Sydney-born actor Joseph Zada cut his teeth on Australian series such as The Invisible Boys and Total Control.

In 2025, after hundreds of auditions worldwide, Zada was announced as the protagonist of Sunrise on the Reaping, the second prequel in the series.

Joseph Zada as Charlie in the Invisible Boys. (Supplied: Stan)

Zada plays a teenage version of Haymitch Abernathy, the heavy-drinking, sarcastic "mentor" assigned to Katniss Everdeen in the original Hunger Games — a role originally played by three-time Academy Award nominee Woody Harrelson.

"I think if I ever thought about it too much I'd start having a mild panic attack," Zada told ABC Arts.

"So it was just more shoving it down and pretending that that wasn't a real thing and approaching it as if it was any other role."

Sunrise on the Reaping takes a precarious middle portion in the Hunger Games timeline, occurring 24 years before Katniss's games and 40 years after the first prequel, A Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

Here's what you need to know before you head to the cinema.

The history of The Hunger Games

Although the concept of children fighting to the death existed before the Hunger Games, Collins's inspiration for her arena came from flipping between reality shows and war coverage on TV.

Writer Suzanne Collins with The Hunger Games star Jennifer Lawrence at the Catching Fire premiere in 2013. (Getty: Eric Charbonneau)

"I was tired, and the lines began to blur in this very unsettling way," she told Publisher's Weekly in 2008.

After an apocalyptic event, the remains of the United States are re-established as Panem, a collection of 12 "districts" — ranging from the luxury of District 1, to the dirt-poor miners in District 12.

To squash any mutterings of rebellion among the lower districts, an annual Hunger Games is held. Two children or "tributes" are chosen or "reaped" from each district and must fight to the death in elaborate, televised arenas until one remains and is crowned the victor.

The Hunger Games chronologically A Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes: Takes place during the 10th Hunger Games.

Takes place during the 10th Hunger Games. Sunrise on the Reaping: Takes place during the 50th Hunger Games aka the second Quarter Quell.

Takes place during the 50th Hunger Games aka the second Quarter Quell. The Hunger Games : Takes place during the 74th Hunger Games.

: Takes place during the 74th Hunger Games. Catching Fire : Takes place during the 75th Hunger Games aka the third quarter quell.

: Takes place during the 75th Hunger Games aka the third quarter quell. Mockingjay: Takes place after the events of the 75th Hunger Games, following the uprising against The Capitol.

The Hunger Games establishes the character of Katniss, a 16-year-old from District 12 whose entrance into the games sets off a chain reaction of uprising and resistance against The Capitol, the home of the ultra wealthy ruling class.

The Hunger Games was released in 2008 with Collins inking a six-figure publishing deal with Scholastic for the full trilogy.

2010's Catching Fire revolves around the "Quarter Quell", a special celebration of The Hunger Games, which takes place every 25 years and involves a cruel twist that sees Katniss return to the games after it is declared that tributes will only be selected from the pool of previous winners.

Mockingjay, released in 2012, does not include an official Hunger Games event, instead focusing on the rebel war against the Capitol and the fascist president, Snow.

The impact of The Hunger Games

By the time the first Hunger Games movie came around in 2012, the trilogy had more than 36.5 million copies printed.

Directed by Gary Ross and with a screenplay co-written by Collins herself, The Hunger Games (2012) grossed $US695 million ($1 billion) worldwide and proved a commercial breakthrough for Katniss actor Jennifer Lawrence.

Film adaptations of Catching Fire and Mockingjay, which was split into two parts, arrived in cinemas yearly after the original. The five-movie series would go on to gross almost $US3.3 billion worldwide, while also largely being critically praised.

Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen in The Hunger Games. (Supplied)

As early as 2015, nine months before the release of the final Mockingjay film, distributor Lionsgate was already exploring spin-off options.

The 2019 announcement that Collins would be publishing a Hunger Games prequel came with a joint statement from Lionsgate that the company was in talks for an adaptation even before publication.

The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes rewinds 64 years from the first book to the 10th Hunger Games, written from the perspective of a teenage president Snow, assigned as the mentor for the unruly District 12 tribute Lucy Gray.

The novel was released in May 2020, selling 500,000 copies in its first week at a time when the COVID-19 pandemic kept most bookstores closed.

By August the following year, a film adaptation was in pre-production and in April 2023 The Hunger Games: A Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes landed in cinemas.

Over the last decade, The Hunger Games has proved its impact through trademarks such as the "three-finger salute", which is used as a sign of resistance by Katniss and has been used by protesters in Thailand and Myanmar, among others.

The three-finger salute became a recurring symbol of the 2020 anti-monarchy protests in Thailand. (AP: Wason Wanichakorn)

What is Sunrise on the Reaping about?

In 2025, Collins published a second Hunger Games prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping, with its film adaptation landing in cinemas this month.

While The Hunger Games chronicled the downfall of a fascist regime and Songbirds and Snakes detailed the inception, Sunrise on the Reaping focuses on living under the dictatorship at its height.

Set 24 years before The Hunger Games, Sunrise on the Reaping's protagonist is Haymitch Abernathy, who audiences know as the alcoholic, disgruntled mentor to Katniss but in this timeline is an optimistic teenager reaped along with 47 other children (double the usual amount to mark the occasion) to compete in the games to celebrate the 50th anniversary.

Haymitch (Joseph Zada) and Maysilee (McKenna Grace) become allies in the 50th Hunger Games arena. (Supplied: Roadshow)

"He's such a different character at the start of this film so it gave me so much free range to do really whatever I wanted," Zada says of embodying Haymitch.

"He's a heartbreaking character so the best job that I could do was to make him loving and caring, so we can see how much this person has been through to reach the cynical, alcoholic, sarcastic person that is Woody's Haymitch."

There was, however, one aspect Zada took from Harrelson's performance.

The picturesque arena of the 50th Hunger Games hides a poisonous secret. (Supplied: Roadshow)

"He has a very specific cadence and trying to see where that fits in my own dialogue occasionally was important but … I still wanted to leave room so I didn't feel like I was overdoing it," Zada says.

McKenna Grace, who plays a fellow District 12 tribute in the 50th arena, says The Hunger Games's longevity lies in Collins's writing meeting the current moment.

"She's managed to write something that feels prevalent throughout the 20-something years that these books have been around, and it still feels very relevant to the world that we're in," Grace told ABC Arts.

"These systems the characters are put through feels very real but at the heart of it, it's about people trying to hold on to their humanity and stand up for what they believe in."

Zada says the series, and particularly Sunrise on the Reaping's story of failed rebellion, delivers an important message to its young fanbase.

"It's hard to wait for change and hold on to hope … with all of these organisations," he says.

"It's just begging younger people to understand that if you do want change in the world it takes time and it takes repeated behaviour."

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in Australian cinemas from November 19.

World.title: Chris Bowen launches bold climate agenda at COP31
World.content:
An ambitious draft climate agreement released at the COP 31 climate summit in Türkiye has called for countries to "accelerate" the phase-out of fossil fuels.

The document argues for a tripling of climate adaptation projects to at least $US120 billion ($178 billion) by 2035 and for 35 per cent of the world's energy use to go electric.

"Overall, this is some of the strongest language we've seen in a draft COP decision," said Greenpeace Australia Pacific's Simon Bradshaw.

"The question now is how much of it will survive the tough days of negotiations ahead."

About 200 countries are discussing environmental targets at the COP31 conference in Türkiye. (Reuters: Murad Sezer)

The comprehensive document arrives at the start of the second week of the annual climate talks, where almost 200 nations will discuss environmental targets, including electrification and emissions reductions and how to implement them.

Australian climate change minister and COP31 president of negotiations Chris Bowen released the 18-page draft in Antalya on Monday, local time, but warned it would not be the final version of the document.

"It is very much to enable consideration over the next week," Mr Bowen said at the press conference.

"There are elements in this draft that not all parties will agree on."

"What we'll be concentrating on in coming days are those issues where people can find common ground. Because the world wants us to act on climate change," he said.

The 18-page document was based on submissions from 160 countries and more than 500 pages of feedback, Mr Bowen said, and detailed 144 provisions.

It expresses "deep concern that global warming is expected to exceed 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels" and reaffirms the need to "accelerate" action to minimise the overshoot, noting climate change was already "harming human health" through disease and heat stress.

It also calls for developed countries to "take the lead" on climate action, and to "achieve net zero emissions by 2030 and net-negative emissions by 2040".

'We cannot afford false solutions'

In a move that appears to have surprised climate advocates, the draft cover decision also calls for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems".

Andreas Sieber, the head of Political Strategy at 350.org, said the credibility of both Türkiye and Australia was now on the line.

"The draft puts COP31's defining battles squarely on the table: the energy transition and adaptation finance," said Mr Sieber.

Climate ambition vs political reality Australia's efforts at this week's UN climate change conference expose the contradictions in current climate politics, both internationally and at home.

But he said the wording stopped short of establishing a clear road map to end fossil fuels, that moved beyond the "diplomatic waiting room".

"After the biggest fossil fuel crisis in history, we cannot afford false solutions," said Mr Sieber.

"You cannot claim to lead the world's climate negotiations while refusing to lead on the transition away from fossil fuels."

Australia's fossil fuel record under scrutiny

The Australian government has come under fire for its record on fossil fuel expansions during the climate talks, as it continues to be one of the world's leading coal exporters.

At least 37 coal, oil and gas projects have been approved since 2022.

Mr Bowen has previously defended the country's record on exports, telling the Guardian prior to the climate talks that Australia was selling fossil fuels to countries that were "in the middle of their transition".

"And they need, in the meantime, to use fossil fuels, and they've got to get them from somewhere," said Mr Bowen.

But the public pressure is escalating.

More than 60 civil society groups released an open letter on Monday, before the draft was announced, to Chris Bowen calling on Australia to use its role as the leader of negotiations to "lift ambition" at the climate talks.

Representatives from the 64 groups, including 350.org, Oxfam and Amnesty International, said, "while the world heaves under the strain of escalating climate impacts", they had seen, "little sign of the leadership needed to meet the moment".

"As the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, Australia's silence can be read as lack of will. We ask you to set out a clear path for the road maps in week two. This is critical for keeping the 1.5C limit alive," the open letter said.

Electrification pledge

Other proposals in the draft cover decision include increasing electricity's share of global energy use to 35 per cent by 2035, known as the 35-by-35 pledge, boosting climate adaptation funding, and expanding carbon capture and cutting methane emissions.

The document also noted the strain geopolitical tensions were causing across global energy markets, and the role electrification could play to address it.

"Such tensions have contributed to heightened uncertainty and volatility in global energy markets and fossil fuel supply chains, with implications for energy security, access and affordability," the draft states.

It noted that increasing the role of electricity in global energy systems would have "significant benefits to emission reductions, energy security, energy efficiency, economic development and energy access".

The wording was welcomed by Natasha Green from climate think tank E3G.

"We welcome the positive language on clean electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels in the draft cover decision," she said.

"And look forward to the Presidency showing more clearly how finance can be a critical enabler of '35 by 35'."

Representatives were expected to deliver strong feedback on some proposals, including an accelerated fossil fuel phase-out, Mr Bowen said, but the draft needed to be ambitious.

"We need to show that the world is keeping up climate action," he said.

"We need to send a message to the boardrooms and living rooms: boardrooms to keep investing, living rooms to give hope that countries of the world are going to keep on tackling the climate crisis, which is still here and getting worse."

ABC/AAP

David Jones’ total debt is more than $400 million, owed across its private equity owner, lender, nearly a thousand suppliers, and over 6000 employees, administrators McGrathNicol has revealed.

The collapsed retailer owes at least $419 million to various parties, including $180 million to 940 brands who have lodged a debt claim, $11 million to 6242 workers, and an estimated 800,000 gift card holders who are owed $33 million.

David Jones’ Bourke Street store in Melbourne. Louis Trerise

The biggest debts are owed to British distressed business lender Hilco, which is owed $115 million, followed by Sydney private equity firm Anchorage Capital, owed $80 million.

But McGrathNicol founding partner Shaun Fraser told around 500 creditors who joined the meeting on Tuesday morning via Zoom that there would be no guarantee that suppliers, which have been left out of pocket by David Jones’ collapse, would get their money back.

World.title: Early draft forecast: These are the players who are about to have their AFL dreams realised
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Early draft forecast: These are the players who are about to have their AFL dreams realised Marc McGowan November 17, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Our first mock draft for the year is here. The AFL draft is this Thursday and Friday night, and we have spoken to the league’s recruiters, junior clubs and player agents to gather as much information as possible to try to figure out what might happen. The Age predicts Dougie Cochrane will be the first player picked in Thursday’s AFL draft, with Ethan Drever and Cody Walker to follow. Stephen Kiprillis This mock includes predicted bids on academy and father-son prospects, as well as the expected trade between Port Adelaide and GWS that will see the Giants secure the Power’s pick 12 for selections 20, 26 and a future asset. You’ll be able to follow our live reporting and analysis of the draft on both Thursday and Friday night.



Pick one (Port Adelaide match Essendon bid) Knee surgery to fix a persistent patella tendonitis issue wiped out most of Cochrane’s draft year, but he was always considered the standout prospect. He is a good athlete, an outstanding kick and projects as a matchwinner who is effective at both ends of the ground and can also make his mark in the midfield.

If not: It would be staggering. Not only is Cochrane the consensus top prospect, but the Bombers would pass up the chance to score a bonus start-of-second-round compensation pick. The alternative would be bidding on Cody Walker. Pick two (Essendon)



Drever is a big and powerful midfielder who wins contested possessions for fun and bursts away from stoppages before driving long kicks inside 50. He kicks his share of goals, proved he could carry a heavy load at the Rebels, and is an A-grade character as well who will be a plus to any club’s culture, which only adds to his appeal.

If not: Arki Butler and Harry Van Hattum are the other players in contention here. The Bombers could also place a second bid on Cody Walker, but that is not expected. Pick three (Carlton match Richmond bid) The Blues get their man, using picks 13 and 18 to match the Tigers’ bid and enable Walker to follow in his 202-game father Andrew’s footsteps. Walker is likened to Patrick Dangerfield for his power and speed coming out of the contest, has no trouble finding the Sherrin, and is working hard to improve his kicking.

If not: Richmond generously let Walker fall down the order, and go for one of Arki Butler, Gus Teixeira, Harry Van Hattum or Heath Mellody instead. Pick four (Richmond)



Butler is outrageously talented, his kicking skills are sublime, and he might be the second coming of Sydney’s star forward Tom Papley. He is cheeky, a bit of a rascal and loves to yap at rival defenders, so expect him to quickly become popular wherever he ends up, but he will need to improve his running.

If not: The Tigers could opt for Butler’s Dragons teammate Gus Teixeira, ruckman Harry Van Hattum or Larke medallist Heath Mellody instead, which would have a major domino effect on the top 10. Pick five (West Coast) Is this too obvious? Maybe. But Mellody’s performance justifies him being taken here, and it makes sense for the Eagles to go local. He started the year as a classy winger/half-back, but proved his inside midfield bona fides at the under-18 championships and WAFL level, including a 34-disposal outburst against West Coast’s reserves.

If not: Perhaps, Arki Butler slips to them, which could at least make the Eagles think twice, while Gus Teixeira is a top-five talent.



Pick six (GWS match Melbourne bid) The Giants will be thrilled to bring in a western Sydney academy product who fits comfortably in the top 10 off his brilliant first half of the year that could have seen him contend for the Larke Medal. A stress fracture in Matthews’ right foot cut his season short, but he is a big ball-winner, smart, runs all day and has a neat left foot.

If not: The expectation is the Demons will bid here, but there is always the chance they leave that to Sydney and grab key defender Mitch Harris, Arki Butler – if he slides – or Harry Van Hattum. Pick seven (Melbourne)



The Demons traded up to secure this selection, seemingly with Harris in mind. That deal originally got them ahead of North Melbourne, who sent their top pick to Sydney in the Nick Blakey swap – and both clubs like Harris. He gobbles up intercepts, is an effective lockdown defender, and had an impressive SANFL finals series.

If not: Maybe the Demons have fooled everyone, and intend to pick Harry Van Hattum as their Max Gawn ruck replacement. Arki Butler would be strongly considered if he were available. Pick eight (Richmond) This is the swing pick of the draft. Ruckman Harry Van Hattum has been linked with the Tigers, but they love Teixeira, too. Richmond are deciding between the duo. The midfielder-forward discovered he had an iron deficiency after dealing with fatigue, but his power, speed and versatility are coveted – and he has star upside.

If not: The Tigers go for Harry Van Hattum as their long-term No.1 ruckman once Toby Nankervis retires or potentially departs for Tasmania. Pick nine (Sydney)



The Swans want key defensive help at this pick, which was the prize in the Nick Blakey trade. They like Mitch Harris, but he is unlikely to be available, so interceptor Snell has become the popular pick here. He is a great size, and his athleticism, composure and skills are all ticks as Sydney prepare for the future.

If not: Tyson Bradley is the other tall defender in top-10 contention. Harry Van Hattum is another option, but they picked ruckman Will Green in the first round in 2023, while Gus Teixeira might be considered if available. Pick 10 (Gold Coast) Bradley put together an outstanding season in the backline, including winning Victoria Metro’s MVP award and being the recipient of Sandringham Dragons’ best finals player. He is a highly intelligent player who reads the play well to be an intercepting force, but is equally proficient locking down forwards.

If not: The Suns also like West Australian midfielder Leo Steed, while key forward Sam Gayfer is an outside chance here, given Ben King’s free agency departure to Hawthorn.



Pick 11 (St Kilda) The Saints could break Collingwood hearts by grabbing the ultra-athletic Gayfer, whose uncle Mick was a 1990 premiership Magpie. The key defensive options are off the board in this scenario, but some think Gayfer might end up in the backline. He smashed the combine’s running vertical jump record and kicked loads of goals.

If not: Tyson Bradley would be considered if available. The Saints might opt for a smaller type such as Lochie Burrows, Toby Krasna or Leo Steed. It would be a surprise if they drafted Harry Van Hattum, but they did lose Rowan Marshall. Pick 12 (Collingwood)



The (potential) slide ends here for Van Hattum, an athletic ruckman with rare kicking skills for his hulking size. Highly touted big men Brodie Grundy and Tim English also went later in the first round in their draft year, and Van Hattum has all the physical tools to be a success as Darcy Cameron’s long-term replacement.

If not: Van Hattum might be long gone. The Pies would love if Sam Gayfer was still up for grabs. The best midfielder likely to be available is Leo Steed, but Lochie Burrows and Toby Krasna could also appeal. Pick 13 (GWS) The Giants are tipped to score Port Adelaide’s pick 12 (13 in this mock draft), in exchange for selections 20 and 26, plus something from the future. GWS are likely to retain this pick, even after matching a bid on Ethan Matthews. Clubs love Burrows, who has AFL traits galore with his versatility, athleticism and combativeness.

If not: Leo Steed could be the pick here, while Toby Krasna may also be in the mix. A left-field option – we know Adrian Caruso and co. love those – might be GWV Rebels riser Archie Elliott or Harvie Cooke. Pick 14 (Brisbane match Melbourne bid)



The Demons place another bid, but the Lions will match with their first two picks in the 20s to secure their latest high-end academy graduate. Murray enjoyed a scintillating under-18 championships where he starred in various roles, with his combination of speed, evasiveness and sharp skills making him an offensive force.

If not: Melbourne leave the Murray bid to Adelaide, and grab Toby Krasna. Leo Steed is another player in this range. Pick 15 (Melbourne) Krasna is highly coveted in this section of the draft and would not make it past Adelaide if the Demons go a different way. He would give Steven King’s Melbourne another speed demon on the wing who is a slick decision-maker, can win his own ball, is tough to tackle and knows where the goals are. Krasna is slight but tough.

If not: There is a scenario where Krasna is off the board and Harry Van Hattum is still available.



Pick 16 (Adelaide) Steed has top-10 admirers, so it is not a given that he would be here for the Crows, but they would be delighted if he is. He is small in stature, but big in impact, and top-liners such as Lachie Neale, Touk Miller and Zach Merrett have paved the way for him. Steed burrows into stoppages and often releases teammates with slick handballs.

If not: The Crows would love Lochie Burrows or Toby Krasna to fall here. South Australian running defender Jake Eime should be available if they are interested. Pick 17 (St Kilda)



The Saints love a bayside product, and the studious and talented Dimer fits the bill. Lochie Burrows and Toby Krasna were on their radar, but St Kilda would need to take them with their first pick. If that happens, Dimer wouldn’t be the selection here. Dimer is fast, clean, creative, a leader, and well-suited to the modern game.

If not: Wil Malady, Harvie Cooke, Archie Elliott, Jake Eime and Jackson Phillips are among the other options, while tall forward Jack Pickett could be in the mix depending on what the Saints do with their opening pick. Pick 18 (Essendon) The big riser, although some clubs rated him this highly for much of the year. Elliott’s switch to the forward line this past season proved a major success. He has an uncanny knack for being in the right spots and marks the ball well for his size. He kicked 43 goals in only 14 games for the Rebels, and won’t last much longer than this.

If not: The Bombers have the chance to select various types in this area of the draft, with another selection early on the second night. The same players mentioned at the previous pick could be contenders here. 19 (Fremantle)



This is one of Eime’s potential landing spots, but he could also last into the second round because the Dockers still have good options here. He is a weapon for his teams off half-back with his acceleration and shiftiness, uses the ball well, and his strong performance at the under-18 championships earned him All-Australian honours.

If not: The Dockers could go in various directions because their list is not wanting for much. They could even go for Jack Pickett here and be patient with his development off his ACL injury. George Gale is a WA product. Second round There is significant uncertainty from the second round onwards. Essendon will kick off the round at pick 20, given Port Adelaide’s top two selections will be absorbed matching the Cochrane bid. West Coast would love Archie Elliott to still be available. Related Article Explainer

Draft Talent is just the start. What do footy recruiters look for in young players?



Players in the mix to be selected in the 20s include Wil Malady, Jack Pickett, Harvie Cooke, Jackson Phillips, George Gale, Noah Williams and Kodah Edwards, while Khaled El Souki and Gabe Patterson could make it to the 30s. El Souki has been linked with Adelaide, but the Western Bulldogs appear to be in a good position to match a bid if he drifts. There is a large group of players with a wide draft range from the mid-20s to the 40s, such as Lachie Hicks, Harvey Spawton-Guy, Keenan Boi, Koby LeCras, Archie van Dyk (linked to Collingwood), Billy Wigmore, Brady Wright (linked to GWS) Albert Macgowan, Wil Antrobus, Jake Soutar, Blake Justice and Xavier Ladbrook. A player who could end up at Geelong or Collingwood is 19-year-old VFL player Zach Stevens. Hicks is among the players Hawthorn are considering at their opening pick, and they hope a Boi bid comes after that. North Melbourne have monitored defender Soutar, while Brisbane interviewed Edwards last week. Carlton are targeting a ruckman, with Ethan Herbert strongly linked to them, even though some clubs prefer Benji van Rooyen. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Good luck to police on this one’: What thieves could do with three stolen Melbourne Cups
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsGold ‘Good luck to police on this one’: What thieves could do with three stolen Melbourne Cups Elias Visontay November 17, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Three historic Melbourne Cup trophies won by Makybe Diva are still missing more than a day after two thieves reportedly disguised as construction workers allegedly stole them from behind a display cabinet at Flemington Racecourse. Now, experts say authorities’ chances of recovering the trophies intact is unlikely. But as attention shifts to the secondary gold market, criminals looking to cash in from the theft must navigate a tricky but achievable path to profit. Loading How much are the trophies worth? A Melbourne Cup weighs nearly two kilograms and takes more than 10 days to make. Each cup is valued at more than $1 million.



The trophies contain about 1.69 kilograms of 18-carat gold, which Adrian Dickens, founder of Melbourne’s Circa Ad Jewels, told this masthead would be worth about $233,000 each, for a combined total of $699,000. The $3 million combined estimate would be the value of the trophies if still intact, Dickens said. Related Article Gold Striking gold is the dream for thousands of Australians. But there’s a ‘paradox’ holding them back How easy will the trophies be to sell? Experts who have spoken to this masthead all broadly agree the thieves would be smartest to melt the gold down as opposed to attempting to sell them intact. This would avoid raising suspicion in the search for a trustworthy buyer interested in the trophies for their historical value - most likely a collector or a black market dealer. Dickens, of Circa Ad Jewels, said it would only take about an hour to melt down the trophies, which would render the gold “totally untraceable”.



“If [the thieves] had any intelligence, they would have melted them down last night,” Dickens has said. “There would be a small amount of extra value [if the trophies were not melted] because they are Melbourne Cup trophies… but with the price of gold as it is, it would be far easier to get away with them being melted down.” How hard is it to melt down a Melbourne Cup without arousing suspicion? Very easy, according to Allan Trench, a professor of mineral and energy economics at the University of Western Australia’s business school. “My first thought is good luck to police on this one,” he said. Not only can a trophy be easily melted down in an hour, “you can literally melt it down in your backyard”.



“I’d be amazed if they (the thieves) hadn’t already lined up a furnace,” Trench said. Where do they sell the melted-down gold? Are there checks and balances to detect criminals? The thieves have a few options as to how they melt down the gold. The current spot gold price is around $US4000 per ounce. Bloomberg Trench said it would be easiest to pour the melted-down gold into a bar-style chunk. But anyone bringing in such a large chunk of gold to a refinery, trader or jeweller would likely arouse some suspicion, especially with an industry in Australia on alert after the thefts.



Related Article Updated

Crime ‘They mean everything to me’: Thieves steal three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva Precious metals fall under Australia’s anti-money laundering legislation. Traders buying or selling precious metal products - including the metals themselves as well as jewellery pieces - valued at $10,000 or more are legally obligated to report the transaction, according to regulator AUSTRAC. “An overseas buyer wouldn’t be on the lookout for this,” Trench said. Transporting such an amount of gold outside of Australia would also be a logistical hurdle. However, if the gold from the stolen trophies is melted down and poured into a vast number of smaller pieces, this would make criminal activity much more difficult to detect. Can anyone just turn up at a gold trader or jeweller and trade in the gold?



In theory, smaller pieces could be taken to a range of smaller retail jewellers in the same way customers can trade in regular items containing gold, Trench said. While anti-money laundering obligations cover transactions above $10,000, businesses buying gold are also required to try to detect and report “linked” transactions when two or more smaller transactions that exceed $10,000 appear related in nature. However, a criminal with a scheme to melt the stolen gold into multiple smaller pieces and delegate the task of trading in the pieces to different individuals visiting various traders and jewellers could avoid detection, experts said. Spacing such efforts out over time could also lower the risk of triggering suspicion. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: The Pauline factor: Why NSW women love One Nation
World.content:
PoliticsNSWNSW Votes The Pauline factor: Why NSW women love One Nation Jessica McSweeney November 17, 2026 — 11:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One Nation is tied with Labor as the most popular party with female voters in NSW, driven by Pauline Hanson’s popularity with women despite hardline comments from the party’s candidates about abortion. The right-wing populist party has consistently outperformed the Coalition with female voters, according to Resolve Political Monitor polling, and now sits neck and neck with Labor at 28 per cent of the primary vote. Pauline Hanson is driving female support for One Nation in NSW. Alex Ellinghausen While women appear to be flocking to One Nation, NSW Leader Mike Newman came in third after Chris Minns and Kellie Sloane when female voters were asked about their preferred premier. Resolve founder Jim Reed said voters did not speak about Newman. “They are focused on Pauline Hanson and what her party are offering generally, and that’s really about forcing change,” he said.



Women in the 35-54 age bracket are a crucial demographic for parties to win over if they are to form government, Reed said. Mothers, often the person at the coalface of household cost-of-living pressures and spending decisions, also can influence the vote of others in their home. Support for One Nation was softer with men, at 23 per cent, trailing Labor on 31 per cent. The party’s lead upper house candidate Stuart Bonds has repeatedly linked migrants to sex selective abortions, and when asked by a social media commenter if men should stay out of decisions about women’s bodies, said, “except when it comes to paying the bills”. One Nation wants to tighten controls around late-term abortions, but these comments do not appear to have affected the party’s popularity with women.



Newly announced One Nation candidate Katherine Deves, who ran unsuccessfully for the Liberals as Scott Morrison’s hand-picked candidate for Warringah in 2022, told this masthead she doubted Bonds’ comments would change their primary vote. “As the vast majority of Australians do not support late-term abortions, I do not believe holding these views will impact the party’s female vote,” she said. Katherine Deves, One Nation’s latest upper house candidate. George Chan Deves, who is best known for her anti-trans campaigning, said Hanson’s no-nonsense style was appealing to women who are fed up with cost of living pressures. One Nation’s NSW president Rebecca Thompson believes the party is tapping into frustrations from women who are forced to work as if they do not have children.



“The majority of mothers just want to be mothers, but it’s a luxury to be able to have one income today. The mental and financial burden on women is immense,” she said. Several One Nation candidates said women were being drawn to the party for its position on sex-based protections for women, which would exclude transgender women from female-only spaces and sporting teams. However, Reed said in his experience talking to voters for Resolve polling, most women are not coming to the party for ideological reasons. “They’re particular ideological platforms that attract people to become MPs and candidates and so on, but there’s a difference between that and the broader electorate,” he said. World.title: Springboks question whether referees are ‘match-fixing’ in Nations Championship
World.content:
SportRugby UnionSouth Africa rugby Springboks question whether referees are ‘match-fixing’ in Nations Championship Fiona Tomas November 17, 2026 — 11:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus has questioned whether referees are match-fixing during an extraordinary rant about officiating standards in the Nations Championship. Erasmus suggested officials are showing more leniency to northern hemisphere teams and incidents of foul play are not being picked up in what he described as a “manipulation of the game”. Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe To illustrate his point, South Africa’s head coach predicted fly-half Sam Prendergast would be available for Ireland’s high-stakes clash with his Springboks side in Dublin this weekend, despite being cited for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji last weekend. He also claimed Maxime Lucu, the France scrum-half, had only been in the sin-bin for seven minutes during his side’s 21-19 defeat by France in Paris last Friday night instead of the mandatory 10 minutes and alleged officials had missed 17 knee-drop tackles.



When asked to expand on his claim that officials had missed 17 knee-drop tackles, Erasmus said: “I’m not saying he’s wrong, I’m saying if he didn’t see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game if you see this injury that happened there, a knee-drop tackle happened there, and it’s been decided that knee-drop tackles are out.” When asked about the possibility of Ireland’s Prendergast missing Saturday’s showdown, Erasmus replied: “I am going to say the right words now. We are in the northern hemisphere. I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play.” France’s Maxime Lucu celebrates after defeating the Springboks. AP Photo/Teresa Suarez When asked to expand on what he meant by “technicality”, Erasmus questioned whether the correct processes had been followed around the Prendergast incident and the one involving Jasper Wiese, who was cited following his red card for a dangerous shoulder clear-out on Kalvin Gourgues in Paris. “It’s Monday, it’s now in the papers,” Erasmus said of the Prendergast case, which has yet to be publicly confirmed by the Nations Championship. “Was it within the period, the 12-hour period? Who cited him? When was it cited?



“When Jasper got cited [for his red card against France], it was six hours after the game. “We got the papers. Northern hemisphere, he’ll probably get cited [suspended] for two or three weeks, so he can’t play in the next two games and then he’ll probably be available. We’ll get that release. “My experience from when we’re here it’s ... I’m not 100 per cent sure how it works. I’m not a legal guy. I don’t have the right to say anything on it. “I don’t have a pleasant experience here from going through Lood de Jager, Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Franco Mostert when we were here, all the things. And then it never seems to go away. I’m not saying anybody’s doing anything wrong. I’m just not expecting him to get... I think he’ll play on Saturday.” South Africa’s Jasper Wiese in the Nations Championship match against France. AP Photo/Teresa Suarez Erasmus also referenced a recent incident involving Ireland’s Tadhg Furlong, who was cleared last month of grabbing Gavin Coombes’ testicles during Leinster’s United Rugby Championship win over Munster. Springboks hooker Wessels received an eight to nine-week suspension in October last year for a similar offence.



Related Article Australian rugby They made the most tackles in a Test match, ever. Will Wales be cooked for the Wallabies clash? “My experience is … like Tadhg [Furlong] got free for the same thing that Jan-Hendrik did,” Erasmus said. “I don’t want to go into details there because I’m not a legal person, but from a South African point of view, that hurt, that we felt it’s more or less the same situation and Jan-Hendrik got nine weeks, the other guy got free.” International coaches were briefed on how hip-drop and knee-drop tackles would be officiated ahead of the resumption of the Nations Championship this autumn. Both tackle techniques were made illegal after a spate of incidents which have led to serious lower-limb damage to the ball-carrier. Erasmus has already named his match-day squad for the penultimate round of the Nations Championship, recalling record Springboks cap holder Eben Etzebeth for the encounter in Dublin. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Father locked in hotel quarantine after child’s death settles case with state government
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCourts Father locked in hotel quarantine after child’s death settles case with state government Erin Pearson Updated November 17, 2026 — 11:50am ,first published 11:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The state government has settled its case with a grieving father kept in hotel quarantine after his daughter’s death just as a Supreme Court trial was set to begin. Hong Kong-based lawyer Hayden Flinn had filed a lawsuit against the state and its Health Department for damages, claiming he had been unnecessarily detained for two weeks after flying home to bury his 13-year-old daughter following her sudden death in Melbourne in May 2021. Hayden Flinn leaves court on Tuesday. Justin McManus At the time, the world was a year into the COVID-19 pandemic and Flinn said he was subjected to “indignity and insult”, a loss of liberty and mental distress when he was refused an exemption on compassionate grounds. What followed, he said, was a distressing two weeks locked in a small Richmond hotel room with his devastated teenage son after the pair were refused permission to quarantine with family at home.



Related Article Exclusive

Courts A father’s rage over daughter’s death has smouldered since lockdown – Brett Sutton is in his sights Flinn said he was also barred from viewing his daughter’s body and could not be with his distressed wife as she planned their child’s funeral. On Tuesday, as the 10-day trial was due to begin, Justice Andrew Keogh was told that the parties had reached a settlement agreement. The court heard there were still “T’s to cross and I’s to dot”, with the matter to return on Thursday if anything needed to be addressed. “I congratulate the parties,” Keogh said.



On Sunday, this masthead revealed that the corporate lawyer, who is now co-chief executive of a large Hong Kong law firm, argued he should never have been detained, with officials failing to properly assess his personal circumstances, vaccination status and the low risk presented by travellers from Hong Kong. Lawyers for the state and Health Department had denied any wrongdoing, maintaining their decision-making was reasonable and justified, and that Flinn had chosen to remain in quarantine. Medical staff outside a hotel quarantine facility in 2021. Eddie Jim At the time of Flinn’s return, there were no lockdowns in Victoria or reported community transmission of the virus. The judge-alone trial was set to hear from a string of witnesses including former chief health officer Brett Sutton and his deputy, Allen Cheng, about the decision-making process around the Flinns’ case and other exemptions given during the pandemic.



But emails revealed a Health Department email, sent on May 4, 2021, read: “The level of distress being experienced by the family was assessed as too high for the family to maintain [detention] requirements. The alternative of going home to wife and family would pose a COVID-19 risk to family and public health.” There were no lockdowns in Victoria or reported community transmission of the virus at the time of Flinn’s return. World.title: Robert Pattinson could make James Bond a little freak. I’m here for it
World.content:
CultureMoviesJames Bond Robert Pattinson could make James Bond a little freak. I’m here for it Nell Geraets November 17, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

To those who’ve done nothing but lament Robert Pattinson’s age and the fact that Batman couldn’t possibly also be 007 since the announcement of the seventh James Bond, I kindly ask you to put a cork in it. As much as some of the other contenders in the superspy race would have looked the part (Callum Turner’s jawline alone would have done serious heavy lifting), Pattinson was arguably the only one guaranteed to sprinkle something different – perhaps something even a little freaky – onto the coveted role. Alright, Robert Pattinson, it’s time to get your superspy freak on. AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt The headlines have predictably highlighted the star’s biggest franchises – Twilight, Harry Potter, Batman – but it’s the 40-year-old actor’s smaller indie roles that make him such an exciting Bond prospect. In Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse, he plays a brooding assistant lighthouse keeper who descends into a mermaid-obsessed madness. In The King, he’s a preening medieval royal in full freak mode with his blonde bowl cut and bizarre French accent. In Mickey 17, he isn’t just one weirdo, but many, playing a bumbling employee who dies repeatedly on an ice planet. None of these oddball characters bear any resemblance to each other, yet Pattinson assumed each like a second skin.



Imagine a Bond that ties in even a fraction of this kookiness. Not only could it help ease away from the character’s womanising (sexist) ways; it could also inject some much-needed unpredictability into this 70-plus-year-old franchise. I’m not trying to say Pattinson’s Bond should drink martinis through a silly straw, or develop a twitch a la Salvador Dalí in Little Ashes. Out of respect for Ian Fleming, the sanctity of Bond must remain intact. But that doesn’t mean Pattinson’s Bond couldn’t be more cerebral or self-deprecating – perhaps cracking more than just one or two jokes per film. Robert Pattinson is crazy and mermaid obsessed in The Lighthouse. What can this man not do? Of course, Pattinson’s franchise work cannot be entirely ignored. This is a man still haunted by Twilight memes, someone who still makes millennials around the world sob while watching Cedric Diggory’s death in the fourth Harry Potter. And he’s still actively working on Matt Reeves’ The Batman Part II. His casting as Bond could therefore feel like an obvious commercial choice by Amazon MGM. But even if it is, who cares? Pattinson has already proven himself an incredible, versatile talent.



Related Article James Bond Robert Pattinson cast as next James Bond Even when Pattinson goes mainstream, he still can’t help but sprinkle in some signature freak flavour. If Edward Cullen – a sparkling vampire whose stare alone could trigger an existential crisis – wasn’t a freak, I don’t know who is. Pattinson’s Batman, meanwhile, isn’t your classic rich-man-turned-superhero; he’s a troubled soul struggling with his vigilante identity. These roles prove he’s comfortable switching up well-known characters. Who’s to say he won’t do the same for Bond? Also, has everyone forgotten that Harrison Ford – the iconic actor honoured with the SAG Life Achievement Award earlier this year – simultaneously played Han Solo and Indiana Jones? Neither of those roles cancelled out the other, so why would Pattinson’s? That said, Ford has long been snubbed by the Oscars, partly because of his willingness to dabble in IP. Pattinson could tread a similar path, as much as I believe he should be a shoo-in this year with The Odyssey (again, getting his freak on with the smarmy, cowardly Antinous). Robert Pattinson as the ultimate jerk, Antinous, in The Odyssey. Universal Pictures via AP It’s also thanks to his franchise work that 007 could finally resonate with Gen Z. We would practically kill for Edward Cullen (#TeamEdward forever). Though it’s been a long time since he sparkled, we’ve followed him loyally throughout his career – he’s partly the reason I became interested in arthouse cinema in the first place. We need more stars like Pattinson, actors who are willing to cross the boundary between arthouse and mainstream, bringing gravitas to blockbusters and straight-up fun to indies.



You may have James Bond’s classic face-card, Robert Pattinson, but we all know you’re a little freak inside. Getty Then, alas, there are Pattinson’s looks. I’m aware I just outed myself as #TeamEdward, but bias aside, I’m convinced he displays the perfect Bond aesthetic. The chiselled jaw, the glorious hairline, the oh-so-full brows – his face-card screams 007. Some have bristled over his age (40, gasp!), but does anyone actually care? He’s clearly fit and able to lean into action, and his whimsical soul makes him seem 10 years younger anyway. This is the man who spruiked the microwaveable “pasta burger”, after all. When Daniel Craig was cast as Bond, people panicked over his blonde hair and muscular physique. Now, they’re freaking out about Pattinson’s lankier figure. Surely it’s time to accept that Bond needn’t fit into a set cut-out. Bond himself said as much in Fleming’s 1955 novel Moonraker: “the man who was only a silhouette”. The good thing about a silhouette is it leaves plenty of room for interpretation – even, perhaps, a bit of freak. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Australian cricket spent the week tearing itself apart and there is no end in sight
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketBall tampering Australian cricket spent the week tearing itself apart and there is no end in sight Will Macpherson November 17, 2026 — 11:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

More than 100 months have passed since Cameron Bancroft smuggled sandpaper into his briefs, but at the end of this extraordinary and often unedifying week of blood-letting, an end does not seem in sight. With two factions poles apart, consensus over who knew what in Cape Town, and the notion of a single version of events for the public to digest and accept, seems as unlikely as ever. The only certainty is that, even after his epic and authoritative press conference, Pat Cummins’s assertion that he had spoken about the matter publicly for the final time seems wishful in the extreme. Gerard Whateley, a respected sports broadcaster, has compared sandpaper to the JFK assassination. It will rumble on. Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins during his 68-minute press conference. Sam Mooy The Test captain’s press conference left those hunting for common ground between Camp Usman Khawaja and Camp Cummins clutching at thin air. Not so long ago, the warring sides in Australian cricket were intergenerational, after Cummins’s team effectively toppled Justin Langer as head coach, provoking the fury of the great group of 25 years ago, led by former batsmen Matthew Hayden and Ricky Ponting. Now the fighting is within the same changing room. While Cummins spoke for 68 minutes, giving the media more access than they could ever have asked for, really the whole engagement boiled down to one one-word answer. He was asked if he was aware of any plot to tamper with the ball in South Africa at all.



By quickly answering “no”, there was no longer any hiding behind semantics or grey areas; not only was Cummins claiming not to know about the taking of sandpaper onto the field on that specific day in Cape Town, he was claiming not to know about any plans to tamper with a cricket ball on that tour of South Africa. He was refuting Khawaja’s testimony directly, all while delivering a personal drive-by, criticising how he had acted as a friend, and questioning why he had not spoken up himself, given he knew what Bancroft was planning. Khawaja had been at pains not to name individuals, but Cummins did make it personal, and operated in specifics. If it emerges that he is lying, there is no way back. The Australian squad that toured South Africa in 2018. Getty Images How on earth does anyone move forward from here? Cummins said he would not be going legal, despite receiving advice that some of the contents of the book were defamatory. That is not to say others will not. For now, the ball is back in Khawaja’s court, and he will have the opportunity to return serve in the coming days, including in Hobart on Wednesday, when he is slated to commentate for Fox Sports, the Australian broadcaster, for the third ODI against England, alongside his friend David Warner and Alyssa Healy, Mitchell Starc’s wife. He is also due to appear on some podcasts, although at least one has been delayed until after Hobart. Khawaja has seemed less assured when receiving a grilling from journalists, such as the ABC’s veteran political reporter Sarah Ferguson than in the breezily-written 17th chapter of his autobiography Sabr where he alleged that “we all knew”. Mitchell Starc speaking to reporters after Usman Khawaja’s book was released. Janie Barrett



So perhaps it is more likely that Warner, the childhood friend Khawaja was trying to protect, moves us forward. On Friday he accused Cummins of “throwing Khawaja under the bus”, betraying his fury. For the remainder of the day in Perth, he stalked around looking mournful and wronged, so it was little surprise that he stuck out a statement on Instagram on Saturday morning, suggesting that more was to come. “As far as I am aware, CA [Cricket Australia] did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation,” the statement read. “If that’s correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn’t know? “It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning [and] ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover-up.” David Warner and Usman Khawaja were long-term opening partners in the Test team. Getty Images Cricket Australia have denied Warner’s allegations. “As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation [into the ball-tampering saga] and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since,” a CA spokesman said.



“Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players’ right to provide their own version of events.” Khawaja’s version of events has been supported by Warner, plus back-up players on the tour Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland, who have no apparent axe to grind. Bancroft said five years ago that the bowlers knew. When he was briefly stopped by the TV cameras at an airport this week, he said he had nothing to say “at this time”, and flashed a knowing smile. Khawaja’s testimony has been refuted by Cummins, Starc, and various coaches from the tour. After his long press conference Cummins headed to the nets with Starc and Josh Hazlewood, with the trio seeming as simpatico as ever. Cricketer Cameron Bancroft is greeted by reporters following the release of Usman Khawaja’s book. Luis Enrique Ascui There are a number of others we are waiting to hear from, with whispers of what they think doing the rounds. Mitchell Marsh fell over himself not to engage in a car-crash press conference on Thursday, while his forgotten brother Shaun, Peter Handscomb and Tim Paine, who replaced Steve Smith as captain, have all kept their counsel, too. In one way or another, all but Shaun Marsh are conflicted. Handscomb is still a domestic player tipped for the Test tour of India in the New Year as a spin specialist, Mitch Marsh is a friend to everyone and Australia’s white-ball captain, and Paine is a CA employee as coach of Australia A. The forgotten man of the whole saga is Steve Smith, the captain who turned a blind eye but copped his punishment. As so often, the intense and restless veteran is keeping a low profile in New York. He will be desperate not to revisit a difficult time.



Related Article Analysis

Ball tampering Two men, two diametrically opposite accounts. A choice must be made: Team Uzzie or Team Pat? Reading Khawaja’s account, it is hard to understand what Warner did wrong at all. But he bore the heaviest punishment for his part in sandpaper, so it is not surprising he felt wronged. If he is so certain he has been stitched up, surely he and his agent have some evidence from the time that they could make public? That would at the least put pressure on Cricket Australia to publish their investigation in full from the time, which was completed by a head of integrity Iain Roy, who left the organisation soon after and has not commented since the episode has been reopened. Better would be interviewing all parties again and coming to a conclusion, which may or may not be the same as the previous one. Given the time has passed there does not need to be new punishments for those who knew – Khawaja would be one of them – but it would give some closure for an issue lacking it. The Telegraph, London
